thread_title: Access to public transportation in Paris
text:
fussyguest, if it isn't too late to answer your question, the answer is "somewhat".

The regional commuter line, the "RER-B" that connects the airports to central Paris have both escalators and Elevators at the "Gare du Nord", "Chatelet", and "Port-Royal" stations. All the other Paris stops on that line have escalators at a minimum.

The new "Meteor" line-14 of the Paris Métro has both escalators and elevators at every station and it connects 5 train stations to the central métro and RER-B line at Chatelet. After that, it's hit or miss.

I'd recommend the bus system which is perfectly equipped for wheel chairs but the bus drivers and Paris traffic can make for a pretty herky-jerky ride and may be a problem for people with bad knees, weakness, etc..

If you are coming to Paris and have an itinerary in progress, I'd be happy to help with info on specific stations.

New Zealand is the most handicapped accessible nation in the world, they put the US to shame. I know, I'm handicapped.

There are non-stop flights to NZ from L.A.

* The amendments hold certain application to U.S. and foreign air carriers - 

* Accessibility of airports as well as changes in airport services including reservations, facilities, in-flight and aircraft acquisitions

* Specific changes that affect passengers who utilize respiratory assistance devices, as well as passengers who are deaf or hard of hearing.

* Changes to the timeframe and possible requirement of advanced notice by some U.S. Carriers for certain accommodations (in addition to those items currently allowed) Previously notice of 48 hours was required for certain requests and services - this time frame is being changed to 24hours

About 10 years ago I developed a disease called scoliosis. To most people this isn't a big deal. A slight curve in their back doesn't really effect them. Well mine got pretty back and I had to have my back alligned with titanium rods about 6 months ago. Although I made a complete recovery learning to do the every day tasks again have been a little challenging. 



So next month I am moving from Phoenix to Boston to start school. Im trying to debate how I should move though. I could rent a Uhaul and pull my car on the car carrie my dad purchase from Uhaul. Or I can pay someone to move for me and fly out there. Seeing how I am a college student.... I'm broke! So driving myself seems logical. However my surgery has made turning my head very painful and kinda limited. I am worried that driving the truck and pulling my car is going to make it difficult for me to stay safe. Any advice?

With the gas prices and great airline rates it just might make more sense to fly. However if you have a friend that could drive you and fly back it may be worth the trip for them to see the east coast. Maybe if you paid for their food/lodging/airfare? Just an idea.

Considering the limitations that you have stated, I would not advise trying to make the drive yourself for safety sake. 

My first suggestion is to contact the local Disability advocates in your area as well as those in the area you are moving to. There are avenues to be explored. 

I do understand that moving is expensive and needing assistance could hold significant impact on your budget. With the short notice it may prove even more difficult. 

Air travel may be the simplest way for you to reach your destination, but the actual moving of your personal belongings will be another matter altogether.

I doubt that you will have enough items to be moved to make it financially feasible to hire a moving company. Most of them specialize in moving entire houses of furniture, and they have minimum prices that they charge.



The answer to this question is predicated on what you are actually planning to take from Phoenix to Boston. I would recommend that you take only your clothing and personal items. You can buy linen and dorm accessories once you arrive in Boston. Or you can order those things online and have them delivered to your Boston dorm. You do not need lots of stuff to get settled in a college dorm, and you could probably do without your TV, game system, stereo and other assorted electronic entertainment equipment. I would suggest that you limit yourself to your own clothing and your laptop.



Likely you will be purchasing new clothing in Boston shortly after you arrive anyway because your Phoenix wardrobe is not going to work well for you after September in Boston.



It might be that the least expensive alternative for you is to take as much with you on the plane and then ship the rest with a carrier like UPS.



I certainly would not even think of driving with the limitations you have described. It is dangerous for you and for everyone else on the highway. If you were in an accident your physical limitations could create an extra level of liability for you.



Were you my son, we would drive you to Boston and then fly back to Pheonix. Is there no one in your family who can do that for you? If not a parent, perhaps a grandparent, sibling, aunt, uncle, cousin? If you do not have help within your family, do you have a friend who would be willing to take a road trip to Boston? I cannot think of a way for your car to be in Boston with you unless someone drives it, and you clearly should not drive it yourself.



You could contact your university in Boston. Sometimes student union buildings have bulletin boards that invite requests from people who are seeking to share transportation. They might have names of other people in Phoenix who are looking for a way to get to Boston.



If it were 15 years ago, I would recommend that you put an ad in the paper seeking someone who would be interested in going with you on this trip. No one reads newspapers anymore so I suppose it would be better to post this request on Craig's List.



I do not know if I would feel comfortable doing this with a stranger I met on Craig's List. The world seems filled with more disreputable people, and I would likely have trust issues with a stranger. It is, however, one alternative to your problem.



Worst case scenario is that you ship some of your things using UPS, fly to Boston and manage without your car until Thanksgiving when you may be sufficiently recovered to go home and get your car. Lots of people do not have cars on campus, and most universities have many mass transit systems to provide easy transportation for students.



Only one of our three daughters had a car on campus. Our grand-daughter is currently a Junior in college and she does not have a car. Like her mother she does not want one. She says it is more trouble to find a parking place with her car than it is to catch the shuttle bus across campus to her next class or the library.



Good luck to you, and please do not drive yourself!

One of the best kept secrets in moving is Amtrak Freight. Contact your local station for info.



Or consider one of the point-to-point storage movers (I used "U-pak" for one move, and door-to-door storage for another). They can be the same price or less than u-haul.

This is not meant to be an advertisement … but I thought I’d throw it out there as it turned out to be one of my better investments. Samsonite makes luggage with four wheels that are called “spinners”. You don’t drag them around – you push them. They stand upright and roll so smoothly (even on carpeting and sidewalks) that you can push them around with one finger. 



Eight years ago I bought two of the medium sized bags for our travels and they have saved me so much aggravation that they have been worth more than the exorbitant price I paid. For example: There is a dead zone between immigration and customs and the “continuing flight” drop-off at most US airports where it is sometimes difficult to get assistance. In Atlanta they line up all the wheelchairs just pass immigration and you have to wait until someone is “free” to help – if your next flight is within two hours, it’s going to be tight getting through and to the next gate in time. We mostly ignore the line up and just push on by ourselves because I can push the wheelchair with one hand and “guide” the two bags with the other – or she can guide them along in front or beside the wheelchair if there are a lot of winding turns to navigate. Either way, I always enjoy the looks we get from the customs folks as we come rolling up.

My husband puts the luggage in the luggage cart, I sit in the wheelchair, he pushes the wheelchair while I steer the luggage cart by pushing it in front of me while I sit.



We've done this in Papeetee, Tahiti & LAX, as there is definitely NOT always any help, especially at LAX.

thread_title: delightfull Brittany holiday with husband who has Parkinsons
text:
We have just returned from our best holiday for years as a family. My husband who has Lewy Bodies dementia and Parkinsons had a wonderfull time with our 2 adult sons and their wives.

We flew to Rennes and hired two cars then took an easy hour twenty minute drive to Le Quillio where we 'took over' the fabulous Manoir de Bolu for a week.

We had a downstairs bedroom and a shower room next door to one another and though not ensuite we managed very well. (there are steps around the ground floor but B. managed them comfortably)

The whole house is fabulous. All newly renovated to a high standard and with all the character and charm of a french manoir (toile de jouey and and four poster bed in one room) plus central heating if needed!

The kitchen is so pretty with a range oven and amazingly well equipped. There was never a thing we needed that wasn't there.

Outside is fabulous, five acres of landscaped grounds all to our selves and a large heated swimming pool absolutely immaculate.There was enough games equipment to keep us on the move all week! Everything from trampoline to rounders and enough bicycles for a huge family (and all perfectly maintained)

B. was able to relax completely and could have freedom to wander around safely without me worrying. He even ran rond the field one day, and I can tell you for a man 10 years into Parkinsons that was a major acheivement. he also swam in the pool which he could access easily.

There was plenty for everyone to do localy. The 'boys' went fishing at a local lake arranged for them by Chris ( who owns the house together with his wife Sue). There were plenty of places to visit Pontivy being a favourite, and we took a couple of trips to the delightfull coast. Eating out was wonderfull, we found plenty of choice and good standards in nearby towns and villages.

We definitely plan to return and though the house can sleep up to 12, B. and I are going to take it on our own next time and perhaps invite some friends to join us for a couple of days. I feel no qualms about being there on our own. Sue and Chris live next door and are so kind and helpfull. They are keen not to be 'obtrusive' but are so approachable if you need anything atall.

B. can walk quite a bit on 'good' days but we also had a wheel chair with us. If we do visit on our own in future Sue has offered to help us find a local english speaking carer just to give me a break now and then. I would definitely recomend this holiday to other people in our possition, but also to anyone else who wants a truly relaxing holiday in brittany ( Oh! and I forgot to mention Sue offers holistic therapies too!)

Two friendly guys did come, but… oh my goodness! The chair they brought seemed to have been made no less than some twenty years ago by a carpenter or plumber who didn’t have the slightest idea it would be used be an adult disabled person. Let me try to describe it. It had a very high back, a few inch higher than the back of the plane seat, so that it was only a tall man that could help me from the back. Fortunately, my husband is over six feet tall. Second, the depth of the seat was less than ten inch. In short, the three men - the two assistants and my husband - managed both to put me on the chair and to take me off it. I was really lucky to return to my wheelchair without any bones broken. On my way back, I warned the staff that I need another type of transfer means and… well, the guys were very tall, but the chair was the same. So beware, ask for very strong and tall assistants!

Hi,



The Air Carrier Access Act requires all airlines to have a properly trained "Complaint Resolution Officer" or CRO, on-duty and on the physical airport premises during all times when the airline has departing flights..



This CRO must be trained in the Air Carrier Access Act guidelines and must know how to properly document and report ACA passenger complaint and he/she must also know the required actions to attempt to resolve the matter at the time of reporting. 



One thing to note is that as Busy-Retired mentioned.. Do know that the ACA does *NOT* grant you any extra time to check-in or similar matters-- you still have to comply with the carriers stated cut-off times and boarding area presence, etc.. The airline does have to provide reasonable timely assistance in completing these matters but you still bear the responsibility to present yourself at to the airline within the stated time line to complete these tasks..



If you feel that any aspect of the ACA was violated by the airline, you should request to speak with the on-duty CRO at the airport. The CRO must contact you within a "reasonable" period of time.



Travel Safe,

hi one and all,hope 2009 is treating you well...being disabled poses many battles for us for travel,have any of you come across especially helpful cabin staff inflight??

Hi,



I'm writing this in part to show "the other side of the coin" with respect to what the2sues says about cabin staff "unwilling" to assist with passenger carry-on bags...



First, let me say that this is NOT to DEFEND nor ASSAIL the staff, but meant to show what may be some underlying reasons for a cabin crew from not helping.



Some airlines actually DO have EXPLICIT rules about cabin staff handling passenger carry-on bags.. This rule is in part designed to limit airline liability for things like damage (the FA dropped it), improper packing (it fell out and hit someone) or matters like that.. BUT, the single BIGGEST reason that airlines put these types of policies in place is with the idea that preventing FA's from lifting bags will reduce back injuries.. Is this true? My experience is that most people don't use proper body mechanics when they lift (lift with the legs and not their backs) and get injured as a result-- so there may be some truth to this claim..



Here's where the problem for the FA comes into play.. 



Let's say that in an effort to "help" a passenger, the FA lifts a bag and hurts themselves (how they injure themselves is irreverent- just that they got injured doing it).. 

Since the injury was "on the job" they are REQUIRED to report it to the airline--failing to report a workplace injury is a discharge eligible offense.. 

So they report it as required, and the company does a workplace injury investigation and finds out that the FA was just "helping" and lifting a bag.. 

Since the policy is "no bag lifting" and the FA clearly violated that policy-- BUT with good intentions-- they end up getting a formal disciplinary action from the company..



So, to a point FA's who are "refusing" to help are in fact caught between a rock and hard place.. They want to help you, but are prohibited by policy from doing so..



Can a reasonable person tell what bags are OK to help with and what ones may be a little too much? Perhaps. I'd guess that a proficient FA would know this, but the airline policy just doesn't allow for this.. They just take a clear path and say "no bag lifting".. 



So what's the answer.. In some cases a ground staff employee will help.. Other times the crew just does it- regardless of policy.



Again, this is not to say who is right or wrong or if there is a right or wrong.. It's only to illustrate some of the roadblocks that the CREW runs into when trying to provide you with services you need.



Travel Safe,

I am well aware of the physical dangers FAs assume when they help people lift their luggage. It always amazes me that they are so quick to offer when I know that they are generally discouraged from doing so. I always try to be responsible for my own belongings because it is not the job of a FA to put carry-on luggage in overhead storage. If they did that for every passenger I imagine many of them would develop their own disabilities.



Whenever possible I like to perform the same things for myself that all able-bodied people do.



What I appreciate greatly from the cabin staff is that they are all so pleasant as we wait for wheelchair assistance, or the delivery of my mobility cart. I know they are tired and want to get off the plane. Instead they stand around and visit with us and laugh and distribute plenty of smiles. Often the pilot will join the group. I often feel guilty because I know they cannot leave until I do, but I appreciate that they do not attempt to make me feel guilty because they are all so pleasant. Last night we waited about 30 minutes, and the pilot kept us entertained with his "old war stories". It was a very unique experience. I am sure that all those people who nearly start a riot in their haste to leave the plane miss these leisurely conversations.



I also have to note, that even though we waited 30 minutes after landing for my mobility cart, the luggage carousel had not even been turned on when we arrived at the baggage area, and all those people who raced off the plane were waiting in the same place I was waiting for our luggage to come up.



Ironically, our luggage was the first to hit the carousel and we were out of the airport before anyone else on our plane.

I really am not sure of the correct forum in which to post this question but I will be traveling from the US to England with a friend who has a machine that helps her breathe at night so therefore, we need to find a voltage converter. This is a three prong machine and it is pretty important that I not fry it when it gets plugged in. Since she has never traveled outside the country before, she is counting on me to solve this problem for her. What questions should I ask about her equipment and how I can be sure we are buying the correct converter?

Hi iamsally;



Electrical converters are readily available for travel overseas, but I would be concerned that they are NOT designed for heavy usage, but for small personal appliances.



I would suggest contacting the manufacturer of the device for some advice / suggestions / information.



As an alternative to taking the unit with you, perhaps you can rent a similar unit in the UK.



Best Regards

I use a C-Pap machine, and I have traveled extensively in Europe and Asia with it. I run it through a power converter and have never had a problem with it. It does not pull an extensive amount of electricity.



I do not know what type of electricity you have in the UK. We have 110 volt in the US. I doubt you would "fry" your C-Pap if you plugged it in because this is low voltage compared to Europe. It is more likely that it simply would not work well if it is designed to work on 220 volt.



Purchase a converter and run your C-Pap through it. I am sure it will be fine.

busy;



The OP is "traveling from the US to England"



The unit would be designed for use in North America where the electrical system is 110 Volts. The UK is on 220 Volts...which WOULD fry the machine if the voltage is not properly stepped down.



Best Regards

I am sorry I read the OP incorrectly. My C-Pap automatically converts for 220 volt, as does my laptop and several other appliances that I use. Before I understood I could plug the C-Pap directly into the wall socket with an appropriate adapter, I ran it through the currency converter along with every other electrical appliance we took with us (and we had lots). I had no difficulty with the C-Pap running through the converter.



Sometimes I still run it through my converter. We seem to always stay in hotels with only one wall socket. We plug our converter into the socket, and then use a power strip and plug everything else, including the C-Pap into the power strip. We have spent over 150 days in Europe and Asia in the past two years with no electrical difficulties at all.





I do understand, however, that 220 volts will fry anything not adapted for that electricity. I plugged in a lamp from our household possessions directly into a wall socket when I was young and dumb. I fried the lamp, the wall socket and I ended up on the other side of the room. Definately have never tried that again. When in doubt, a converter is best.

I appreciate all the suggestions on this. It is a C-Pap machine and I have read that some of them will do the voltage conversion automatically so I definitely need to check with the manufacturer and find out if her machine will do it. If not, I'm back to finding a voltage converter. I just don't know about the ability to rent those machines in London. I'm sure they are available but as to whether or not it would be practical is a different question.

A voltage converter is not expensive. We paid about $17USD for ours. I have seen them as cheap as $10USD. I see them at almost every department store where luggage is sold. I have two. I purchased one at Kohls and one at the Samsonite Factor Outlet Store near us.



You do not need to worry about renting one when you reach London. Just buy one and take it with you.



My greater problem with my C-Pap is not the voltage converter, it is locating distilled water I need to use the humidifier portion of the machine.



I can only buy it at service stations in Turkey. They use it to fill car batteries. It always smells a bit like oil, and I am not sure it is good to breath the fumes from the water. You will not, however, have that difficulty in the UK.

I also travel with a C-PAP machine and my only gripe is

the availability of an accessible electrical outlet near the bed. Many hotels/motels put them behind the headboard and you have to physically move the bed out enough to be able to access the outlet. Fortunately I carry a long extension cord and am usually able to snake it from another outlet to beside the bed. Don't forget to take a couple of small night-lights for those trips to the bathroom.

In the early days of using a CPAP (1995) I never traveled without an extension cord, multiple outlet adapter, light socket converter (to turn it into an outlet) and duct tape!



Thankfully, it seems I have been the benefit of business travelers needing additional outlets for laptops, etc (at least in the U.S.) as in the last 10 years or so I seem to be able to find outlets more plentiful. Sometimes they are in a lamp base, sometimes on a wall sconce, etc. And I haven't needed the extension cord in many years so that I never travel with any of that gear anymore. I did end up needing one at a hotel in Reno once, and housekeeping was happy to lend me one for my stay.

My husband has a C-Pap and when we travelled to Paris two years ago we used a heavy duty converter that I bought through Magellens and it worked just fine. If your friend has a new C-Pap it may have a built-in converter which you could see by examining the machine.



Definitely doable!
For the person who suggested renting a C-Pap overseas, this would not work. The machine is calibrated to the person using it.

Greetings Travelers! I just have to vent here: To attend a family wedding, my husband patiently spent 45 mins on the phone personally to set up 2 seats at the economy bulkhead for my 78 yr. old extremely limited in mobility, (cannot bend his knee at all or walk much) disabled, wheelchair-bound Alzheimer's suffering Father and accompanying 77 yr. old senior Mother, BOTH WAYS, while arranging wheelchair assistance at departing Tampa & arriving BWI, ~ AND ~ the RETURN only to have my parents re-seated (?), seats separated !! ( they NEED to be together) and NOT at the bulkhead !! as pre-arranged for leg-room but in MIDDLE seats !! and apart from each other! 



 My parents are unfortunately very timid and not frequent flyers, so they did not plead, beg, INSIST, argue or fight during early assisted pre-boarding to be re-assigned back to their original seats. I do not know HOW they managed an unbendable person into a middle seat but my mother reported my father was perspiring with pain and discomfort so profusely he was nearly blacking-out by landing 2 hours and 15 mins. later! It took several persons to remove him from his seat at Tampa.



 I find this horrifying and appalling! This is the first time we have arranged travel for disabled loved-ones and wonder if this treatment is SOP, the usual? If I could ever persuade them to fly again, or if they NEED to for medical treatment, a family emergency, funeral, etc, how can I better manage their care without being there personally as we live cross-country? Is there an airline that provides better care of seniors and disabled travelers?? Any suggestions?? And while I'm at it, my sincere hat's off to disabled travelers who can maintain a good attitude ! Safe Journeys! --Sandy

<<how can I better manage their care without being there personally as we live cross-country? >>



You can't. Accompany them personally (flying cross country) or pay for someone to travel with them. Anything else is irresponsible.

 

As someone who has direct personal family experience with Az, I am going to castigate you by saying there is no way you should have allowed a person with Az to travel with just one person, especially another senior. 

What happens if your mother visits the bathroom? OK your father may have "limited mobility" but to me that means he could walk off, to who knows where. 

I don't know if you are familiar with the story of the elderly couple, IIRC the husband with Az, wife went to the bathroom, wife asked airline employee to look after the person for two minutes, came back, both were gone, the husband was never seen again. They never even found a body. This was at DFW airport maybe 10 years ago.



<<Is there an airline that provides better care of seniors and disabled travelers??>>

Airlines aren't set up to provide nursing care, they certainly don't understand the needs of people with Az, arrange it yourself with additional people, either you, another relative, or a nurse.



Consider this a lucky escape, it could have turned out far far worse.

Thank you sincerely for your response. My father has just been diagnosed with AZ a few months ago, has no or little signs of dementia at this time, and his limited physical conditions are more of a issue currently. We are, in NO way , expecting nursing skills from airline personnel, only the seating consideration that was pre-arranged and assigned; and obviously in need of.

 

 As a family, we are all learning new ways we must all adjust to the changing requirements of our loved ones as the age and infirm and one of our struggles is when & what to do when they INSIST they are fine and can handle things just FINE Thank You Very Much!! Obviously, it's difficult to demand they relinquish their power and independence, over-rule their own Authority, and be forced to "parent our parents". We have a lot to learn! Thanks Again, Sandy

Sorry to be harsh, but the sad truth of AZ is that wherever you are in its progress, as someone once said to me, "remember, now is is as good as it gets" , so whatever difficulties with travel you have now are small compared to whats coming :-( 



Simply forget them travelling alone any more, its not practical or safe.



Limited mobility is perhaps a blessing in disguise, but if he is mobile at all, then one day you'l find your mother will say something to him like "wait here for 2 minutes while I go to the bathroom" and after a minute he'll wander off, looking for her. Unless you've experienced it yourself, you cant take on board the fact you can say to someone 'stay here' and 30 seconds later they forget you said that, they forget why they are there, where they are, and the next thing is to go wandering off.



Off topic, but you need to get help for your mother, its incredibly wearing for just one person to look after another 24x365, and longer term, its simply not doable. 



As for travel, *you* and your family will have to change, because you can't change old people, you most certainly can't change or reason with an Az sufferer (even if you convince them, they'll forget and go back to their old behaviour :-) , and so its you that will have to accommodate the Az, not an airline. Sorry and good luck..

If your father is wheelchair-dependent then the airline should have escorted him and your mother from the checkin desks to the gate and on board the plane as well as off the plane at the destination. If he truly has minimal to nil flexion of the knee(s) then flying at all should have been considered very carefully as no seat in Economy would be truly comfortable for someone with limited joint movement.



Airlines do allow airside passes for family members to accompany travellers who need support between check in and boarding; I'm a little surprised the airline did not offer such a thing and that you or your husband did not ask whether it was available.



If your father's pain control regime is still being titrated, had you not discussed the need with your mother to ensure he had sufficient analgesia before and during the flight? Is his pain of new onset or chronic? If the latter and yet pain is still uncontrolled then a discussion with his GP is in order sooner rather than later.



If your mother is unable to manage your father's care then should either of them wish to travel in future then you or another family member will need to accompany them, it is that simple.



Without wishing to sound too harsh, if your father has been diagnosed with an Alzheimer's type dementia then he will have congnitive deficits, otherwise making a diagnosis would be tricky. 



To travel anywhere - even to visit family in your city or to go out to dinner - you and your parents will need to make some changes now and in future. Ensure that mobility aids (walkers or wheelchairs) are fitted properly in consultation with a Physiotherapist and/or Occupational Therapist. Again if your father has chronic pain issues, please ensure his analgesic regime is adjusted to suit his needs. Has your father had his hearing checked recently? If he has decreased hearing and it can be addressed with a hearing aid then things may be better all around in that respect for him and for the rest of your family too.



Contact the Alzheimer's Society for help and support. Good luck to you and all of your family members.

thread_title: Self-Drive with limited mobility around UK
text:
Hi,



My daughter is coming over from Australia next summer and we would like to do a self-drive (own car) tour around the British Isles. She was living in London when diagnosed with leukemia and almost died from a brain infection that has now left her with brain damage and limited mobility. The intention is to see as much as possible within a four week period to compensate for all that she didn't get to see before, as she spent over 12 months in a hospital as opposed to doing the planned tourist bits. I am planning on traveling to India (Delhi/Faridabad area) the first of the year. I use a power wheelchair and have very limited mobility, I have never traveled outside the country, so never flown with my chair either. Any advice on 1) air travel with a power chair and 2) accessibility in India? 



Thank you!

Hi HindiPrincess;



I would suggest posting your question on the India forum as well.

http://www.tripadvisor.ca/ShowForum-g293860-India.html



Best Regards

I do not know how all airlines manage a powerchair. We fly almost exclusively on Delta because our loyalty program is with Delta, and they fly to more places than any other airline. With Delta I take my scooter directly to the door of the plane. It is then gate checked. When we land I wait until all the passengers have left, and then I often wait a bit longer. Ultimately the chair comes to the door of the plane. I am mobile enough to get myself from the scooter to my seat on the plane, and I do not need assistance during the flight.



I have heard that some foreign airlines want the chair to be checked with checked luggage, and some ask that the chair be taken apart if possible. There is also an issue regarding the type of batteries your powerchair uses.



I would suggest that you contact the airline that you are using and discuss your situation with them so that you at least know what their policy is regarding the way your chair will be handled in flight.



As for the issue of accessibility in India, I have never been to India so I cannot comment from personal experience. The best advice was offered by RescueTeam, and that is to seek advice from people on the India forum.



I can tell you that in my world travels I have never found a country that offers so much protection for disabled people as the US. Few countries have any legislation regarding the rights of the disabled. It also seems to me that the less economically developed a nation is, the less access you can expect for your disability.



We travel frequently to Turkey, and in the past three years my mobility has seriously declined. I seriously contemplated bringing my scooter on our current trip. Remembering the number of stairs necessary to reach so many places along with the lack of elevators, plus the high curbs and cobblestone streets discouraged me from bringing my scooter. I am glad I left it at home. It would have been virtually impossible for me to use here.



My inability to walk has resulted in my inability to be a companion to my husband. He spends a portion of each day walking to places we would like to visit. I either wait in our hotel room or in a near-by park or restaurant. He shares his photos with me when he returns.



I have only a finite number of steps I can manage each day, and I have to make sure that each and every step is an important step. When I walk I use my cane, walk very slowly and keep my eyes on the ground so I do not trip. My greatest fear is that I might break a bone.



I go very slowly, and when I become fatigued or in pain I stop and rest. I also make good use of the taxi system. Managing a taxi in any foreign country is a learning experience. I am sure people on the India forum can offer advise on avoiding typical taxi scams that are prevalent in any large city where a taxi is part of the daily transportation system.



When my mobility becomes so limited that I cannot take short, slow walks, I will bring my scooter. We will put it in the trunk of a taxi and I will use it in places where I know I can manage it, such as museums, The Grand Bazaar, and more modern neighborhoods. This will further restrict what I can see and do, but I am determined to continue to travel as long as possible.



I do not know how advanced your mobility issue is. Probably you do not appreciate the barriers you will experience with your chair in India. You can certainly plan on the lack of sidewalks, high curbs with no cutouts for wheelchairs, a multitude of stairs without ramps or elevators, uneven pavement or cobblestone streets/sidewalks, lack of space for your wheelchair in restaurants, shops, and entertainment locations, and, of course, the lack of handicapped equipped hotel rooms.



Even with these barriers, if I were completely restricted to my chair, this is a trip I would still take, and hope to make necessary adjustments to maximize my experiences. Basically, I suppose seeing any part of India, regardless of the difficulty is better than not seeing India at all.

thread_title: How to visit Cambodia & Thailand with a disability, I did it
text:
Last spring my husband & I did a 3 week trip to Thailand & Cambodia, which I organized & booked myself. If you are disabled or in a wheelchair & you want to go to either one of these countries, email me & I'm happy to advise on where to stay in Bangkok, Siem Reap & Khao Lak... YES there are wheelchair accessible hotels in Thailand & Cambodia... I spent weeks researching hotels in Khao Lak (56 miles north of Phuket) as we did not want to stay in Phuket, as I found it too touristy when I visited 20 years ago! LOL! If you want to visit Khao Lak there are 3 accessible hotels, have no fear.



Siem Reap is definitely do-able. I hired a licensed guide (who hired a van driver & 2 porters) to enable me to see Angkor Wat and other temples (including temples in the remote countryside)... So, do NOT allow anyone to tell you (as travel agents told me) that you 'can't see Angkor Wat if you're in a wheelchair or if you're disabled & can't climb stairs'... because I did it. We spent 6 nights in Siem Reap & it was the experience of a lifetime with our incredible guide Leng Tek who made it all happen for me.



The Peninsula Hotel in Bangkok also has portable handicap toilet seats (with steel handrails) that they will attach to a regular toilet seat if you are (like me) not in a wheelchair & do not wish to stay in a handicapped accessible room but need the seat to use the toilet. If you call their 800 (the calls go to Hong Kong) they will tell you that the Pen in BKK doesn't have portable handicapped toilet seats, it's not true. I called housekeeping & described it & within 5 minutes a porter arrived & attached it to our toilet, plus two rubber nonslip mats around the toilet (the bathroom is all marble) & waited while I tried it out. Fantastic service. Deluxe rooms have walk-in showers with separate tubs, the entire hotel area is ramped.



Both Bangkok Air and Thai Airways were fantastic with wheelchair transfers between our numerous flights, putting us in the First Class Lounge at the BKK airport on our return flight.



Our only problem was getting a bulkhead seat, they don't seem to understand that disabled people need the bulkhead seat. They kept offering the aisle seat & I kept having to demonstrate that my husband needed to LIFT me out of the seat, so he needed room (the bulkhead) to do so.



So, don't let your disability prevent you from visiting Cambodia, or Thailand.

As far as public sidewalk & curb issues, best to avoid them by hiring a guide/driver with an accessible van, so you don't have to walk anywhere on sidewalks... we did have a guide/driver in Bangkok (Jerry whom we hired through Tong -- ugh) & Jerry was wonderful & expert on navigating with the wheelchair we borrowed from him, as Jerry's father had had a stroke... so Jerry offered to take me about in his Volvo sedan w/ his father's LIGHTWEIGHT wheelchair... and although the curbs in BKK are VERY high, there ARE small wheelchair ramps in some blocks & if not, he wheeled me up the driveway. The MBK shopping center is totally accessible to those in wheelchairs.



As far as Siem Reap, our guide Tek (reached via LengTek@yahoo.com or

via his new website www.siemreap-tours.com) is very experienced touring with the handicapped, he can rent a van or an SUV & hire a porter (or two) to help carry the wheelchair (which we borrowed from our hotel) up the stairs of Angkor Wat & over tree roots at other temples.



There ARE other accessible lower cost hotels, as Raffles Grand d'Angkor is not wheelchair accessible, that are accessible... the Sofitel is totally accessible with accessible rooms, but we chose not to stay there as it is very spread out & no A/C in the main areas... and heat can be very fatiguing to the handicapped.



There are moderate priced guest houses that are accessible, but you have to contact them individually & ask them about ground floor rooms, bathrooms or stay in a western hotel with an elevator & a ramped entrance.



Just to be clear, Raffles in REP does NOT have a wheelchair ramp entrance to the hotel... I was carried up by the doormen & my porters... and I was able to walk down the stairs by myself. We used the service elevator to get to our poolside room in the new wing.



A 5K GBP budget is enough to cover a great trip to Siem Reap, you just need to hire a great guide like Tek (who knows how to do it) & not stay at Raffles.

thread_title: How to visit Cambodia & Thailand with a disability, I did it
text:
Hi,



OK. With a nightly budget of about THB3200 to THB3300 a night you'll have no problems finding suitable accommodations.



Off the top of my head I can think of the Holiday Inn on Silom, Radisson (Rama 9), and Novotel (Siam Square). All these places have elevators and rooms that can be requested that are better equipped for mobility impaired..



I think where you'll encounter more difficulties is navigating the streets.. For the most part Bangkok sidewalks are uneven, poorly maintained, rutted and often partially blocked by sidewalk vendors.. 



On the smaller side streets (called a SOI, in Thai language) there really is no technical sidewalk, as motorized traffic and pedestrians share the same area.



The BTS or Skytrain has a selected number of stations that are equipped with elevators from the street level to the concourse/ticket level and the train level. However, as mentioned, they're not at *every* station in the system.



My best suggestion is to hire a private car and driver for the day.. While not nearly as cheap as using the SkyTrain or taxis, it will be by far more convenient and a time saver.



For the most part, the major malls and attractions are much more mobility impaired friendly, but the same is not true for the older buildings which haven't undergone recent renovations.



Travel Safe,

text:

thread_title: In USA, what sot ot "tip" is expected?
text:
Hi,



While there is obviously no tip *required* for this service, as I've seen it, commonly it's $5 or less.. What I tend to notice is mitigating factors are: the distance of the journey-- some airports require you cover a great distance from plane-side to baggage reclaim and other not so much.. 2) did they assist you in any way with your cabin/hand carry bags (if any)? 3) did they just get you to baggage claim and leave you or was there some sort of effort made to facilitate your baggage reclaim (most chair services don't handle bags, but work closely with the airlines or airports 'porter' service), and 4) what was their overall level of professionalism-- was the ride smooth?...



Many people who operate the chair service have unfortunately never spent any real time *in* a chair to understand that there is a sizable difference in how the ride feels to the person seated versus the person pushing.



$5 would be more than appropriate for most situations.. Do remember that most all employees of these services are paid a standard wage *in addition* to any passenger gratuities received.



Travel Safe,

thread_title: In USA, what sot ot "tip" is expected?
text:
In the US I tip based upon the level of service. If someone just picks me up at the plane and pushes me to the luggage carousel, and if it is not a great distance, I tip $3 to $4. If a person helps with my carry-on luggage, retrieves my luggage from the carousel and helps me reach ground transportation i might tip as much as $20.



There is no obligation to tip, and some people will not accept a tip. There is a gentleman who works in the SEA airport who pushes wheelchairs all day, and absolutely will not accept a tip. He also works as a volunteer so he is not paid by the airport either.



I visit with the person pushing my wheelchair, and I suppose I tend to tip more if the person seems sincere, hard-working and deserving. I once had a young man who attempted to read a book and talk on his cell phone while pushing my wheelchair. He ran into three people including my husband who had all of our luggage on a cart. He knocked the luggage off of the cart and did not offer to help load it. I did not give him a penny. In fact, I told him to go away. I pushed my wheelchair to the curb myself.

thread_title: Wheelchair assistance travelling from Manchester via dubai t
text:
I assume you've notifed the airline you need assistance.

When you get to check in let them know you've asked for help (they may already be aware).

They'll tell you what to do.

You'll be collected by a wheelchair, and taken on the express route through security. Then left in the special needs section of the departure lounge (unless you've booked space in a lounge).

They'll come for you when it's time to head for the gate. And depending on your disability will wheel you to the aircraft entrance, or to your seat if you're unable to walk at all.

I'd expect the same service in Dubai, and in Brisbane you'll be taken through the express line for immigration.

You'll be looked after. For me, the worst time at airports was the period when I found walking difficult, but not bad enough to use a wheelchair.

If you have a carer, he'll accompany you at all times, and will benefit from the attendant's help.

thread_title: how to still be able to enjoy traveling on limited diets
text:
Hello everyone, We are at the beginning on the long journey to repair our guts but love to travel. We know it is tough to travel on a strict diet (Gluten, Diary... Free) but don’t want it to become a barrier to pursue our dream. we thought of an alternative to travel by car instead of flights; that way we will be able to carry little more essential stuff to prepare our meals just in case there is no option that accommodate our diet. However, we have never been traveling on such limited diets before so don’t really know what to expect. We heard there is an helpful “Find Me GF” app that can assist us but would love to hear more suggestions from traveling experts for international traveling or roadtrips within US on how to still be able to enjoy traveling on limited diets. Thank you very much.

Kay

thread_title: how to still be able to enjoy traveling on limited diets
text:
In the U.K. and the EU there are strict rules about labelling food and in restaurants you’ll be offered menus noting allergens and other food options, everything from vegan and vegetarian to GF, DF, even lupins. If the information isn’t on the menu you can ask for details; very often you’ll be given a folder with more details than you’ll think possible. 



As an example. A friend who is Coeliac joined us in London for a meal at our local fish and chip shop. Not only were the fish and chips GF, so was the vinegar, beer and everything else he was offered. 

Supermarkets too label foodstuffs, often having separate large sections for GF and dairy free options. 



Overall we’ve found it far easier in Europe than in the US to trust ingredients meet our requirements.

thread_title: how to still be able to enjoy traveling on limited diets
text:
I'll give a thumbs up to Bestcornishcat's post. While I'm not GF, I am vegan and honestly I find it's much easier to travel in Europe than the US.



I spent a month in France last Sept/Oct after not having traveled since October 2019 (for obvious reasons, lol). One of the things I found is that there were fewer vegan choices this time as many restaurants in Paris have limited their menus. I suspect that is because of many factors but I could usually find something to eat. I'm going back in a couple of weeks and will be challenged as I'm meeting some friends at a very "meaty" restaurant (their choice, of course,lol) so will try to not be terribly hungry when I go. 



What countries are you considering? For myself, I've got translation cards that say "I am vegan" in French, Dutch, German and Italian. I've got them taped to a 3x5 index card as occasionally I've had a server take it back to the chef, then come back out to point things out on the menu that will work. I have a translation app on my phone but I don't relish my phone being taken away from me, lol!



I would learn the phrase for "gluten-free" in the language of the country you are visiting and do some research on menus for restaurants you might want to visit. Often they will have little icons beside menu items that will tell you what allergens they have - such as a little loaf of bread with a line thru it or in my instance, a green leaf.



As far as the US, I go to Yellowstone for a couple of weeks each summer and have always traveled with a cooler. The choices there were pretty pathetic before the pandemic and were dismal last summer and the summer before! I leave home with a block of ice frozen into a large plastic container that fits in the bottom of the cooler. When I leave I usually have a couple of salads organized such as a couscous salad and/or a pasta salad. Something that travels well. I also travel with an electric kettle so I can use hot water for oatmeal in the AMs and some vegan soups for evening after I've plowed thru my salads. I replace my homemade ice block with block ice from a grocery store once that melts. 



I also have a plastic bin of dry goods - crackers, bread or bagels, peanut butter, etc. Since there can be problems in the cabins in Yellowstone with mice I have a lidded bin to protect that food. I always carry some Kind/Luna/Clif bars in case I'm out and about watching wildlife or geysers and need a quick something for my stomach.



I do figure out kind of a meal plan and know when I need to head to a gateway town to stock up on hummus, salad greens, etc.



A good friend and fellow DE on the Yellowstone forum is GF and she and her husband also travel with a cooler. It's just much easier for her instead of taking the chance to get slimed by a careless restaurant. 



Good luck on your travels. I'm not wanting any food issues I have to limit my wanderings!

I live in the U.K. and have taken my #cooter to inumerous countries, including Italy and Rome.



First of all, as long as you have the correct two pin plug adaptor you will have no problem in charging your scooter in any European country.



My scooter is very similar to a Pride Go Go Traveller. It has suspension, which is an advantage. Yes, there are cobbles in Rome, but not everywhere. Rome is a compact city, so it’s easy to get about. The main problem I had was that if there was a dropped kerb, there wasn’t one on the opposite side of the road. I spent a lot of my time riding in the road.



I also found that cars often park across the dropped kerb.



The trams are accessible, but not all buses are. I found most people very willing to help.



Most museums and attractions are accessible and all details will be on their websites. Book all entrance fees via the official websites. There is free entrance for all disabled visitors plus a carer and you get priority entrance.

The Pantheon is now requiring that you reserve tickets for weekends or holidays, apparently to control crowding. The tickets are free: https://pantheon.cultura.gov.it/en/. However, they are both within the historic center, which is where I always suggest first time visitors to Rome stay, so they have as much access as possible to the many wonderful sights as well as restaurants and such.

But many people pointed out that it might make more sense to look at vans and plan to stay in hotels. The reason we would still want a van is so my mom could still lie in a bed whenever she gets tired (which is often). I am aware that it is technically illegal to have someone sleeping in the bed while we're driving, but I'm just being honest, it's going to happen so it is what it is... Yes it is a safety concern, I know! I'm sure we have all "broken" that law with a snooze in a backseat on a long car trip so... Anytime my mom would need to move from one spot to another (like the bathroom), we'd pull over.



My mom is not bound to a wheelchair- It's just the stairs getting in that will be the challenge. She walks but not well. Many people offered good advice and questions like "why not take Amtrak?" The whole point is there is a series of things we want to do along the way- visit family, see some national parks, etc. I want my mom to see the Grand Canyon! It's a bucket list thing. My original idea was "get a big RV and then mom will always be "home" cuz she can sleep, go the bathroom, etc, pretty much whenever she needs to". But people made the good points that setting the RV up at RV sites etc isn't exactly fast/easy. So now I'm thinking, maybe it would be better to get a van and then stop at hotels for the night. 



Does anyone have any experience with this? To start, I can't even find many wheelchair-accessible RVs. I know RV bathrooms aren't exactly easy for mobility-challenged persons either. I know we would need to take a route that avoids high elevations out of concern for her ease of breathing. thread_title: Flying UK- Texas with 2 autistic children
text:
Hi

I'm starting to look for deals to fly to texas (Houston area) next April with my 2 boys. Both autistic, although relatively 'high functioning'. They will be 14 & 11 when we fly & younger one may have his birthday while we're out there.

I have sleep apnoea & use a cpap machine & neither of my boys are dry at night (yet).

As I have never flown by myself (someone else has always organised/been in charge), let alone with these added complications, I'm wondering what advice people can give me to help thing go as smoothly as possible. 

 

My plans so far include: none stop flights, booking either direct through airline or via a trust worthy travel agent with experience in these issues, notifying airports in advance so we have access to quiet areas while waiting, trying to ensure we are seated together- this might be harder on way back if Mr 11 turns 12, but don't want that to be a time limiting factor. Ensuring I know the rules for extra baggage allowance for medical equipment (cpap & incontinence pants). Double checking medication rules for US (I'm on several different medications).

We're going to meet my dad & other family & really don't want things ruined because I forgot to check or mention something months before.

thread_title: Flying UK- Texas with 2 autistic children
text:
You might not like this as it is going to cost money but if you want to be seated together which makes complete sense I think you should pay seat reservation fee then you don’t have to worry about this a know your seats in advance. You should book directly with the airline. As far as I know BA and United are the only airlines with non stop flight from U.K. to Houston both depart from London.

thread_title: Flying UK- Texas with 2 autistic children
text:
I agree 100% with Alex. To me, this complex set of circumstances means you should not look for "deals". I am not saying to not grab a good fare if you see it but certainly pay for seat assignments. Look at the seating charts for whatever route you settle on and see if they have 3 seats across the middle vs 4 seats. I fly Delta usually (no direct flight to Houston) and the economy seats are 4 across in the middle whereas the Economy Plus seats are 3 across. In your situation it might be better if you can pay up to whatever the Economy Comfort level is for the airline you choose just to get a row to yourselves.



"notifying airports in advance so we have access to quiet areas while waiting," I'd do some research on this one ahead of time. If you are in touch with Autism Spectrum groups in UK someone may have accessed a room at either Heathrow or Gatwick and can give you specific information. I did a quick search and only came up with prayer rooms at Heathrow. I did check out the prayer room recently at Schiphol in Amsterdam but there was a person in there praying and it would not have been a good place to sit and wait while they were doing their devotions. I didn't come up with anything for Gatwick on a quick google but that doesn;t mean there isn't one.



I'd also recommend you get to the airport way earlier than you might think you should. It does depend on what the current state of affairs is for the airline industry next spring but prepare for it to not have improved much from what is happening now. I'd probably plan to get there 4 hours ahead of flight time. 



I hope the trip goes well and that your boys enjoy the trip!

thread_title: Flying UK- Texas with 2 autistic children
text:
This is what I have done regarding my trip. In terms of assistance, I let my airline know that I need a wheelchair to get from the desk to the aircraft. In UK airports you will find a special assistance desk, I know in Gatwick and Heathrow they have a specific lounge for those who need special assistance and their carers/family. I would look on the airports site and more than 2 days before travel, let them know of your needs. You'll want to confirm your inbound flight too so if you need assistance when returning, they can help. 

Special assistance, at least in the UK, has a dedicated security lane which should ease the stress of the loud and busy environment. 

I booked my seats since it is a long haul trip. It was about £50 and I am doing a layover in each direction, so 4 seat bookings total. For the small price, I would really recommend it. 

Your CPAP machine shouldn't account as baggage allowance if you take it as hand luggage from the airlines I've seen as it is a medical device. So you should be able to bring it as an additional carry on with no issues. Make sure you confirm this on the airlines website, some like you to just let them know you are bringing it on board.

From my experience dealing with Expedia, I would book with the airline themselves. I was in a back and forth with them for months with the airline as they both refused to take responsibility. If you book directly, it is their problem should you have issues. Deals on travel agent sites aren't that great either. They often lie about the 'original price' vs their 'discount' of the ticket. I would rather pay the extra £100 or so if I book directly. 



If you really don't want to pay for your seat choices, you could email the airline and let them know about your needs. They might accommodate you and put you together, but you might just be put at the back of the aircraft where people tend not to book seats as first choice. It is a gamble but you can decide on that.

thread_title: Flying UK- Texas with 2 autistic children
text:

thread_title: Flying UK- Texas with 2 autistic children
text:
Incontinence supplies (including for adults/older children) are readily available at any drugstore in the US; pack enough for the trip (including possible delays) but not for your entire trip. You should be able to carry any prescribed medications (including liquids), but don't count on being able to fill a UK prescription in the US. 



I've known other people with an autistic family member who arranged a specialized tour of the airport ahead of their travel day, so the person could get familiar with the airport and the routines of flying. If it's their first flight and one or both of your kids would benefit from that, do ask.

Hi, I've also seen your question on Air Travel and the advice you've received there.

I'd be very unhappy with such a tight connection, so understand your concern.

I think you will need wheelchair assistance throughout the trip, it does sound as if you'd struggle to cope without it. This is not unusual, airports are huge and can involve a lot of standing and waiting. I needed wheelchair help before I was seriously disabled.

With a tight connection, if you buy as 2 separate tickets, there's a real risk that a slight delay on the first flight will mean you'll miss the connection. In that case, you'll either have to abandon the trip, or buy a ticket at the last minute, which could be very expensive.

If you buy the whole journey as a single ticket the airline is responsible to get you to your destination.

First see if they will sell it as a single ticket, if they won't it means the connection isn't safe, and you should abandon the route.

If they do give a price (this will be more than buying as 2 separate tickets because the airline is taking a risk if anything goes wrong), I'd call them and see if it's suitable for a disabled person.

As you realise, you'll be last off the plane, but will get express clearance through secuiry, So it probably won't take you any longer than any other passenger.

thread_title: air travel with leg immobilizer on
text:
Hi Meg,

Just a couple of points. I am disabled and fly transatlantic fairly frequently . 

If the seats that you have booked are next to an emergency exit, be prepared for the crew telling you that you have to move. They consider that ALL the people in those seats must be able to operate the exit door in the event of an emergency. I have needed the extra legroom ( shortly after a surgery with my left leg totally immobilized ) 

Because I needed wheelchair assistance to board the plane and because I could not fully support myself using both legs I was deemed “unable to assist in an emergency “ and I was told that I had to move. After disagreeing with their assessment of me, I eventually HAD to move or disembark the plane…Captains orders!

This may not be the policy on the airline that you are flying with but I wanted to make you aware of this “rule”



As for supporting your leg during the flight, you are probably going to be far more comfortable if you have crutches, to assist you in transferring to/from wheelchairs, seats, the washroom etc. With crutches, you are able to totally none- weight bear through your injured leg, plus if you lie a crutch across your hip of your “good” leg, towards your foot on the injured leg you can then lie the injured leg up across the crutch…. This is very supportive and surprisingly comfortable. I use forearm crutches, they have a band that holds on to your forearm. Regular crutches are cheaper but not as comfortable to use.

An Inflatable neck pillow can be used behind your knee to offer some “padding” if you and your wife have carry- on bags that you can stack to form a support for your leg.

Please make sure that you have enough pain medication for the flight/s as the transferring and hopping around can really aggravate an injury. Good luck with your flight and I hope that you get home safely xx

We visited Thailand quite a lot over 10 years ago, and some of the beaches there are very peaceful. But nobody outside the hotels speaks English. You could ask on the Thailand forum for suggestions.

thread_title: Advice on European air travel with a scooter?
text:
There are all sorts of problems when flying with a scooter, the batteries can be a major issue, as lithium batteries can catch fire, so you may have to avoid them. There are rules about size as well. When you hire, you should discuss this holiday with the company you hire from.

I would trust the airport to get you to the gate by wheelchair. I've flown from Heathrow several times, and it's the airport, not the airline, who organises help for the disabled. You must make sure the airline is aware of your needs before departure date.

It is worrying that BA haven't responded to your email.

it would be best to have a scooter which breaks into pieces. Make sure your carer can handle comfortably the weight and bulk of the heaviest piece. Otherwise you'll need a large vehicle which can also hold a ramp.

thread_title: Advice on European air travel with a scooter?
text:
I have travelled throughout Europe on a regular basis with my scooter. I have the type that breaks done into 5 separate parts, but never have to do that on an aircraft.



Airlines do have weight and size restrictions, but shouldn’t affect a small scooter. All details will be in the T&Cs on their website.



I have taken my scooter on BA flights with no problem whatsoever. My scooter has a dry cell battery which I leave on the scooter. If the scooter has a lithium battery, then you are normally asked to take it in the cabin with you.



You need to book Spacial Assistance direct with the airline. I do this at the same time as I book my flight. You will be asked to supply the specifications of the scooter.



At the airport you will be fast tracked as are all disabled passengers. I ride my scooter to the door of the aircraft. It is then taken and put into the hold . I take out the key and take it with me. I also show the handlers how to operate the brake. It really is very easy.



When I arrive at my destination it is waiting for me at th3 door of the aircraft. I don’t disembark until I see it waiting for me.



It really is quite simple and efficient.



Both Copenhagen and Stockholm do have some cobbled streets, but the majority are ok. They both have accessible public transport systems.

thread_title: Advice on European air travel with a scooter?
text: My scooter weighs 30 pounds (13KG) with battery and I have never had a problem with any international airline (although I hear China and Emirates are a problem). Because my scooter battery is lithium I have to take it off the scooter and carry it on the plane. Basically, I ride the scooter to the plane door, remove the battery, walk to my seat while my scooter is put in the hold. The scooter is generally waiting for me when I deplane.

thread_title: Advice on European air travel with a scooter?
text: I have a Titan 4 from https://www.tzora.co.uk/ I travelled to France with my scooter in May this year. I downloaded the certificate from the website CE compliance and presented it to check-in. The scooter was taken on board as luggage. I was then driven around the airport. At the other end, I was again driven to collect my luggage, including my Titan scooter. The process was relatively comfortable.

thread_title: Advice on European air travel with a scooter?
text: Thanks to all who responded to my post. Unfortunately, my own experience was far from positive. I have already contacted British airways without a response from the company. I have flown the LAX-LON-CPH route several times before with BA but without a disability requiring a wheelchair or scooter. Without hesitation, this was the worst trip, by far, of any I have ever taken on any airline (and I am a veteran of 1970s student charters.) Despite submitted forms and emails from me, and many hours on the phone over several months, no promised accommodations were provided by BA for my flights. When I was boarding at LAX, a BA staff member touched me repeatedly in ways that had nothing to do with boarding (despite my loud requests that he stop touching me.) There was no aisle chair that fit the plane aisles on our long outbound flight (requiring me to haul myself over several rows of seats to reach my seat) and no opportunity to use the bathroom during or between flights either direction because, according to the flight attendants "there was no way to get [me] there." I cannot recommend that anyone with a mobility issue rely on British Airways at this time.

Presumably you are going to use Eurostar to travel from London to Paris so the following may help.



From Eurostar’s website



Can I take my mobility scooter on Eurostar?

You can bring a battery-operated mobility scooter free of charge, as long as it’s no more than 70cm wide by 120cm long. This is to make sure it fits in lifts, on ramps and in one of our onboard wheelchair spaces.

 

Scooters that use combustible fuel aren’t allowed on board any of our trains.

 

If you book a wheelchair space, you’ll need to sit in your scooter all the way.

 

If you’d rather sit in a seat on board, you need to be able to walk 200m unaided and get on the train using the steps.

Therefore, I naively assumed SATA would be the same... unfortunately this was not the case and I was rudely informed that it was not the airline’s problem and they have no power to ask passengers not to consume their own snacks. Hopefully this will be different for you if you notify them in advance! I took a chance as it was only a 45 minute flight and I knew they did not sell any food, and luckily was ok. text:
You say “ I'l looking for a big site (or sites) where people can search for or place an ad to find a travelling companion, preferably for a very long stay abroad. I mean up to a year or even more.”



Firstly, I doubt there’s anyone in cyberspace who would want to do what you suggest. Even if you aren’t actually in cyberspace, it’s unlikely any rational person will be in a position to take a year off work/their daily life to go travelling with a stranger. Why would they? 



I’d echo keshgrammy’s comment. I realise it’s not what you want to hear, but whether disabled or not, advertising online for a travel companion is unwise unless you plan to interview them, take up references, get to know them well enough (in person, not just online) to know you’d be happy to spend 24 hours a day with them (and they with you). 



You need to establish who pays for what, how much care is to be provided and to what extent your habits are compatible eg drinking, spending, whether you’re an owl or a lark, what will happen if you disagree and/or one of you wants to return home or move on and the other doesn’t. 



If you don’t have friends or relatives willing or able to join you then your choices are employing and paying someone eg via a reputable agency, placing an ad on something like Craigslist (and doing a lot of due diligence checks), trying to find someone via groups to which you already belong. 



I suspect you haven’t thought through this “trip”.

If you “ don’t have what is generally considered a disability, but am not healthy” then welcome to life... you are not alone, and you are not special. Believe me... 



There are millions of people like you, yet you want a website to buddy up with someone to look after you, for a year or more, or are you seeking vulnerable disabled people to buddy up with and look after them?



Rather than saying responses to your question are “kinda irrelevant”, and quoting a chunk from Richard Dawkins, ( which is totally irrelevant anyway but whom you seem to hold in high regard) I suggest you try your best to make friends in your own cyberspace community and see if anyone there wants to travel with you.

text:
I really don’t know where ou have been getting your info from, because it is totally incorrect. If you found Italy easy, then the U.K. will be a breeze.



In London all buses are free of charge for wheelchair/scooter users. They have recently introduced a system where you need to egister a scooter, so they have the dimensions and the bus driver knows it is authorised to travel. Museums, attractions and theatresoffer ‘carer goes free’ tickets.

thread_title: Flying with Total Knee Replacements TKR
text:
I have made several 12+ hour flights, first with one TKR and now with both knees replaced. The first was 16 months ago, the other 7 months ago.

Speak with your surgeon about wearing compression stockings...my knee high ones keep leg swelling down. Ask about inflight exercises to do...remember the ankle pumps after surgery? Those still work...

I do try to go business so I can get the legs UP and straighten them. But I have made several 5-6 hour flights in regular seating and it was ok.

I make a point of walking up and down the aisle every couple of hours. 

Honestly, I do better now kneewise than I did before surgery. I am 66.

I wonder if you might benefit from some additional physical therapy before you go, and in general...something to consider to improve your ability to stand unaided and also to stretch muscles to reduce stiffness. If I do not do my home program, I get much stiffer in the muscles. The joints themselves are fine, it is the rest of me that needs work! :)

thread_title: Flying with Total Knee Replacements TKR
text:
I got to put my feet up in the lie flat business seats, and I was fine on arrival afterht eh 12+ flights. Walked all over airport and city on arrival. 

On the 5-6 hour flights in regular seats I was a little stiff and legs swollen a bit but still fine.

But my feet and legs have always swollen even before surgery and I have used Jobst compression stockings for about 11 years. https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B008CKK83E/ref=oh_aui_search_detailpage?ie=UTF8&psc=1



I used to be groaning getting up after sitting or in a car. Both legs. Then after my first TKR, after the rehab (which worked on both sides) no more difficulty standing, much less stiffness, much better overall. Even better after the second TKR.



I do not consider my TKRs a disability, do not use special assistance in airports, walk 2-3 hours at a stretch sightseeing, climb stairs without difficulty, am so grateful for the surgical outcome and my wonderful physical therapists.



I attribute this outcome to my surgeon and also to the EXERCISES and STRETCHES I was given by my physical therapist and the home program I am to follow every day for the rest of my life. If I slack off, I get stiffness and pain. It goes away when I do my work. Surgery just puts in a new joint. It was the exercise that built up the tissues, gave me range of motion and mobility. Stretches give me range of motion and flexibility. 



 After going through the surgeries, it is foolish of me not to do the continuing work to get my virtually painfree knee life! I had not realized how limited I had been until I wasn't limited anymore. I still tense before I stand expecting pain--and then remember why there is none :)



I suggest you go for it and also am quite forward in suggesting you look into more physical therapy to address your strength issues. You may be very pleasantly surprised.



Good luck and happy travels.

thread_title: Is travel possible for patients with dimentia
text:
Google “air ambulance “



Companies that provide air ambulances often can also arrange appropriately trained doctors and nurses (including mental health staff) to travel on “normal” flights. 

They will assess the patient, arrange clearance with the airline in advance, can provide medication where necessary, and will be suitably trained to handle the patient in flight. They can also arrange appropriate land transport to the final destination. 



This won’t be cheap, but it will be a darn sight cheaper than a chartered plane (where you’d still be expected to provide medical staff anyway)

Good Morning,

As an Australian badge is not recognised within the UK, you are going to have to contact the authorities of the places you are visiting to see if they will allow you to use your Australian badge or if they can issue you a temporary badge.

From Traffic & Road Safety, Glasgow -

text:
I really don't think letters from a specialist will help you if you are confronting a Parking Attendant any letter can be a forgery. Some PAs are very diligent and will give genuine Blue Badge holders parking tickets if the badge is displayed incorrectly e.g. Back to front. For a pass to be valid the expiry date must be seen, not the picture. As soon as a ticket is issued it can not be retracted. 



In the U.K there is a great problem with passes being used fraudulently and stolen passes. If your Australian pass is not accepted you are likely to get a parking ticket and your only hope is to appeal it. It will be very hard to get a temporary pass as the issue of passes is linked to now much more linked to Benefit entitlement. In the past local authorities issued passes on a discretionary basis but this is being tightened up due to misuse. You need to contact every authority you park in to see if they will accept your pass. It's a difficult area to research with little advice.



If you need extra room to get in and out your best bet is to use a disabled space to transfer and then have someone move the car. If this isn't possible you have to be prepared to maybe get a parking ticket. Also be aware that disabled parking is not always free in private car parks. Parking on roads and places with time limits require setting a clock.



Hope it helps.

I travel with insurance from Holiday Safe after looking at several companies including ones heavily advertised on daytime television. I had an estimate of £950 for a one month holiday in Japan from one of those.

Holiday Safe uses a different model from most. 

They have one deductible amount for most things people claim for (lost property, twisted ankles etc.)and a larger deductible for claims arising from a preexisting condition.

When you buy the insurance have telephone call where you go through a a list of questions from an actual human being who appears to have some medical knowledge (as opposed to a teenager with a tick list)

The end result of their model is a lower price for your insurance. 

My last policy was around £180 for a world wide (including the USA and Japan) annual policy. The deductible for most things was £60, for preexisting conditions it was £600.

I had a heart attack in Japan at the beginning of the 4th week of my trip in January/February 2019. 

Although the insurance aspect wasn't hassle free, they did pay up.

I paid the hospital £11,500 (20% of the bill) because I wanted to catch my flight which was due to leave a week after the heart attack. 

The insurance company did make it clear that if I was willing to wait for them to get the response from my GP, they would pay the costs coming from the wait and re-booking the flight but I had work on the Monday to get home for and the hospital was willing to let me go and certify me fit to fly.

I did get paid back by Holiday Safe in time to pay the money back into my saving-for-taxes-account and they told me when I enquired 6 months after the heart attack that they would continue to insure me by an annual policy. The cost would be more and the deductible for a heart attack would be higher, but my greatest fear was that I would no longer be able to get travel insurance and therefore no longer be able to travel.

I hope now that 14 months have passed and more time will pass before we can travel again, the cost is likely to go down again.

I like this model of charging because if any of my preexisting conditions go wrong, the cost is likely to dwarf a £600 (or even higher) deductible. My hospital bill in Japan was £57,500. (Although the care was superb and the food was delicious)
