I travel with a service dog. In fact, he's been with me 24 hours a day since 2009. I have multiple medical conditions that are USUALLY invisible unless I'm having an episode. 



Because of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), travel in the US rarely presents problems, except for those ubiquitous nitwits. Tell them what they must do, and what you must be allowed to do, according to federal law. If you know the state law for the place you're visiting, inform them of that one too. State laws may only expand our rights. Any abridgement is a violation of federal law.



Be prepared to show the gatekeeper the applicable section(s) of the ADA, or print out the appropriate pamphlet for businesses. If that doesn't work, say that you'll be happy to wait while they call the police. That's a fairly hard-nosed approach, but it often works.



Also, be sure that your service dog is adequately trained and behaves like a service dog, whether your disability is visible of not. The security screeners get a kick out of me stripping off my dog's vest, collar, and leash, putting him on a down-stay while I walk through the metal detector, and having my naked dog come to me on command. :-)



We (dog and I) have been on 3 cruises. Royal Caribbean has been great! 



We just returned from Israel with an extended layover in New York city. Israeli law addresses guide dogs, but not service dogs for other medical conditions. I could write a very long essay on our experiences in Israel. 



Here are a few pointers:

1) Every country has entry requirements (called import requirements) for domestic animals. 

http://tinyurl.com/o368m2x

http://tinyurl.com/ptyr3pj

Plan ahead! Complete every form. Paperwork must be signed off by the DOA Export Office nearest you. Also, there are a limited number of airports from which one may transport a live animal. 



2) Inform the airline and hotels before you leave that you travel with a medical service dog. Make sure they understand what that means. The conference planner smoothed out the problems with the hotel, as did a phone call to the hotel's corporate office in the U.S. I had huge problems with El Al Airlines until I contacted the TSA disability helpline (http://tinyurl.com/q79xlfj). Every carrier that flies out of American airports is required to have a person to deal with disability law violations and problems -- can't remember what they are called. After TSA involved El Al's problem resolution specialist, the problems disappeared. He promised to train the reservations agents regarding service dogs.



3) I ordered business cards in English on one side and in Hebrew on the other side to inform people of his job and simple service dog etiquette (i.e., "don't pet me"). Keep the text short. Contact me if you would like to see mine.



4) I also purchased a custom patch for his vest and a leash slider that say "Medical Service Dog" in Hebrew.



5) My biggest obstacles were taxi drivers who do not want dogs in their vehicles. The doorman or front desk at my hotel was often able to explain why the dog must accompany me. Use local people to assist you in communicating with gatekeepers.



Those are the high points. Let me also plug a book by a local service dog handler, Marcie Davis, "Working Like Dogs: The Service Dog Guidebook." I spoke with Marcie before my trip. She answered questions and reassured me that it be an adventure that would work out in the long run! She was right. :-)
Please be aware that Hawaii has very strict rules, even for service animals. We do not have rabies here, so the laws are different for bringing an animal with you.

Unfortunately a lot of the resistance to service dogs comes from hotels and others who have been abused by pet owners who are trying to get around the "no pet" rule by claiming the dog is a service animal when it is no such thing. These pet owners who cannot bear to leave their dog with a responsible pet sitter or stay in places that will always accommodate pets ruin it for those who truly need a service animal. ADA laws protect the legal rights of disabled people and their service dogs when they enter hotels, restaurants, businesses, and other public areas. You can check it in as checked baggage or you can ride it through to the boarding door of the aircraft. Your choice. You will either have it back at the aircraft or at baggage collection, depending on the airline and if baggage handlers can read the special instructions. If you aren't going to receive it at the aircraft, they will collect you in a wheelchair and the attendant will stay with you until you collect your scooter.



There is no charge for checking your scooter as it is classified as medical equipment, which is carried for free. You will need a letter from your Doctor stating you need to use the scooter. It is a good idea to insure the scooter for overseas travel as that won't be included in your domestic policy. Also take a walking cane with you, it required. If wooden, ensure it is a hardwood.. I travel with a hardened modern day polypropylene.



You need to notify your airline in advance (like three weeks to a month) that you are travelling with it, supplying Make etc., as well as your battery Watt Hours (WH). I travel with a copy of my scooter details, including folded measurements, weight and battery Amp hours as well as Watt Hours. You need a compliant bag to place the battery or batteries in, as you need to remove the battery (s) and place it in the overhead locker on the aircraft. I photocopy all my scooter paperwork, including battery information. I take with me, a copy of all documentation for each flight so they can keep the paperwork, plus a spare copy to keep with me.



Check the regulations of your airline regarding batteries for use with medical equipment, it is not always in plain sight but is different from ordinary lithium ion batteries. If you scooter uses two batteries to power it, both batteries must be under 300WH each. If you scooter uses only one battery to power it, you may also carry a spare battery. Again, each battery must not exceed 300 WHs each. Remember, if you carry two batteries, they both must be contained in the battery carry bag, or if needed, you will need to purchase a second battery compliant battery bag. Lithium Ion Batteries used in small items suchnas cameras, computers etc, have been known to catch fire. Your battery bag, if supplied by the scooter manufacturer, will be fireproof.



Don't forget to take a power adapter compliant with the power outlet in your hotel room. It can be handy to travel with a power board and or short extention cord to make charging easier. Ensure you are compatible with the power supply of your destination country. Check your battery (when on charge) can accept either 240 or 110 volts. Many can be varible. If unsure regarding the battery technicalities, contact the retailer you purchased it from. 



If your scooter folds down, it may pay to place a luggage strap around it, while in transit, to help elliminate damage in the haul. Also ensure you have a sturdy luggage name tag on the scooter.



In most cases when flying, if you need to change flights before reaching your destination, they may transfer your scooter direct to your connection. In which case, you should be met with a wheelchair. The upside to that, is the attendant knows where to go. At Immigrations, insist your career stays with you (if needed, say you are dependent on your career, there don't know any different). I have known of a case where the wheelchair was taken through Special Assist and it took her career another hour to pass through immigration. Stay together.



This may all sound daunting, but if you are compliant with this, then you shouldn't have any problems. Always ensure you have plenty of time for check in. We usually arrive three hours before departure. Some check in staff need time as they have never checked in a scooter before. All airlines have different policies. Provided you are compliant with your airline, you should have a fuss free time. If you have any questions, feel free to ask. Have a great holiday. Today (12/03/2020) the US Dept. of Transportation ruled that dogs are the only animals defined as service animals. Their definition is as follows - "a dog trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of a person with a disability." They received over 15,000 comments on the notice of proposed rulemaking. 

Emotional support animals are no longer considered to be service animals but the ruling still requires airlines to allow dogs that are psychiatric service animals.

The ruling becomes official 30 days after publication.

Ask your TRAVEL INSURANCE COMPANY who to consult, either a General Practitioner (GP) or a Hospital Haematology Clinic where your blood can be checked. After battling advanced breast cancer in 2007, then undergoing IVIG (intravenous immunoglobulin infusions) in early 2008, I took a long direct flight from Houston to Honolulu. I was high on my own endorphins once I arrived there in paradise (where I had grown up as a child). 

Soon after arriving, however, I began having crushing pains in my chest and I tried to ignore it. My friend urged me to go to the ER but I said I did not want to get hooked up to all sorts of monitors and IVs, so I would just ignore it, even if I was having a heart attack. It may sound silly, but I told my friends, "If I am having a heart attack, then this is where I want to be when I die, and I do not mean in the hospital!"

However, two days later I could not even function from the excruciating chest pain and my friend finally talked me into going to the hospital. After a flurry of getting hooked up and a contract CT scan, I was told I had a massive attack of pulmonary emboli (blood clots in my lungs) and it was truly a miracle I was alive. I was later told that my own endorphins were probably what had protected me.

Anyway, then I got stuck in the hospital for ten days while they used Lovenox and Coumadin to thin and stabilize my blood. I was chomping at the bit to be released, and as soon as I could, I got out of there and enjoyed every moment to the fullest.

Now I am stuck on Coumadin/warfarin for life, and I was told that it may have been the combination of having had cancer (which can predispose you to blood clots), having been on IVIG, and then the long flight which caused all this. 

I monitor my own INR at home, which tends to stay pretty stable, but I am terrified to fly again, especially for long distances. I did try one (round trip) four hour flight which went well, but if I do not get up the nerve to try a long flight to Europe, I may never again see many of my best friends over there.

Does anyone else who is at really high risk (esp. after cancer) have any advice about this? There is almost the exact opposite problem with one of my best friends in Holland. She has spent years battling cancer and is on warfarin, but would love to come visit me here... but is afraid of the long flight.

Who can give us some good solid advice?

text:
I checked past threads, but I could not find the information I was seeking.



My sister is currently traveling and now needs wheelchair assistance between gates. I asked folks on the Dallas forum for assistance with transiting that huge airport, and they were helpful. They confirmed that a wheelchair is essential for someone who cannot walk far. 



A wheelchair was requested when the ticket was booked. My sis reminded American Airlines staff when checking in (at a small airport, so she just walked to that gate.) The flight attendant on the flight said that a wheelchair would be waiting for her as soon as she exited the jetway into the vast DFW airport. Nope. No one there. The American gate agent tried to tell my sister the directions to get to the next gate. My sister insisted, and a wheelchair was called. 



First question: is that usual? If a wheelchair is requested, does it usually show up? Should we have contacted DFW instead of American Airlines?



Second question: the attendant said that she does not receive any pay and only works for tips. Is that usual in US airports? Or was this a sob story (hoping for a larger tip)?



Third question: what is a 'usual' tip? If the transport takes longer due to tram/train rides between gates or concourses, do you tip more?



And final question: do you think the wheelchair will be at her next airport? At least now she knows that it is reasonable to insist on getting help when needed.



Thanks for any replies or ideas you can offer. These are new experiences for us.

thread_title: Q: Wheelchair assistance at DFW, maybe other airports
text:
My first experience of using a wheelchair was at an airport. Even if somebody walks reasonably well, airports are large and it's perfectly reasonable to request a wheelchair.

The request has to be made to the airline, and they should arrange it. In my case I wasn't sure if I qualified for a wheelchair the first time, so had not arranged it. After the long journey to the airport, a helper saw I was walking badly, told me to sit down, and helped my wife check in, and sorted us out. Since then we've always arranged a wheelchair in advance.

We've done so with both Thai Airlines, and Singapore Airlines and never had any problems.

Things can go wrong. We normally contact the airline when or shortly after booking to make the initial arrangement, and again a few days before the flight unless we know the airline well, but as I said, we've never had problems.

Regarding tips, I know the USA has more of a tipping culture. We've tipped for good service at Heathrow and Bangkok, but not in Singapore (tipping there is not encouraged). In the UK we tip about UKP1 (about S1.20) but only for good service, we withheld a tip last time when it took 2 hours from getting out of the taxi to the departure lounge. When we have tipped, the tip has been received with pleasure and often with surprise.

I've no idea what's normal in the USA, hopefully somebody else can answer that.

Reading your post, I think your sister did all the right things, the fault lies with the airline or the airport. Hopefully her future experience will be better. Flying when disabled is tough, but beats staying at home!

Hi and welcome to the disability forum.

I can set your mind at rest. As the carer, the wheelchair attendant will be looking after you as well as your husband.

At security, you will be separated for a few minutes, while you (often with the attendant's help) sort out your carry on luggage. Then you'll go through the scanner.

In my experience they always pat down a person in a wheelchair. Perhaps they don't want somebody falling in the scanning tube, and causing delays.

So you'll need to explain to the attendant about the monitor - they're used to all sorts of problems, so they'll understand. Security will almost certainly query the monitor. The wheelchair attendant may prefer to explain what it is, or may invite you to delay passing through the scanner until you've explained it.

Don't worry. For my wife and me, flying has been easier since I've been disabled, I appreciate the generous care I'm shown. The worst time for me was for a few years when I was struggling with my health, but not bad enough to get assistance.

Enjoy your trip.

text:
My husband and I are travelling for essential reasons soon. He's mobile but he has a suprapubic catheter. We plan to use the large 200ml drainage bag for the 12 hour journey - concealed in a privacy bag - because he really doesn't like the leg bag. Should I request assistance from the airline/airport? A lot of the assistance from airlines seems to be for those in need of wheelchairs and more hands-on assistance and I don't want to use up resources.

thread_title: Suprapubic catheter - should I request assistance?
text:
I'd say you definitely should request special assistance. IMO your DH has a genuine reason. even if you both just get a ride on one of those golf-cart things and some priority going through Check in, Security, Passport Control, getting to/from gate, Baggage Collection and getting to your onward transport, why not?

I would not begrudge you.

thread_title: Suprapubic catheter - should I request assistance?
text:
I agree with EssexWanderer

Walks through airports plus the queues take a lot of time. Therefore many who don't normally need a wheelchair do need one for the airport.

The only time I use a wheelchair is at an airport, but I walk slowly and would struggle to cope with long queues, so I consider it justified, and airlines have never queried it. In fact it was the airport which encouraged me to use a wheelchair when I wasn't sure I needed one. 

Don't feel bad at using resources, they are there for people in your position. If the airport gave all a better experience, then perhaps you wouldn't need help!

Let the airline know you need assistance before the flight, and they'll sort it out for you.

thread_title: Most Sensory-Friendly Places for Solo Traveler w/Autism
text:
Hi everyone! So I don’t have a trip planned at the moment, but I’m curious about your thoughts when it comes to a solo, 19 year old traveler with autism (me) spending time in sensory-friendly destinations in the US. It’s a complicated issue I’m facing currently, but in summary, the noises from loud cars and motorcycles are what trigger me exclusively. I’m always trying to problem-solve with myself to figure out how to get over these specific sensitivities, but until then, it’s a huge challenge I’m facing. While I’m dealing with that, though, my love for travel hasn’t diminished at all. My goal is to travel across all continents someday and really embody the type of person who, say, dives into cultural celebrations or rides public transit in India. THAT kind of traveler, not someone seeking out all-inclusive resorts near theme parks all the time. Hopefully that makes sense.



With that said, I was just curious if anyone had thoughts about good destinations (any kind) to start. I’m not looking for locations where motorcycles are completely banned or all vehicles are off-limits, but somewhere where traffic is less likely to be amplified. And definitely somewhere unlike DisneyWorld, places where I can experience an authentic sense of the local culture/environment. 



Sorry to phrase this so open-endedly, but I’m fine with any thoughts on the matter! And just to remind you, I’m sensitive only to loud cars (like sportscars) and motorcycles that people have made very loud. I love being on airplanes and navigating airports! :)

thread_title: Most Sensory-Friendly Places for Solo Traveler w/Autism
text: Look at Hawaii, Ben. If you stay away from Oahu-esp the Honolulu area, you can find a very nice mix of things.

thread_title: Most Sensory-Friendly Places for Solo Traveler w/Autism
text:
There are two places in the world where we tend to forget our son is on the spectrum: the North Shore of Kauai in the summer (May or September is better if you are able to get away) and Yosemite in September. It is not easy to explain but it has to be experienced. 



The immense, mesmerizing nature in these places especially in the shoulder season when there are fewer tourists provides a spiritual experience where the loud sounds which are fewer in the shoulder season seem to not bother him as much. We spend our days hiking and at the beaches in the North Shore of Kauai...our heaven on earth.

thread_title: Most Sensory-Friendly Places for Solo Traveler w/Autism
text: I'd say travel off the beaten track and try to go to more rural areas and towns, afraid I know nothing about America but in Europe many towns are pedestrianised in their centres so you don't have to cope with too much traffic noise. In England and France definitely visit smaller villages as that way there won't be so many people or traffic but you still get to experience allot of the culture and history and sometimes you learn more about the area than if you were to go to a hectic city! I find google can be helpful as well as it will show where traffic is heavier and when so that can be helpful to know when to avoid. I'd also avoid rush hours and school run times and use that time to find a nice café to grab a cupper as that's when most people will be on the roads and streets. Hope that helps a little x

thread_title: Trip Report---------Wheelchair Problems in Atlanta Airport
text:
We just recently flew to Harrisburg Pennsylvania. Our itinerary was Tucson - Atlanta - Harrisburg, with the same itinerary coming back. On our way there, we had 3.5 hours in Atlanta, and although we had never been to that airport before (nor had we ever flown Delta), we figured we should have no issues getting from one Terminal to the next one, as we had so much time. My husband had back surgery in the early spring, but still has back problems. He cannot walk more than 300 or so feet, without having to sit down to rest for a few minutes. So, it was no problem navigating to our connecting flight, as we would walk, and then, we would reach a gate (lots of seats in waiting area), he would rest a bit, and we would continue walking.



Coming back, we only had 1 hour and 23 minutes to change flights in Atlanta. As we would be getting the last flight (of the day) to Tucson, we wanted to be sure to make that flight. So, I requested a wheelchair for my husband. This all went nicely, and a wheelchair was supposed to meet us at our gate (Gate C55), when we arrived from Harrisburg. We deplaned around 7:30 pm, and Boarding for our next flight (Gate B26) would begin at 8:10. That means we had 40 minutes.



As we were getting off the flight, three wheelchairs with assistants wheeled by on their way to pick up passengers at their seats. When we came into the Terminal, there were some wheelchairs standing to the side, but no assistants. I made my husband sit down, and looked around. A woman (employee) came over, and asked for our boarding passes. Then she took the boarding passes to the Gate, and began scanning them. I suppose they did not scan (why should they, when we were not going to board the flight to Detroit at Gate C55? ). So, she moved over to the next Gate (I think it was C53), which was empty. Since this was the first time we ever requested wheelchair assistance, we had no idea what the procedure was, so we waited. 



Then, someone came over to her, and she had a conversation with them. In the meantime, every passenger had deplaned from our flight, the 3 wheelchairs (with passengers from inside) had gone by us, and we are still waiting. I was afraid to look at my watch, but I did, and now, it was 7:48, and we had not moved an inch. I ran over to her, and asked her what the issue was. She replied that, "These boarding passes do not scan, and I have to scan them". I asked as to why the other wheelchair assistants did not scan any boarding passes at the Gate, and she just shrugged. We were frantic, as nothing was happening, and our next flight would be boarding in 20 minutes. We think that my husband would have made it, if we had started walking immediately. Now, there was no way he would make it.



She came back to us at 7:54, gave me the boarding passes, and left. What were we supposed to do now? Anyway, all of a sudden, an assistant appeared, and I told her what had happened, and that we were frantic not to miss our flight. She scanned the passes on her hand held device, and we were off. The trains were packed, and we had to let four go by, (they come every minute) until we could board. By the time, we arrived at Gate B26, people were boarding. We had missed our group, and we don't like to cut in line, so we sat down and waited until everyone had boarded.



We made our flight, but it was all so stressful. Delta sent us a survey regarding wheelchair assistance, and I wrote them what I am writing here. I have no clue, who that employee was, why she took our boarding passes, and why she was trying to scan them, first at the entrance gate to Detroit, and then, at an empty gate.



If we have to do this again, I will call and clarify exactly as to what the procedure is when one deplanes, and needs a wheelchair. This was an unnecessary stressful experience.

text:
Delta has two ways of booking wheelchair assistance, either they meet you at your seat, or they meet you at the Gate. We requested that they meet us at the Gate (C55). Perhaps, overseas , you call that the door. Here we say, "I exited at the Gate", which is the area where passengers enter or exit the aircraft. A Terminal has many Gates.



When we exited, there were a couple of wheelchairs there at the side. When my husband sat down, that employee came over, and asked for our names. She immediately found it on the short list. So, we were booked, the wheelchair was waiting for us, and we never went wandering around the Terminal. Everything was as it should be, and as ordered. The BIG trouble was this employee, who insisted on scanning our boarding passes at Gates, when our Gate of departure was B26, not even in Terminal C. She wasted all this valuable time, and got nowhere. We could have walked ourselves over from Terminal C to Terminal B. It would have been difficult, but we could have done it, had we known the stress she would cause us.



I've talked to several neighbors, and they find all this scanning very unusual. Never happened to them. However, none of them fly Delta, so maybe the rules are different. I don't know, but next time, I will talk to a Delta person, and find out the exact procedure.

In a few weeks my boyfriend and I are flying to Lanzarote from London Luton Airport. We both take prescription medication and know we need ‘proof’ or this for airport security, but we’re not sure what proof we need.

I don't see why security would be interested in your medication, unless you are carrying significant amounts of liquid or powder. In that case, it would be better to put most of your medicine in hold baggage. Security is only interested in things which might affect aircraft safety, I'm not sure if anything would be enough to satisfy them if you are carrying liquids/powder, you risk having them confiscated, which is why I suggest putting them in hold baggage.

Customs is the main problem, but I think a copy of your prescription should be enough proof, I've never had any problems. You might want to ask on the Lanzarote forum in case there are certain medicines you cannot take into Lanzarote.

You never ever put your prescription medicines in your hold baggage!

Any liquid medicine is allowed to be carried seperately from your standard liquid allowance. But you must have a copy of your prescription with you.

https://www.gov.uk/hand-luggage-restrictions/essential-medicines-and-medical-equipment

 You can have your medication in an extra bag.

thread_title: European river cruises w/best views elderly limited mobility
text:
We had several people with disabilities on our river cruise (APT for Australians, AMA waterways for Americans). There were a few occasions when we were moored next to another boat meaning that the view from the cabin could be obscured, but this was not for a long period. There was always a view forward from the lounge or front deck.

Several times we left the ship over the top deck of a ship next door, and several times we walked through their foyer. Other times we disembarked directly along a ramp between the ship and shore. It was never particularly steep as the rivers are not generally tidal and the canals maintain the same height at all times.

The ships had an elevator for reaching the accommodation decks and restaurant, but because of height restrictions this could not go to the upper deck.

Excursions happened every day, sometimes twice a day, as well as various happenings on the ship itself.

They were graded by activity level but most involved some walking. The opera visit in Budapest, the concert in Vienna and the dinner at Castle Namedy were very easy.

Food was excellent and plentiful. The cabin easily accessible.

A wonderful but expensive holiday.

thread_title: London Heathrow airport - Disability Assistance Problems
text:
We travelled last month from Tel Aviv via London to Chicago and return. Owing to some health issues I cannot stand for too long nor can I run, but I can walk short distances. I consulted with my doctor and decided to ask for disability assistance. I did that while booking our flights with British Airways for all three airports. I made sure to call BA Customers Service BA a few days before our departure to confirm, again, the wheelchair assistance at all the three airports I will be going through.



At the Tel Aviv airport, while checking in, the BA agent told me she was not sure when the wheelchair assistant will arrive but soon enough the assistant arrived and all went well. When we arrived in London the plane did not park near a slot so busses had to transfer us to the terminal. There was no wheelchair in sight when we left the bus so I had to take quite a long walk until we found the Assistance office, which acknowledged that I had a reservation for a wheelchair but they had no wheelchair for me. A guy with a buggy offered to transfer us to our departure gate to Chicago and I was so very glad he took me as I most certainly could not walk the distance. In Chicago the assistance was just great, the chair was near the exit of the plane and took me to my destination. 



I complained to BA customers service who told me it is not their fault and I should contact Heathrow Customer Service, which I did on November 15. They promised to investigate. 



On our return flight, Chicago's airport assistance was once again perfect. But, we landed in Heathrow there was no wheelchair at the gate. In the terminal, there were no chairs either but one of the airport personnel said they could not provide me with any assistance and I should wait. We actually had a bit of a rush to catch our flight back to Tel Aviv, so I decided to walk because I was reassured that the gate to our next flight is just a short distance away. I made it safely to Tel Aviv, where there was no wheelchair waiting for me either, but I found someone in the terminal who helped me find assistance and got safely home.



I wrote to Heathrow Customers Service again mentioning my previous complaint. I got their reply about two weeks ago: We apologise for the extended nature of this process and would like to assure you that we are intent on providing a response as quickly as possible". 



I want just to add that I asked the BA stewardesses about my wheelchair and they promised me that a wheelchair will be waiting for me in London, that they made sure of it. Unfortunately, that did not help me to to get the promised assistance at the Heathrow airport. 



I am writing the above just to share my experience so people can decide how to go about booking disability assistance at the various airports.

All in all, it is doable and I encourage you to call AMA and ask.

Most hotels, when accepting reservations, take “requests” for such things as views, room types etc, and for most people this is satisfactory. thread_title: Requesting extra baggage on British Airways flights
text:
Hi,



Next year I'm going on holiday with my father and we are flying with BA out of the UK and then back.



I'm severely disabled and due to my disability, I need to be fed and given drinks by someone. Therefore, I carry a lot of what I'd call "drinking towels" or small hand towels, as they need to be held under my chin while eating & drinking as I spill a lot out. Also I take more clothes, because they get messed up daily.



Usually I email the airline I'm flying with, explain to them my disability and the amount of drinking towels and clothes I take and ask for extra baggage allowance. They all give me this with no problem.



Yesterday, I emailed British Airways and asked the same question. They replied saying,



We can approve extra baggage for prescribed items and equipment, unfortunately we are unable to approve clothing or towels to be checked in without charge.



I can understand it isn't prescribed medication or medical equipment as such, but I consider my drinking towels as medical equipment, because I cannot do without them at all.



My dad phoned them today, but they won't budge.



Can anyone advise me on how I get around this please, as this is a first for me?

thread_title: Requesting extra baggage on British Airways flights
text:
Use compression bags, it's amazing how much you can get into them. Just watch your bag isn't over 23 kg. Also remember BA give you a very generous cabin bag allowance.



I use Eagle Creek packing cubes. I roll all our clothes and put them in the cubes. I can get clothes for a 2 week holiday in just a cabin bag. These compression bags should help.



Google Eagle Creek packing cubes. Good luck.

Hi everyone,



I have RA and am on humira syringes fortnightly for this. We are travelling from Australia to Europe in July/August for 5 weeks and I will need to take two syringes with me. The first dose will be at the end of week one, the second dose at the end of week three. Then I will have another dose the day we get home. The latest information about humira is that it can be kept out of the fridge for 14 days so I at least need to keep the second dose cool for the first week.



I have a travel wallet that was provided to me when I first started humira but it only keeps the product cool for up to 9 hours. The wallet needs to be placed in a freezer for some time prior to use to ensure it is at the right temperature and maintains that for the 9 hours.



I have several issues.



1) Our flight from Adelaide - Dubai - Warsaw is obviously longer than 9 hours. Flight time inc. stopover is about 22 hours. Plus the time from home - airport and then airport - hotel. It is also possible that we will be going from Warsaw to Poznan or Wroclaw which is another 2.5-3 hour train ride. So basically, I need a way to keep it cool for at least 30 hours to be safe. I am waiting to hear from the airline (Emirates) if I can store it in the fridge on the plane but I doubt it. And there's the still the issue of the 3 hour stopover in Dubai.



2) We are staying with family for the first 5-6 days of our trip, so I can keep it safely and securely in one single fridge for that duration. Then I would likely do my first injection before leaving there. Worse case scenario, I can then take my second dose out of the fridge and just keep at room temperature for another 2 weeks before doing that dose. It'd be 1-2 days early but that's okay.



Alternatively though, if I was to try and keep it cool in hotel fridges, that would be fine. We generally always ensure our accomodation has some sort of fridge. But the freezer sections in these bar sized fridges would not be large enough to fit my travel wallet and adequately chill it prior to our next move.



Obviously, the flight is the largest concern at the moment. I would love to know what other people have done to keep their medicines cool while travelling long distances. I contacted the company and they were next to useless, simply recommending their own product - the travel wallet - which as discussed, does not meet my needs! My pharmacist is doing some investigating for me as well.



Thank you!

Alanna

I can walk short distances and manage some stairs and did find I had to get out a few times.

I'm a wheelchair user and I went to Rome alone for three nights three years ago. With respect, PLEASE don't listen to the person who dismissed Rome as "not wheelchair accessible". This is just plain wrong. The only attraction you'll have a major problem with is the Roman Forum (uneven ground, difficult path down to it). Everywhere else WAS FINE!! Hell, they even have a lift in the Colosseum!! The Sistine Chapel has an accessible entrance. You name it, you can go there as long as you've done your research. 



The downs? It's hilly... Not the end of the world - take taxis. I found taxi drivers in Rome to be some of the most helpful and accommodating I've ever come across anywhere in the world. Cobbles - consider investing in a Freewheel attachment. They're expensive, but they give you so much more freedom and open many more doors for you. They eat cobbles for breakfast. I've taken mine all over the world with me. And that's about it really for major downs. GO!! Please go! Rome is somewhere EVERYONE should experience!

thread_title: Obese passenger with disabilities - how will I fare?
text:
For your flying question maybe worth asking also on the TA Air Travel forum. Say which airline you are flying with.

If you do need special assistance, with any airline, then you need to book that well in advance, don't turn up at the airport then ask for it, that will be too late.

Have you flown ever before, or is this a first time?

Also, where are you flying from?

If you add your home location to your profile so that it shows inder your avatar & screen name (like Essex shows under mine) that can be very helpful to those who would reply and try to help you.

text:
Sorry, only seeing this now. 



Is your grandson verbal or non-verbal? Do you need to use PECS or another form of symbolic communication with him? 



Acclimatisation is good. But also draw up a schedule for him. Get a calendar and mark in the number of days left to the trip. Allow your grandson to have a level of control and input over what he will be bringing.



And in the days leading up to the holiday, choose the battles wisely. Allow a lot of leeway in terms of behaviour. Also if he is big into computer games, allow him choose a few for the airport and the plane. And get some ear defenders if it is noisy.



Our son also finds dark sunglasses very helpful. (He has Aspergers). They block the glare from the lights and stop him having to work at making eye contact. A hat helps as well.

thread_title: In Spain, if Able to Pre-Board by Walking, NO Wheelchair!!!
text: I didn't where I should post this however, had I known about this beforehand, it would've saved lots of headaches and time. Yes, ADA compliance has its faults in the States, but Spain makes the U.S. look like a well-oiled machine! We were flying from Madrid to Barcelona (to most able-bodied people, a relatively short flight). The whole process of deplaning in Barcelona to get to the curb took about as long as the flight! First, to get off the plane I had to exit through a door opposite the jetway (normally I see plane-catering trucks use this door). I was placed in a wheelchair, was strapped in. Then the truck was hydraulically lowered. Then the truck drove to the terminal. When we got there, we all had to go out to the back, this platform was again hydraulically lowered to the ground so they could wheel me off. Inside, I had to get out of that wheelchair and sit in some seats to wait for an electric car. Finally it arrived. The electric car drove us to baggage claim where I had to get out, go through some sliding glass doors and was ushered into yet ANOTHER wheelchair! Finally, I made it to the curb. I suppose they are providing jobs, but my husband remarked, "Never have so many people done so little for so few!" So armed with this new-found knowledge, on our flight from Barcelona to JFK New York, I used a wheelchair through security, an electric car took me to the gate, and I pre-boarded slowly walking with my cane. The gate attendants asked if I needed a wheelchair which was met with a resounding NO THANK YOU! from me and my husband.

thread_title: In Spain, if Able to Pre-Board by Walking, NO Wheelchair!!!
text: I forgot to add for benefit of those who don't know how it's done in the States, a wheelchair met me at the jetway. It was this same wheelchair that took me through customs, baggage claim and out to the curb!

What is best way to know which unit to rent/buy and how to have oxygen on a long distance (abroad) flight? 



Is there any way to fly with oxygen for long distance? I only need it for sleep but on 13 hours flight, I hope to sleep!

Check with the airline you will be flying with. Below is the link from Delta, I guess all airlines will have similar rules.



http://www.delta.com/content/www/en_US/traveling-with-us/special-travel-needs/disabilities.html
As already stated.. Check with the airline you are booking / flying with.

A lot of airlines will supply free oxygen on long haul. Check with them. Be aware though that often it is for only one person per flight. You will need to supply a fit to fly form detailing settings. See you GP and get tested. You should also be aware that even though you normally only need it for sleeping you may well need it for the whole flight due to cabin pressure which is normally about 8,000ft but will sometimes go to 10,000ft. At those altitudes your oxygen needs change.
Do portable-oxygen-concentrators work for this kind of flight? Or does life/weight of the batteries become too big an issue?

You would need a lot of batteries on a long haul (mine cost £300 each) although this would depend on how you use it and at what setting. Check with the airline if it is possible to charge them. Your best bet is to fly with a company that supplies free oxygen. Lots of airlines will supply free oxygen and others will charge. You will need a fitness to fly certificate (see your GP) and a copy of your prescription. If you have an FAA approved concentrator it will be suitable.

My husband had this problem last year. There was a lot of red tape but we did get to Tenerife with sufficient oxygen for the week. Jet 2 were helpful for the flights, but the airports were obstructive, despite a "fitness to fly" certificate. thread_title: Traveling on foreign airlines with medical devices
text:
A couple of weeks ago, I was flying from SDF to DTW and on to LHR on Delta. I travel with a percussion vest in its rolling case, a portable nebulizer, a small carry-on with all my meds in it, and my handbag. The ADA allows this. The only problems I have encountered have been with the overhead compartments on the small planes out of SDF not being big enough to accommodate my percussion vest in its case. In the past, I have asked the Gate Agent for pre-boarding so I could remove the device from its case and place it in the overhead compartment, and then gate check the carrying case.



With gate check for luggage becoming something that is possible only if one is willing to have it check through to ones final destination, this is now a major problem for me. Many of these small planes do have a very small closet but it is reserved for First Class passenger's coats. 



So this time I used my FF miles and booked First Class to DTW and DeltaOne to LHR. I got on the plane and it had no closet! I was lucky that the Flight Attendant look pity on this old lady and hoisted that 20+lb device, case and all, and managed to stuff it into the overhead. 



Forty-five minutes before departure from DTW, I received a text that my flight to London had been cancelled due to mechanical problems. I was now to fly to Amsterdam and then on BA on to London. Not happy - arriving 5 hours later than expected with wheelchair ordered for airport delivery and a car ordered as well - also many other arrangements for that day had to be re-scheduled. And of course, it was the middle of the night in London. My son was already there so I texted him and forwarded relevant emails so he could reschedule things for me when I arrived the next afternoon. 



There were 6 of us on the flight from DTW who were going on to London. There was a 2 hr layover in Amsterdam. The first thing that happened was the gate agent informed us that she would not allow us to board the flight as 2 hrs was not enough time for our luggage to accompany us, and that they do not allow passengers and luggage on different flights. I was unaware of this and she was not able to tell any of us when we might get on a later flight. She later came back and said that since we all were Sky Priority customers, our luggage HAD been transferred so we could go on the flight. 



When I went to board, she told me that I had too many carry-on items - I had to choose between my medical device and my carry-on. My meds would not fit in my handbag so this was not a good choice at all, and the medical device could not be checked re instructions from the manufacturer. I showed her the letter from my doctor and I was holding up the boarding for everyone, and she finally agreed to allow this.



I later found out that in order for any medical device to go on a foreign airline, one must have a notarized letter from ones insurance company that it is medically necessary. I don't want to even think how long it would take to get such from Medicare! Of course, I had no idea at the beginning of my trip that I would be going on a foreign airline.



Does anyone have experience with this? No wonder old people just stay home - WAY too much red tape for us to fly anywhere these days!

thread_title: Travelling with own small luggie mobility scooter
text:
Hi we travelled with KLM to Alaska from Spain using. Travelite folding scooter which is similar. They lost it for 36 hours on outward journey. The return journey was with a 7.5 hour layover in Schipol and the treatment there of both my disabled husband & myself was appalling, total mistreatment of disabled/ill people. They told us that as we had more than a 3 hour layover he could use his scooter airline door to door and have it loaded from there to the hold for the second leg flight. We had booked assistance months before. On disembarking the flight at Schipol the scooter had been dumped on the walkway the steering column on the floor and the ignition key on the floor 3ft away from the scooter, so we had to get assistance to get us to the scooter, the assistance then just abandoned us with vague directions to make our way thru this enormous airport on our own so we ended up at the wrong gate. After serious abuse from a security staff member on the X-ray check we found out we were at the wrong gate and if the security staff should have checked our boarding cards and passports initially and redirected us to the correct 1. We were again left to our own devices and when enquiring at the information desk that our departure gate had been changed (if assistance had done its job and accompanied us they would have known this) also that THE BAGGAGE HANDLERS HAD REFUSED TO HANDLE THE SCOOTER TO THE HOLD. This meant we had to leave secure arrivals and re book onto the flight thru check in to book the scooter in as secure hold luggage. They did not tell us that we could not book in till an hour before the flight so, as we had gone to do so immediately, we were expected to hang about the check in hall airport entrance for 4hours. I was suffering angina heart pains and asthma attacks with the stress and when we went on numerous occasions to the KLM info desk they just did nothing when we insisted after about an hour as I was so ill we were treated abusively and very rudely by the check in staff on the special hold luggage desk and even the assistance supervisor had problems getting us booked in so we could find somewhere comfortable to sit. I collapsed twice and we were continually informing them that I was ill but they never offered advice as to where to go to for help or to summon medical assistance for me luckily I had plenty of melds handy and managed to control it myself. When we booked the scooter in we asked for a self propelled wheelchair as I was not well enough to push the big heavy sit up and beg push wheelchairs they were giving us, they said they had non. When I asked how my husband was supposed to take himself to the toilet or for a drink or food they said you will have to take him with all the hand luggage etc (even in the midst of my angina and asthma probs that they had caused) he is a leg amputee so not a dependent disabled so how humiliating for him they just did not care. When they DUMPED us in a freezing cold dirty running with mice assistance waiting area eventually there was LOCKED UP WITH CHAINS self propelled wheelchairs and when we asked for 1 they said the did not have a key as they were for the use of the assistants doing airline door assistance!! 

PLEASE TAKE NOTE OF THIS AND STAND YOUR GROUND BETTER THAN WE DID AND INSIST ON PROPER SERVICE

thread_title: Travelling with own small luggie mobility scooter
text:
I am so sorry that this happened to you Maureen. Seasoned travelers would tell you that you could have avoided some of your difficulties by being more proactive. Schipol is huge, and depending upon someone for vague directions is dangerous. It would have been wiser if you had checked the board for departing flights so you did not waste energy going to the wrong gate. It would also have helped your position somewhat if you had taken something in writing indicating that KLM and Schipol would permit your scooter to be gate checked. I find it interesting the baggage handlers were able to remove the scooter, but not able to load it again.



I have no difficulty believing your evaluation of the way you were treated at Schipol, as we have had similar experiences both with this airport and with KLM regarding their treatment of our special needs. I think you generally summarized our evaluation when you wrote that at "Schipol the treatment there of both my disabled husband & myself was appalling, total mistreatment of disabled/ill people."



It is my opinion that the staff of KLM and the staff of Schipol believe disabled people should be shot on sight rather than accommodated. Like you, we have never been treated so rudely as we were on our first trip through this airport, nor have we ever received worse treatment in terms of assistance for our disabilities.



I learned some critical facts. Regardless of what you are told about having access to your mobility scooter, this can all change based on the airport and whoever is in charge of your airline at that airport. We check our scooters ad pick them up at our destination.



If you need wheelchair assistance to connecting flights, or to get your luggage, you must request this through each airline that you use. After our terrible experience in Schipol I called KLM almost weekly to insure that we would be allowed to ride on the electric carts they use to transport people with disabilities. If your name is not "on the list" no one in that airport will help you. I am positive that they would force a person with no legs to crawl to his connecting flight if his name was not "on the list".



You cannot expect any sympathy from anyone at this airport. They each have a specific job to do, and that is all they are going to do. No one will do anything except that job. If you have a heart attack I assume someone would eventually call some emergency response team, but I do not know.



I am not always able to prevent it, been when I can I do not fly KLM and I do not transit through Schipol. I agree that there is a general attitude that is not remotely helpful to those of us with disabilities. Hopefully the rest of your trip was pleasant.

thread_title: Travelling with own small luggie mobility scooter
text:
A resident of Amsterdam told me that the citizens of The Netherlands are a very precise people. They have clearly defined procedures for everything, and they never violate those procedures. They do not exercise independent thought. They will not participate in problem-solving. They will never acknowledge that there is a possibility that your name is not on "the list" because of their error, even when you can provide written documentation that requests for special assistance were made correctly. The most dreadful thing is that they simply do not care. My husband was forced to walk nearly a mile. He was ill in addition to his regular disability issue. No amount of logical argument, no amount of begging not even the promise of a financial award would persuade anyone to assist this poor elderly gentleman who was not allowed to ride to his connecting flight because his name was not "on the list". 



I do not like to stereotype people, and I have several friends who are Dutch and share no similarities with the people at Sciphol. After the first catastrophe I avoid this airport when possible. If I have to connect I make written and verbal requests for special assistance many times. 



When their system works it is impressively efficient. Although they provide no assistance down the jetway, they are generally waiting at the arrival gate & they move you quickly to your connecting flight. If you are not "on the list" no one will do anything for you. I suspect that they have no word for compassion as the concept seems totally foreign to them. In fact every person who refused to help us seemed to take great pleasure in those refusals. The experience caused me to believe that many of these people are just sadistic individuals who derive pleasure out of watching others suffer. 



This is unfortunate because at one time we had planned to spend a week in this country. Now I work very hard to avoid even changing planes there.

thread_title: Travelling with own small luggie mobility scooter
text: Re travel with mobility scooter: My wife and I have traveled by air and ship for many years with our mobility scooters without any problems except occasionally with securing ground transport for the scooters in some countries. I have found that when making arrangements to fly one must contact the airline well ahead of time to advise them of your scooter type and size. When traveling by ship one must secure a "Access" cabin to park the scooter overnight since scooters are not allowed to be parked in ships passageways due to the resultant blockage of said passageway for other travelers and crew attendants. I have usually been successful with securing ground transport transfers for the scooters through the Cruiseline's Special Services department when making reservations. To date, I have not been charged any additional fees by the airlines or the cruiselines for travel with the scooters, however there is always an extra cost for ground transport that is capable of transporting the scooter(s).

Last year we organised a trip around NZ for a friend who is confined to a wheelchair so I thought I'd pass on some suggestions / tips.



She travelled with a companion for assistance and they flew Air New Zealand via LA and were very well looked after by the cabin crew on all legs, and by the Air NZ ground staff at Heathrow, LA Auckland & Christchurch.



We were able to arrange for a Disabled Parking Badge through CCS here in NZ at their Christchurch office.



A bike rack that clipped onto the tow bar worked perfectly for strapping the chair to and a roof box meant that we had room for the luggage for the 4 of us.



We managed to book a CCS house in Orewa on the North Shore for using as an Auckland Base that worked brilliantly. The house could sleep 6 and was fully accessible with wet room, laundry & a second bathroom available (in the garage!). You needed your own bedding however & we were lucky with friends in Auckland we could borrow some from so didn't need to carry that too in the car.



Travelling around NZ we had little to no difficulty finding accessible accommodation with wet rooms available at a high percentage of the motels in all the destinations we went to.



We booked on a 3.30pm cruise in Milford Sound with Southern Discoveries. They asked us if we wouldn't mind swapping to the 12.00 cruise as that boat was easier to access (they honoured the cheaper price for the 3.30 trip though). With the Disabled Parking Permit we were able to park right outside the cruise boat terminal (where the coaches park - the public car park is over 500m away).



Biggest surprise of the trip was that in the Waikatio the Ruakuri Cave is completely wheelchair accessible. We had a fantastic guide who ensured that we went ahead of everyone else so she didn't have her view blocked by the person in front of us. At one point there is a lot of water dripping in the middle of the path - most people could walk around it but the wheelchair couldn't - without any hesitation he simply took off his jacket to protect her from the drips.



Also in the Coromandel Peninsula the Driving Creek Railway has an accessible carriage.



Our driving tour covered Christchurch, Arthur's Pass, the Tunnel Terrace walk, Hokitika, & Hokitika Gorge, Greymouth, Reefton, the Seal Colony at Tauranga Bay, the Pancake Rocks at Punakaiki, back to Christchurch, Akaroa, then down to Tekapo, Cromwell, Queenstown, Te Anau, Milford Sound, Dunedin, Timaru, and back to Christchurch. This was followed by Kaikoura, Picton, InterIslander Ferry (accessible), Wellington, Waiouru, Te Kuiti, Waitomo, Rotorua, Coromandel, Auckland & Warkworth. 



Happy to answer any questions for those locations with further hints & ideas.

thread_title: Mini Break Next Year, When to buy Travel Insurance?
text:
Whenever you take out insurance you will need to tell them about asthma or any other pre existing conditions



You should always get travel insurance as soon as possible after booking a holiday. Otherwise if an insurable event happens now which prevented you from travelling you would not be able to claim. 



If you developed, say, a new medical condition between now and taking out travel insurance that would further load your premium, but once you have travel insurance based on answering questions correctly they won't keep loading your premium and making you pay more if you have an asthma attack, break your leg or anything else covered by your policy. 



.

thread_title: Mini Break Next Year, When to buy Travel Insurance?
text:
I have just made a claim on my travel insurance as I had to cancel due to my accompanying passenger not being able to travel due to an injury. One of the questions was "on what date did you buy this policy". I had bought it the day I had booked the cruise. I have also heard stories where a person is not covered even when they have insurance if they have to cancel due to a preexisting condition of their travelling partner. When getting insurance you should declare every illness etc you have been to doctors or hospital for the past 5 years. Buy your insurance Asap. I used justtravel who offer cruise insurance for preexisting conditions. My annual policy was very good value.



On the cruise ensure you book a trip as this will guarantee you get off the ship as you should have priority getting on the tender into port. Hope u have a great time. Another thing to note is that Guernsey is one of the most missed ports due to bad weather. I finally got there this year on my third attempt

The ADA was passed in 1990. No buildings constructed prior to 1990 were "grandfathered" under the act. Existing buildings were required to begin eliminating barriers by January of 1992. 



The ADA is not a building code law. It is an anti-discrimination law. It is therefore controlled and enforced through different mechanisms than building code laws. 



Buildings that are open to the general public must provide equal accessibility to every person who wishes to enter the building. If the owner of a building elects not to make these changes he can be sued for large sums of money. Very few property owners are willing to gamble by ignoring the requirements of this law. 



If you do business with private on demand service providers such as Uber or AirBnB the law is less clear. These automobiles and homes are private. In the tourist city near me, Orlando, owners of private homes who rent out part or all of their home do not have to comply with some of the ADA provisions. If they don't the owners will generally make it clear that their home is not ADA compliant. 



Since the city of New York has declared that AirBnB cannot operate in New York, partially for just these types of issues in addition to safety and inspection issues I do not believe the OP will find NYC remotely as challenging as the major European cities. Just make reservations early and request a room for your disability. Hotels have to have a certain percentage of rooms that are accessible. 



While no law works perfectly the ADA has been successful in providing people with disabilities an equal opportunity to have the same experiences as those without disabilities. I believe that equal opportunity is represented better in the US than any other country where I have visited. 



Old buildings or new construction - all public buildings must comply.

By "grandfathered in" I guess I was referring to the part of the ADA law that reads as follows - "Under the ADA, existing business facilities that serve the public must remove physical barriers where that is readily achievable (easily accomplishable without much difficulty or expense). The "readily achievable" requirement is based on the size and resources of the business. Barrier removal is an ongoing obligation. The ADA Standards for Accessible Design (ADAAG) guide businesses. " So because many of the older buildings in NYC cannot accomplish totally removing physical barriers without difficulty (there are no elevators, for example) then they do not have to do so. Here's the link to the website for all the answers - http://www.access-board.gov/

It is true that if it is determined that an old building cannot be renovated to be ADA compliant, the ADA may not require extra ordinary efforts. 



The ADA is enforced when disabled people sue a business that doesn't provide equal access. The law requires the property owner to pay all legal expenses for the plantiff. There are huge law firms that specialize in this type of law suit because it is a win/win for them. Win or lose the suit the attorney is still paid. 



The fact that these law suits are frequent and can be initiated without formal notification to the property owner makes the owner of a non-compliant property exceptionally vulnerable. Many hotels that could not achieve compliance are simply closed, sold or converted to private clubs or religious organizations which have lower thresholds for ADA compliance. 



While some hotels are not ADA compliant, the vast majority of hotels are compliant. Visitors to NYC are also protected by local law in the form of the Human Rights law, which also prohibits structural discrimination. 



Of all the major cities in the world I expect that there are more accessible properties in NYC than any other city. Certainly those of us with disabilities should inquire directly with the hotel to guarantee compliance, but there are few hotels that do not have access, so locating one should not be a serious problem.

IME, US travel insurance usually covers preexisting conditions if purchased within a certain amount of time after the first trip payment (usually 14 or 15 days but I did find one that was longer). I have purchased travel insurance through TravelGuard, both the Gold and the My Travelguard policies (that one because I hadn't bought it in time for the waiver) but have never had to (fortunately) submit a claim. You would need to read the policy to see if you met that criteria. Generally there is a clause saying that preexisting conditions are not covered and then another one saying the first one is waived if you purchase within the correct amount of time and insure the full cost of the trip.



Usually there is a dollar amount for medical coverage and a dollar amount for medical evacuation. I have always been able to purchase a rider for a small fee that increases the dollar amount for evac (doubles it, IIRC) and also allows you to be evacuated to the hospital of your choice rather than the one TravelGuard picks. It's mainly for that reason I pay it as I would want to end up in a hospital near my home, not whichever one TG thought was cheapest to get me to. The $50000 sounds like the medical expenses amount. My last Gold policy from TravelGuard (bought Feb 2016) included $25,000 in medical expenses and $500,000 in evacuation. That was with the rider.



When I went to Poland, I asked on the forum for Poland if $25,000 would be enough, and it seemed that it would be as medical expenses in the EU are much lower than in the US. It's a little hard to get information on that as EU residents don't pay so don't always know how much things cost but from people who had paid for private care, it seemed like most hospitalizations would be less than that. So I think $50,000 (each, I'm assuming) would likely be sufficient for that but I'm not sure it would be enough for medevac.

Here's a link to that thread:

http://www.tripadvisor.com/ShowTopic-g274723-i959-k7446010-Medical_Costs-Poland.html



I've also seen some threads from France where people required medical care. I think someone posted their experience of being hospitalized after breaking an arm or a leg and included costs. You could search on the forum. I'm not sure if it was the Paris or France forum where I saw it. Obviously, Poland and France are not Italy, but I'd expect prices to be in a similar range.



My only other suggestion is to talk to your mother's doctor (perhaps go to an appt with her) to see if s/he recommends taking any medications in case they are needed - i.e. if she is likely to need stronger pain medication than usual if she falls (even if nothing's broken), she may want a prescription here to take if her dr is willing to do that. Also make sure she knows the generic name of all of her medications, including over the counter medications as the brand names are different in other countries. I believe acetaminophen is called paracetamol in all of Europe. I'm not sure if they would recognize acetaminophen. That's the only generic name I've heard of that's different. We found the pharmacist in France to be very helpful when we needed more dressings for a burn my daughter had (she left the ones I bought her in the car at our home airport...) and also the one in Rome when I needed cold medicine. She did not speak fluent English and I did not speak Italian, but she spoke enough to figure out that I needed cough drops, and they worked quite well. We took the box for the dressings from home into the pharmacy in France and he found us something essentially the same. Pharmacists are utilized a lot more in Europe, and many of the OTC meds are actually behind the pharmacy counter (although in the UK they're sold more like they are here).

is it necessary to state that you are a wheelchair user when booking travel insurance?

It will depend on a number of factors..... The nature of your mobility impairment, what caused that impairment, how long you have been reliant on a wheelchair, etc.



Many UK travel insurers have a health screening system, which assesses the applicant in terms of " risk" and calculates the premium accordingly.



If you would like to provide some more details, then myself and other members may be able to assist you further.



I would just mention that a lot of UK travel policies exclude cover for wheelchairs in the " baggage and personal effects" section of the policy. It is therefore a good idea to have your wheelchair covered ( " specified" on ) your household contents insurance policy.



This is especially important, because if it gets damaged in transit by an airline, their liability is very limited indeed, and as wheelchairs are expensive items, any payout from the airline will almost certainly not be enough to replace yours.



Mon

thread_title: Possible new law about faking service animals in Colorado
text:
Interesting article in today's Denver Post. Colorado has a pending law moving from the House to the Senate. It would criminalize misrepresenting your pet as a service animal. The law would have a penalty phase similar to parking in a handicapped parking space:



a $33 surcharge plus a fine of:



• $350 to $1,000 for a first offense;



• $600 to $1,000 for a second offense;



• $1,000 to $5,000 and up to 10 hours of community service for a third or subsequent offense.



Here's the link for the article for more info - denverpost.com/news/…



This of course would impact Denver International Airport, the 5th busiest airport in the USA in addition to rental vehicles, hotels, etc. Hopefully those folks who abuse the system and make it more difficult for those who need service animals will get the message.

thread_title: Possible new law about faking service animals in Colorado
text:
I do not understand how this law will reduce abuse of the use of fake service animals. State law cannot take priority over federal law. The ADA only requires the owner of an animal to state his disability and explain how the animal is trained to assist the disabled person. This loophole allows a person to claim anxiety disorder as a disability and state that the animal is trained to cuddle and provide comfort thus reducing anxiety. I saw a very elderly lady make this exact claim when boarding a plane with a tiny, poorly-groomed dog that appeared even more frail than the old lady. Who is anyone to deny this claim?



So long as people can provide justification for an animal they identify as a service animal there is no way a Colorado law can circumvent federal law. 



Of course, Colorado has a recent history of violating federal law with state legislation. Perhaps the lawmakers reason that if they can legalize marijuana while it remains an illegal drug at the federal level they can also criminalize a service animal that is not criminalized at the federal level.

thread_title: Possible new law about faking service animals in Colorado
text:
What you described is not a service dog, it is a companion dog or a therapy dog. ADA law does not cover the latter, only the former. This information is from the US Dept. of Justice - "When it is not obvious what service an animal provides, only limited inquiries are allowed. Staff may ask two questions: (1) is the dog a service animal required because of a disability, and (2) what work or task has the dog been trained to perform. Staff cannot ask about the person’s disability, require medical documentation, require a special identification card or training documentation for the dog, or ask that the dog demonstrate its ability to perform the work or task." So they may not ask what disability the person has but the dog has to be trained to perform a service. 



Also - "Under the ADA, you have a disability if you have at least one of the following: a physical or mental impairment that "substantially limits" one or more "major life activities"; a record of such an impairment; or. you are regarded as having such an impairment." 



"Major Life Activities. These consist of functions such as caring for yourself, (including bathing, dressing, shaving, preparing a meal, and going to the restroom), performing manual tasks, eating, sleeping, standing, walking, lifting, reaching, bending seeing, hearing, speaking, breathing, learning, reading, concentrating, thinking, communicating, interacting with others, and working.



As a result of the ADAAA, major life activities now also include the operation of any major bodily function, including but not limited to, functions of the immune system, normal cell growth, digestive, bowel, bladder, neurological, brain, respiratory, circulatory, endocrine, and reproductive (procreation) functions. 



Major life activities do not include the following: caring for others, driving, ability to have a relationship, and grocery shopping." http://www.illinoislegalaid.org/index.cfm?fuseaction=home.dsp_content&contentid=167



Airlines are able to turn away pets in the situation you spoke of. If someone claims they need a therapy dog then they would need to have a letter from a medical provider showing they are receiving mental health care at the time of travel and therefore, need to have the dog with them. Here's Southwest Airlines info on therapy dogs - it's quite lengthy so I'll just post the link. https://www.southwest.com/html/customer-service/unique-travel-needs/customers-with-disabilities-pol.html#unique_travel_needs_allergies_disabilities_pol_tab_list_tab_10



So, yes. Just as folks who are not disabled and use disabled parking are fined, CO says enough is enough. If you aren't disabled stop faking and pay the fees for bringing your animals along. If you are disabled, then you and your service dog are welcome.

Any suggestions how a quad individual can transport from Nevada to Colorado without prohibitive costs? Cannot fly and cannot sit in motorized wheelchair longer than 4 hours? Any suggestions would be helpful. Thank you.

Transportation in this area is limited to planes and buses available to the general public and private auto transportation. I assume that one could also obtain the services of an ambulance that could convey your to Colorado, but I am sure this would be exceptionally expensive. I do not believe there is any train service between these two states.



You cannot fly and you need to spend no longer than 4 hours in a sitting position. This eliminates the two public forms of transportation. Presumably you might be able to use a public bus and arrange your trip in four hour increments, but I think the waiting times between these rest periods would be lengthy and undesirable.



This leaves you with only the option of private transportation. You could rent an SUV or a van. In some locations you can rent specialized adaptive vehicles that will accommodate your chair and you without serious manipulation. You would obviously need a driver. Hopefully you are traveling with a friend or family member who can provide this service for you. If you are using a private vehicle you can plan rest stops so you will not be sitting longer than four hours. This may not be very comfortable, but I think it is probably your only choice.

There is a man in my neighborhood that has done this with his wheelchair. He enjoys taking his dog for a walk. He sits on a bench and ties the dog to his wheelchair and spends the afternoon delighting children, exchanging ideas with teens and enjoying the appreciation of adults. It operates very well. It isn't a heavy vehicle built for hiking trails, but it isn't a little portable unit either. I do not think the weight is a big issue in the technology.

There are a couple of forums where geeks discuss this regularly and I'm sure there are also You Tube presentations available. You might also look at this web site: http://cwhatidid.com/view/?t=Twenty%20Buck%20Power%20Wheel%20Chair%20Wireless%20Remote%20Control&itemParent=304



Just be sure that the instructions you are reading do not change the function of the wheelchair in to some other device. 



In the school where I used to work we had a robotics department. If I wanted a remote control power chair I would go to a school with a robotics department and see what they could do. I was always not only satisfied but completely amazed by what these young people can do. If they take on this project you would probably only need to pay for the parts. I would look at technical colleges or even a technology high school.

thread_title: Flying with an orthopedic boot - my experience
text:
I recently flew round trip on United from a medium-sized city to a small city – with a plane change in Houston - while wearing an orthopedic boot. I was able to walk short distances wearing the boot, remove the boot and walk short distances when going through security, and get from the gate to my airplane seat without assistance. 

Following the instructions on the United website, I requested a wheelchair when I booked my flight, and when I got to the airport I requested a wheelchair to take me to my gate. I also got a “special services” card which I later showed to the various wheelchair attendants and gate agents. The wheelchair attendant took me through the ‘express lane’ for security. This is quite a benefit if the line is long and you are unable to stand. The attendant also was willing to stop for food, water or the restroom. As I waited at the gate, there was an attendant waiting with another passenger. I don’t think the attendants are allowed to assist you in the restroom and I don’t know if they are allowed to physically move you from the wheelchair to your airplane seat.

The ‘special services’ card allowed me to get on the plane before everyone else. This was good because I did not have to stand in line with my boarding group, in the jetway, or on the plane. 

Once I arrived in Houston, a series of attendants took me from the concourse to the tram waiting area, onto the tram, to another waiting area for regional flights, and finally to the gate for my flight. 

When I arrived at the small city, the only way to get from the plane to the terminal was via a flight of stairs. After a long wait outside sitting on a storage bin, a wheelchair arrived.

For my return flight when I was leaving from the small city, there was no line at security and I knew my gate was just a few yards away – thus, I decided against the attendant. This was a mistake as there was no place for me to sit and take off my boot. While wearing the boot I was unable to stand ‘correctly’ for the body scanner; consequently I had to have a pat-down. I should have opted for the wheelchair. 

When I returned to the medium-sized city, the wheelchair attendant at my destination took me from the gate to baggage claim and then to my car in the handicapped parking area right next to the terminal. 

A few suggestions:

- Plan extra time between flights since you will probably have to wait for wheelchair assistance.

- Pay the upcharge to check your bag. If you are dealing with a boot, you don’t want to deal with your bag.

- Pay the upcharge for an extra leg room seat. The extra room will make it easier to maneuver the boot. 

- Get a window seat if you don’t plan on going to the restroom. Since you are getting on the plane before everyone else, having a window seat means that your seatmates won’t have to crawl over your boot.

- Keep plenty of cash handy to tip your wheelchair attendants. Keep in mind that you could have several different ones to get you from one gate to another. Every attendant I had was polite, patient, and exceedingly helpful. All appeared to be contractors rather than airport/airline employees and none refused a tip.

- If you have a handicapped parking placard, see if it allows you to park in a special area at the airport.

text:

thread_title: Travel insurance covering cost of prescriptions (Caremed?)
text:
I also believe it will be very difficult to find travel insurance that provides coverage for a medication you regularly take for a chronic condition. Travel insurance is for catastrophic events rather than the treatment of known chronic ailments. Many policies may even have exclusions that permit them to deny coverage for health issues that are caused by a known and chronic condition. 



I take several medications on a daily basis. I generally make arrangements with my insurance company to obtain the amount of medication I will need for the length of my stay. Failing that I have a family member pick up the medication and mail it to me. This is occasionally more difficult depending on how difficult it is to mail packages into the country where I am.
