does anyone with cerebral palsy or any other neurological disorder very bad motion sickness and does not go away for a few days? I've had this on all of my trips and the drugs only seem to work for a little bit. Any tips

Hello,



You really should talk to your physician to see if they can offer you another medication, but I might offer a few tips..



GInger is a well tried and trusted remedy for motion sickness. It has a natural anti-emetic action. 



You could try crystallised ginger pieces from a health food store, or ginger biscuits to nibble whist travelling.



Lavender oil and eucalyptus oil, with a few drops of each sprinkled on a Kleenex and sniffed gently can be helpful too.



Some folks use " pressure bands" on their wrists to combat motion sickness. They are supposed to alleviate the worst symptoms, but I don't know if they are proven to help.



Small meals, snacks rather than usual meal sized portions, are a good idea, and try to stay well hydrated all the time you are travelling. Obviously, avoid alcohol! 



Dehydration can play havoc with your metabolism, and with the semi-circular canals of the inner-ear, which help govern spatial awareness and your sense of balance, so plenty of water and non-carbonated drinks will help.



If travelling by car, bus or train, look out of the windows at the horizon as much as possible. If travelling my plane, try to avoid reading as it usually means your head is pointing downwards and your sense of " horizon" can be distorted and upset.



I hope this might help, and I send you my very best wishes for happy travels in the future.



Mondial

The UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities came into effect in 2008 to promote and protect the equality of disabled people under the law. That includes equal rights to take a taxi and no, taxis cannot refuse passengers simply because they have a disability.

I don't know how well that convention is followed in Germany but it should indeed be illegal to refuse to carry a person because they have a disability (or a service animal). That doesn't mean that everyone knows the law or is prepared to carry it out. 

A formal complaint, not necessarily asking for redress but bringing the matter to the attention of authorities, may help to spread information about the rights of people with disabilities more widely.

Germany is currently discussing some of these issues http://www.thelocal.de/20150327/germany-seeks-to-improve-disabled-rights so it may be a timely instance.

Do you need a CONvERTER to charge a go go scooter in Europe?

The charger will need to be a dual voltage device which can accept both 110-120V and 220-240V. If so you'll only need a plug adapter, to convert your US plug to a European plug. 



If your charger only accepts 110-120v you will need a charger adapter. Contact the manufacturer if in doubt.

I recently went on a trip to Russia where we boarded a 1980s river cruise ship that had 110 volt electricity supply. As most mobility scooters used to 12 volt batteries they are very very often 24 volt output therefore your charger already scales up the electricity and can often do that from either 110 volt or 240 volt At either 50 or 60 Hz

Look on the label which is on the charger itself and it will say something similar to mine.

There are only two basic input voltages which are either 100/110 or around 240.

My battery charge reads 

INPUT AC 100-240 volts 50/60hz 1.5 amp

OUTPUT 24 volt 2000ma (the OUTPUT is kind of irrelevant ad it is not related to the problem)

HOWEVER basically this means as long as I can adapt the three pin to a 2 pin using a standard travel plug it can take any electricity from all over the world the only exception being where it is supplied by a DC current which is from a battery and it is extremely unlikely you will ever come across something like that! Please read your label and if you are not sure after my explanation feel free 2 post the readings on here and someone if not myself will be able to advise you but my experience is that of the two mobility scooters I have both the adaptors are capable of taking 100-240 volts and both have an output of 24 volts therefore I am fairly confident you will not have any issues

I am looking for a rental (Adapted) RV for disabled. So far rental companies (all major ones) do not offer adapted RV's. Rental period Summer 2014, area West USA round trip. Driver's + 2 pax are abled, 1 passenger disabled (elec. wheelchair).

I'll be interested to hear how you get on, but surely accessible RVs to rent are as rare as hens' teeth? The adaptations are too likely to prove expensive and inadequate for a high number of "standard" vehicles to be produced - the manufacturers adapt accordig to the individual buyer's needs.

I'm in a wheechair myself, and I'd always prefer a hotel - adapted bathroom, accessible rooms - and to travel by car. Interested, therefore, to know why you'd go for an RV. A car is so much easier to drive, fuel costs so much lower, only one tank to fill (and none to empty) on a daily basis ...

I have spent lots of time on the West Coast of the US, and lots of time in RV Parks and RV Sales Lots. Renting an RV is difficult in and of itself. There is really only one major rental agency and they only rent Class C motorhomes, which would certainly not be large enough for three adults. I doubt that a Class C would even have room for an electric wheelchair inside the unit. At best you might be able to remove a chair and put it near the table, but I am not sure that would work and you would not be able to move around in it.



I would be very surprised if you are able to find this type of a unit. As johnb points our, traveling in an RV is not really cost-effective. People who do this now are not doing it to save money as much as they are committed to the lifestyle. Fuel is very expensive and an RV rarely gets 10 mph, and usually much less. Nightly parking fees can be as much as $80/night at an RV Resort; although certainly less expensive in parks with less to offer.



A reasonable Class A RV sells for about $100,000, and those are the motor homes made in assembly line factories. Custom motor homes start at about $400.000 to $600,000. I have toured through the three largest custom factories in the US and none of them have ever made an adaptive coach. I think the cost would be prohibitive, and even if someone had one, it is unlikely they would be willing to rent it.



We traveled in an RV for 30 years when I was much more mobile than I am now. We gave it up about 15 years ago because it was too difficult, and when our children left home it was no longer a cost-effective system for just the two of us. We travel by car, or by plane and a rented car. We like the convenience of having a place to cook so we generally do short-term apartments. If we are interested in a specific place we might stay a week. On some occasions we have stayed a month, and sometimes only a couple of days. It is always less expensive to rent a short-term apartment than to stay in a hotel.



We are planning on spending part of the summer on the West Coast. We have reserved a couple of apartments on vrbo.com. We will fly into Seattle, rent a car that gets good gas mileage and has room for our two mobility scooters and explore. Of course, if you cannot leave a wheelchair it is more difficult to locate vacation apartments that are adapted for the disabled, but it is not nearly as difficult to locate these places as it will be to locate a motor home adapted for a wheelchair.

Only one day after my assurance that it would be difficult to locate an RV to rent in the Western US, I have discovered that there are a few large RV's available to rent. These are tow behind travel trailers, and I have never seen them for rent because the renter would require a tow vehicle or the person renting the RV would have to provide such a vehicle. I had never seen that.



There is now a company called Airstream 2 Go that is renting Airstream Travel Trailers with an appropriate tow vehicle, a 2013 GMC Yukon Denali SUV. These are not adaptive RV's, but they will provide much more floor space than you would get in a Class C Motor Home. If you are exclusively confined to a wheelchair you would need a ramp to enter the RV. You may not be able to use the RV shower, but every campground has showers, and they are almost always of generous size so you could possibly use these facilities.



Airstream travel trailers, for those not from the US or not familiar with RVing, are widely recognized as the most luxurious travel trailer on the market. They are instantly recognized by their rounded shape and aluminum exterior. The rental Airstreams come with all the necessary luxurious including 650 thread count sheets, flat screen TVs, Sony DVD players, fully supplied kitchen with microwave and cooktop, Weber Q grill and automatic awnings.



If managing a tow-behind RV is intimidating these units also provide the renter with an iPad containing an owner's manual and lots of instructions for trouble-shooting the various systems in the RV.



There are two sizes available for rent. One is a 23' Airstream that can sleep four and the other is a 28' Airstream that can sleep 6. I would expect that there is only one permanent bed in either of these units and extra sleeping arrangements are in the form of fold-out dinettes and/or hide-a-bed couches. 



The starting price for renting one of these units for five days is $5300, and depending on your need for a customized itinerary can be as expensive as $7500 for five days.



You would also be responsible for the gasoline, and you can probably not expect anything better than 10 mpg, regardless of what they tell you. You can use your own auto insurance, but you need to make sure it will cover you for this type of rental. Our insurance would cover the tow vehicle, but not the travel trailer, so we would need to add that coverage before we rented something like this. You would also have to pay for your own campground fees. On the positive side, most Walmart stores will let you park in their parking lots over-night if you do not require any water, sewer or electrical connections. I would need A/C and probably a TV so this is not an option for me because the travel trailer, unlike the standard motor home does not come with a generator. We would need a some type of campground.



This is not something either my husband or I would do at this point in our lives. We have traveled hundreds of thousands of miles towing an RV, and we enjoyed our experiences. However, driving is much more difficult when you are towing something nearly 30' long behind you. It is also a bit difficult to set up the trailer each night. You have to level the trailer, jack the corners for stability, hook up the water, electricity and sewer connections, and sometimes all of that takes much longer than it sounds like it should. As much as we enjoyed traveling in our RV, we are no longer willing to put in this much work. As you can see, it is an expensive adventure. I have never paid $1000/night for a hotel room, but I am confident that I could get a very nice suite for that price. So, at a minimum of $5300 for five nights, this is still not a practical solution for us.



If, however, much of your vacation is to have an RV experience, this is one way you could manage it. Camping in a lovely National Park campground is a great experience, which I really believe everyone should enjoy at least once in their lives.

Hmm, that's one helluva price! Here's the website http://airstream2go.com/

As always, the Airstream caravan looks amazing! But then, so would a $1,000 per night suite...

And 10 MP (US) G that's more than 23.5l/100km, as we continental Europeans would put it!

Reason for wanting an adapted RV - My mother is handicapped. She has wanted to travel to the West Coast with many many many stop-offs along the way. When she was able-bodied she first had children to rear then a career. Now that she's retired and has the time for such things, she is not able to move around freely. She needs to have a 'home base' that she can go back to quickly if she is fatigued. She has a severe light sensitivity. She needs a CPAP at night. She's only 65. I am sure you have read all of the previous posts in this thread. To my knowledge there are currently no companies renting adaptive RV's on the West Coast of the US. You understand that you cannot always be only a block from your RV. in most cases you have to park your RV on the outskirts of a city. While driving an RV provides quick access to a bathroom, but if you are sight-seeing in downtown San Francisco your RV will not be close to you. 



RV's also provide sleeping for a minimum number of people. Our current RV can sleep a total of 6 people, but two of those are on an air mattress in the dining area, which we have to empty before our guests arrive. It is not practical housing for large numbers of people.

Purchasing an RV with the intent of using it briefly for a vacation and then selling it seems like a most unwise financial decision. These units depreciate about 20% the minute you drive a new vehicle off of the sales lot. In addition there are many extra expenses when getting a RV ready to travel. You have to pay taxes to obtain a license as well as insurance. These things can cost thousands of dollars.I am confident that you could stay in a five star hotel and have money left over compared to what you would spend if you do a short-term purchase of an RV.



Unless you want to own something for at least a couple of years it is never a good financial decision to buy something. When you are using an RV exclusively for an annual vacation owning a vehicle makes no sense, and you should probably try to manage in a rental RV.



I can understand that a toy hauler was an effective way for you to move three wheelchairs down the road at the same time, but as you acknowledge, you were not able to use the RV for the purpose of sleeping, which generally defeats the purpose of using an RV in the first place. If your only goal is transportation, it seems as if there would be more practical solutions such as a full-sized SUV.



We have used an RV for more than 45 years, and are now pretty much full-time users of our RV. While it is certainly possible to make adaptations in an RV, these units are not made like real homes. The walls are flimsy. Space is at a minimum. It has been impossible for us to make some of the most basic adaptations such as creating a roll-in shower because there is simply not enough infrastructure in our RV to support this type of structural change. Our current RV has a very unique floor plan, and it took us several months to locate this particular unit which gives me access to all of my kitchen and adequate room to move around in my wheelchair or with my walker. I also have full access to my bed, but shower access is problematic and does not provide me with the type of privacy I would like. Apart from changing the cupboards so I can roll them out rather than dig around in the back of them, we have not successfully made our unit more friendly for my disabilities. We manage quite well with our unit, but this is only because we knew what we needed and did not purchase until we found something that already had a workable floor plan.



Unless you are exceptionally talented in all areas of construction including plumbing and electrical work, and unless you are willing to purchase a top of the line RV with a metal frame that can support significant changes in the floor plan I would recommend that you have an RV custom designed by the factory. Several RV companies will meet with buyers, listen to their needs and provide adaptations when the RV is originally constructed.



I do not believe creating an adaptive RV is a DIY project unless you have many specific skills, have enough disposable income to support your goals and lots of experience in re-structuring one of these homes on wheels.

text:
We are flying from Denver to Knoxville on Frontier, then from Detroit to Denver on United. Both airlines tell us we can either check the scooter with the luggage, and get wheelchair assistance to the gate, or take the scooter to the gate, and gate-check. Which is preferable? My husband can walk short distances, and climb a few stairs, but stairs would be impossible with a scooter. 



Any suggestions from experienced travelers would be much appreciated.

thread_title: First time flying with mobility scooter
text: I have flown with my mobility scooter (small, folding 35 lbs) and it's been very easy. If your husband's scooter isn't one of the large monster scooter's than he can ride it to the gate, notify the gate agent and he will be allowed to ride it to the door of the plane. The scooter will be placed in the hold and will be returned to the door of the plane when you land (it will probably take a little extra time). It doesn't matter whether you gate check or check it with the luggage you will have to go through the regular security line (although upon occasion they will open up a seprate lane for you). As for whether or not there are stairs I would suggest you check out the airports website for accessibility. As one time you had to walk out to Frontier planes and climb the stairs, but I haven't flown on Frontier is years so I don't know if that's still true.

thread_title: First time flying with mobility scooter
text:
Thanks for your response. We flew in last Saturday, checked the scooter with the luggage, and were taken to the gate by wheel chair. It was easy! And we were so grateful to be able to avoid the massive line at the Frontier desk. Even with the luggage check-in, the scooter came out at the gate at our destination. We wouldn't have known that except for the wheelchair attendant. He helped assemble it, and handled the carry on luggage. The rental car agency (Budget) kindly delivered the car to the curbside and helped load the scooter into the trunk. 



We do not have the foldable TravelScoot, but do have a small one that is easily disassembled. It is easier to handle with the van we have a home than putting it in the trunk, but it is possible,

I have flown on my own with a mobility scooter, albeit not to Egypt. You need to book the Special Assistance with the airline when you book your flight.

Looking for the portable shower/bathing & commode solutions. Please give opinion for those items which can be carry on a trip.
amazon have shower chairs and stools.

Just in case you don't know already, most cruise lines and high quality hotels have these items available for use during your stay. Simply call/email to arrange ahead of time. If they are not available and you are staying at a hotel for a decent amount of time, I would call a medical supply place and rent them for the duration. Most medical supply places will rent shower chairs/transfer benches but you will probably have to buy the commode accessories. Either way would be easier than trying to carry them with you. However, if all else fails, a cane with a foldable seat can be utilized as a shower chair and a backwards walker with its breaks on as a way to get up off a toilet easier.

I got my current chair from Amazon for like $35. It is very sturdy and adjusts to many heights. It comes with a back and arms which are removable. The legs unscrew from the chair and the whole thing stores flat. We take it everywhere we go- but I agree with another poster- many hotels have attached seats in roll-in shower stalls or chairs like the one I mention (which is where we got the idea for it). Heck, for $35, you might consider getting one when you got to your destination and leaving it behind! 



Another option- I have a shower/commode chair that is designed for travelling- it comes apart reasonably well and comes in a box designed to be used as a travelling case. it is marked as durable medical equipment which I believe, by law, airlines must let you check free of charge. Drawbacks- it's really bulky and takes up a lot of room in the van and it was really pricey (like $1000).

thread_title: Advice re Malta travel during hip replacement rehab post op.
text:
Hi



First of all have you got the all clear from your doctor, and secondly have you declared this operation to your travel insurers?



Flying with your leg stuck out into the aisle isn't really practical and if you are immobile the airline might not allow an aisle seat unless it is your own family who are on the inside seats. You do have to inform the airline and although you say you don't think you will need assistance there is nothing lost by having it in place anyway.



I've never been to Malta but I have only ever done one package tour bus transfer over twenty years ago and ablebodied and crippled (I've been both) I would never do it again. So book yourself a comfortable transfer from airport to hotel. There's nothing like arriving at your destination and seeing your name held up on a board, knowing you'll soon be relaxing over a nice glass of chilled wine.



No baths, showers and get in touch with the hotel to see if they have one you can put a plastic stool in.



Have a good holiday.



Jackie

thread_title: Advice re Malta travel during hip replacement rehab post op.
text: I'm not sure what your recovery issues are. At age 65 I had a total hip replacement. Following surgery I had three weeks of physical therapy and then I flew from the US to Istanbul. The flight was not uncomfortable, and I had a middle seat. I had no difficulty using the shower in a standard-sized bathtub. Our hotel had no elevator, but I managed the narrow winding steps quite well. I was overly careful walking on cobblestones for the first couple of days, but after that I managed fine. I took only my walking cane. I would think that you would have few problems three months following your hip surgery. If you are nervous about some physical activity ask your PT person to focus on tasks that will help you be more confident.

Mobility Assistance at Airports

Hello in the last 12 months I have developed a knee problem which means I can’t stand or queue for long periods, hence I have had to start using airports mobility assistance when going on holiday.

Below are my findings, please feel free to add you own to this forum.

Manchester Terminal 1

Staff very friendly & helpful, but at peak times the provider OCS is under resourced, leading to longish waits.

Agadir, Morocco

Staff friendly & helpful, but being outside the E>U>, they expect tips.

Corfu, Greece

Very Poor, in either direction no assistance was provided, although pre-booked.

Las Palmas, Gran Canaria, Spain

Excellent, staff could not be more helpful. Plenty of resources.

You might add LAX - mean well, but are not physically fit to push a wheelchair from the UA 80 gates to the 70's. We just took over the wheelchairs, threw a tip at each attendant and made the connection, leaving the wheelchairs at the gate. Now, the ideal would have been to have a motorized cart, but we were denied that service. Not sure why, as I see all sorts of folk riding in those, and at LAX? In our case, we were flying elderly, and infirm family members FC to HNL, so maybe one needs to be GFC on international?



Hunt

Hi can you post this on Traveling with disabilities forum please.



http://www.tripadvisor.co.uk/ShowForum-g1-i12336-Traveling_With_Disabilities.html



Deb

Toronto is pretty chaotic too.



Last month on arrival we were made to wait at the top of the jetway while we waited for a second passenger (who of course came off last). Apparently it is impossible for two pushers to work independently when meeting the same flight! They had to check and cross-check which passenger they were pushing. Then they only took us part of the way. Before we went down to the customs hall we had to wait for another set of pushers. At least we were fast-tracked through passport cotrol.



On the way back (we were flying United) we waited ages for the pusher to turn up at the desk. (Fortunately there were a couple of seats next to the priority check in desk). Again, this pusher took us only as far as security. Once through security we were met by a cart driver who looked at our boarding passes and exclaimed that he couldn't help us as we were leaving from small gates for regional aircraft where his buggy couldn't go. He eventually relented and pushed the wheelchair, but not after muttering something along the lines of "I'm a driver, not a pusher!") He left us at the gate and I pushed my wife to the aircraft, which was fine (I often choose to push her on departure so we can be independent).



Contrast that to Heathrow's new Terminal 2. We were three hours late, arriving at around 1am (special dispensation to break the curfew). Again two parties being met, and we waited at the jetway for the second party. There was a reason for this as we only went a short way by wheelchair and were then transferred to a buggy for the rather long trek to passport control. Waiting meant only one buggy was needed. The lifts at T2 are designed to accommodate the buggies, so the whole trip to passport control is seamless. There we transferred to wheelchairs. The pusher took us out to arrivals where our driver had not yet arrived. Despite the fact that he was already way past the end of his shift, he offered to wait but we told him we would be fine.



(On the way out we flew from Man where we just picked up a chair and I did all the pushing.)

I know I'm probably out of line and this will get zapped but I've got to make the comment.....

It says something about out society when our luggage gets taken from the check in counter to the plane for nothing but the elderly and infirm have to tip someone to do the same for them. Sad.

BTW, people who assist less mobile passengers to and off aircraft in Australia are not allowed to accept tips.

No I agree with you post 4! 

Now how do I get this thread moved to TWD forum ? 



Deb

When my husband suffered back problems we found Stansted to be really good, we rang ahead to book a wheelchair and assistance, then we waited in a special area until a member of staff came to take my husband and I through security, we were then taken to departures and left there until another member of staff came to take us to the gate where we were fast tracked onto the plane. No problems whatsoever.Very smooth and painless. Sadly at the Fuerteventura airport all was not so plain sailing but the airport is mercifully small and we had a private care waiting.

x

correction - we had a private car waiting not private care.

Must also add that when passengers are walking or queuing and there is someone in a wheelchair please be aware of your handbags etc., because my husband was whacked about the head by various bags whilst we were at the airport.

I have used wheelchair assistance in airports for the last 15 years. I cannot really say that some airports are bad while others are good. It seems to me to depend more upon the person pushing the chair than the airport itself. My only reservation is AMS. If your name is accidentally left off the "list" you will not receive assistance even if you have to crawl to your next gate. Overall my experiences have been positive; although not always personable. Some wheelchair pushing people are so helpful and kind that they make my entire journey seem more pleasant. The wheelchair guys at the IST airport are among the most helpful, but they work with the most dreadful equipment of any airport I use.



I do not know what these people are paid in Europe. In the US the average wheelchair pusher is paid $5/hour by the airport or a sub-contracted service. This is not even minimum wage. When a person helps me through security, passport control, customs and also helps me manage my luggage I feel that this person should receive a tip. I generally reward exceptional service with a $10USD bill.

In 2013 mum & I decided to try our first flight holiday since she lost her leg so we booked a week in Benidorm flying Ryanair from Leeds Bradford airport (as it is quite a small airport) so I booked mum assistance as she is very slow at walking up stairs (and I knew ryanair don't use the jetway at LBA) and wasn't 100% sure she could get up the whole flight on her own under the time pressure.



When we arrived at Leeds Bradford when to the assistance desk we were asked whether we need a wheelchair, which mum didn't as she is able to walk a reasonable, the very helpful staff member explain we could take as little or as much assistance as we needed and as she only needed to use the ambi lift to board the plane to be at our gate 15 minutes before our flight was due to board, when we got to the gate we were politely greet as Mrs XXXXXX & you need to use the ambi lift so along with another passenger our boarding passes were checked and I wasn't expecting to be able to accompany mum but it was no issue, so were walked out to the ambi lift and driven across to the plane and loaded to the rear of the aircraft, a stewardess was there to check we were ok and where we needed to sit. 



At Alicante what a performance if we had known there was a jetway we would have abandoned the assistance. When we arrived the ambi lift took quite a while to arrive, they made mum sit in a wheelchair when there were seats that she could have easily used, when we arrived at terminal mum said I am fine to walk, but no she had to stay in the chair until we got through passport control & once we got to luggage collect mum had to firmly say no I don't need the chair any long I am quite able to walk the short distance to the coach pick up area, the staff member seemed most upset. 



On return to Alicante for our return flight it was also very disorganised not helped by 4 UK flight which had quite a few assistance passengers all being due out within 25 minutes of each other. We went to the assistance desk which had quite a queue so thought OK lets get rid of the luggage so returned about 15 minutes later & then waited another 20 minutes to fill the form in we told the staff member who spoke very good english & understood us very well that we only need assistance to board the aircraft, but again they insisted that no if you book assistance you use a wheelchair. We then had to wait another 15 minutes for somebody to push the wheelchair even though there was about 10 chairs available & I was happy to push if they insisted we had to use a wheelchair, once we were through security we where pushe to an area near to another assistance desk & told somebody would could to help board about 10 minutes before boarding commenced. 



So I pushed mum around for a bit and returned, when we got back to the designated place there was 3 assistance passengers but only 2 staff so I ended pushing mum, down the jetway, by which time other passengers were boarding so we had a few issues getting to the designated disabled seats on the plane.



Back at leeds the stewardess came and said we are sorry there is a slight delay on the ambi lift so we had to wait about 5 minutes, the staff member asked who needed a wheelchair which was only one passenger of the 3, he then told us he was sorry but he had to pick up some passengers off another flight so there would be a slight delay.



Once we got across to the terminal be bypassed the passport control queue and took the group of us to the front of the queue & then checked whether anybody needed any more help before he disappeared off to help other passengers.



Overall I would give Leeds Bradford 9 out of 10 & Alicante 6 out of 10 & if we knew it would be a jetway would not use assist at Alicante.



I would also recommend Benidorm as a good destination to visit from the UK as its very easy to hire wheelchairs & scooters if you need to. We did hire a wheelchair to make life easier for a few days around the market etc, it cost less than 10 euros for the 3 days.



THanks to this break mum is happy to travel by plane with no fears of access etc.

I have a mobility problem but last time I used the wheechair service my poor friend who was travelling with me 

had to nearly run to keep up with the fast ride. If she had not have have kept up I would have lost her along the way. Any sugestions as I need her for help even getting out of the chair with luggage.

I have a mobility problem but last time I used the wheechair service my poor friend who was travelling with me 

had to nearly run to keep up with the fast ride. If she had not have have kept up I would have lost her along the way. Any sugestions as I need her for help even getting out of the chair with luggage.
Yes, speak up. Tell the airport assistant to slow down if necessary, to make sure you stay together as you need your friend to be an assistant.
Yes, I would mention to the wheelchair pusher that they are going too fast. I am sure this has happened to us in the past and we just ask them to slow down. Not really difficult.

I can walk a short way, but no stairs at all, so always ask for wheelchair from check-in to airplane. I've been around the world twice plus all 7 continents all by myself (no "pusher" or escort) and have been transported by garbage lift (with accompanying wilted lettuce, etc.) by kitchen chair with and without arms to hang on to, by my own legs when they finally brought a ramp after pusher left me standing on the tarmac, by nice and by swearing people. Worst was in Miami: I was refused to go to the concourse I wanted. Their instructions were all handicapped must be isolated in America's North Terminal D until 1/2 to 1 hour before departure. No food, no bathrooms, and they take away the wheelchair so you are captive. I had 5 hours between flights & rather than being a captive, spent 4 of them hobble/sit/hobble/sit getting back to my exit gate that the pusher had passes 4 hours earlier. Heathrow United is also segregated, but at least they have vending machines and bathrooms. They both assume, if your legs dont work, your brain can't either. In Heathrow, I will not again sit meekly letting them sooth me until after my flight is missed (because they couldn't find my non-existant "keeper"), but will speak up as soon as something is out of order. As for MIami, I will just avoid it like poison. Other airports are a grab-bag. LAX is usually ok, but both International and Domestic sometimes have big problems wheeling people. I always double-check at every arrival to verify transfer departure gate and transport. Having maps of the airports is a big help. Ditto having the airline print out handicapped card with boarding pass. Every time a connection flight time is changed, your reservation can get reset to destroy your previous seating and wheelchair reservations (especially when travelling in Asia) so keep double-checking all the time. Pay attention to what gate you are landing at, find it on the map, and see how far away your departure gate is before you even get off the airplane, then, sometimes, the stewardess can help you make additional arrangements.

Thanks for your message. Sometimes more trouble than its worth but I will persist and not get pushed around

Mobility Assistance at Airports

Hello in the last 12 months I have developed a knee problem which means I can’t stand or queue for long periods, hence I have had to start using airports mobility assistance when going on holiday.

Below are my findings, please feel free to add you own to this forum.

Manchester Terminal 1

Staff very friendly & helpful, but at peak times the provider OCS is under resourced, leading to longish waits.

Agadir, Morocco

Staff friendly & helpful, but being outside the E>U>, they expect tips.

Corfu, Greece

Very Poor, in either direction no assistance was provided, although pre-booked.

Las Palmas, Gran Canaria, Spain

Excellent, staff could not be more helpful. Plenty of resources.

Overall, our great experiences vastly out number our less than positive experiences. We have learned that rules vary from airline to airline, airport to airport and country to country. Some places provide only the assistance you need. One of the largest differences we notice is simply the difference between employees. Most of the time our wheelchair assistants are personable and pleasant, but occasionally they are difficult and less than helpful.



It is good to know what your airline and airport will provide. Understanding their services helps you prepare for different procedures. A map of the airport helps you direct your wheelchair person to the correct location. When I travel I am never as comfortable as I am when I am in my own home. I know that my mood reflects my level of discomfort, and I am very careful to be as pleasant as possible regardless of how I feel or what other bad experiences I have already had. A positive attitude can generally generate a more professional and personable performance from the wheelchair pusher.



I know the procedures my airline follows. I never attempt to leave the plane until the last passenger has left, but I also refuse to leave the plane unless there is a wheelchair waiting at the door. Remaining on the plane means that some of the flight crew must remain with me. The flight crew is much more motivated to do what is necessary to provide a wheelchair when they cannot leave until I leave.



With the exception of AMS there is no airport that I feel consistently provides poor service. AMS can be managed, but you have to check, re-check and re-confirm your arrangements many times to insure that you are on the official list for disability services.



My father had the same disability that I have. He really stopped leaving his home for the last 25 years of his life. With better equipment, great legislation and a general improvement in compassion, life is so much easier for me. We still fly 50,000+ miles each year. My father's greatest travel experience was a trip to the grocery store where he then waited in the car for my mother to complete her shopping.



People with disabilities have obtained huge advantages for themselves in the last couple of decades. I feel very fortunate to be able to take advantage of these improvements in service.

Greetings Busy-retired,



Great post, been there, waiting for the assistance & the wheel chair, we also waited on the aircraft till personnel arrived, I would walk to the aircraft gangway, to make sure all was in order, before deplaning.



Kind Regards,

Any new opinions for DFW to JFK, then on to Heathrow as easily as possible.

Will stopover at a hotel close to JFK for 2 nights to rest.

Also any suggestions on hotels close to there with shuttle service.



Thanks bunches!

I frequently fly from MCO to JFK and then on to IST. Wheelchair service used to be hit or miss at JFK, but in the last four to five years we have had excellent experiences at JFK. It is an old airport that has not been maintained well, but the staff has been excellent with us.



We did overnight at JFK four years ago. It was more problem than benefit for us. We selected an inexpensive hotel near the airport. Reaching the shuttle area from the airport was difficult. The airport staff would not push the wheelchair beyond the airport and that was several blocks away from the hotel shuttle area. Our return was fine. The hotel shuttle driver took us right to the door of the airport. There was construction going on which may have made exiting the airport to the shuttle area temporarily difficult. It was such a mess we just opted not to do it again.

My daughter took Virgin Atlantic flight 8 from LAX to Heathrow, landing today (Jan 10, 2014). We had confirmed in advance with the airline that she needed mobility assistance on landing to get her to her connecting domestic flight. She confirmed at the gate at LAX and with the flight crew that she would need assistance. 



To set up her situation: apparently the flight was somewhat of a nightmare, as she was seated across the aisle from the epitome of the Dursleys, with three very young children who screamed nonstop, banged on the tvs with empty chip cans, slept in the aisles, kicked seats, and, while holding over London, apparently vomited in a barf bag which the mum did not bother to seal and toss - thus leaving all the neighboring seatholders retching. So, minimal sleep for my daughter and the entire cabin (including the poor soul nearby who had taken sleeping pills) the whole trip. [Apparently, also, the parents of said evil spawn were absolutely obnoxious when various of their neighbors requested that they have their children not kick seatbacks, scream, run up and down the aisles, etc..- so I guess a posh accent can be learned, but class cannot. ;) ]



So, after all that, and when everyone was off the plane, my now totally frazzled/exhausted daughter disembarked and was left waiting at the door - no wheelchair was there to meet her. The staff left her, telling her to remain and someone would be with her shortly. "Shortly" turned out to be approximately an hour. She was panicking and starting to think that they'd totally forgotten her when someone did finally arrive. She says that the gent who brought the wheelchair was very nice, but horrified that she'd been left alone there for that long. He told her that someone from the airline should have remained with her.



She did make her connecting flight, but only just, as her carry-on caused problems in the screening area, and they unpacked her bag as the person screening her bag did not recognize her knitting needles as knitting needles and she said something about it setting off an explosives detector. Apparently they swabbed everything in her bag for explosives, and the needles failed. They sorted out that it was the ball of yarn doing it, and finally passed her through. (No, really! I have NO idea - it was ordinary, commercially produced wool yarn. She thinks it might have been the moth-proofing they put on it at the factory. Well, that's a trip that will be retold for years....)



Anyway, I am wondering which party would be the one with whom we should lodge a complaint about not having mobility assistance there as scheduled? Would that be Virgin Atlantic, who said everything had been arranged and basically left her by herself at the airplane door, or some office at Heathrow? 



Thanks.

Special Assistance is booked via the airline but provided by the CAA ( in this case, Heathrow). I am very sorry to hear about your daughter's bad experience. I would never have got off the aircraft. Normally the crew, or somebody from the crew will stay with you.



The only thing I can think of that made this such a bad experience is the extra security and checks because of the atrocities in Paris.



She needs to complain to the CAA.

Thank you. She arrived only a few hours ago at her destination and IM'd to let me know she'd arrived and what had happened. I'll pass the advice along to her. Thankfully, her onward flight was almost textbook perfect on Little Red, and she arrived home safely.

New Hamad ( Doha) airport is disgraceful. Dumped in barren corridor areas with no access to toilets or source of a drink/ food. Grossly understaffed service with no spare wheelchairs. Avoid if you can but if not they do at least get you to the plane on time( just).

Dabolim ( Goa) Hey this is India what do you expect? Very old wheelchairs, very small pushers. Do not panic when they say they will be back having dumped you half way there. They will come back but at their own pace and time!

Heathrow- deserve the Oscar for the most improved service over the last 12 months. It felt like a different service

Gatwick- really have it cracked. They are consistently the best service we have had anywhere.

Dublin Airport with Ryanair.

Travelling with my partner's mobility scooter through Dublin Airport, assisted by OCS, was convenient and straightforward though the OCS assistance desk was not easy to find. The scooter did not have to be broken down or boxed for our Ryanair flight and, although it weighed 38kg, it was accepted free-of-charge as her 20kg hold luggage.

We parked our car in QuickPark and took the free transfer bus to the terminal but found that the transfer bus was not scooter-friendly, it probably would have been OK for a wheelchair, but the boarding ramp was too high up for the small scooter wheels. On the outward journey, other bus passengers helped me lift the scooter, but on the return journey we were the last ones off the bus but the driver just watched me struggle.

Overall, we would be happy to travel via Dublin with her mobility scooter again.

Milan Orio Al Serio Airport with Ryanair.

Travelling with my partner's mobility scooter through Milan's Orio Al Serio Airport, assisted by OCS, was convenient and straightforward. The OCS assistance desk was not easy to find so we headed to the check-in desk where the Ryanair check-in clerk acted as if she had never even heard of assisted travel and faffed about for ages before phoning for help - language was not the problem as the clerk spoke good English and my partner is bilingual in Italian. The scooter did not have to be broken down or boxed for our Ryanair flight and, although it weighed 38kg, it was accepted free-of-charge as her 20kg hold luggage.

Orio Al Serio airport has a special waiting area for assisted passengers that has machines for beverages, soft drinks, and snacks, but they are quite happy for you to visit the main departure facilities so long as you return to the special waiting area 1 hour before boarding. We were a bit concerned because our assistant did not appear until well after the final boarding call, but it turned out OK.

The rental car return point is a considerable distance from the terminal and there is no bus, however, the nice man from FireFly processed our return then ran us round to the terminal door in the car, so we didn't need to assemble the scooter until we got there.

Overall, we would be happy to travel via Orio Al Serio with her mobility scooter again.

thread_title: Timing of connections with wheelchair assistance
text:
I'm looking at booking a US domestic flight for my mother with connections likely to be ORD, DFW, DTW, MSP, or ATL (if that matters). Currently American and Delta have the best prices, but United could also be a possibility. Flights will be on one of those 3 as they're the only options. She can walk, but quite slowly and is getting to where she wears out fairly quickly, so I was thinking of booking her wheelchair assistance for the first time. (She'd be able to walk off the plane, and could even just do one of those carts, but I don't know if you can book those.) She may also have more carry on luggage because she might need to carry more medical supplies than she has in the past.



Previously, I would always try to allow her 2 hours between flights, although for myself with no mobility issues I would take 1 hour if the price was significantly better. However, I have no idea if wheelchair assistance speeds up the connection or if it slows it down because you have to wait for the wheelchair or staff or something like that. 



Would I be ok booking her the same length connection I would book for myself, or do I need to build in extra time for the assistance? Does it make it more likely that you'll make a connection since airline staff are in charge of your connection, or does it not affect that? (Obviously if the first flight is significantly late, it wouldn't help that.)



Any other tips on the process would be great as I have no experience with the wheelchair special assistance.



Thanks for any advice. I posted on Air Travel too, as I wasn't sure where was best to ask.

thread_title: Timing of connections with wheelchair assistance
text:
The airline staff is not in charge of wheelchair service. Each airport provides a wheelchair staff. Generally they do not bring the wheelchairs to the plane until everyone has left. So I probably stay on the plane about 20 minutes longer than a walking passenger near the front of the plane. 



I usually give myself 2 hours for connecting flights. Sometimes this isn't an option. Last summer the only connecting flight I had in DTW was 30 minutes. However since my airline offered it, it was a legal connection. If I would have missed it my airline would have put me on the next available flight. 



Your mother should remain on the plane until the wheelchair arrives. The flight crew cannot all leave until all the passengers have left. If your mother leaves the plane and no wheelchair arrives there will be no one to help her. If she stays on the plane they will make sure someone comes for her. On my last flight the wheelchair didn't arrive and the pilot got on the phone and then the wheelchair arrived. Generally airports do an impressive job of meeting planes and making sure you reach connections in s timely fashion.

thread_title: Timing of connections with wheelchair assistance
text:
btgm, The electric carts that you occasionally see in airports are rarely part of the scheduled system that the airport uses to help those people with disabilities move from one place to another. Generally this is managed by a coordinated operations of wheelchair pushers. The airport in SLC occasionally uses these electric carts in conjunction with wheelchair pushers, but it is the only airport I use in the US where these carts are employed as part of the system. In Europe it is much the same with the exception of AMS. At this airport electric carts are virtually the only thing that they use to assist disabled passengers. If you need help on the jetway they will provide a wheelchair for that distance only; otherwise passengers are moved on electric carts.



Just because you mother can walk does not mean that she should attempt to walk in an airport. These places on often congested and difficult to negotiate. The distances between gates can be huge. If she is carrying a bag it will be even more difficult. I would not have let my mother try to negotiate her way through an airport alone in the last five years of her life (85 to 90). She could walk, but she was frail, and not very fast. I thought an airport was a perfect place for her to fall and break a hip. We always arranged for wheelchair transportation for her. I would recommend the same thing for your mother.

hi, i was wondering if anyone knows where can i hire a mobility scooter in Istanbul? Any contact information to provide? .. Thanks to you in advance!
You may have a better response if you put your question on the Istanbul Forum

I have found this web site for scooter rentals http://mobilityturkey.com/ I have no personal experience with this company. In the ten years I have been a DE for Istanbul I have never known anyone to use this company. I am providing it because it is the only thing I have.



Istanbul is exceptionally difficult for mobility scooters. I leave mine at home. Every year I carefully examine my environment hoping to see that some obstacles have been replaced by infrastructure that is more accessible. This is an ancient city with a huge population, and I do not expect to see it friendly to disabled people in my lifetime.



Barriers include many hotels with no elevators, or elevators too small to accommodate a scooter. Stairs everywhere. Even in new construction rooms are placed at different levels for the sake of design. Shops that are much too small for a scooter to enter. Cobblestone pavement that is very rough on equipment. High curbs at every corner that require that a scooter be manually lifted over the curb. Sidewalks that disappear half way down a block forcing you into the narrow street to compete with tour buses and taxis. Sidewalks that suddenly convert into stairs on steep hills. Sidewalks that have been appropriated by a sidewalk vendor and turned into display space. I would not say that Istanbul is impossible for use of a mobility scooter, but I would say that it is exceptionally difficult.



The modern malls are all generally accessible. Generally you can manage most of the Grand Bazaar in a scooter. You may not take them into mosques, but larger mosques will provide a mosque approved wheelchair for your use while you visit. Public transportation is hit or miss. The ferry system is generally impossible. Some tram stops accommodate scooters, and others do not. The Metro has elevator access, but it is hidden and you have to know where to find it. We use taxis almost exclusively because I really need door to door service to manage the city.



I do not leave home without my scooter, except when we travel to Istanbul. For the last two years I have taken a little three wheeled walker that I use to walk two or three blocks. I depend upon taxis and the kindness of our many friends in the city to manage. Each year I walk a bit less and spend a few more hours sipping tea and visiting with Istanbul residents.



Even though I have significantly reduced mobility, I am determined to continue to visit my favorite city, and I am able to do this mostly because of the hospitality and kindness of the people in the city. I have never known a more helpful culture. I have had dozens of experiences where strangers just appear to help me. I have never crossed a busy street that some stranger did not take my arm and usher me across. Occasionally brave college students just stop traffic while I cross. Last year a sidewak just disappeared into a big construction hole, and four men just picked me up and lifted me across the chasm. When the turn style does not have an alternative entrance, someone always picks up my walker and lifts it across. When I stop to catch my breath a shopkeeper immediately appears with a chair, and a glass of tea.



Last year in Cappadocia, one of my favorite hotel owners constructed a series of ramps making it possible for me to reach my room from the street in a cave hotel constructed on many different levels. There is not enough money to even start making Turkey compliant with the needs of the disabled, but the people are exceptionally clever, and they have never failed to help me.



Good luck, and if you to have any success with this company, please let us know. We would also like to know how you manage the city with your mobility issues.

text:
I would like to hear of other passengers with Stomas experiences at Airports, both good and bad. My husband was treated appallingly at Birmingham Airport when we went on holiday in June, my husband should have been taken to a more secluded area when he accidentally set the alarms off in Security at Birmingham Airport as his Stoma Bag wasn't completely empty, so he was 'padded down' in full view of other passengers, when he explained again (although told a female member of security moments earlier he had a stoma bag and was ignored). Although the man 'padding him down' did apologise when my husband had to explain again that he had a Stoma Bag and that he should be taken to a separate area with a doctor or nurse available. However worse was to follow, when my husband presented the necessary equipment required, e.g. Imodium Medicine, sprays to remove the bags and spare Stoma Bags along with a doctor's signature on correspondence, Health Passport and information from the Tour Company/Airline, which also included that the passenger has a Stoma on the Airline ticket he was treated with contempt by the man checking our hand luggage, no apology, or treated with tact. I bet the White Widow would have been treated better! 

 I appreciate that they have a job to do in Security/Passport Control, but it does not entitle staff with no empathy and lack of people skills to treat people who have a health condition with contempt. It really put a dampener on the start of our holiday, and instead of being able to relax and enjoy wandering round the Duty Free shops etc, it made my husband want to go home. 

In contrast my husband was treated very well by the cabin crew of Thomas Cook, and also had no problem with Security/Passport Control when coming home, once he told the staff of his health problem he was treated with compassion and the utmost consideration, in fact it was not he who set the alarm off on the scanner but myself, due to my underwired bra.

Or have I completely misunderstood ? 



In 1978, the ECMT Council of Ministers agreed that all Member Countries of the ECMT would grant the same parking concessions to people with disabilities as they offered their own nationals. These concessions usually allowed special parking in areas reserved for people with disabilities, or allowed longer parking periods or exemptions from charges.



This Resolution was updated and extended in scope in 1997. In addition to all the Member countries of ECMT this Resolution now applies also to the ECMT Associated Countries (Australia, Canada, Japan, Korea, New Zealand and United States). This means that disabled motorists from all ECMT Member and Associate countries are now entitled to the same parking concessions as nationals in all ECMT Countries. The only condition is the display of a badge showing the international wheelchair symbol.



In 1998 the EU adopted a Resolution along the same lines for the Member countries of the EU. The badges to be displayed are to be standardized to facilitate recognition and to avoid difficulties at local level.

thread_title: What's the best adventure when you can't walk much?
text:
My husband and I visit Turkey for five to six weeks each year. We are both 70, and both have mobility issues. When we go anywhere but Turkey we use mobility scooters. Turkey's infrastructure makes it impossible to use them there. The cobblestone streets are too rough. There are stairs everywhere. Sidewalks disappear into a set of stairs or a sidewalk cafe or just an enterprising person who has put a blanket on the sidewalk to display his wares. This forces you into the narrow streets where you compete with huge tourist buses and manic taxi drivers. The streets have very high curbs. Istanbul is not friendly to those of us with disabilities. 



None the less, we are determined to continue our visits to our favorite city so we make adaptions to manage. I take a little three-wheeled walker that I bought on Amazon for less than $80. Without the walker I can manage about one block. With the Walker I can walk a couple of miles if I rest every two or three blocks. The Walker is light enough that I can just lift it over the barriers like high curbs, transportation turnstiles, the two step entrance you often find in stores, hotels & restaurants. 



There is excellent public transportation in Istanbul. If our hotel is near a tram stop and my destination is also near the tram line it is convenient to use it. If I have to walk many blocks to reach the tram I use a taxi. We probably use a taxi at least once a day. The taxis are clean and the fares very reasonable. Tourists are often victims of taxi scams, but if you are prepared you can easily avoid their tricks. Over 99% of my taxi experiences have been pleasant. 



There are beautiful ancient buildings, hundreds of fantastic restaurants, amazing ruins, exotic markets like the Spice Bazaar and the Grand Bazaar, gracious and hospitable people who will make every effort to help you if they see you have a physical problem. 



Domestic air travel is very cheap. You can fly to Cappadocia and enjoy a sunrise over the unique geological landscape in a hot air balloon. I can no longer hike into the underground caves, but a good driver can take me near enough many places so I can see things very well. 



This country is decades away from making infrastructure changes that will make it easier for those of us with mobility issues, but the amazing hospitality of the people compensate. Turkey straddles Europe and Asia. It is a modern metropolis with very modern and trendy malls and neighborhoods. Unlike Europe, however, there are elements of the ancient Ottoman and Byzantine cultures. It is both modern and ancient. We lived in Turkey for two years, and in the last decade we have spent hundreds of days in the country. I never fail to experience an elevated heart rate when we drive along the Sea of Marmara from the airport to our hotel. Every day holds a surprising new adventure. I would obviously encourage you to investigate this amazing country.

text:
Hi folks, 

 Well my report on the wheelchair assist at Manchester Airport and Alicante! 

First Manchester - We tel called en route to the airport and the man was waiting at the doors as our minibus taxi pulled up, he set off at a high rate of knots while the rest of us some with walking problems struggled with all the bags and tried to keep up as I kept saying please wait for the rest of us as we have all the bags and can't walk fast. He went to the bag drop desk and the scales were not working properly and one lady was kicking bits back onto the weigh machine, our bags despite being weighed at home and taking the same things as we always do in the bags, were told we were overweight and had to pay £45 for another bag as that was the best way to do it. (I complained to Jet2 on their facebook page on return home but got no reply surprise surprise.)

 He then set off at a rate of knots past the security gates to a desk on the left for to register the disabled person and show his passport and boarding pass, my husband gave him £5 in the hopes it would make him more helpful he took the money and then turned back talking to the others, he was more interested in chatting with the others at the desk and turned and said well you just go down there and through the part I told you for wheelchairs, and we were left to our own devices to struggle with the bags I said but we have all the bags and some others have problems, it took us ages to get through security not because they were checking electrical stuff so god knows why they were soooooo slowww.

 The disabled person had to have his cabin bag on his knee while I struggled with mine and the wheelchair till one of my other sons took my bag as well. We didn't have time to look at the shops or go for a drink and went straight to the boarding gate, nobody came to help as they started boarding so I asked if we were getting any help she said can't you manage, we said we would have to, and then the man came to help, he set off with the wheelchair and never asked if he had a bag and just left his bag so good job he wasn't alone as the man didn't listen to him asking where his bag was, so if we had not been there the bag would have been left as he didn't listen to anyone. 



Alicante - it took ages for someone to arrive and they wouldn't let us all go together as there wasn't room on the truck thing which had wheelchairs stuck to the floor, and some people had got on before us so we were split up, not knowing what was going to happen, so I had said if we get split up make your way to bag collection which they did. 

 I went to the toilet and my husband gave the lady €5 and she then left us saying are you OK to manage. 



The return journey meant a long wait at the wheelchair assist office for someone to come to take us through. 

The hold bags were all under weight albeit only 2 bags had been on the boarding passes and I had to tell the lady that we had 3 bags under the lead passenger and 1 under my name as only 3 were allowed per passenger and that saved paying for online check in, and Jet 2 had said it would be on the booking records even if not on our boarding passes, but the bags all went through OK and a lot better that in the UK. We then set off and in fairness she did wait for the whole party when asked to slow down but at one point she said only the wheelchair and one person can go this way so the rest of you will have to go the normal way, I gave my husband his passport and boarding pass and she told them what area to head for after they got through to meet us, we all met up at that point and arranged for to be taken to the gate from that point, and a man came when the gate opened and we were taken through and he waited for the whole party the wheelchair person was left at the plane door we gave him €5 the only one that was deserved of the tip in my opinion, and we boarded and put the bags away, and the wheelchair people were boarded after everyone else had boarded.

I emailed Chris on return home but got no reply.

I can only say that of the 2 airports Alicante was the less stressful and they were a lot better than Manchester for the assistance and they have the language barrier although they did understand English.

 

I would say that if we use the service again we would not take any cabin bags, just small shoulder bags, as once we drop off the hold bags it would be much easier and less to moider about, and would also make sure everyone has their own passports and boarding passes, in case of being separated.

 Hope this helps people decide what is best to do and how to arrange things.



 I will say that it was annoying that we had to wait around 20 minutes longer at Alicante because of some people in a party and one had their own manual wheelchair and had a person in an airport wheelchair with the group and they wanted 2 assistants to push both of them, while others in the party just walked at the side of them, when one helper would have been sufficient as the one in the manual wheelchair obviously wheeled herself around normally, and did not have anything wrong which prevented her wheeling herself as some people obviously do as well as walking problems.

Carol

My trip through New England included stops in Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont and Boston. Most of the towns we visited even the small ones where accessible with a few caveats. 

1. Most of the sidewalks are inset brick which while a bit bumpy are manageable as long as they’re reasonably flat

2. Most of the inset brick sidewalks are not flat. Due to tree roots, settling and weather the sidewalks have small hills and valleys and slope. Doable, but you need to be careful.

3. Sidewalk cut-outs were plentiful except in Boston

4. Many small shops are not accessible unless you can walk in. Sometimes it is due to one or two small steps, sometimes the shop is too narrow, but mostly it’s due to the hordes of tourists.



The Portland, ME art museum (http://portlandartmuseum.org) is small, but has a nice mix of artwork and its fully accessible. We also visited the Victoria House (http://victoriamansion.org) in Portland. There is a lift in the back of the house, but only the first floor is accessible if you can’t walk. The Victoria House was interesting and had some of the first modern conveniences in Portland.



Boston was a disappointment as far as accessibility except for the subway. The subway or “T” is 90% accessible and the employees are awesome! Any MBTA (http://www.mbta.com) employee I asked a question or had any interaction with went the extra mile. Not only were they polite and friendly (and funny) many times they would walk with me to wherever I needed to go just to make sure I got to the right elevator or platform.



The streets in Boston’s historic district are bad. Again, the sidewalks are inset brick, but rarely is one flat. Gas and water connections stick up out of the sidewalk; you may have a sidewalk cutout on one side of the street, but not have a matching one on the other side of the street and there are missing bricks which leave a wheel catching hole. The Freedom Trail is in bad shape in several spots. I took a tumble on one section and my friend (very agile) nearly fell on another section. Most of the sites on the Freedom Trail are not accessible unless you can walk. I know Boston Is old and that provides its own set of problems, but frankly I was disappointed in the condition of the streets and the accessibility.



On an up note, both the Isabella Gardener Museum (http://www.gardnermuseum.org/home) and the Boston Museum of Art (http://www.mfa.org/) are fully accessible and while quite different both wonderful.



New England is lovely and I’m glad I had the opportunity to visit at such colorful time of the year. 

As for JetBlue, they were great! No problem in Seattle or in Boston and my TS was delivered within 10 minutes of the plane landing in each location.

so this might be an odd query but hopefully someone has experienced it..... The background is that my husband had radiation treatment for prostate cancer nearly 2 years ago. All went well, no side effects etc, 12 months later complications began and the upshot is that the radiation has done damage to his bladder. Im probably over thinking this, worse case he just detaches from the bag and uses a pad for the spell through security but it's a lot more cumbersome.

text: Its a long and tiring way to go for 3 days and yes you would definitely need medical travel insurance cover would never travel without it, especially with such a major pre-existing condition!

thread_title: Travel to Hong Kong with father who has dialysis
text:
You are traveling a long distance with the possibility of many variables. I wouldn't create a life or death schedule that depended upon the whims of the airline industry. Your return flight can be delayed or even cancelled. It will not matter that your father's life depends upon returning on his original schedule.



To protect yourself against these events as well as health issues that may surface you really cannot travel without health insurance. Medicare does not provide coverage outside of the US. If your father has a Medicare Advantage Plan they may provide for some foreign coverage. You should determine what coverage you have. 



Obtaining travel insurance is likely to be difficult and even a bit expensive because he has a pre-existing condition. You should start to research this as soon as possible. 



I have one final thought. This is an exhausting trip. Your father will spend over 30% of his allotted time just getting there and back. Is this trip something he truly wants to do or a treat you think he will enjoy? My husband and I are older and have some serious chronic health issues. We still travel internationally, but neither of us would consider the schedule you are suggesting. When we travel we stay at least a month. We spend at least one day recovering from jet lag. We no longer schedule marathon days of sight-seeing. We have rest breaks and occasionally even rest days. I think this itinerary is complete madness; however, if it is something he wants badly personal determination can overcome even serious physical disabilities for a short time. Just please be sure that your gift of this trip is something he wants badly enough that he can fight through the physical difficulties and still have a meaningful experience.

I am staying in a Holiday Inn where all the handicapped rooms are way in the BACK of the building. As far as possible from the. lobby, elevator, etc. Are there any ADA rules about this?

A handicapped room where you need to use an elevator? That's a new one. The ADA rules are pretty specific that those who have mobility problems need to be able to move around the facility without any steps, stairs or other abrupt level changes. In case of a fire, how would a person with mobility problems who has to utilize an elevator to get to the lobby (and in this case I'm assuming the main level) get out of the building? So in the future when you are booking a handicapped room, imho, inquire it's location. Should be main floor to be truly ADA compliant. Check out the rules at the US Dept. of Justice's website - http://www.ada.gov/hsurvey.htm
Every ADA room I have ever booked, has been on the first floor/ground floor.

My issue is how far you have to walk to get to the room. They should be near the lobby and where you have parked your car.



I have had handicapped rooms on upper floors and that does not other me as much as the long walk to the room.



Obviously, I walk - slowly with a walker. A person in a motorized device would not have to worry about distance.

My issue is how far away the rooms were from the lobby. My car was conveniently parked near the front entrance of the hotel, and the lobby. My room was the last room down a very long hall away from the lobby. There was a back door, but no handicapped parking there. A very long walk for me with my walker.



(I have stayed in handicapped room on upper floors, and I wondered about that, but I didn't mind. I felt someone would carry me down the stairs if the elevators weren't working.)

If you are staying on a floor other than ground level then you need to know where the Areas of Rescue Assistance are on that floor. Here's the ADA law "In hotels that do not have a supervised fire sprinkler system serving every room, are there two 30"x48" wheelchair waiting areas (a.k.a. an "area of rescue assistance" linked to the primary entry by intercom) at each required exit (i.e.: stairs) on levels above or below the ground floor for persons with disabilities who cannot exit the building in case of a fire or emergency? [ADA Stds. 4.1.3(9)]" 



I would not expect the staff to come to your assistance. Hopefully you are traveling with someone who is able to carry you or I would not take a room that requires you to do stairs in an emergency. Also if you can't walk very far you may be better off in a non-handicapped room if you can walk. Many hotels now have walk-in showers (no tubs) and you could find these rooms sufficient for your use.

thread_title: Hotel didn't mention there was no lift and refuse to refund.
text:
When you book with a 3rd party booking company you are contacting someone in a cubicle or little office who probably has a notebook/online screen with some information about the hotel (much like what you would see online). They are not at the hotel. They may never have been to that hotel or even in that country. But when you contact the hotel directly then you can ask important questions. 



I noticed when I looked at the hotel's website that they are a "budget" hotel. That would indicate to me that they probably would not have spent the money to put in a lift, since that is an expensive part of construction. 



You can call the hotel directly and mention the rate you saw online with a 3rd party - sometimes they match it. But sometimes the 3rd party rooms are the ones that they have a tough time renting out. The ones on the top floor when there isn't a lift or the room next to the trash bins that get emptied at 3 am or that overlook the cooling towers that rumble all night long. There's a reason for getting a cheap rate sometimes.

It was not mentioned in the hotel info that there was no lift, the building is a least 4 or 5 stories high. I cancelled more than 24 hours prior to the date of stay. They retained my payment, £119 for one night and refused a refund. Booking.com contacted the hotel, who claimed the hotel was overbooked that night so they wouldn't issue a refund. I understand overbooked rooms, where I wouldn't be guaranteed a room despite them having already taken my payment, is a breach of contract. I find that many stepfree or wheelchair accessible hotels have impossible ramps and tiny lifts.

My only choice was to let my foot drag on the ground or stand up in the footrests (on my surgery knee) and held myself off the chair with my arms for the 30 minutes it took to get to the gate. 



I'll be doing the same procedure in January. How do I avoid this problem next time?

thread_title: Going through airport with a knee replacement
text: Is your knee still not bending? My husband had a knee replacement and was up and walking the next day. Few weeks of PT at home and then a few more weeks at their office. But even from the first week his knee was able to bend. I hope there wasn't a problem with the surgery. You should be able to bend your knee for placement on the W/C footrests now. Best of luck and a speedy, full recovery.

thread_title: Going through airport with a knee replacement
text:
I was able to bend my knee immediately after surgery. It took some weeks of PT to get full range-of-motion when I had to kick my leg forward, but no problem with a natural bend. I didn't use a wheelchair extensively at that time but I had no difficulty sitting in any type of chair, and this was 20 years ago. Replacement technology has improved dramatically since then. 



What you are describing sounds absolutely horrific, but I have never heard of the problem before. I think you need to discuss this situation with your PT and your doctor.

thread_title: COPD, oxygen and travel insurance; information
text:
This information may be different to what applies in other countries but I thought I would sound a warning at least for fellow Australians.



We took a long trip this year and paid additional insurance fees to have husband's COPD covered. At the last minute, well after we took out the insurance, his doctor prescribed oxygen for the flights. The original policy still stood. All went well with a hired oxygen concentrator and 6 battery packs.



We were planning a trip to Alaska and the Rockies for 2015. We thought the same insurer would cover us again, but no, the prescription of oxygen for the flight now means he cannot be insured for anything related to his lung disease. We have not been able to find a single insurer who will cover him for the COPD now.



Luckily we hadn't paid any deposits though we were within a whisker of paying the airfares last week. Possible hospitalisation in the USA without medical insurance doesn't bear thinking about. It would wipe us out financially.



Moral: If you intend to fly with a medical issue, get approved for the insurance first, before making any downpayments.

We declared: husband Osteoarthritis which had required treatment for his back in the past. No treatment in almost 20 yrs (more than reqd min). Husband had a mini stroke ~22 yrs ago, nothing since, again answered all Qs correctly. Me: Osteoarthritis (knees, though they do not differentiate). No treatment, medication etc etc. Gallbladder removal Jan 2012 (they ask if any probs in last 3 weeks)
