Husband was told he had COPD last August after actually being referred for his excessive snoring. We are still not sure which type (apparently there are several types, but the registrar was dismissive and our Doc has not yet had the letter.....) I mention this as the specialist COPD insurers ask which type of COPD.



Now, some insurers ask for ANY condition, some only in the last 2 yrs, some last 5 yrs. I'd rather be totally honest. My gallbladder removal was in Jan 2012, so 4 yrs ago. The 3 week question is crazy when it was so long ago, and any further issues are well in the past? Hubbys mini stroke was 22 yrs ago, and several Doctors have cast doubt on diagnosis since. 



I am well aware I have osteoarthritis in knees, and declare it. It runs in my family, and I have lived with a certain amount of pain since age 14. I am now almost 39, and know I cannot get a knee replacement until age 50 in UK. Regardless, I graft daily and do not need physios to tell me that regular exercise will prolong joint life, not only cos I keep active but also due to family history and their replacements. (Great Gran was 96 when she had her last one, and was only accepted as she was SO active!)



Same for hubby, osteoarthritis of spine, diagnosed 25 yrs ago, told to expect a wheelchair within 10 yrs. We currently run several pubs, and my hubby knows to look after himself and maintain his core muscles to protect his back. 



Is there actually ANY insurance company that actually takes into account lifetsyle rather than just diagnosis? We've tried all the ones above but our premium has gone from £16.67 to £180 with hubbys COPD diagnosis(the only difference other than date of travel). We've obviously been honest, and there is only 1 site that has asked for details of medication rather than just condition. Just despair of getting reasonable cover tbh

text:
Hi there,

I recently did Turkey, Greece, Israel, Egypt, Jordan, Oman, and the UAE with my father in a lightweight wheelchair. While we did cruise part of the time, our excursions and day trips I booked with Toursbylocals.com. You can search their site for wheelchair accessible tours (look for the big, blue wheelchair symbol) or choose a guide and create your own customized tour based on your needs and limitations. I didn't know what to expect with a different guide in each country, but every single person was fabulous, without exception. All their tours are private, but if you have 2-3 people, not much more that you would pay for a large group tour per person. Because it's JUST your group, you can make whatever accommodations you need to make sure your disabled family/friend has an awesome time and participate in everything. Also, because the person is LOCAL, they probably already know all of what it needed, like whether something is wheelchair accessible or not, and how easy/difficult a given site is. I can not recommend this highly enough, our experiences in some very challenging areas of the world were superb. Please feel free to ask me more if needed. Also, feel free to call the customer service folks at Toursbylocals as well, they were super helpful for me.

I travel internationally with my father who can walk very little and uses a lightweight wheelchair. First, please don't take the airlines BS that someone HAS to sit in a given seat due to a disability. YOU tell THEM what will work for you and they accommodate, call in person, ask to speak to a reservations manager, be insistent when necessary. That being said, as far as getting to the bathroom, explain the situation and demand a seat that will give them access. Use these words: "Anything else is completely unacceptable." If someone needs assistance in the restroom, meaning they need help with personal hygiene, that is where you and a flight attendant come in. There is no rule that the bathroom door has to be shut when someone is in there. Bring your loved one back to the rear or obtain permission to use the first class (front-most) bathroom. Put your loved one on the throne and leave the door open so you can assist them. The job of the flight attendant is to make sure you are not disturbed and the privacy of your loved one is not compromised. Explain what you need in detail to a flight attendant when you board and recruit their help then so you are ready when your loved one is ready to go. Please feel free to ask more questions, I will answer if I can help.

thread_title: UPDATE:Traveling with refrigerated liquid meds/TSA & Hotels
text:
Back from Las Vegas vacation and wanted to update everyone on how TSA and the hotels handled my med situation.



I had traveled to Phoenix first then Vegas, so for this three week vacation I had three flights. I let TSA know at each check that I had liquid medication with a ice pack in my carryon. On not one of the flights did they need to see it. On one flight they told the person scanning my bag that I had medicine and a cooler pack in the bag. I was pre-check on two of these flights, even after telling TSA about my meds.



Luxor Hotel Casino in Las Vegas - I called ahead of time to request a refrigerator for my meds. They told me that there would be a $25 charge per day.



Fremont Hotel Casino in Las Vegas - When I called and requested a refrigerator, they told me that they had to say that they would charge me, but that they wouldn't. 



When I checked out of the Luxor, I asked if my "play" would comp the charges for the fridge and told her that I had not planned on needing one, but was prescribed these meds just before I left for vacation. She talked to her manager and rather than remove the fee for the refrigerator, they took off most of the resort fee ($28 a night) So, I ended up paying nothing for the fridge.



When I checked out of the Fremont, there was no charge for the refrigerator.



So, for all the worry and pre-planning, it all ended up being a non-issue - but I am glad that I did my homework and knew what to expect. Thanks to all those that helped me through this, especially Keshgrammy!

text: We are flying to Mexico on Delta through Atlanta. thread_title: can I carry on a wheelchair on Delta
text:
The U.S. government requires that airplanes with more than 100 seats must have a space inside the cabin for a foldable wheelchair to be stowed. Here is some more information:



http://wheelchairtravel.org/summary-of-your-rights-under-the-air-carrier-access-act/

thread_title: can I carry on a wheelchair on Delta
text:
Delta is very good with wheelchairs, and they do have limited space on the plane to store small collapsible chairs. I am not sure why you need to have the chair on the plane. You cannot use it on the actual plane because the aisles are too narrow. If your mother-in-law cannot walk at all you will need to make arrangemens with Delta to use a special aisle chair.



We take our mobility scooters of power wheelchairs to the door of the plane. We are both able to walk from the door to our assigned seats. When our flight lands, the chairs are delivered right to the door of the plane. We never have to take a step in the airport. Unless she is limited to a wheelchair all of the time I would opt to use it to the door, have them store in it the cargo hold and deliver it back to you when you arrive.

thread_title: can I carry on a wheelchair on Delta
text:
There are many reasons to stow the wheelchair in the aircraft's cabin. Foremost, it protects the wheelchair from damage. On international flights, it is not standard practice to return gate-checked wheelchairs to the door. The space exists for wheelchair stowage and is guaranteed by the ACAA.



If you travel internationally with a powered chair or scooter, you must be aware that it is often a fight to have it returned to the jetway, even at major hubs such as AMS and NRT. I have seen the same struggle for others with standard wheelchairs.

45 minutes more of desperate passengers, pointing to their boarding passes, pleading to be taken to their planes, some in tears, Flimsy wheelchairs finally arrived, manned by greasy shirted grounds crew men. hoping I'm not too late with this posting. I travelled to Italy (Rome and Florence) this time last year in a power wheelchair. I thoroughly recommend booking a customised tour with Rome connections. My husband has MS. He uses no canes in the house; one cane for shopping, etc, and 2 canes when we travel taking tours, on cobblestones, etc. On longer walking tours , he needs to rest occasionally. We have taken 5 river cruises all with Uniworld. He can manage steps providing there is a handrail. I'm his extra support on wide staircases without hand rails. If an excursion seems too daunting, we stay on the ship or visit the local town or village. Our recent experiences. We are in Australia so things may differ for you.

This all happened within the last month before we flew out on a 12 week trip, so a bit of a nightmare. Especially as we had 8 flights and 4 different carriers.



Our specialist really knew nothing about the intricacies of obtaining oxygen in flight. He assumed it was automatic and free when you asked.



Airlines all have support staff who will provide you with the paperwork required to submit to them. You can often find this on-line as well. You MUST have their knowledge and approval to use oxygen in flight.

Dr's letter as already outlined.



Very few airlines provide oxygen cylinders for free. I think Emirates does. Otherwise it is at your expense and sometimes also an additional seat for the cylinder.



There are portable oxygen concentrators (POCs) which can usually be hired from a medical gases company. You will also need enough battery power for 150% of the length of the longest air trip in case of delays. This solution was a godsend for us.



Only a very few airlines allow you to plug in the POC, most insist on battery power.

Only some POCs are approved for use on airlines.



We used the Airsep Freestyle which is approved. It comes as a small box and with battery belts and rechargers. We needed 6 belt packs for our longest flight, Vancouver to Sydney. We stored the equipment in 2 backpacks, each ended up weighing about 5kg.



The airlines are obliged to allow you to carry these for free as medical equipment, in addition to your normal carry-on baggage, but not obliged to provide you with power, hence the need for batteries. We labelled the bags prominently as "Medical equipment required on flight"



For a 12 week trip we paid $1250 in hire fees.



Only once, at one security check, were we asked to open the bag of batteries, and once at check-in the woman asked to see the batteries. Otherwise we sailed through despite all the fuss with getting permission to begin with.



I can see no reason at all why the hotel needs to know. Of course if you need it in the hotel you will need it walking around and so a portable, small system seems the way to go.



Now for the nasty bit.

We had trip insurance. We advised the insurer that N now needed oxygen in flight and that was fine, though they wouldn't insure the equipment itself. We got that covered by our home contents insurance.



Then we were just about to pay for a trip for next year and checked. No one will insure him for another flight because he now requires oxygen in flight. Full stop. As the holiday was to Canada and the USA, who have no reciprocal medical agreement with Australia, we cannot take the risk of going and perhaps incurring ruinous expenses if N needs hospitalisation (which he hasn't ever for this condition but forseeably might somewhere down the track.)



I hope the system there works well for you and that our experiences help if things aren't quite so straightforward. I also hope the insurance thing is better in the UK than it is for us here in OZ.

Happy travels

Lynn

We spend part of every year in Istanbul and have done so for many years. It is not a city with friendly infrastructure. I do not take my chair because there is simply no way to manage the high curbs and numerous other obstacles. I use my walker & depend on taxis for door-to-door service. Taxis are very economical. There are some annoying scams, but if you pay your fare in exact change you will have no problem. Read the Istanbul forum for more detailed explanations. When I can no longer survive with my Walker I will just eliminate using public transportation & use taxis exclusively. 



Many hotels are old Ottoman buildings that have been converted to boutique hotels. Many of them have no elevators. I would try to find a property with an elevator. There will still probably be a few steps to handle, but a very helpful hotel staff will help you manage. I recommend the Sirkeci Mansion or the Neorion. These are four star moderately priced hotels. 



While the infrastructure is poor, the warm hospitality of the Turkish people compensates. When I see a person in a wheelchair I always see a few strangers pop up to help the disabled person around any physical barrier. 



Istanbul is significantly more difficult than Rome. We used our chairs there with no problem save the tiny size of the elevators. Expect a greater challenge in Istanbul, but know that the magical experience here will compensate for the inconveniences.

Taxis looking more and more attractive as a way to get around! Definitely looking to stay in a hotel in a newer building given what I've read. Almost there with a booking. Just making a few final checks on the hotel. (My travel agent is really good with that sort of thing. They really go the extra mile for me there).

We spent two months in Istanbulnlast fall, and I used a taxi at least once every day with no difficulties. New visitors seem to have some difficulties. Drivers accept your money and then quickly switch it for less so your 50'TL note suddenly becomes a 5 TL note. I keep lots of small bills to pay my fare in exact change. If you need change you become vulnerable to this scam. I also determine the cost of the trip before I take a taxi. There are several web sites with this information. I do not pay a fare greater than 20% more than the correct fare. I ask my hotel to call my taxi because there is less of a chance these drivers will be dishonest. Some of my most enjoyable experiences in Istanbul have been with taxi drivers. I am not remotely intimidated by them. 



There is now a taxi app similar to Uber in Istanbul. I have not used it because my iPhone does not work in Turkey, but people who have used it report great success. If you go to the Istanbul forum and put "taxi scam" into the search block you can get web sites that will give you estimated taxi fares. You will read many accounts that report unpleasant events, but remember that no one writes about a good experience. There are over 20,000 taxis working 24 hours each day, and when you think about this huge number the complaints are not exceptionally significant. 



I hope you will let us know how you manage with your clever chair. It is a challenging, but very much worth the effort.

thread_title: oxygen and air travel within the US & abroad
text:
I travelled round the world with a POC last year, so have some experience.



All airlines will make arrangements for a POC, but the details vary and you will need to consult the web sites of the airlines you intend to use.



Qantas allowed me to plug the POC into the aircraft''s power outlet, but Swiss and Air Canada insisted that I had to use battery power, with Air Canada saying I had to have enough batteries for 150% of the scheduled (trans-Pacific) flight time.



We carried the POC and batteries in 2 backpacks, and had no problems with Security during our journeys. One security person asked to see inside one of the backpacks, saw it had the batteries, and sent us on our way.



in mainland Europe, Customs formalities usually consist of walking through a doorway labelled "Nothing to declare". Once your luggage has entered the EU, there are no further Customs formalities when crossing EU borders.

thread_title: oxygen and air travel within the US & abroad
text:
Just be aware that it may be very difficult to get travel insurance for anything connected with her use of oxygen and I strongly recommend you check this before booking tickets.

It is against the law in America for any airline flying into or out of the US to refuse to carry POCs that are approved but the airline does not have to provide power to these devices. We hired both the POC and sufficient batteries. (Sydneynick and I are a couple)

text:
In addition to insurance demands, renting a vehicle from a mobility company will be exceptionally expensive. I think your most cost-effective solution is to rent an SUV and rent or buy some ramps to help you load your wheelchair and your scooter. My husband and I deliberately selected very portable electric mobility scooters so we can travel with them. They come apart, and no part weighs more than 25 pounds. I can manage my scooter completely on my own, both putting it together, taking it apart and stowing it in the car.



When we travel in US we are able to manage with either a regular (not compact) passenger car. If a small SUV is available for not a significantly greater cost we select that because we can just load our scooters inside without taking them apart. Even completely together we can easily lift a scooter into an SUV.



I assume that you are traveling with very heavy wheelchairs and scooters, so there is no way to get these units into a vehicle without a ramp. Do the car rental companies have the names of any local places where you could rent or purchase a ramp? We do have ramps, which would work for our scooters but are not needed. We purchased them for under $100 from a medical supply house.



You might go to the St. Louis Forum and see if anyone there can get any information on renting or purchasing ramps that will make as SUV workable for you.



Even if you had to pay $200 to $300 for ramps, it would still be less expensive than going through a mobility service. Hopefully you could find someone who would deliver them to the car rental facility for you.



This is a tough request. We really do not have car rental companies that provide transportation for wheelchairs and scooters. Good luck!

thread_title: Dealing with TSA when you have an ostomy
text:
I am not convinced that any form of written information about your disability is useful when moving through TSA. As one TSA official once explained to me: If a terrorist is going to hide himself behind a disability would not he produce a perfect counterfeit piece of documentation to explain that condition? My doctors no longer even provide cards or letters because they are useless for TSA purposes; although I still carry letters when I travel in the event I should need some emergency medical care while traveling.



I am not sure why you felt you were treated as a cripple. TSA is not famous for their sensitive management of the full range of disabilities that travelers have. Most of these people have no more than a high school education, and minimal amount of training time. They are often rushed and pressured to move people through lines quickly while trying to be aware of potential threats. I try not to take offense at any way I am treated so long as my basic physical needs are met.



I suppose that technically I am a cripple. TSA agents are generally sympathetic to my needs, but they do not make me feel less significant as a person. I absolutely detest the invasive pat-down procedure, which I think would be a sexual assault in any other setting. I try to avoid pat downs whenever possible, opting for the screening circle when I set off the metal detector.



I do not have huge expectations for my TSA experience. If I can move through the line fairly swiftly and keep people from grabbing my naked skin beneath my underwear I feel as if the process has been successful. I do not let the way other people treat me define me, and neither should you. I agree with the previous poster that you should read the TSA web site, and if you are not completely informed, make a phone call and ask for the proper TSA procedure for someone in your situation. This does not mean that a TSA person will follow protocol, but at least you will know what is supposed to happen.



I elect not to be offended as I move through TSA. There are frequent circumstances where I feel a complaint to someone in a supervisory position would be justified. I just do not go to this place in my head. TSA is something I endure so I get to fly on a plane and enjoy the benefits of travel. Like root canal therapy or the day after Christmas at Walmart, I just endure because that is the quickest way for me to clear the area and go to the gate for my flight.

thread_title: Review: Gatwick and Funchal Airports using Easyjet and...
text:
This is a review rather than a question, but I couldn't find anywhere else on tripadvisor to review the 'interesting' experience of travelling with a wheelchair user at Gatwick/Funchal Airports with Easyjet.



I recently accompanied my parents on a trip to Madeira flying from/to Gatwick (MS-sufferer mum in wheelchair, can't move without assistance, can only stay on her feet with great difficulty and with assistance). I had spent much time beforehand emailing the airline (Easyjet) about her needs and was expecting the worst but hoping for the best. 



We checked-in online and the bag drop at the airport went smoothly. We were then directed to the Special Assistance desk at the South terminal. We advised that we didn't need assistance with wheelchair pushing as mum has her own wheelchair (dad was pushing and I had the hand baggage). That was our first mistake.



Our second mistake was to try and use the oh-so-state-of-the-art disabled loo ground-side. After a 10 minute wait Easyjet's (able-bodied) check-in agent finally exited the facility and informed us that the (automatic) door was broken. Thanks for that.



We then joined the queue at the 'special assistance' lane through security. We should have requested a wheelchair pusher as those lucky few who did leapt the (long) queue of families-with-screaming-toddlers. Queuing and security checks are a necessary part of airline travel but why the need to herd elderly, frail and/or disabled people through a process akin to a school-holiday, superstore check-out?



Mum (and wheelchair) were frisked as usual but, other than that, we made it airside safely. Then the fun began with Frankie and Benny's 'fast food' restaurant. I've reviewed this elsewhere but, for the record, avoid it unless you like slow, cumbersome lifts and have hours to kill (we didn't).



We had allowed plenty of time to eat (but not at Frankie and Benny's) so arrived at the boarding gate later than we had planned. Luckily our aircraft was boarding via an extending walkway (although we had requested the ambulift via Easyjet just in case). Wheelchair to the plane door was simple and then the fun started with moving mum into her seat. I had requested the 'aisle' wheelchair to facilitate this but mum refused to use it (it's designed for those who are blessed with a petite build so don't bother unless you are under 5 feet tall and weigh less than 100 pounds). We therefore had to support mum with walking (at her usual snail's pace) to her seat. Mum hates to stand in public as she feels like a spectacle and, in this case, she certainly provided a diversion for the couple of hundred passengers already seated on the plane.



Thankfully we boarded from the front of the plane and had booked seats in row 2. Only on the return flight did we discover that we could have booked row 1 as the extra leg room (seats 1 E and F on this route) are not in the emergency exit. Knowing this would have been a life-saver as transferring someone who can't stand/walk unaided into an aisle seat with fixed arms (and two people seated inside of her who need strong bladders as they will be stuck in their seats for the duration) isn't something I would recommend. 



Note that international rules prevent disabled people from 'blocking' the emergency exit rows on aircraft so the extra legroom seats are usually unavailable. In future on this route I shall contact the airline and request one of these row 1 seats immediately before online check-in opens. Note that online check-in doesn't inform you of this fact - and nobody from the airline advised us before we boarded. I am therefore deeply grateful to the crew on the return flight for telling us. It's a piece of cake to transfer a disabled person into a seat with extra legroom space in front and ironic that such seats are usually unavailable to them.



Easyjet staff were as helpful as they could be during both flights (given that they are not trained, nor expected, to provide specialist help) but were especially so on our return from Funchal four weeks later. 



Thanks to requesting the ambulift, disembarking at Funchal was straightforward. Their lift is a motorised vehicle which provides a short ramp from the airline door to the passenger cabin of the vehicle. It requires a short (assisted) walk or seated transfer using the aisle wheelchair. Passengers are then transported in this vehicle directly to the terminal. We were provided with a wheelchair pusher at Funchal (not specifically requested) from the point of arrival and he ensured that passport control and baggage collection went smoothly. The Special Assistance staff at Funchal couldn't have been more helpful or friendly. What a contrast to Gatwick!



Note that the ambulift at Funchal isn't guaranteed and you MUST request it in advance (via your airline) for those who are unable to walk. I couldn't help but notice that several passengers cheekily took advantage of this facility to avoid walking/queuing through the airport. Note to the cheeky: there is a reason that the disabled need these facilities and, by abusing them, you are adversely impacting facilities and services provided for those in genuine need. 



Our departure from Funchal was as well-organised by the airport as was our arrival. The hire car company (Avis) kindly met us outside the departure terminal so we were able to avoid the walk from the car park with mum/wheelchair/walking frame/6 pieces of luggage (in unseasonable rain). We immediately went to the Special Assistance desk (on the far right rear of the terminal) and the agent escorted us from there (including pushing wheelchair) through baggage drop and security. No queuing, no hassle. Bliss. He left us in an area designated for disabled passengers (with seats for their carers) and asked us to go to security as soon as announced. We were met at security by another agent who took us through security and to the gate. From the gate we were transported via the ambulift vehicle onto the plane before the remaining passengers boarded (this sparing mum's dignity during her awkward transfer to her seat).



Mum was allowed to transfer to the empty 1E seat next to dad during the flight (much to my 'relief' and that of window seat passenger also seated in row 3) and the airline staff were helpful and friendly throughout.



Then we arrived at Gatwick - at 9p.m. - in the driving rain and wind and cold. 



Unexpectedly the aircraft parked on the apron so the Gatwick ambulift arrived to disembark mum (and a few extras of both the genuine and cheeky variety). This lift isn't a vehicle so requires a transfer from both plane to the lift via an 'open-air' 3-metre ramp to the passenger cabin, and also from another external lift to the ground. At mum's 'walking' pace she was quickly drenched during stage one of this process. This lengthy and cumbersome process was not helped by the need to retrieve her wheelchair from the hold and assemble it before she could be transferred to the mini-van. Yes folks, a mini-van. This apparently is the best one of UK's largest airports could provide. The walking wounded had to to step up into the vehicle (so much for mobility problems) whilst mum waited (in the rain) to use the wheelchair lift at the back.



We were driven the short distance to the terminal and the walking wounded were loaded onto a buggy. Only one airline agent accompanied us and he was needed to drive the buggy so we (soaked, exhausted) were dismissed with a hand wave in the general direction of passport control and told to go through the 'Special Assistance' lane. We found it eventually but the lane was closed off so I approached an airline official to ask if we could use it. She undid the tape without a word and, stony-faced, escorted us along the lane to the desks where we were told to 'wait for the next available security officer' at passport control. Luckily we avoided the queue this way but more by accident than design.



Our bags were the only ones remaining on the carousel by the time we arrived in the vast baggage collection hall. Then we discovered that mum's (checked) walking-frame was missing. Cue: a long walk to the other side of the hall to baggage information. Cue: a long wait there whilst they tracked down the frame. The dismissive agent who met us at the plane had taken it on the buggy with the walking wounded (against airline procedure) as he had 'assumed that it belonged to the elderly gent with the walking stick'. It was eventually returned to us the other side of customs by the same agent. His belated jollity at his mistake was somewhat lost on me at this point and I admit to being short with him to the point of rudeness.



Summary: 

1) If you are disabled you will do well flying Easyjet but make sure that you communicate with the airline in advance re: your requirements. Don't bother phoning Customer Services (they never answer) but email them. They reply quickly and are very helpful and efficient.

2) Avoid flying to/from Gatwick if you can. It is the antithesis of disabled-friendly.

3) Take your own food rather than eat in Gatwick's terminal. The departure lounge is overcrowded, noisy and difficult to negotiate. The one good thing being the disabled loos (clean and well-equipped)

4) Always pre-order the ambulift via your airline if you are genuinely immobile. Airports and airline disabled facilities are abused by so many mobile passengers that there is an assumption of mobility unless you contact them directly.

5) Funchal is a model of facilities for disabled passengers but emphasise your need for the ambulift when you book your flight, and again directly to the airline, and again on check-in. The alternative will be a manual lift (in wheelchair) off/on the plane.

6) Easyjet are good-to-excellent with disabled passengers but engage with them directly in advance to ensure your trip runs smoothly.

7) Avis in Funchal were very helpful when we left. Make sure you hire a car that is big enough to take all luggage and mobility aids (we had a Renault Megane). It will be expensive but worth it.

We are planning to visit Greece and Istanbul in Sep. I walk short distances with crutches but use a small size scooter for long distances. Can anyone recommend a hotel at a good location with accessibility to the tourist attractions and not too pricey in Istanbul. Will I able to ride my scooter to the attractions? Rent a taxi or use public transportation? Any private tours? 

I am planning to take a 4 day Louis Cruise of the Greece Islands. Will I be able to go to the excursions in my scooter? Is it better for us to take a private excursions? Can anyone recommend any private excursions contact info. Thank you all.

I cannot comment on Greece, but I have spent hundreds of days in Istanbul in the last decade, and a couple of years in Turkey 40 years ago. Turkey has made huge changes in the last 50 years. I recognize virtually nothing from the years we lived there except for the historical buildings and sights; however, the one thing that has not changed is the infrastructure.



I also can walk for only short distances, usually not more than a couple of blocks. I use a cane, but in every other location except Turkey I use an electric wheelchair or a mobility scooter. I have taken my scooter all over in Europe with differing levels of success. I have never attempted to take either of these in Istanbul. The streets are cobblestone, The curbs are impossibly high. The sidewalks may just disappear if a restaurant converts the space in front into sidewalk dining or some one has rolled out a blanket, set out his wares and is operating a small retail operation. This forces you into a narrow street where you try to avoid crazy taxi drivers and gigantic tour buses.



Most of the economical hotels in the old city have lots of stairs, and only a few have elevators. While I have seen elevators in the historic buildings, I have never seen one that worked. Even some of the newly constructed buildings do not have facilities that are designed for people with disabilities.



To make this even more difficult, Istanbul is built on hills, so it seems as if you are always walking up an incline or down one. Down is physically easier for me, but up is safer as I tend not to trip on cobblestones while walking down.



There is a good public transportation system in Istanbul, and if Turkish people notice that you have a disability they will quickly give you a seat. Public transportation is not, however, designed for us. At some tram stops there is absolutely no way for a wheelchair or mobility scooter to even get through the entrance to wait for the tram. The more modern Metro is easier to use. I have been told that there are some kneeling buses in the city, but I have never seen one.



I rarely see anyone with walking issues on the street. We were in Istanbul for November and December. I saw one man with a mobility scooter in the Grand Bazaar, which does not have serious barriers. I saw one man with a regular wheelchair, and his friends were helping him by lifting him and his chair over the obstacles. I think most people in Istanbul with disability issues are confined to their immediate neighborhood, and possibly even in their own homes.



I chose not to stop traveling to Turkey, so I make things work for me as well as possible. If I know I am going to have a day involving much walking I always premedicate. I look carefully at my map and plan each step. I hate wasting precious steps wandering in the wrong direction, so I simply never get lost.



If I am going to have to walk I plan on stopping every two blocks. Often I can find a public bench, and over the years I know where these are located. On other occasions, I just stop and a shop owner rushes out with a chair. Often more than one shop owner comes with a chair. Occasionally I stop to rest in a tea house. I do not push any longer than two blocks because my objective is to endure the experience as much as possible.



Turkish people are very hospitable and very helpful. A couple of years ago I got into a situation where there was construction, and there was a large hole in front of me that other people were managing by walking over it using a plank. Three big men just grabbed my arms and lifted me over the barrier. They do everything they can to help you. I have had people walk into the street and stop traffic so I could pass.



When my hotel and my destination are very close to public transportation I use public transportation. I much prefer, however, to have door-to-door service, and I make generous use of the taxi system. There is an abundance of taxis in Istanbul (except during a rain storm) and they are inexpensive. If you decide to go to Turkey you should PM me for taxi tips. Like any huge city, there are a few scams that take advantage of a new visitor. You should not be afraid of using a taxi. The vast majority of drivers are honest and helpful.



This year I did something I have not down before. I took a little three-wheeled walker because my husband begged me to try it. I knew it would not work, but I ordered it anyway. It was so light and flimsy I did not think it could begin to improve my ability to walk. I was amazed to discover how much easier it was with the walker. I could walk much longer with the walker......sometimes as much as 1/2 mile without a rest stop. I was also about twice as fast. I often left the rest of my party behind me. The fact that the walker was so light permitted me to just lift it up and over the high curbs. I set the brake and had a steady guide when stepping over the curbs myself.



For the first time in several years we were able to leave Istanbul and visit more primitive areas. We went to Eastern Turkey, often as near as 5 miles to the Syrian border, and had many experiences in villages that had absolutely no facilities for disabled people. I struggled at times, but I managed to see things I have dreamed of visiting for years.



I do not know if this walker would help you. I purchased it from Amazon. It is called the Minnie and this is the link http://www.amazon.com/s/ref=nb_sb_ss_c_0_18?url=search-alias%3Dhpc&field-keywords=three%20wheeled%20walker&sprefix=three+wheeled+walk%2Caps%2C323



I have seen this exact same walker for sale in my local drug stores, but it was twice as expensive.



If you cannot manage a walker, you should take your crutches, plan your trips, use public transportation when possible and save steps by using a taxi when necessary. Be sure to take extra tips for your crutches. The cobblestones eat those tips in about a week. Probably sooner if you use them extensively.



My philosophy is that I am going to continue to travel so long as I can manage to get myself around regardless of how slow I am, or how awkward I appear. I am able to manage a medium to serious level of pain if I am doing something I really want to do. I am nearly 70 years old, and I do not have a long time in front of me to experience the places I wish to visit. I am not ready to spend the rest of my life sitting on my front porch in a rocking chair.
Thank you so much for giving me an insight. Can you please advise which hotel do you stay in.

When we were in Istanbul, we stayed at the Adamar Hotel. It's as good as it can get. The elevator worked all the time and the observation top deck is to die for. Have a look at their web site for the photos. To Sophia(2 blocks), Blue Mosque(6 blocks), the Sistern(1 block)and the nearby main street and a series of restaurants(1 block), Grand Bazaar(6 blocks), it's level ground or close to it. For location, you can't get any better. If you book there, pick a room at the front, as it is much bigger than any other rooms, which is an oval shaped room with 2 beds shown of their photos.

For convenience my favorite hotel in Istanbul is the Sirkeci Mansion or Sirkeci Konak. They are in the process of changing their name. They have lovely rooms that include virtually everything you would find in a five star property. There is a good sized reliable elevator. They are one-half block from the tram stop, and the immediate neighborhood has wonderful restaurants and shops on level pavement. I do not think there is an easier place for a person with a disability to stay than this hotel. The staff is also absolutely amazing.

I own a lightweight mobility scooter but haven't traveled with it yet. I walk short distances and go up or down a few steps, and the rest of the time my husband pushes me in a very light folding wheelchair. We made travel arrangements through Sage Traveling, which specializes in accessible travel in Europe (and Turkey). We were staying in Istanbul only one night before boarding our cruise ship where we would spend another night before setting sail. Sage listed for us three possible hotels with accessible rooms, and since we were spending only one night on land, we decided to book a room at the Golden Horn Sultanahmet Hotel so that we could soak up the atmosphere of the old city. We were very pleased with our choice. The room was comfortable, the elevator was reliable, and the view from the top floor breakfast room (also open in the evening for drinks and snacks) has to be one of the most spectacular in all of Istanbul.

Through Sage we arranged for a private full-day tour of Istanbul before we set sail, and we were well satisfied with the guide's skill in showing us the easiest ways to see many of the fascinating sights of the city. Before we boarded the ship, we went by taxi to one thing we wanted to see that we knew would not be on the tour, and that worked well, too. The hotel called a cab and arranged that it would also pick us up for the return trip after we had spent an hour at the site.

If you visit things on your own, we recommend going to the Basilica Cistern. If you enter through the exit rather than the entrance, there is a wheelchair lift available, but some people miss visiting because they don't know about the lift.

In addition to listing the tours they can provide, the Sate Traveling website has very good accessibility information for Istanbul and also for Athens.

What ports will you be visiting on the four-day cruise? I know of accessible tour possibilities for a few places.

Hi I had a wonderful time in Singapore and I did go on the MRT trains. The first thing I did wrong was try to ride straight onto the train when a door opened. NO - you must make sure there are the disabled stickers because those doors are flat for easy riding straight on and off. Once I realised this never had any problems getting on and off trains. It did take us about half an hour to get out of Bayfront station and at one stage finished up in the staff quarters. The lifts are sort of scattered about and there is the Metro Station, a casino and a shopping centre and I managed to find all of them before I found the exit I needed. The signs told you what floor you needed but I didn't realise you might be on the right floor but could be in the casino, shopping centre or one of the ways out so you needed to go back to the lift down to the other floor go to a different lift on that floor that would get you to the exit. I was confused but I'm sure that if I went again I'd find my way ok. Everyone was helpful and it is an easy way to get around the city. 



The bus stop wasn't really close to our hotel but we were told many of the buses including the hop on buses would be OK for my scooter. 



Mostly though we did take taxis as they were very reasonably priced between £4 - £7 pounds. My husband could lift the scooter into the taxis and the taxi drivers were very helpful. The MRT trains would be ok even if you were on your own they are well laid out. It was quite a way to our nearest metro station but they are now building a new one right near our hotel.

The Disability Discrimination Act in Australia has laid down certain rights

https://www.humanrights.gov.au/dda-guide-ins-and-outs-access

Just as a general knowledge thing

Curb cuts are everywhere, city and suburbs.

Most buses are accessible. Many train stations have lifts and the platform staff use ramps to assist people on and off. This may need to be planned in advance.

There is a good selection of drive-in accessible taxis

All attractions should have accessible toilets and accessible entrances and pathways

Most big shopping malls have scooters available at their offices

There should be accessible areas in theatres. The opera house is a bit difficult as it doesn't have an elevator to the higher seating areas but entrance to the floor area in front of the stage is possible for the main theatre.

Many restaurants are accessible but not all will have accessible toilets (like up 6 stairs out the back)

Some older premises will not have been modified.



Seeing people on mobility scooters is common. If you hold an International Parking Permit that will be accepted in all Australian States except Victoria, which issues a temporary pass. This info may help also

http://www.disabledmotorists.eu/en/world_map/oceania/oceania_new_zealand_and_australia.htm



Have a great holiday

Lynn

Hi,

I have PPMS and use a powerchair and a frame to transfer form chair to seat / bed etc.

I am starting to plan for a holiday aboard, and wondered if anyone has any advice / experience about how I would be supported at the airport and during the flight. I ideally am looking to travel from the UK to Spain initially - so a reasonable flight time, but wondered how this has worked for others.

Any advice / recommendations / tips appreciated - about which airlines are good etc.

thanks

Sue
This post was determined to be inappropriate by the Tripadvisor community and has been removed.

Sue, I wonder how you will transfer in the plane. They need to have you on a narrow airline chair for getting to the plane and then to your seat. I doubt there would be a frame for transferring.

I could, of course, be entirely wrong, just something to check on.

All airlines will arrange for you to be assisted at the airport to reach the plane and your seat. You arrange through the airline but the service is provided by the airports. They are not responsible for transfer lifts nor assisting you at toilet and if you need that you will have to travel with a carer.

Not all airlines accept all sorts of battery powered chairs. Most are OK and transported for free but some sorts of batteries are not accepted. Something else to check on.

But Spain is a great place to go. They have really adopted the rights of people with disabilities and most cities have fully accessible train services etc.
Airlines won't allow powerchairs on flights because of the pressure. At least I've never been allowed to.

My partner travels with his Invacare Mirage power chair, weight 73kg 



We've done Lanzarote, Fuerteventura and Alicante all with ease!
I see powerchairs on planes all of the time. To what "pressure" are you referring? I do not think they are a problem, at least not in the US or the areas of Europe where I have traveled.
Something to do with batteries exploding in the hold. We travel from the UK.

Traveling on an airplane with a power hair is generally not difficult, if you stick with the major air carriers .... Especially if they land in the USA at all. 



For the airlines the biggest concern is the chair's battery. the airline will want to know that it is safe to put on the plane - we disconnect our dry cell battery. the next concern the airline will have is the weight and multiple dimensions of the chair - many airlines will have a form to complete for this info. Our chair is about 175k.



 For the wheelchair owner you want to ensure that the chair arrives at your destination without damage which generally means protecting the joy stick and any other equipment attached to the chair. we remove the joy stick and head rest and wrap the whole thing with cling wrap. We take the seat cushion on board with us.



we use an airline manual chair to get to the airplane and then transfer to an aisle chair. While some airlines do have frames most that we've flown on will use airport personnel (not airlines personnel) to help transfer into the seat.



Our big concern is that the airline we choose have sufficient experience with wheelchairs - usually not a budget airline. If we are concerned we google the airlines to find out how they treat disabled passengers. That helps!



have fun!

Hi Sue, I have traveled as an attendant with a few clients over the years to various destinations. As far as you power chair goes, the big thing that most carriers look at is that you have a "dry cell battery". This is important.

As far as transferring to/from the plane/seat, that depends on the carrier, the airport, and which individuals you are dealing with. I have experienced where the carrier at one end will not do a physical transfer, but at the other end will supply 4 strong men who actually know what they are doing. Of course this all depends on Health and Safety Policies and Union/Company Policies. Your best bet, is to call the airlines directly and ask for specifics. Most have a department that deals with accessibility issues. If you do choose to fly with them, make sure you have a plan in place with them and call and remind them 48 hours before your departure. Try to get all this info in writing!!

 All this being said, good luck. All the planning in the world doesn't always equate to a smooth trip. We have had some really bad experiences and some that were amazing too.

My wife has a disability, we don't need any special facilities except to be guaranteed a room with a walk in shower as she cannot use a bath, but Thomsons, and other companies, always say that they can only request this, they cannot guarantee it. The alternative is to book directly with the hotel, but this can be more expensive and in some cases impossible if the hotel has a fixed contract with the holiday company. thread_title: Why can't holiday companies guarantee disabled suitable room
text:
I have no rational answer for you, but I cannot resist responding to someone who also waited for Godot. I nearly gave up my theatre minor after that particular production.



I think people in the UK do many more vacations with groups than we do in the US. So my experience is somewhat different. I make all of my own hotel reservations and I make them directly with the hotel. I do not use third party agents like Expedia. One of the reasons I do not use them is that they also will not guarantee a specific type of accommodation. They will not even guarantee a no smoking room.



Rooms with walk-in showers are not as common as standard four piece bathrooms, but there are many more of them today than there were ten years ago. I have not been in any new construction hotel in years where these rooms were not readily available. My goal is to avoid them because I prefer a bathtub. Many people, however, actually prefer a large shower, and I see them very frequently.



I do however, have specific requests and when I make a reservation I make it clear if they cannot meet my requests I will go to another hotel. I have rarely had any problem getting exactly what I have requested. This is particularly true when I book into hotels I have used in the past. Sometimes I just walk up to the registration desk, and the clerk says: "Same room. Here's the key card". So from my experience it helps if you are a returning guest. Absent this factor I am just very firm. If everything is not correct, we go elsewhere, even if elsewhere is not as desirable.



As to your situation, I agree that we have the technology to be able to more accurately predict if there will be rooms available that meet the needs of your wife. There are just not that many people with disabilities that travel. I believe it is easier to give us some meaningless response because we are more trouble than we are worth. Until there is a financial reason for meeting our requests we can probably expect similar treatment wherever it is legally permitted. While I am completely confident that Thomson's could get a guarantee if they threatened to pull their contract absent such a guarantee, I just do not think the odd person with a disability is going to motivate Thomson to issue such a threat.



We have seen lots of improvement in meeting our needs in the past couple of decades. I really do not believe I will live long enough to see a large agency such as Thomson's make such a demand of a contract hotel, but I did not think I would live to see many of the changes I now just take for granted.



So unlike those poor people who waited for Godot, perhaps there is some hope.



In the meantime, our medical supply facilities sell a nifty little thing called shower in a box. The box consists of quite a few thick towels pre-treated with some type of soap that does not need to be rinsed. You heat them up in a basin of hot water, and you can feel quite refreshed. They are a bit expensive, but I have no objections to paying $7 for the occasional unusual bath. You can also purchase a shampoo product which works really well.



I have only used these once when I was forced to go camping with a grand-child. I did not think they were a bad alternative. I do, however, have an even better review. I would often send them to my son-in-law when he was deployed to war zones over the past ten years, and he loved them. He would rather have a shower in a box than any food item I could mail. Sort of sad because if you intend to remain in an unfriendly country for more than ten years, you really should construct showers for your soldiers, but that is a topic for another forum; although the people there are also waiting for Godot.

thread_title: Why can't holiday companies guarantee disabled suitable room

I'm with what the others have said. There are all sorts of reasons one of the hotel's very small number of disabled rooms might beckme unavaiable (and remember, it's like to be only 1% or 2% whcih are adapted) so they will never give you a cast iron guarantee. 

Think of something simple like paying to reserve certain seats on the plane ... then they're gven to someone else at check-in, or you;re asked to move ... there's nothing you can do because even though you paid to reserve, the airline has the right to change your seat assignment.

Over the last ten years we've stayed in a fair spread of hotels - Norway, Poland, UK, Japan and India, Dubai, France, Belgium and Germeny staright off the top of my head. Some places we have had wonderfully adapted rooms in really nice hotels, sometimes poor adaptations and/or crappy hotels, sometimes we arrive and get the standard version of the room becuase our request got over-ridden. It's part of travel, abd if you do not want to be restricted you have to be adaptable and do all you can to make sure you will be able to function wherever you land up (our trip around Rajasthan was accompanied by an excellent American airbed which we only had to use a couple of times, but we took it knowing there was a chance we'd (I'd) need something more than the standard hotel beds we came across. We also carried an anti-slip mat for the shower, torches and lord know what else!) Was I pissed off sometimes - heck yes - but did I let it get me down or discourage me from travel? Hell no! (Except at the Taj Mahal - the most famous inaccessible building in the world. There is "managed, just" but it was not easy and wuld be impossible now.

So - look on the bright side. Be happy when all goes well but be prepared for the odd let-down and, most importantly ENJOY YOUR TRAVEL!



(Incidentally - next big trip is fly Warsaw to Tokyo and spend some more time in Japan, me, partner and wheelchair, now at early planning stages!)

text:
First, let me say again that I'm in a wheelchair. I can stand, but not long enough to tae a shower, and on two crutches my walking ability is still negligible.

Over the last few years we've stayed in some hotel rooms which we found perfectly adapted to suit my needs and others which were rubbish. And of course some of those rooms were in hotels which were themselves rubbish! 

I guess the basic problem, though, comes down to the economics of it. hotels are not high profit businesses, they rely on high occupancy rates for what profits they do make, and that means having the maximum number of rooms suited to the maximum number of people - how else could Travelodge offer rooms at £19 a night? Adaptations means extra thought, planning and expense and not all adaptations will be suitable for all disabilities so a hotel owner wil never know exactly "how adapted" a room needs to be. 

I don’t think hotels are discouraged by other people's reactions to seeing disabled people - that isa terrible thing to suggest - but they, given their choice, figure that their business model is better served by not catering for disabled folk rather than risking getting it wrong or having adapted rooms standing empty because, TBH, most able-bodied people don’t like them. Maybe there are also liability issues.

I don’t mean to be an apologist – just saying that if you accept the hotel is a business, you also have to accept that it will take decisions to maximise profitability. Legislation can force hotels to adapt some rooms, but they’ll only adapt the number they’re required to unless there is an expectation of a very high occupancy rate.

thread_title: Power wheelchair to Tanzania? It is possible
text:
I am glad to let you know that my trip using my power wheelchair in Tanzania was surprisingly successful. With some improvisation, creativity and grasp of basic Swahili - travelling with powerchairs to Tanzania is possible. 



Let me tell you about my experience beginning with the airport. People I came across at the JKN Airport in Dar es salaam were nice, very helpful and very cooperative to how I wanted things to be done.



I got off the plane on an aisle wheelchair onto the skylift vehicle as the plane was at the tarmac. Once there I transfered to a manual wheelchair then we descended down where I found my powerchair all set at the tarmac. 



I transferred to my powerchair assembled the controlled and other detachable that I had removed and took it with me on aircraft from Toronto, Canada.



There is no wheelchair level surface to fill out forms and no place for the customs/immigration staff to reach you if you are in a wheelchair. However the porter who was assisting us was very helpful in obtaining the visasa and other required formalities.(it is very important to be friendly to people who are assisting you, you'll be surprised who smooth the entire process unfolds)



The biggest challenge I encounter in Tanzania is wheelchair accessible transportation and accessible washrooms but with little planning ahead this is also possible. 



There are no buses, vans or vehicles that accommodates wheelchairs. Atleast not yet!! So here I had to be a little creative and using local people to find me a vehicle that could carry my power wheelchair while Im on it as I have hard time to transfer on and off from car seat.



The next day we found a guy who does private transportation using NOAH, a Japanese make van that are plenty in Dar and everywhere in TZ, it had a super roof. Perfect for my powerchair, Next I spoke with locals to direct me to place where they work with scrap metals. There is a place called GEREZANI in Dar here I made my make shift ramp to get into the NOAH.



People using mobility devices in Tanzania and Zanzibar have to really look around when it comes to Hotels, restaurants, cafes and bars. To resolve that challenge I went back to Gerezani where I asked craftsmen there to make for me a small curb ramp that I tied at the back of my powerchair and used it when need. 



There are no public accessible wash-rooms anywhere in Dar. However, found one in Forodhani in Zanzibar. bars, cafes and restaurants also don't have accessible washrooms. I suggest bringing your own toilet seat raiser and portable handle bars that can be attached to the toilet in hotel that you staying. 



Visiting Arusha, National Parks and Zanzibar is also very possible.



During my trip I also visited Tarangire National Park, snake park in Arusha and Zanzibar. 



We travelled by road to Arusha in NOAH. After spending a day or so we embarked to Tarangire national park. New Arusha hotel has rool in showers and pretty much accessible bar and lobby. Roads in Arusha are doable by powerchairs encountering some obstacles. However people are friendly and willing to assist you when you ask for help. There are plenty of street food places selling Nyama Choma, a local delicacy of grilled meat.



Trip to Tarangire went without a hitch, was surprised how the NOAH which we were travelling in could withstand the rough terrain.



Zanzibar ferry is accessible by powerchair and the narrow streets in Zanzibar is like perfect fit for powerchairs -Hotel accommodation for people using mobility devices is totally different ball game! It took us almost 5 hours to finally find a hotel that was accessible. AL-MINAR in forodhani is one of few that can accommodate persons on wheelchairs



Good news: 



During my trip I met Tanzanian businessman who is planing to introduce wheelchair accessible vans and buses. For now his plans is limited to Airport-city shuttles. He's in talks with major hotels and guest houses on providing and retrofitting rooms to be wheelchair accessible.



He told me he is also considering the National parks tours for people using powerchairs. Lets keep our finger crossed.



If anyone planning trip to Tanzania feel free to contact me I'll try my best to assist you make the trip possible.

thread_title: Travelling with over the counter meds
text:
The first thing that I put in my carry-on is all the medication my husband and I will use while we are away. Sometimes we are gone for three months at a time, so my carry-on looks like a pharmacy kit. I would not put anything more than an easily replaceable bottle of aspirin in any checked luggage. Morphine and codeine have street value that makes them very attractive to a thief, and Tramadol, while not producing much of a "high" is also in demand. It is just so easy for a bottle of morphine to slip out of a suitcase during a routine inspection. I would never take that chance.



John, in my home state of Florida, not only does morphine require a prescription, it can now only be prescribed by a surgeon or a board-certified pain management doctor. A regular general practice doctor can no longer prescribe any narcotic medication. You absolutely want to bring all your own medication before visiting Disney World.

thread_title: Travelling with over the counter meds
text:
Prescription medication, as a general rule is 5 to 10 times as expensive in the US than almost any other country in the US. My husband takes a blood pressure medication that costs $400/one month supply. He can purchase the identical medication in Istanbul for $27/one month supply. 



We live in a retirement community and several times a year there are organized "tours" to Canada. The primary reason for these excursions is to fill prescriptions. Coming back thru customs takes a great deal of time. Every passenger must produce a doctor's prescription for everything they have purchased. OTC drugs in Canada like Tylenol with codeine that are OTC categorized in Canada, but require a prescription in the US are confiscated at the border. I have seen 250 passengers clear customs at JFK faster than 35 who clear at the Canadian border. 



In my experience Custom officials know who they are looking for. Older people receive much more attention. I am sure it is because they take more prescription medication, live on fixed incomes and have time to invest in a quick run across the border.

thread_title: WestJet will not accept mobility scooters!
text:
This is something really important that those who use some of the most popular brands of mobility scooters must be made aware of. I called WestJet to inform them that I am traveling with my new Go Go Elite Pro scooter, and to request a wheelchair as I made my booking. I was told that new rules are in place and that they WILL NOT TRANSPORT MY BATTERY.



I have flown with airlines throughout the world and have never had a problem, until now. WestJet now classifies the batteries as dangerous goods and will not accept them. They are not lithium, and are a standard AGM non-spillable battery. I was told that the update clearly states that they will take my scooter, but it is ME who is required to transport the battery by calling a dangerous goods air carrier.



How can the airline get away with this? It is impossible for me to fly without the scooter, as I cannot be mobile without it, due to a childhood disease. Shipping the battery makes it impossible for me to get to the airport without renting a wheelchair to get me around, and what happens when I get to my destination? The scooter will be sitting there with no battery until I can get it from this other carrier? 



Essentially my mobility has been cut off, my ability to leave my home city has been taken away when flying WestJet. Are they planning to call all of their customers who may already have flights booked, or will they just tell them at the airport?



Please spread the word on this, and provide feedback directly to WestJet.



Note the following information directly from the WestJet website:



At this time, powered collapsible mobility aids containing batteries that require removal for transport and stowage will not be accepted in the cabin, as checked baggage or as cargo. This applies to lithium and non-spillable battery operated units. If a manufacturer does not provide detailed instructions for proper battery disconnection for stowage and transport, please have the make and model of the scooter available and contact us for approval prior to travel.

 

It is your responsibility to arrange transportation of the battery with a dangerous goods carrier if your mobility device and battery falls into this category. Examples of common powered collapsible mobility aids include, but are not limited to:

 • CTM H2-125

 • Pride Go Go Elite

 • Pride Go Go Regular

 • Pride Go Go Sport

 • Pride Victory

 • Shoprider GK10 Spirit

 • Travelscoot Deluxe

 • Travelscoot Standard

 • Tzora Easy Travel Elite

 

Batteries intended for use with a powered collapsible mobility aid or for the models listed above, will not be accepted.

 

WestJet will accept those mobility devices with non-spillable batteries where the battery is encased and attached to the base of mobility device as long as you or your attendant are able to disconnect the battery and/or confirm that there will not be any accidental activation of the battery during transport. If you are not able to disconnect the battery you should be prepared to provide verbal instruction and the original manufacturer's manual, as well as any disassembly instructions you may have related to any modifications made to your mobility device.

 

Scooters that are up to 45 kg (100lb.) and have a battery specifically designed for easy removal, which is not encased at the base of the scooter, are considered a powered collapsible mobility device. The batteries for these types of scooters are not accepted for transport in the cabin, checked baggage or as cargo at this time. It is your responsibility to arrange transportation of the battery with a dangerous goods carrier. WestJet strictly adheres to the individual manufacturer recommendation for proper disassembly and stowage as described in the owner’s manual.

I am travelling to the UK next year and wanted to know if I could use my Disability Permit In the UK so I emailed The Blue Badge Administrator UK to get a ruling form them and below is the reply I received. 



Good Morning, Thank you for your email. There is currently no agreement in place between the UK and Australia regarding the use of Australian parking badges in the UK. The decision as to whether you could use your Australian parking permit in the UK would therefore lie with the Blue Badge team in each Local Authority area where you would be using it. thread_title: Travelling in Myanmar with a mobility disability - a report
text:
The itinerary - three weeks travelling in Myanmar on a self-organised trip for two retirees, taking in the three tourist hot spots of Yangon, Mandalay, Inle Lake plus a 10 night cruise down the Irrawaddy from Mandalay to Yangon.





The context - my wife has suffered from MS for many years, which means that she can only walk very short distances unassisted. Although she is not wheelchair-bound, to get around efficiently and quickly she does use a wheelchair which we take with us wherever we travel abroad. We can now add Myanmar to a growing list of countries this long-suffering wheelchair has visited!





Remarks and comments:





International flights - as you would expect no real problems at all. We used Heathrow and transferred through Doha (Qatar Airways) to Yangon. Typically the worst experience was on our return to Heathrow, where an inordinate wait for assistance was prefaced with the excuse that there were not enough staff to cope with the sudden influx of passengers requiring help - deal with it! 





Internal flights - no problems at all using Yangon Domestic, Heho and Mandalay airports and two different local airlines. There was apparently the normal chaos at these airports, but we had no extra issues, even if my wife does somewhat blanch at recalling being wheeled across the tarmac at Mandalay in the rain dodging moving aircraft!





Hotels - we had carefully chosen hotels where we knew their facilities matched our requirements. Clearly a lift is vital in any bigger establishment.





Getting around - in accordance with our previous practice I had hoped to be able to wheel my wife around the streets of the major places we visited. Not a chance. First of all the traffic in Yangon and Mandalay is far too frenetic and dangerous to allow me to contemplate using the roads themselves. Even the side roads were full to bursting with cars, bikes, vans and people etc. Secondly pavements were generally much higher off the road surface than here in the UK, making getting on and off them resemble a mountaineering exercise and a physical nightmare, drop-down pavements were non-existent, whilst the pavements themselves were uneven with holes and broken paving slabs, or simply blocked by masses of people, stalls and street vendors. As a result we soon gave up using our own steam and just relied on pre-hired cars with guides. We had never done this before, so were perhaps a little apprehensive. But in the end all our arrangements made before leaving the UK worked to perfection and without the help of all the guides/drivers that we used we would not have been able to see all we did see, and in such comfort. We had informed the guides that my wife had a mobility problem and that we would be bringing our own wheelchair and they responded accordingly, in one case clearly bringing along a bigger vehicle than they would otherwise have used. We got to rely on them for physical assistance, such as lugging the wheelchair around, helping my wife when she was able to walk short distances required ('slowly, slowly' became a much-used and very meaningful phrase!) and realising what would and would not work by way of sites to be visited, where to park and so on.





Visiting sites. Clearly some sites were beyond our ability, although a number of pagodas do have lift access, markets can be negotiated in a wheelchair if due care is exercised, and in smaller towns and villages (which we visited as part of our cruise - see below) roads can be used. Just be realistic and discuss any issues with your guide/driver.





River cruise - we had done river cruising before in Vietnam and Cambodia and knew that it suited our particular needs. On originally applying to Pandaw to come on the Irrawaddy cruise they had said no as they did not have sufficient facilities for disabled passengers. On explaining more fully our specific situation, they reassessed the itinerary and having worked out what would or would not be possible, or what extras they could provide, said yes. In the end my wife only missed out on one excursion, otherwise taking a full part in the trip. (Have a look at the detailed itinerary to see what that involves.) Without the full cooperation, help and assistance of Pandaw and in particular the staff/crew of RV Katha Pandaw (the boat we sailed on), this would not have been so successful. If you are contemplating a river cruise, make sure you square it all openly and realistically before hand. Pandaw will do all they can to make it possible.





Conclusions - a truly memorable, exciting and exhilarating experience all round. Travelling around present day Myanmar with a limited mobility disability is doable - we have serious doubts as to whether this is true if you are completely wheelchair bound. My wife was at least able to walk short distances when necessary. Be realistic as to where you can go, what you can do and see. Even in November (the beginning of their cool period), it was hot, dry and very humid. Plan properly, use cars and guides to get around and take their advice.





People in Myanmar are really delightful, friendly, open and ever ready to help. If you are in a wheelchair, you will be stared at, but only as a brief curiosity as they rarely see their own inhabitants in wheelchairs. They always gave us the feeling that they were really pleased to see us. Enjoy it.

thread_title: What is your Experience with "Wheelchair Access" icon.
text:
Here in India there is a very serious problem with wheelchair access. Laws have been passed since 1996 and further building regulations in 2014 however wheelchair access is very nearly non-existent. Even hotels that actually make an effort usually do so with very poor advice as the implementation is usually a nearly complete failure.



This is not helped by the "Accessibility Checklist for Hotel Accommodation". If the reception staff don't understand the needs of wheelchair users they may think that their 40 degree slope at the hotel is ok. They may think that the fact the wheelchair can actually get through the door into the bathroom is enough and not realise that the cupboard under the washbasin is an obstacle or that the fact there no seat in the shower is a serious matter. They may think that a couple of steps here and there is not a big issue!



It is my experience that the general awareness of the needs of the disabled in India is extremely low. To expect to get good information by asking specific questions who already don't speak your language as their first language is unrealistic.



Tripadvisor developers seem to be either unaware of this problem or unable to fix this by removing or repairing this feature. Here are some suggestions:



1. If you can't fix it remove this feature. I don't think this a very positive solution but it would be improvement on 99% failure of Indian hotels/facilities that don't have disabled access but say they do. No information is better than disinformation.



2. Remove the self-nominating aspect of "Wheelchair Access" and allow the users to rate the hotel in the way of "Hotel Style" voting feature with "Disabled Friendly". They can expand on why they say it is disabled friendly in their written part of the review but at least the person browsing can "filter" for "Disabled Friendly". This is a little weak as each persons needs are different.



3. Change the functionality of the review page by putting the "Disabled Access" in the "Hotel Ratings" They can expand on why they gave that rating in their written part of the review but at least the person browsing can "filter" for above 3 stars in "Disabled Access". This is better than the previous options because people who already have a disability usually have a better idea of how disability access features should be.



4. Make a separate section where the reviewer can make more specific votes and comments for all the critical elements of disabled access from front access slope, through size of lifts, height of dinning tables to bathroom shower seating... This requires far more programming/development but would actually provide useful information.

The TSA worker ignored the suitcase and pointed me to the area for a physical pat-down. This person laughed at my certificate and said "We are looking for terrorists. I did think that it would not be impossible for a terrorist to have scars in the appropriate location, but since I was forced to remove my clothing, it would still be difficult for a terrorist to smuggle a weapon on board after he had been forced to remove his clothing.



Bottom line is that you do not need a certificate, and offering one just makes the whole system work a bit more slowly and generally annoys the TSA workers as well as the people standing behind you.

Sorry in advance if I am not on the correct forum for this query! My mum and her partner are having a big holiday this Oct/Nov to Florida. Her partner needs to take out additional travel insurance, for pre-existing conditions. They have apparently been told by an insurance company that they cannot take out this type of insurance 'too far' in advance incase the medical condition stops them from going away!! You are quite right, holiday insurance is to give you cover and peace of mind, not only whilst you are away, but before you go, should you need to cancel. My partner and self have pre existing conditions, but buy an annual insurance as we go away a few times a year and it works out more economical. So, theoretically, we are buying our cover a full year ahead.



Like you say, it is very important to have travel insurance in place and should be bought at time of booking. In addition we have our EHIC which are easy to get and are FOC.
Thank-you! I think I might suggest the annual cover to them, because they have 3-4 holidays a year.

The insurer may not want to issue a "single trip" policy a long way in advance of the trip, because, depending on the type of pre-existing conditions, they may feel that a long run up on the policy means they have a greater exposure to the risk of cancellation.



If you do decide to buy an annual policy, in order to have cancellation cover in place, the cover should start as soon as possible.... Don't nominate the departure date for the trip as the day you want the policy to commence.



I know these 2 statements seem contradictory, but single trip and annual cover policies are rated differently, especially when there are declared pre-existing medical conditions that the applicant wants covering. 



I hope this helps and that you can find suitable cover.
