thread_title: Air Canada - Unbelievable Questions re Wheelchair
text:
Hi,



My Mum's friend is flying with Air Canada and needs to take her own wheelchair (she is only flying one way with them, the other is with another airline). When she phoned to advise them she ended up being questioned for almost an hour regarding all her medical history (including medicines) which was as in depth as when arranging travel insurance. The agent kept having to go away and check with someone else before coming back and asking more questions. Then later that day the agent called again with more Q's and yesterday she called again asking for the wheelchair measurements again! The lady is now extremely stressed out about it and feels like she is being harrassed. I have offered to write a letter of complaint as I know this is not standard practice on other international airlines.



My Mum travels with her own mobility scooter and I always arrange the assistance with airline (American, BA, Virgin Atlantic, United and others) and have only ever been asked questions about the scooter and whether she can climb stairs and walk to her seat, never about her specific health issues.



So, I was wondering if this had happened to anyone else, particularly with Air Canada?

thread_title: Air Canada - Unbelievable Questions re Wheelchair
text:
It certainly shouldn't! I would demand to speak with a supervisor right away! Air Canada's wheelchair policy(http://www.aircanada.com/en/travelinfo/before/specialneeds/wheelchair.html) is here. For a motorized scooter, they will of course have questions about the battery type, but there should be no issue, this is totally routine.



I have not flown with Air Canada, but have flown with a manual push chair on 5 other airlines.

thread_title: Air Canada - Unbelievable Questions re Wheelchair
text:
It's called fitness to fly. Thne airline does not want any in-flight medical emergencies and by requesting assistance you've triggered the questions they need answered to satisfy their medical officers that the friend is, indeed, fit to fly.

Unpleasant, clearly, for the lady concerned, but not exactly something one could complain about.

I had the same procedure myself a few years ago, thogh that was with the CMO of Virgin Atlantic, and I knew what he was doing. Maybe the problem here is that the agent did not make it clear what the reason was for the questions - or the caller did not realise FTF was even an issue.

I received an email from them stating if I wanted handicapped considerations I would need a letter from my physician stating I was fit to travel and that that I must pay the expenses of having a physician fill out the form. thread_title: EU destination - Can I put my mobility scooter in the hold?
text:
Airlines transport mobility scooters FOC. I take a Pride GoGo Traveller with me. Normally scoot to the gate, steps, or aircraft door and then it is put into the hold. Generally, when I arrive at my destination it is waiting for me on the tarmac. I can walk up and down the aircraft steps, but if you are not able to, then you will be assisted.



You need to advise the airline at time of booking you wish to take a scooter with you. They will then ask you for the specifications. You also need to take the details with you. I normally take a couple of copies and hand it to them.



The procedure is very easy and makes a big difference to your holiday when you arrive at your destination. You do need to choose your hotel and destination carefully. Where are you planning to go? In Europe, Barcelona has to be one of the most disabled friendly places.

looking for information on wheelchair accessible hotels in Istanbul,preferably with roll in shower .

Try posting on the Istanbul Forum the local experts who have far more knowledge of the area might be able to help you.



Deb

Istanbul and Turkey in general has very few special accommodations for people with disabilities. Even before you reach the point where you need a roll-in shower, you will need to manage serious difficulties with a wheelchair. Sidewalks are difficult. Sometimes they just disappear, forcing you into the road where traffic is crazy. Sometimes vendors have spread a blanket and merchandise on the sidewalk, forcing pedestrians into the street. Occasionally sidewalks convert to stairs if the elevation is particularly steep. There are no curb cut-aways, so every time you need to cross a road, you need to physically lift your wheelchair over a high curb. In addition, much of the area is covered in rough cobblestone that can prove difficult for some people who use wheelchairs.



You will also need a hotel that provides easy access, and I cannot think of a hotel currently that does not have a couple of steps somewhere in the lobby. Few of them provide an alternate ramp. You will also need a hotel that provides an elevator, which is not common in the smaller boutique hotels in the city.



You can enjoy Istanbul in a wheelchair, but you need to be prepared for the obstacles. I use a mobility scooter everywhere I go except for the 1-2 months I spend in Turkey each year. In Turkey my scooter would create more difficulties for me than my limited mobility. I take my small, three-wheel walker, plan my routes carefully, take a rest break every block or so, and use public transportation and/or taxis to get from one place to another. Finally I depend upon help from others. I also have some mobility. I can easily manage my own transfers, and with a walker I can manage a block of walking before I need to stop and rest.



It is rare to see people in wheelchairs in Istanbul. I suspect that local residents who are forced to remain in a wheelchair do not venture out of their homes very often, but much of Istanbul is modern and sophisticated. You would have no difficulties in any of the more than 100 modern malls, and actually not too much difficulty in the ancient malls of the Grand Bazaar and Spice Bazaar. If you have a portable wheelchair you can put it in the trunk of a taxi.



I have been thinking about hotels in Istanbul for the last hour or so, and I cannot remember a hotel that has an actual roll-in shower. However, some hotels have budget European-style bathrooms. In these bathrooms the shower simply includes that entire bathroom. You remove anything from the surfaces of the bathroom before you shower and then the entire bathroom is covered by the shower spray. These types of bathrooms would work for you because they would provide enough room for a wheelchair. Just remember to remove the toilet tissue and extra towels or make sure they are covered before you turn on the shower.



Unfortunately, while I know of hotels with these types of bathrooms in other cities in Turkey, I am not aware of any in Istanbul. The best I could offer would be the suggestion that you read hotel descriptions and/or reviews to see if you can locate either this type of bathroom or a bathroom that offers a Turkish-style bath. A Turkish-style bath would not have a shower, but there would be a large basin and a drain. You soap up using the warm water and soap from the basin, and then rinse off using a bowl and fresh water from the basin. It is actually similar to a shower experience, and certainly cleaner than sitting in a bathtub. You could certainly email any hotel and ask about their bathrooms.



In Sultanahmet we stay at the Apricot Hotel, and Room 4 has a Turkish-style bath that would work for you. The problem is that Room 4 is on the third floor and reached only by a winding staircase with no handrails. The stairway is probably not even wide enough to accommodate a wheelchair if someone wanted to try to manually take you up those stairs. I do not think I would want to attempt this. I manage these stairs by walking very slowly and carefully and paying complete attention to where my feet are going.



If you cannot find an appropriate bathroom, there is always the alternative of using a real Turkish bath where someone else will cover your with soap, provide a bit of a massage and then rinse you off. 



The reason that you can manage in Istanbul in spite of these barriers is because the average person in the street is filled with a rare sense of hospitality and generosity. If you come to the curb barrier and stop it will only be a minute or two until several men appear to lift you over the curb. You would receive this same assistance in the Turkish bath, and certainly in hotels that have only a few stairs in the lobby area. There are very few physical adaptations of the infrastructure to accommodate people with disabilities, but there are millions of people who will help you.



Once I somehow wandered into a construction area, and the only way across a deep hole was a single 2 x 6' piece of wood. Before I could even think about how to turn around, four men appeared and simply lifted me over the hole. I have never crossed a street by myself. I stand at the curb waiting for traffic to break, and someone always appears to take my arm and often to walk into the street and stop the traffic. When we reach the other side these kind people disappear so quickly that I often do not have the opportunity to thank them. Similarly, I have never had to stand on any type of public transportation. Someone always gives me a seat. Waiters are careful to select tables I can reach easily. There are some shops in the Grand Bazaar that are so tiny that a wheelchair will not fit through the door. If you see something in one of these shops that you want to examine more closely the shop keeper will bring his merchandise to you. Most shops have no barriers. The Grand Bazaar is essentially without barriers in the general halls.



The ancient attractions you will want to visit also have stairs which can be obstacles. The Blue Mosque did have a ramp. I think it was at the exit, but they will permit you to enter this way. You have to switch to a mosque wheelchair because they do not want street dirt to be transferred to the carpets. People in wheelchairs switch to one used only inside of the mosque. Aya Sofya has a couple of thresholds that are high, but someone will help you. I do not visit the second floor in this museum, but I can be very happy just exploring the bottom floor and then look at my husband's photos of the second floor. There is an elevator to visit the Cisterns. Topkapi has a few stairs scattered about, but people will help you manage these.



I would try to locate a hotel that has an elevator because there are very few hotels with rooms on the first floor. I also stay in the Sirkici Mansion. There are two steps to enter the building, but there is a ramp to enter. I think the lobby is flat, and there is an elevator that serves all the floors except for the roof-top terrace. I think that every room in this hotel has a bathtub/shower combination, but I am not sure. You could email them and ask. I would probably just ask for lots of extra towels and take a basin bath if there is no roll-in shower.



When you email hotels to make this inquiry you should describe what you need in terms of shower facilities. They probably will not understand the term "roll-in shower".



Although visiting Istanbul in a wheelchair is more difficult than countries that mandate adapted infrastructure, it is still possible. I depend upon the kindness of strangers, and I have never been in another country where so many strangers demonstrate so much kindness.

thread_title: Travelling with an adullt with Aspergers
text:
I really cannot imagine a scenario where you would be separated from your family, unless one of you is singled out for extra security. I would make very sure your son does not have anything on his body that would trigger a metal detector and then force him into either a screening device or a personal pat-down. He might find either of those disturbing (I find them disturbing).



Without additional screening, you just put your luggage on the X-Ray table, walk through the metal detector and pick up the luggage again.



My concern would be more about how he handles crowded situations. Some people I know who have children with Asperger's need to move to the front of lines because the child does not tolerate waiting in line, and security lines can be quite long. If this is his situation I would probably request a wheelchair for him so he can move through a shorter dedicated line. 



This suggestion would generate some stiff feedback on a regular airline forum, and I would not make it there. However, if your child becomes extremely upset with long lines I believe this situation would justify the use of a system that would help him move more quickly. In an ideal world you could just explain this to some official in charge to security and he would be moved to the front of the line, but I tend to think that these security workers are not trained to address situations like what you have with your son. They do all recognize a wheelchair.

text: I also have limited mobility and have done a number of cruises, but not river cruises. I suggest you look on Cruise critic where they have sections on disabled travel and river cruises.

thread_title: European River Cruises for mobility challenged
text:
We went on an APT river cruise recently, Budapest to Amsterdam. There was a small elevator on board though not to the sun deck. Several people with mobility issues came on our trip, one with a walker, one with a stick and a shorter leg. (Note that APT and AMA waterways use the same ships. APT is mainly for Australians)

They had walks of different levels of difficulty so the gentle walkers went in a group of their own. Some situations were unsuitable of course, but in many cases adaptations could be made. No one used a wheelchair or scooter but it might be possible in some situations. Many excursions were by bus from the pier to the destination, so being able to board a bus would be important.

The cabins are compact though you could use a small manual wheelchair on the window side of the bed. The bathroom is supercompact with a step in shower and no room for a wheelchair.

Hope that helps.

thread_title: European River Cruises for mobility challenged
text: if your mobility issued requires wheelchairs, scooters, walkers, transit chairs ect don't bother booking : gangplanks are too narrow (have to collapse aid and carry and walk-on-off vessel). send Avalon River Cruises and email at - consumersvacation@globusfamily.com - review their main web page re Traveling With Disabilities and take it all as "generic" comments - ie - take their suggestion you try a different type of vacation : the biggest problem is the various number of "mobility issues" that you can have ... if you only require a 'stick" - cane - and can maneuver stairs ect you should be ok

thread_title: Health episode cause me to miss flight- insurance procedure?
text:
Hopefully this is the ideal sub-forum to use for this.



A fortnight ago I developed a delicate health issue which I had expected would pass before now. I am due to go to Antalya, Turkey on Friday the 12th, which I had already been pretty anxious about, being my first trip in fourteen years and my first 'holiday' involving a flight.



I'd paid for travel insurance. My flight, with Turkish Airlines, is one I can't be refunded for by them at least, not even with a medical reason - they do sound a tight lot. In retrospect I was a bit delirious when I booked everything, with inconvenient times and a stop at Istanbul that had made the flight feel intimidatingly complicated to start with. I am hoping a doctor's letter will get my my flight money back through the insurance company but I wondered whether it's okay to cancel the flight now or would that forfeit the insurance refund. This morning I cancelled the three rooms I'd paid for (one near Heathrow, two in different bits of Turkey) as this was simple enough, on booking.com. Is the reimbursement likel to be long-winded? I was hoping I might just about be able to rebook for ten days later and still see some sun and so on.



I am so annoyed with what's happened, it seems like a major case of Sod's Law. The health issue is unrelated to my regular health problems and sprang up out of nowhere. Hopefully getting the doctor's note itself will not be like getting blood out of a stone. My soon-to-be-ex-GP is hellbent on doing nothing for me regardless of what I go to the surgery for but i'll need his assistance this one last time if it's not too much toruble for him...



There is still a slim chance I can go, if the medical assistance I got today pans out, but i'd like to get advice here anyway.



Thanks for any advice.

text:
Have you called your Travel insurance company and asked their advice? That would seem the sensible thing to do.



You need to inform your insurer and they will send a medical questioner to your GP who fill it in and send back.

Then they will decide if they are paying out or not, if your health problem is any way shape or form an old one or not declared you will not see a penny.







Deb

thread_title: India. Hotels with listed with disabled access in Amenities
text:
99% hotels are not accessible. However there are some hotel groups that have a policy to provide a least one adapted room. However many of these are still not really suitable because they have adapted them incorrectly. For instance we stayed in a really nice business hotel, Ibis, in Jaipur but the room had a bed that was too high and the room was so small that it was not possible to get to the bathroom in a wheelchair.



Try Ibis hotels, Lemon Tree and I have also heard Ginger hotels are ok. All the five and 4 star hotels should have accessible rooms but they can also be wrongly implemented.



The best hotels I have experienced are Raj Palace in Jaipur, Rajasthan (the owner's wife uses a wheelchair) and Mayfair Gangtok,Sikkim. 



It really depends on your level of disability. As my wife is fully paraplegic and has little upper body strength life travelling in India can be very difficult.

Like a number of Americans, we've never used trip insurance. In the past we've always been able to work with the airlines and hotels and get our trips cancelled or postponed. In my own case, I have always been able to provide the requested proof and have the penalties waived. My health situation however has changed and I now find myself planning a trip where I will need insurance coverage.



We are in the very early stages of planning a trip to Europe for April/May of 2016. This trip will include France, Italy and The Netherlands, with possible day trips to Belgium, Germany and Switzerland. At present France and The Netherlands are certain, all other destinations are flexible.



I'm looking for suggestions on what companies provide the best and most comprehensive insurance options. In particular, I'm lookimg for companies that will cover pre-existing conditions (more than one, as I suffer from several different issues) as well as one that will allow cancellation for any reason.



As stated. we're in the very early stages of planning this trip. However, without the insurance coverage, there's no need to even continue any further. Right now, both I and my GF are both eligable for Medicare, but get our medical coverage at the VA.

Hopefully Busy retired a fellow countryman of yours will see this post and might be able to help, I know they travel to Europe and have mobility/health problems.



Deb

HI vegas-guide, You are correct that trip insurance is not as common for US travelers as it is for Europeans. Before our health insurance shifted to Medicare we also managed to cancel our own reservations and control our own cost consequences if we had to change a flight. We generally fly Delta, and we always buy the least expensive non-refundable ticket available. Even with that ticket, Delta will give you credit if you cannot take the flight. They will evaluate the reason why you cannot fly, and may even waive the $150 change fee. Because of these generous policies we just carried a inexpensive major medical repatriation policy so we could transport our bodies back to the US if we should die while traveling.



 Prior to shifting to Medicare our Blue Cross policy reciprocated with other insurance companies and health care providers in the foreign countries that we visited. Medicare will not cover medical services delivered outside of the US. I have not been able to find any supplemental policy that will cover expenses incurred in a foreign country. Almost all secondary insurers refuse to pay anything on any claim that Medicare rejected.



So, now we purchase trip insurance for health care, medical evacuation and repatriation. I generally purchase my travel insurance with insuremytrip.com. I have Lupus and Parkinson's Disease in addition to significant mobility issues. I have to pay a higher premium, but they have not refused to cover us. It is quite expensive, but I feel that it is something we cannot afford to be without.



The problem with selecting a trip insurance company is that it is difficult to utilize reviews to determine which insurance carriers are preferred. Most people never use their trip insurance, so they provide good reviews because they have not criticisms. When one has a crisis and requires assistance, it is almost never a simply and easy transaction. Generally I find that people who never use the insurance give the companies great reviews, while almost everyone who does use the services has numerous complaints. So I do not use these reviews as a decision criteria.



Before I purchase trip insurance I ask for the actual policy to be emailed to me. I read the policy carefully making sure that I am familiar with everything in fine print. I check the Standard & Poors Rating as well as the Better Business Bureau. As I have never had to use trip insurance, I have no idea if I am selecting the best company and the best policy. I hope I never have to actually evaluate any policy.



If you have no success with insuremytrip.com you can Google Trip Insurance and compare some of the other products. My criteria include a significant amount of coverage for medical expenses and medical evacuation expenses. I am not concerned about insurance for missed connections, or unplanned strikes or missing luggage. The only reason I purchase trip insurance is to provide medical coverage.

Thank you Busy-retired, that's what I was looking for. I'll check to see what they have to offer and see if it suits my needs.



All my previous issues were either one of a kind incidents (IE: broken bones) or unexpected (anemia induced geart attack). However, with these pre-existing conditions, I need to take the responsibility to purchase insurance to provide additional coverage. 



I have AFIB (requiring warfarin), borderline stage 3 Kidney failure (no dialysis required) and due to Glaucoma and Cataracts have been declared legally blind. Other than those minor issues, my health is pretty good. All ny issues are under control so it should not be a problem making the trip.



Like you, we're just looking for emergency coverage. We're not interested in lost/delayed luggage, missed connections, etc. We do want the cancel for any reason coverage as we tend to use advance purchase options extensively and they are usually non-refundable/non-changeable (especially for rail and/or hotels).



Once again, thanks for the information. I'll find out some more about them and see if they have what we need (or at least close).

text:
The US has excellent laws that prohibit businesses from discriminating against people with disabilities. Obviously you cannot expect a taxi to accommodate a $10,000 4-wheel drive motor scooter, but you can reasonably expect a taxi to accommodate a general use small, portable mobility scooter or wheelchair.



I have never used a passenger bus in the US. I think I would be afraid to use this type of transportation because of the places where they stop and the other passengers who select bus travel. We do occasionally travel in tour buses. There is never a problem with our mobility scooters. Usually they fit into the luggage compartment without even being taken apart. The driver generally meets us at the door of the bus with our scooters. I am sure that bus transportation could accommodate a mobility device. I think they are legally required to do so.



I have not been on a passenger train in the US in 50 years, so I have no idea what you can expect. There are lots of commuter trains in the Northeast corridor of the US. I assume people with disabilities use these, and that they can accommodate mobility devices. I have used light rail systems in downtown areas with absolutely no difficulty at all.



I can tell you that not many B & B's provide rooms for people with disabilities. I do not know how they get around the ADA laws, but I live in a town with lots of B & B's and I am sure they do not have disabled rooms. Since you do not need a mobility scooter all of the time, I am confident that a B & B would store your mobility device, and you could manage inside the property with just your walking sticks.



The problem that I would have were I planning to do what you wish to do would be obtaining a mobility device. Even if you could locate a device in every town you plan to visit, it could take several hours to take a taxi to the rental facility, complete the paperwork and take your mobility device. In larger cities, or in areas that cater to tourists, there are always places that will rent mobility scooters and/or wheelchairs.



This is a link to a web site that lists many places around the US that do rent mobility scooters http://www.scootaround.com/ I have used this web site to locate a rental unit, but not for several years. You need to fill out a form, and they call back with rental locations in the areas you wish to travel.



This is a link to some other rental companies, including a couple in the UK. http://seniortravel.about.com/od/seniortravelbasics/a/Rent-A-Mobility-Scooter-Ecv-For-Your-Vacation.htm

The very most simple thing you could do would be to rent a scooter in the UK and just bring it with you to the US. Then it will be available in whatever city you wish to visit.



I do not know what charges are in the UK. Renting a mobility device in the US is generally rather expensive. Before I purchased my first scooter, it was not unusual for me to pay $50/day for a scooter delivered to my hotel room. Weekly rates will be less expensive, but I paid less than $800 for my scooter, and that is just 16 days worth of rent. Have you ever considered purchasing a mobility scooter? It seems as if it might even be useful to you at home. These clever devices have made it possible for my husband and me to do all kinds of things we would never have even thought to attempt.



We spend part of every year in Turkey, and our scooters are more trouble than benefit in this ancient country. I continue to search for some type of device as my ability to walk becomes less and less every year. Last year my husband insisted I purchase a three-wheeled walker. I could not imagine that this light-weight little gadget would be of any advantage to me at all.



I was wrong. It skimmed over the cobblestones. It was so light I could lift it over the high curbs. It folded so I could use public transportation. I actually walked faster than the rest of my party on several occasions. This is the link to the walker I purchased http://www.amazon.com/s/ref=nb_sb_noss?url=search-alias%3Daps&field-keywords=three-wheeled+walkers&rh=i%3Aaps%2Ck%3Athree-wheeled+walkers It is the Medical Winnie Light, and it is the best $80 I have ever spent on any mobility aid. It is light weight. It has a pocket to carry things. It folds up and stores easily. It increases my endurance enormously.



My preference is my mobility scooter because there are absolutely no boundaries on what I can do with it. I never have pain that prevents me from seeing what is around the next corner. My next preference is my Winnie Light. It still does not make sense to me that this is helpful, but it is.



You have an ambitious travel itinerary, and you are planning on using transportation systems that travelers in the US normally do not use. We are generally airplane...rent a car at the airport people, or we drive our cars. Few of us travel by bus and train. I think it is fantastic that you have worked out a way to see the US without having to drive an automobile.



I hope this has been helpful. If there is anything else I can do to provide any additional information, please do not hesitate to ask.



Good Luck!

text:
Hi, does anyone know of websites or chat forums which actually customer review the disabled facilities offered by hotels? Research by asking each hotel to expand on their description, email pictures and measurements, etc is incredible time consuming, and not always easy. My friend's recent experience showed that even after a lengthy exchange with the hotel about details, the bathroom was still unsuitable for her very disabled husband. Spending a lot of money on upmarket hotels does not necessarily get away from the problem either, and is not to every travelers' taste or pocket. 



Surely offering disabled travelers the same opportunity to review rooms in detail in a way that can then be searched by others is out there somewhere. And being able to see recommendations of accessible rooms by location, so you know whether it's even worth doing all the detailed work? There must be enough people needing and wishing to share this kind of information. Time to get to grips with this on your otherwise very good website, Tripadvisor?

Hi Leboff;



This idea has been discussed many times on the "Help Us Make TA Better!" forum. It's not a bad idea, but many hotels / motels claim to be “handicapped accessible”, but just what does that mean ? 



As an example, a number of years ago my wife called a hotel directly and asked if they were “handicapped accessible” ? The hotel replied with an enthusiastic, YES !



Fortunately, I used Google Street View, beforehand. When what we were told and what Street View showed didn’t match, we went to double check in advance. It was a good thing that we did, as my father in his wheelchair could NOT be accommodated by that hotel – period.



When we arrived I immediately noticed that there were steps leading to the entrance. We went inside and were told that they were “handicapped accessible” because they had grab bars around the toilet and in the shower. None of the rooms were on the main floor and there was no elevator...just stairs. How is THAT “handicapped accessible” ?



Here we had first hand information from the exact hotel, not through a chain’s toll free reservation number, not from a website like TripAdvisor, or through an online booking site. 



"Is this hotel disabled friendly". Disabled in what way ? 



To one person, it could mean automatic doors and ramps, to another person it could mean Braille on the elevator buttons.



Without clear definitions and standards that can be applied to every accommodation listing on TripAdvisor, in every city & in every country, “handicapped accessible” or “disabled accessible” is just too broad a term, and would be left to each individual's interpretation.



Best Regards

thread_title: Reviews of facilites in hotel rooms for the disabled
text:
Hello.

My wife and I are both full time wheelchair user.

 We travel all over the world and stay over 100 nights a year in hotels in various countries.

After over 40 years of travelling I have learnt that the only way to find out about a hotel is to contact them direct and ask as many questions as you can about the bathroom facilities, access to the hotel, bars, restaurants etc.

I always contact the hotel after I have booked and get them to confirm back to me by e-mail that they have allocated a disabled room to us. If they won’t do this I find somewhere else.

When using TA you can filter the results for hotels at each destination to find hotels that purport to be wheelchair accessible.

 That gives you a start, then you can further whittle down the list by using whatever other filters you want e.g. free wifi, free parking, etc.

Able bodied people in general have no concept of what a wheelchair accessible bathroom is! Bolting grab rails everywhere, which may help a person who can stand but needs support, my in fact make it impossible for a wheelchair user to position there chair in the right position to use the toilet.

Another gripe of mine is putting the seat in a roll in shower on the opposite side of the cubical to the shower head and controls so that they are too far away to reach.

In the USA most hotels comply with the ADA. But that doesn’t mean that you will be able to use everything. Western Europe and North America have far more accessible hotels than else where. But you should be able to find somewhere in most major cities in the world, but the standards will vary. I hope tat this is helpful for you.

Just google hiring mobility scooters Orlando loads come up.

There are, indeed, many places that rent mobility scooters in the Orlando area, and most of them are significantly less expensive than renting a scooter in one of the theme parks. In addition, if you rent from an outside source you have your scooter to use between the parking lot and the amusement park. Although everyone provide parking for people with disabilities, the walk can still be long and difficult.



I would just offer a couple of pieces of advice. Mobility scooters come in a huge variety of sizes. A minivan with five passengers will not be large enough for one of the larger scooters, and it will also be much more difficult to load and unload. If I were selecting a scooter rental facility, my first concern would be how portable the scooter is. We use Pride Go-Go Scooters. When we travel in our daughter's mini-van, where we are a party of five, we are able to put both of our scooters in the small space at the back of the van without difficulty.



Some rental places offer lots of bells and whistles with their scooters including sun shades that also protect you from the occasional shower. We leave all of these things at home when we visit the parks because they are just more parts about which we have to worry. We just take our basic scooters with the single basket mounted on the front of the scooter. We even leave our arm rests at home to reduce the amount of space we need, as well as the amount of time we take to assemble or take apart our scooters.



Before we purchased our own scooters we rented in Orlando. We generally rented from this company http://www.walkermobility.com/mobility-scooter-rental-orlando/26/ because they provided the portable scooters we needed along with the most reasonable price. You might want to check to see if there are other places that have better prices now, but we were very happy with Walker's.



You should also be aware of what type of insurance you need should the scooter be damaged or stolen, and be careful to follow directions regarding caring for the scooter during rain storms and restricting use of the scooter to qualified adults.



I am positive that you will enjoy your holiday much more with the independence that comes from being able to manage your own movements, and, as you note, you also free your family from the burden of pushing you. I resisted using any mobility assistance until my daughter pointed out that I walked so slowly that the rest of the family only experienced one-half of what they could accomplish in any given day and it was selfish of me to protect my vanity at the expense of the convenience and enjoyment of my family.



I rented my first scooter on that day, and I have never visited Orlando without one since that day. People do occasionally stare at me, and some people make comments about lazy Americans who would rather run around in a scooter than walk to their destinations. I just enjoy being able to keep up with the grandchildren and ignore the comments of people who do not know better.



Occasionally Disney gives some preference in lines to people using mobility scooters or wheelchairs. There are a few attractions where people with disabilities are permitted to enter through the exit or move to the front of a complex line. In these situations your family may also take advantage of this small benefit.

Hi Harry, This is rather embarrassing. I have always considered myself a bit more educated in insurance than the average person; although health insurance is really my area rather than personal liability. Nonetheless, I am ashamed to admit that I have never once even thought of the possibility that I could be held liable for something I did while operating my mobility scooter that would justify my need of liability insurance to protect other people or property from me.



My husband would likely disagree, as I did, on one occasion, take down an entire huge display of beer which had been stacked in the center of the aisle where people walk. I did have a fleeting thought that someone might want me to pay for all the beer, but the store was concerned because the display had actually blocked the aisle and they were much more anxious to determine that I had not been injured and get me to sign a document stating I had not been injured.



I rather think that my homeowners policy might cover a situation like this, but I am currently in Turkey and do not have my policy with me so I cannot read the fine print spelling out the terms and conditions.



I honestly do not think this will be a great worry for me even if I am not currently covered. I would probably call and ask if the coverage could be added as a rider to my existing policy. If not, I likely will continue to use my scooter without concern about personal liability. It is small. It does not move very fast. It is quick to maneuver and turns quickly. I have been using it, or other less nimble scooters for nearly 20 years, and I have never hit anything or anyone. The beer incident happened in an electric grocery cart provided by the store. I really do not know how I would go about getting liability insurance if it is not available through my home owner's insurance company.



I rather think of my mobility scooter as another model of an electric wheelchair than as a substitute for a motor vehicle, and I do not think anyone feels it necessary to carry liability insurance on electric wheelchairs.



I own my own. I do not rent. I would expect that if liability by user is any type of a problem that the renting agency would carry that type of insurance as it would ultimately be their liability were an accident to happen. I am sure that if this is any type of a real danger scooter rental companies in the US would have this type of insurance. People is the US are so prone to sue each other and various companies over the smallest events, that I am confident large rental companies would carry liability insurance in the US if this is even a remote possibility.



I am not nearly as confident that rental agencies in Icmeler will automatically carry liability insurance on the scooters it rents to people. Turkey seems much more casual about insurance than we are in the US. Even if there is a national law requiring rental companies to carry such insurance, I can imagine situations in which operators would simply forget to obtain it or claim they did not know it was necessary.



Generally I doubt that such insurance is required by Turkish law. Again, I think the mobility scooter, unless it is one of those huge $10,000 ATV scooters, is just an alternative to an electric wheelchair, and I do not see it as a risk to the people or property around you. My only concern for insurance has always been to make sure whatever I rented was covered for theft in case someone took it while I left it parked outside a restaurant.



While walking is exceptionally difficult for me, and I never leave my home without my scooter, there is one exception to that rule, and it is Turkey. I have never brought my scooter with me. I examine the infrastructure every year with the hope that some of the many barriers to using it will have been eliminated. Unfortunately, the high curbs with no cut-outs still exist. Sidewalks suddenly disappear when someone spreads a blanket and places his merchandise on the blanket and open his little store. In the neighborhood of my hotel they finally replaced an ugly cracked and broken concrete sidewalk, with a set of broken stairs in the middle of it, with a lovely cobblestone sidewalk. I still have to walk in the road because now the lovely sidewalk is completely impossible to use because people park their cars on the sidewalk. Then there are all the buildings, including some very modern buildings, that have stairs. Some provide entrance ramps, but then sink a public room with three steps, without any thought to how a person in a wheelchair or with a mobility scooter would get down those steps. The ramps are often ridiculous. There is a Starbucks in Sultanahmet that offers a ramp that is so steep a person would tumble right out of whatever he was sitting in if he attempted to go down the ramp.



It has been decades since I have been in Icmeler, and when I was there I had no reason to look for disabled access facilities. I hope it is very modern and you will have no difficulty navigating the streets and shops and restaurants. I would, however, be amazed if this is the situation. I am sure that if you have made the decision to rent a mobility scooter, and if there are places in Icmeler that rent mobility scooters there must be large areas of the city where they can be used.



I know you can use a mobility scooter in Turkey and survive. Two weeks ago I met a woman who was paralyzed from her waist down. She used a mobility scooter that was huge. She and her husband rented a very large (by Turkish standards) SUV. They hired a private guide, who also agreed to drive the SUV. The guide made arrangements with hotels all throughout Turkey to provide ramps and first floor rooms. When the lady could not get into restaurants, the guide brought out a portable table and brought her meals to her. The guide also had ramps custom made for the rented SUV. This lady and her husband visited Istanbul, Ankara, Cappadocia, Konya, Antalya, Kas, Fethiye, Pammukale, Bodrum and Ephesus and claimed it was one of the best vacations they had ever experienced. So with the right preparation, a person who cannot walk at all can still discover this magical country. It is, however, very difficult and much more expensive than many people with disabilities can afford.



Were I renting a mobility scooter in Icmeler I would ask the rental agent about liability insurance. If the rental agent does not carry it, I really do not think I would worry about it. Just be careful and do not have a collision with a taxi or a tour bus or a group of school children.

My local council lends me a mobility scooter FOC whenever I need it. It is fully insured and if I go abroad I pay them a returnable deposit in order to take it. I think it is also so they know I am away should I have to make an insurance claim. I have never thought about thir party liability either. I think you need to ask the company in Turkey you are renting from. Maybe they can send you a copy of their T&Cs.

I do not think that one forum can always answer all the questions you might have about a specific location. If I need specific information for people with disabilities I generally post both to this forum and the forum of the specific destination about which I am researching. Often local people are more familiar with places to rent equipment, and they can advise about the suitability of a specific destination for use by those of us with disabilities.



On the other hand, I have learned a great many things sharing a forum with people who have similar challenges. This forum is particularly useful in helping me discover information about transportation. I have learned tips about traveling with medications. I have picked up tips to improve my ability to manage travel with mobility issues.



I try to make appropriate information available on this forum regarding specific destinations with places with which I am familiar. I seek similar information from others in the hopes that they have already traveled to the locations I am researching. If no one has that experience I go to the destination forum. I think we all appreciate any information on destinations that people with disabilities can post on this forum.



I firmly feel that in "this day and age" there is an enormous need for a forum dedicated to those of us with disabilities who are not ready to stop traveling and spend the rest of our lives sitting in a rocking chair on the front porch.



The people on this forum give me the energy and motivation and information to continue to explore traveling opportunities, and my world would be less rich without their encouragement.



If our individual experiences even could be divided among the many other forums on TA, they would be virtually unavailable for us as a group. A thread on disabilities on the Orlando Forum would disappear to the second and third pages in less than one day. In addition, it would attract a huge discussion of why Europeans hate to go to Disney World where fat Americans use ECV's because they are too lazy to walk.



On this forum I know that there is little risk that I will be required to defend my specific disability or my use of wheelchairs and mobility scooters. This is a safe place for me to find others who are like me.

thread_title: Buying crutches and walking aides in Patong
text: My partner and I travelled to Patong beach Phuket during May - June 2013. On our first day, my partner stepped on a broken glass bottle in the beach water and cut his foot. thread_title: Nappy/diaper change facilities on the plane for Asd child
text:
To start with, I would not put my child on the floor of a restroom on a airplane. I can barely put my own feet on those floors. This would leave you with the back galley area or your seats. Neither of these are ideal, but I would not feel intimidated from making my child comfortable if it was necessary to do a diaper change at your seats. I am sure by now you are quite fast and skilled and can complete the process quickly, and you will carry a plastic bag for instant disposal of the diaper. If you need their seat space to change a diaper your other family members will be standing briefly which should provide some privacy for you and your child.



People might get a few whiffs, but it is an airplane. Two weeks ago we flew across the Atlantic with a gentleman in front of us that suffered from some type of serious digestive disorder, and we whiffed for nearly 8 hours. Passengers have to be prepared for life as it happens. Children, obviously cannot wait until the plane lands to meet their bodily functions.



There will be passengers who will be quick to conclude that your little one drinks from a bottle and is not toilet-trained because you are a poor parent. I am sure you have seen these people before, and you cannot be intimidated by them. If someone makes a verbal complaint you could offer a two sentence explanation about your child's condition, but avoid lengthy explanations, justifications or confrontations.



A trip to Bali has to be a very exciting event to plan. I would not waste time or increase my stress levels worrying about this. If it should happen, a diaper change is a five minute event and no one should overly stress about it.

During the Eastern holidays of april 2014 my girlfriend and I visited Madrid. Since she’s in a wheelchair, there are a lot of things to take in mind. Maybe other people can be helped with the information we gathered.



First thing to consider: the metro. If you arrive by plane, you can go to the city center by metro. You have to take 3 different metro’s, which could be quite difficult, but it is manageable if you change in a station with elevator service. For daily transport in Madrid we used the metro a lot. From my own experience I can say: Nuevos Ministerios, Moncloa, Plaza de Espana, Opéra, Callao, Atocha Renfe are well adapted for wheelchair, so don’t be afraid to use them. Metrostations Retiro, Atocha, Alonso Martinez, Banco de Espana, Bernabeu, Manuel Becerra, Ventas, Anton Martin are not that good. This means you have to take at least one big staircase. We didn’t use the other metro stations, so I can’t tell anything about it. If you can handle some staircase, every metro station is possible. Keep in mind that very few metro stations have a toilet. You better look for a bar or restaurant before using the metro!



Metro Sol, the center of Madrid, is a difficult one: there are elevators all around, but it’s a real mess to know which one to take. My advice: try it and ask for help. Spanish people always were kind to help us. If you pick a metro filled with people, everybody steps aside to give you the space you need.



The city of Madrid is well adapted: most of the steps are lowered for wheelchairs and the roads are in good shape. Some parts of Madrid (near the big museums and Atocha) are quite hilly, but nothing extraordinary.



Here you’ll find a list with things we visited:



Mapfre Foundation (a place with free temporary art exhibitions) to see Picasso. It was well adapted, so no problem there.



Museum Cerralbo (a must see, according to us) is fully accessible in a wheelchair, with adapted toilets as well and it’s free for wheelchair-users!



Templo de Debod: a lot of stairs if you take the front entry. Better is to go all the way around to the end of the park and walk the road up again in the park. Inside the temple is impossible for wheelchairs (but not so interesting as well)



Téléferico: well accessible if you can step out the wheelchair and put yourself in the cabine. You can take a round trip for about 6 euros (takes 25min) and leave your wheelchair at the desk. With a wheelchair you must enter through the exit doors, where you’ll find toilets and a photo shop.



Easiest way to reach: take the declining road in the park, parallel with the big road.



Museum of America. You can get there by metro till Moncloa and then take the cycle path over the highway. It’s well adapted and nice!



Palacio Royal: also very well adapted and free! Someone will guide you from the entrance to the elevator, then it’s easy: all public rooms are on the 1st floor. Toilets available.



Atocha garden: hard to find (maybe our fault?) but not that overwhelming. If you don’t need a train, you might consider skipping this part.



Botanic garden: once you survived the cobblestones at the entrance you get free entry and may enjoy a nice, relaxing garden with nice flowers. Full accessible and toilets.



Toros de las Ventas: you get a discount, but still rather expensive. Overall it’s an interesting tour after all the big musea. Tour is fully accessible, toilets in front and at the end of the tour.



Bernabeu: you get free entrance but you can only see a small part of the tour. However, we managed to take the full tour for free, since my girlfriend can still take some stairs. Warning: if you want to do so, there are A LOT of stairs.



Of course the big musea like Prado and Reina Sofia are easy for wheelchairs. No problem there!



Overall conclusion: Madrid is a nice city, and it’s quite well adapted for wheelchairs. Only warning when you take the metro: only half of the stations are adapted with elevators.

Good review lots of good information 



Deb

text:
My husband and I took our mobility scooters with us to Italy two years ago. You are not permitted to use them in the Vatican, and I am not aware of any place where they can be stored. We took a taxi from our apartment to the Vatican so we left our scooters in our apartment.



The Vatican did provide a wheelchair. It was in dreadful condition, and our daughter, who pushed me through the Vatican had a dreadful time managing it. We hired a private guide who was able to help us move from floor to floor using private elevators. At a cost of nearly 500 Euros, I would probably not use a private guide again. 



Since you must provide a person to push your wheelchair, and we traveled only with our daughter, my husband decided to attempt to view the Vatican on foot. He had a dreadful experience, and while he was able to see rooms he had only dreamed about for most of his life, his level of pain made the experience far less pleasant. Overall, our experience with wheelchairs in the Vatican was not exceptionally good. I am sure there have to be better ways than what we did. I simply could not discover any other method.



I was advised to simply go to the ticket office at the Vatican and they would make arrangements for wheelchair transportation. When we arrived at the Vatican on a rainy weekday in February an hour before they opened the lines were already exceptionally long. We simply could not have endured standing in such long lines, so we opted for the guided tour, which bypassed all of the lines. Our guide claimed to provide all the assistance with wheelchairs available in the Vatican.



I have to add the information that I trust absolutely nothing this guide said to us. She spent four hours lecturing us about the secret association between the Bush Family, the current Pope, the previous Pope and the rulers of the former USSR. After the first hour we just stopped accepting her explanations because everything she said was clearly tainted with contempt for the Catholic Church, and almost everything she said was completely untrue. She was useful only to the degree that she forced us to go back and do some research just to make sure that the claims she made were as untrue as they seemed at the time.



It is possible that there is some way to obtain a functioning wheelchair in the Vatican; although I doubt that the Vatican would provide anyone to push it for you. If I planned to return I would try to do some more research because this was the only place where we had difficulties because of our disabilities.



Obviously you cannot manage a scooter around all of the ruins in Rome, but many were retrofitted with excellent access using elevators. We had to hunt around for them a bit, but generally someone would point us in the right direction.



Using our scooters in Italy was not as difficult as I expected. We were able to manage the streets and sidewalks in all kinds of neighborhoods. Our greatest problem was that, while the sidewalks are cut out at street crossings so scooters can move across the street between sidewalks, Italian drivers simply claim these cutouts as parking places. We had to take our scooters apart once to reach the sidewalk. Normally, we just turned around to hunt for a better crossing spot.



We used the train through out Italy. They have a special compartment for people with disabilities, and your scooters are stored right in the compartment with you. You need to make advanced reservations with the train. We were required to arrive at the station 90 minutes prior to departure. We sat in a little waiting room until 20 minutes until departure and were then ushered to the appropriate track and loaded on the train car. It was very easy. I have no idea why we had to arrive so early. Maybe they configure the train or something. We just enjoyed breakfast while waiting in our designated location. It was very pleasant and the train people were very pleasant and helpful.



The only other unusual thing we experienced was the size of many of the elevators. The apartment house we used in Rome had absolutely the smallest elevator I have ever seen. We had to take our scooters apart and send them up in the tiny elevator in pieces. We stayed in small boutique hotels through out the rest of our stay in Italy. We did not have another elevator that would not accommodate our scooters, but we also did not find one that would permit more than one on the elevator at the same time.

Noah
I don't know what prices are in the US, bt in the UK you can buy a complete CPAP system for about £300 - 350.

I found I just could not adjust to my CPAP machine so it was suggested to me to try the TAP3 or aka: Thorton Adjustable Positioner. It repositions my mouth so it corrects the sleep apnea. I went to the dentist and he ordered and fit my TAP3 for me. I have used it for a couple of years now and it works just fine. I especially like it for travel because I do not have to lug the CPAP machine with me. It is just a small case like you would use for a dental plate and I just throw the case into my purse.

Hi Ms Slush. That is interesting. I'd heard people can't adjust to CPAP but I have yo say my first night on CPAP was a revelation and - save for some bad decisions on masls - I've never looked back. The design of the mask can make a huge difference to comfort ond effectiveness - I now use only the fabric dereamweave masks bt I went through some bad times with plastic masks in the past. 

I also have a lightweight cpap machine, so ,uggibg it is not exactly a joy, but not a big issue either. I'm going to check out your device, though

Lisa, If your father has true sleep apnea he needs to see a sleep specialist and get a C-Pap. Sleeping in a recliner is not a cure for sleep apnea. He may breath a bit easier, but if he has apnea he will still stop breathing many times during the night. This is the thing about sleep apnea that makes it so physically dangerous. So, you need a better solution, not just for travel, but also for his comfort and health every night.



I used to travel with a business associate who had some weird type of gastric reflux, and she could only sleep in a recliner. Our travel agent always ordered a recliner from a health care store to be delivered to our hotel. My associate's health insurance paid for the rental of the chair. When there was not a health care store available or we could not get a chair, she sat up in bed with a large wedge similar to the link provided by PDXNoah. She did not like this solution as well, but it worked better than nothing. Again, this is really not legitimate treatment for sleep apnea.



I just saw an ad for the TAP3. I asked my dentist about it, and he said he had never heard of it. I am going to do some more investigation. I have grown to absolutely loath my C-Pap. It could be because it is 8 years old, and I do not think it was fitted correctly when I bought it. Every night I have the struggle between wearing it and breathing so I do not wake up with a head ache versus fighting the nose piece all night long. I probably should at least get a new one. In truth I have moved since I saw my sleep specialist and I cannot get a new C-Pap without a prescription. So.....going to find a sleep specialist who knows about the TAP3 and maybe get a more modern C-Pap, maybe with a dreamweave mask.



Is the US the only country that requires a prescription for a C-Pap, and do we have the only sleep doctors that require an official over-night study every 24 months? It is an obnoxious procedure.



I truly hate carrying my C-Pap, and I purchased the most portable unit available. No airline has ever protested when I have two carry-ons, but it is always a mess getting it through TSA, and there are some places in the world where a C-Pap is an exotic machine no one has ever seen before. That really makes clearing security fun. The first year I tended to forget it and would have to return to the plane. 



Once, in Antalya Turkey I changed buses to continue to Cirali. I left my C-Pap on the first bus, and I was so sleepy that I did not remember it until an hour had passed. Thank goodness my husband can speak Turkish. We found our bus company in the bus station. My husband explained what had happened. The ticket agent sat me down, ordered tea and said "wait wait". He contacted the driver of my first bus, and the driver of a bus coming in the opposite direction. They met and exchanged my C-Pap and delivered it to me.



None of them had ever seen a C-Pap before, and my husband told them it helped me breath while I was sleeping. I think they thought I might stop breathing at any minute because I have never received such a level of care and concern before, and certainly not in a bus station where no one spoke English.

For ref I know that you can but a cpap machine w/out any prescription here in Poland and in the UK, so I expect the same rules applies throughout the EU. Of course, after diagnosis, your machine will be free or subsidised by your local health scheme - so it's free in the UK.

Once diagnosed, I was not allowed to go home until they gave me a cpap machine, then I was called back a couple pf times over the next couple of years for a night so they could check me over in general and use a more clever machine to monitor my sleep breathing. 

I've never had problems with the basic system - only with masks. My first mask was excellent, and I got a new one every few months, so I was happy. Then that model was discontinued and a series of different models followed - some better than others, some bloody awful - until I got an original Sleepweaver ... still the best of the lot, and I include the newer design in the "less good" category! 

Get it right - it pays dividends - I'd never go anywere without my cpap.

I was diagnosed with sleep apnoea 10 years ago and getting my CPAP machine was definitely the best thing for me. It does take time to get used to the headgear or the nose pillows but the difference it made to my life was amazing. Before I was diagnosed I went to Australia and the flights were horrendous, I was so scared of keeping people awake with my snoring that I forced myself to stay awake! I know that I kept my family awake when we were staying with them too so getting the machine changed my life.



I've not flown long haul since so haven't used it on a plane but without taking it on holiday with me, my husband and I (and the other guests in hotels or apartments) would not get any sleep. Luckily, living in the UK I managed to get my machine through the hospital that diagnosed me, I've had one change of machine and several changes of headgear/masks. Like Johnb121, I wouldn't go anywhere without mine and as you can take it on flights as 2nd hand baggage it makes life so much better.

I posted this for Heather, who needed some help and reassurance on how she and her husband could continue to enjoy a holiday in the sun. I thought I'd re-post it because, reading through it again, I think it's damned good advice and, though i'm in no way an evangelist, damned good advice to live our lives by, as age and/or disability starts to limit what we (think we) can do. With the love and help of my partner and the assistance of airlines, airports, tour guides and tour companies, I've had two wonderful holidays in the last three years - one touring in Japan, using the Shinkansen (Inside Japan), and one touring in Rajasthan by car (Delhi Magic). Knowing in advance that I'd covered all my bases and that my loving partner was by my side (or pushing from behind) has meant we can live a wonderful life, and continue to see more of this wonderful world.



********



As H has said, airlines and airports are very disabled-friendly and you can arrange a wheelchair via the airport or airline (could you walk from mini-cab to check-in?) If you would find a wheelchair helpful, they'll usually collect you from check-in and take you through the security etc to the departure lounge, then collect you again to take you to the gate and down to the plane. If your husband can push the luggage on a trolley from mini-cab to check-in, that's the last you'll see it till the other end. Or you could pick up a porter, curbside. (Maybe it would be worth visiting the airport in advance and talking with the porters and info desk about what can be arranged?)



At the other end, you'd again get a wheelchair to the arrivals hall and you could pick up a porter in baggage claim so all your husband has to do is identify your cases and they'll go with you through to arrivals. What happens in and after arrivals is down to what you've booked. Your husband may have to push the luggage trolley, and you walk, to your car/taxi/transfer bus. But the key point is to check who can arrange what, book it early and check it again just before departure.



Incidentally, I believe the right order of things in the UK is for you to arrange assistance via the airline, but for the actual assistance to be provided by the airport. Same process overseas, so you'd not have to arrange anything with the foreign airport - the airline will do it for you.



I think we all try to do too much, and not to see or consider or ask what help may be available (some of it free-of-charge, like wheelchairs and a pusher to get you through the airport, some at a cost, like porters). As we get older and/or less abled (I'm 53, but have to use a wheelchair, or crutches for short distances) we either draw back our horizons and accept a limited existence or we accept out limitations and plan to get the most out of things, whether it's arranging a wheelchair place at the cinema or theatre, accepting stares and being dealt with in the third person (and would he like a drink? Is there anything he needs? Well, asking me direct might be more polite, for a start!) or broadening your horizons, choosing a wonderful holiday destination, researching just how you're going to get there and how you'll get around, checking that you and your husband will be able to tackle what you must while others do all they can to help, and going for it. Don't forget, there is a worldwide industry which can come together to make your journey and holiday as easy as it/they can



Go for it Heather, the world really is still your oyster.

Hi 



My name is Kevin and I am an English guy living for the past 13 years in New York City and Brooklyn, New York. I thought I'd write a quick advice piece to those of you traveling to NYC who have mobility issues, so that you can enjoy your trip even more. 



The first thing to say is that New Yorkers are kind and generous and used to seeing and dealing with disabled people. I once fell over in Oxford St London and two people stepped over me and kept walking. That would NEVER happen in New York. EVER. So, feel free to ask people for help here (using common sense precautions, of course) 



Like all cities there are places in New York City you are simply not going to be able to access. Not all buildings have level entry and not all are accessible to wheelchair users. 



The main tourist attractions, of course are. All of them. In this town, wheelchair users are normally escorted to the front of the line (queue) and as this is common practice, no-one will bat an eye or criticize you for this HOWEVER, do not just go to the front of the line by yourself - that will annoy people. 



I am going to start my mobility guide to New York by talking about public transport and getting around. 



Use the buses. Yes, the buses here are awesome, regular, clean and all buses have little elevators at the front door or middle door or ramps at the front to allow up to two wheelchairs onto each bus. Wheelchair users are supposed to pay their fare as normal, but most drivers won't ask you. However, have quarters (25 cent coins) with you for the fare, just in case. 

Drivers will help you onto the bus, tie your chair down with straps and untie them again at the end of the journey. You must let them do this, it is the law. Offer the fare when you get onto the bus and put fare into the metal "bucket/container" as directed or if you have a Metro Card (recommended and available everywhere - ask your hotel or buy in deli/store) put that into the slot. A Metro Card will enable you to do multiple journeys on buses and on subways. Make sure you have enough credit on the card for your journey. They do have inspectors here. You WILL be fined if you don't have enough credit or don't have a ticket or the fare. Ignorance is not a defense. Also, a new generation of buses and bus routes - mostly in high congestion areas require you to buy your ticket at the bus stop itself before you get onto the bus. The idea being that it reduces congestion at the bus entry and people can get on and off more quickly. 



Also, when boarding a bus all wheelchair users get on the bus first and off the bus first. People are used to this again and will make way for you to get onto the bus before themselves. Don't feel self conscious of this - it's the way it is here. 



As I said, most wheelchairs get off the bus first. When you arrive at your destination, the driver will lock the door, leave his seat, untie your chair, go back to his chair, unlock the door, lower the ramp or elevator and you will roll out. This all happens BEFORE anyone gets on or off the bus. Again, don't feel self-conscious - it's the law. Now having said all of that, of course, there are going to be exceptions. Lazy drivers forget (you will be sitting at the front of the bus close to the driver so its worth reminding them you are there when you are getting close to your destination) and sometimes passengers also forget and will rush past you in their eagerness to get out of the door. Be patient. MOST New Yorkers won't behave this way. Just bide your time and you'll get off the bus and be fine. 



OK. Subways. I would say avoid these if possible, unless you really know your way around. Why? Because MOST subway stations in NYC are NOT wheelchair accessible. Now you may find that the one you are getting on at near your hotel is accessible but you may well find that not the case when you try to leave the station. You can visit the excellent MTA Info online site to work out what is and isn't accessible, but again for safety's sake, avoid the subway if you can. MTA Info also has an excellent online "Trip Planner" where you can input your start and finish address and work out how to get their by cab, bus, train, car or walking or any combination of the above. USE IT. 



Cabs: There are very few wheelchair accessible Yellow Cabs in NYC. If you use a chair and are fit and can transfer, you can flag down a Yellow Cab and hop into the back and the driver will, with your instruction, break down your chair, stow it in the trunk of the cab and take you to where you need to go. It is illegal here for a Yellow Cab to refuse to carry you because of your mobility issue. That said, some won't stop for you. The best place to get a cab will be your hotel or tourist site or main transport hub. Then you'll be OK and you'll be able to get to the front of the line and get a cab, but from the street it can be a problem. 



Yellow Cabs used to be a law upon themselves, but are much more regulated now and there are little screens in the back that give you travel info, annoying commercials and messages from the city and details about your fare. ALWAYS tip your driver. Round up to the nearest whole dollar or bill note (if fare is $8.20, give $10, if the fare is $35.70, give $40) 



Town Cars: Town cars or livery cabs are normally sleek, black nice looking cars that are normally run out of a regulated car service office. They will always be more expensive than a Yellow Cab BUT they can carry more people, making fare-sharing better) they can carry more luggage, are more comfortable, will have helpful drivers and so on. I use them regularly for airport runs or for client meetings etc as they look better and are more comfortable, but again they are ALWAYS more expensive than a Yellow Cab. One more advantage is that the fare is set PER CAR and in advance, so you know what you are paying - there are no meters (normally - some do, most don't) Tip the same as Yellow Cabs, but with a little more generosity. Round up to nearest big bill ($23 fare - $30 total etc) 



As with any tipping in New York - tip two times the sales tax. This will give you a tipping rate of about 17%. Perfect for this tipping culture town. Sales tax is always on your invoice, ticket or bill before the total is given 



Enjoy the Big Apple, Wheelers! 





Trains: Over land trains are going to have disabled access cabins and access. However not all stations are going to be accessible. It is unlikely you will use these when in NYC but if you travel out of the city, you will. Check with the hotel or contact the train company you are traveling with and they will be more than happy to help. 



So, this rounds off my guide to getting around New York in a wheelchair. 



Next in my guide: Where to wheel around to get a real taste of this great city 



More later: Kevin Fetterplace 

Kevin@Mojoworking.com
My partner is semi disabled uses sticks and electric wheelchair she would like to go Rhodes in Greece with private accomadation with whom I know out there do Thomson cater for these situations

Not sure I understand, Stephen. Thomson, like all airlines, will accept a booking for a "typically disabled" person - here I'm thinking of anyone who needs some, but not total, care and assitance. They will pass on the booking for assistance to the airports in the UK and Rhodes who are responsible for providing the assistance - in this case a wheelchair or electric buggy from check-in to the plane door and from the plane to baggage claim ... or if your partner needs the chair to get to the plane, it will be taken from her thmere and put in the hold. I'd have thought it will need some sort of dismantling. She'll get her chair back at baggage claim in Rhodes. Same process coming back.

Check the Thomson website for specifics - like maimum weights, battery types and so on - as some electric chairs are not accepted and you need their info on dismantling or folding the chair. Some people have reported chairs being rejected because the parts are individually too heavy or otherwise unsafe for handling - check this. Maybe even do a trial run - take the chair to the airport you'll fly out of and discuss things with the local Thomson and airport staff. Except when they're really busy, they're usually happy to help.

At the plane door, your partner will either be abe to walk with her sticks to her chair or the cabin crew will take her to her seat in a little chair they can move around the cabin.

Sticks - I use elbow crutches - go in the overheads during the flight, so she can get to the bathroom and so on unaided, if she is able.
Oh, and see this and related pages http://www.thomson.co.uk/editorial/faqs/disabled-passengers/airport-assistance.html
Some might find my blog of interest , some missives regarding a villa stay in Florida plus Hotel in Portugal. http://onmybiketoo.blogspot.co.uk

Hi Stephan, 

I am not clear if you are planning to stay with a friend/relation or are asking if Thomson has suitable accommodation for wheelchair users. 



we visited Rhodes 2 years ago with Thomson, be aware that they cater for mass tourism and are no experts in disabilities. My husband has mobility problems following a stroke but is not a wheelchair user. On arrival at Rhodes airport there was no wheelchair to meet him and the very young courier expected my husband to walk from the terminal across a huge car park to the coach. My husband said he would wait for a wheelchair but the courier seemed unsure of who or how to organise this. Before booking the Ibiscus hotel we asked Thomson to confirm that the showers were of the walk in variety and not over a bath. This was a request too many, my local agent said they were not allowed to call the hotels themselves and could only request such a room with NO guarantee of availability on arrival, they did not seem concerned that a guest could end up with a 10 day holiday of sponge downs . We emailed the hotel ourselves who not only promised to keep a room with a walk in shower but as my husband would not be out and about all day long, promised to keep a room at the back where the sun shone on the balcony until sunset. The hotel and staff are excellent, the hotel is opposite a beach which has a ramp down to the beach and wooden walkways on the beach suitable for wheelchairs. The walk into Old Rhodes is approx. 15-20 mins, but the Old Town would be a challenge for a wheelchair of any description. Infact, one day I did help a tourist who could hardly push her husband's wheelchair over the cobbles. The dining room at the Ibiscus is on the lower ground floor accessible by a ramp and then you go down in a lift type piece of equipment for wheelchairs. However, it is small so I would contact the hotel to ask if it is big enough for an electric wheelchair. 



This year we were given some holiday vouchers for Thomson. Again. we choose a hotel in Garda that suited us . Again we asked about the showers and number of stairs etc. This time at least we were put through to the special assistance department who said that their computer stated that none of the bathrooms were of the walk in type and there was no information regarding accessibility. However, again we contacted the hotel ourselves and have been promised a suitable room . 

So my advice is to always contact the hotel with specific questions if you are using a mass market type company and ALWAYS book assistance with the airline in advance . 



I hope you enjoy Rhodes as I am sure you will.

Since my husband is on an oxygen concentrator I really try to research everything that we will do on our trip to make it easier for him. Apparently I did not do enough for I was not prepared for the Kona, Hawaii airport. We arrived way early thinking that we could get all checked in and through security which takes awhile with his machine. We know that, no problem. He is always patient and courteous to TSA. We get there only to find the airport is open air. No AC so here we sit on a planter in the hot humid shade waiting for the Delta agents to arrive. When they do, they take five groups of travelers first even tho only one group was ahead of us. They took them cause they had boarding passes gotten online! We can't do that due to his machine. We have to go to an agent. So they took all the youngish able bodied people FIRST while he waits in the hot humid line. Then we have to lug our bags over to agriculture with the man saying "put your bag up here". It weighs 45 pounds and I have RA but I did it. Then on to security. Then to the inside. Guess what no AC it is all open air but there is no air. Only place to wait is a kind of AC café. No gate number on our passes said to look at the monitors but no monitors. Then we had to wait and wait cause we had gotten there early. No electrical outlets so he could charge up. He had extra batteries but that's why we go early to get all settled and he can recharge. Finally time to board. He had to walk up steps to the plane. Oh my! Here's the lady with a cane struggling in front of us. I thought my husband would need to be resuscitated by the time we got in. No one offered to help or anything in that whole airport! We will need to rethink next time we come to the Big Island. It was almost as bad at Honolulu except it had AC. No people to help, no train, no signage to where the train was. A long long, long walk from our flight to the Hawaiian air terminal. Again no offer of help. Just be aware that Kona airport is not set up well for disabled folks and the part of Honolulu airport we were in was not either.

Thanks for posting that, cropsis. We really need to know when and where these issues arise.
