If you would find a wheelchair helpful, they'll usually collect you from check-in and take you through the security etc to the departure lounge, then collect you again to take you to the gate and down to the plane. If your husband can push the luggage on a trolley from mini-cab to check-in, that's the last you'll see it till the other end. Or you could pick up a porter, curbside. (Maybe it would be worth visiting the airport in advance and talking with the porters and info desk about what can be arranged?)



At the other end, you'd again get a wheelchair to the arrivals hall and you could pick up a porter in baggage claim so all your husband has to do is identify your cases and they'll go with you through to arrivals. What happens in and after arrivals is down to what you've booked. Your husband may have to push the luggage trolley, and you walk, to your car/taxi/transfer bus. But the key point is to check who can arrange what, book it early and check it again just before departure.



Incidentally, I believe the right order of things in the UK is for you to arrange assistance via the airline, but for the actual assistance to be provided by the airport. Same process overseas, so you'd not have to arrange anything with the foreign airport - the airline will do it for you.



I think we all try to do too much, and not to see or consider or ask what help may be available (some of it free-of-charge, like wheelchairs and a pusher to get you through the airport, some at a cost, like porters). As we get older and/or less abled (I'm 53, but have to use a wheelchair, or crutches for short distances) we either draw back our horizons and accept a limited existence or we accept out limitations and plan to get the most out of things, whether it's arranging a wheelchair place at the cinema or theatre, accepting stares and being dealt with in the third person (and would he like a drink? Is there anything he needs? Well, asking me direct might be more polite, for a start!) or broadening your horizons, choosing a wonderful holiday destination, researching just how you're going to get there and how you'll get around, checking that you and your husband will be able to tackle what you must while others do all they can to help, and going for it. Don't forget, there is a worldwide industry which can come together to make your journey and holiday as easy as it/they can

thread_title: International Travel for Father with Dementia
text:
First, I suggest you accompany your dad to his next doctor's appt. Tell the doctor about his plans--and see what the doctor says. This may take a little persuasion on your part with Dad..........elders tend to know their choice is prob not the best and will try to keep you out of a session where the doc agrees with you.



Second, instead of saying no--start a plan with Dad for a date in the future. Tell him you want to be able to go and see the relatives too--but need to save the money and time off first. "So, Dad--let's do this next summer".

People with dementia fixate, as you have learned. One of the most effective ways to work with it is to be **agreeable** and have an option or backup plan.



If you can get the doctor's help, then Dad has to go with that--and you aren't the bad guy. It becomes, "Dad, the doctor said you should wait till next year, remember?" Dad will grumble and say the doctor is an idiot.........but it's not YOU in the hot seat. You should just say "I know you think that, but let's do this so you have a wonderful time".



When he returns to it, you now have a plan, too. "Dad, I'm sure you remember that we are going to go next July". Then change the subject to stories about his youth, his relatives, the food, etc...........let him take the trip mentally, and help him there. You may learn things you will enjoy, honest.



Good luck; you are in a very tough place, and I feel for you. But the best advice I can give you, based on dealing with this many times-is try, try, try-not to personalize it. Easier said than done, I know. My motto is often: Divert, Distract, Move on. But you have to be kind of sneaky about how you do it, not confrontational!!



P.S. Something else.......please understand that his desires are strongly linked to his feelings of mortality and his illness. He is seeking closure.

text:
Hello



My wife and I are hoping to take our first holiday abroad since my wife became disabled, hopefully sometime between September 2013 - May 2014. We are understandably apprehensive about booking, travelling and hotel arrangements (especially as we are relatively new to this change in circumstances), so are looking for some advice from others who have experience travelling with a disability. We have been reading the forum posts with interest and see how helpful and supportive everyone is. I apologise in advance for all the questions, which may seem abit basic but important to us - sorry... Hopefully our questions won't be too much!



Background - my wife is in a lot of pain which impacts upon her mobility. She can walk a very short distance but otherwise uses a wheelchair which I push when out. She is unable to hold anything but very light objects for the shortest time due to her condition. Her one (relative) pleasure now is bathing in the sea.



Question 1 - Which UK Midlands/ Southeast/ Southwest airport would you recommend for disabled access?



Question 2 - What do you find the best way to get to the airport is? Train (we can park for free unlimited at local train station) but wonder about logistics of suitcases/ wheelchair etc? Car? If travelling by car what is the best way to arrange parking etc (again bearing in mind I will have to manage two suitcases and a manual wheelchair)?



Question 3 - Similar to question above, we are aware we can arrange assistance at the airport, but where/ when does that start from? Bearing in mind I will have to manage two suitcases and a manual wheelchair.... 



Question 4 - Is it best to take your own manual wheelchair on holiday with you? Or use one provided by the airport whilst there and then hire one on holiday? My wife's is provided by the NHS and we are concerned about its safety in the plane - eg. do they get damaged/ go missing etc? Also how easy is it to insure? Any recommendations for insurance?



Question 5 - We will obviously do lots of research regarding the resort/ hotel etc to make sure it meets our needs. But one major concern is that to keep things "easy" we will probably go all inclusive, however we are concerned how we will handle the dining room. Unless we can get a table close to the food (which may not be possible), how will manage, as my wife probably won't be able to walk far enough to look at the options herself, so we will need to use the wheelchair, which will mean my hands are not free to hold her plate and serve her food, and as she can not hold her own plate - it will be tricky to have a hot meal together. Any experience of this, thoughts, or suggestions? 



Finally any recommendations of hotels in Spain or the Canaries in peaceful resorts which are all inclusive, relatively disabled friendly, preferably have an accessible beach, flat promenade/ access to some shops, would be very welcome. 



We would be grateful for any advice, experiences, thoughts or recommendations on any of the above points. 



Thank you so much in advance.

Padv

thread_title: First Disabled Holiday Abroad - Some Questions
text:
1) Choice of airport - not important, All airports can provide assistance through the terminal and onto the plane. For places without ramp access to plane they will have an ambulift to lift the wheelchair to the door. 



2) Some airports will meet you at the carpark if requested but for most it starts at check in desk. Off airport car parks usually have accessible buses and driver will help with luggage. You can book special assistance on trains. Airport taxis get you closest to the front door and save the need to park.



3) Especially on budget airlines I try to manage with one wheeled suitcase and a large bag with shoulder strap. For longer trips you can usually get a luggage cart to carry multiple cases. I have mastered the art of pushing a wheelchair one handed while steering the luggage cart/case with the other hand. Get a wheelchair bag that hangs from the handles. My wife made one to the maximum size allowed as carry on luggage!



4) We always take our own and just use standard household insurance cover, Never had any problem or damage in flight. It is usually collected from and delivered to gate, sometime it is taken to baggage claim (but not put on the belt)



5) I usually take my wife on a 'drive past' the buffet so she can see what is on offer and she either holds her own plate or she places her order and I get both plates after I park her at the table. We don't bother with all inclusive (unless a good deal) - most restaurants are quite happy to clear a path to a table.



We usually hire a car so that we can get about easily without having to get on/off coaches - very few are accessible. Cost is usually less than the cost of airport transfers and excursions.



Beaches are not wheelchair friendly so try to find a resort that has special beach wheelchairs and easy beach access if she wants to to swim in the sea.



Many resorts have a good long promenade - Fuengirola is one.



We don't always go for easy, we have done Luxor, Egypt, next trip is New Zealand via Vietnam and Australia

thread_title: First Disabled Holiday Abroad - Some Questions
text:
Some of us have set up a Facebook group called Access All, which tells the stories of diabled gravllers. Three of us are Destination Experts and the others are well-travelled.https://www.facebook.com/groups/651478171544602/



 I'm like your wife - mostly using a wheelchair but able to walk short distances.At the airport you have two choces - use a porter or get a fmaily member to go with you. You need to book assitance via the airline - book is via the airline but provision is arranged by the airport - and when you check in ask where the assistance desk is. It's pften the closest enquiry desk. Go there, give them your name and someone will collect you and puch your wife's chair. Usually, they get you as far as the departure lounge, then agree where they'll meet you to take you to the plane. At the door of the aircraft, they'll get your wife to climb out of her chair and either walk to her seat or they'll use the skinny aisle chsir to sheel her to it. If you're lucky you'll get a disabled seat, with the aisle arm rest fodling out of the way for an easier transfer. Meanwhile, the chair will be taken down to the ho,d. 

At your destination, the cabin crew get your wife to the door, the airport wil have someone to meet her - sometimes with her own chair but more often with one belonging to the airport - hers will be waiting at baggae claim. The pusher will usually get you to the arrivals hall, then you're on your own.

If I were you I'd book an independent transfer to your hotel - they will meet you in arrivals and take the trolley with the cases and leave you to push the chair. 

You'll have to accept that not everything will work how you'd like it to, and that you may have to be your wife's legs - like the buffet ... you can push her along so she can see what's on offer, male her choies, but then you need to park her at a table and go back yourself to collect your meals.

Thank you all so much for your help & advice. It is very much appreciated. 

It is always difficult to know what to expect the first time you use a service. Only 2 days until we go now!!

I arrived into London Gatwick yesterday. We had two big suitcases and a wheelchair.



The airport assistance guy put my wheelchair on to the buggy and my OH got a lift on another buggy as it was a very long walk to baggage reclaim.



Once we collected our luggage he took us to the bus stop to collect our car. He really went out of his way to be helpful and I would have felt very guilty if we hadn't given him a decent tip.

I can't speak so much for other countries, but here in the US, I generally tip $5-10, depending upon distances involved, amount of extra help given, attitude, etc. If I find that the distance is only a couple of close gates for a plane change, as occasionally happens, I might not tip, or certainly not as much, but otherwise I always do.



In Chile, tipping practices are much more modest than they are here, so I've tipped the equivalent of about $2-3.



I find that most wheelchair-pushers don't expect a tip, likely because most people don't *give* one, but that it is definitely appreciated. And here in the US, tipping protocol pretty much requires tipping for almost any kind of personal service rendered unless the provider is the owner of the business.



You'd tip $1-2 per bag handled, or for a parking attendant to deliver your car, so I just up the amount more or less correspondingly for carting me, hand luggage, the chair, etc. around, for the extra care involved in making sure the chair doesn't run over my dog when I have him with me since he's not yet fully trained to deal with chairs, schlepping us to and from the pet relief areas on top of baggage claim and gates, and for getting my stuff on and off the TSA conveyor belts and baggage claim carousels, etc. 



These people really work hard in a very physically demanding job, and I think they deserve a decent tip. 



Compared to the cost of the plane ticket and getting to and from the airport, I find that it's generally a very modest increase in the overall transportation cost and just figure it as part of the same.



I would add that it's really important when abroad to follow local tipping customs (which are usually far more modest than here) so as not to make yourself out to be a target, and to not risk being part of upsetting the local economy, but further elaboration on that belongs in a different thread.

Having traveled as a companion aide through London, Paris, Toronto, Johannesburg, as well as other small African airports, I have never tipped a member of the airport's accessibility team, nor would I. This is a service that is required by law in most jurisdictions, and part of what we all pay for in our air travel taxes and fees. Everywhere I have traveled, from bustling Heathrow to the tiniest backwoods African airport have had staff who will assist you. Do not accept "help" from people who are not in the official employ of the airport, as this creates a scammy obligation for tipping, encourages their poor behavior, and also creates a liability risk, both for the airport and the individual. 



More tips for navigating the airport in a wheelchair can be found in my article here:http://www.squidoo.com/navigating-the-airport-in-a-wheelchair

With the exception of a couple of European airports where a tip is always refused, I always tip the person who pushes my wheelchair. On our most recent adventure my husband and I gate checked our mobility scooters at our departure airport all the way through to our arrival airport. This required wheelchair service when we changed planes mid-way through our trip. The people who pushed our wheelchairs arrived early at the door of the plane, and delivered us directly to the door of our next flight. They were pleasant and efficient and we tipped each of them $5.



When we arrived we had two wheelchairs from the plane to the luggage carousel. They helped us get our two suitcases from the carousel and we tipped them $7 each. They were pleasant and very fast. Our scooters had not arrived, so we ask a porter to take our suitcases and our carry-ons. Eventually, when our scooters did not show up, this nice gentlemen went and found an employee who eventually found our scooters. This was approximately 40 minutes after the man assumed responsibility for our luggage. He then escorted us across up the elevator to the bridge across to the parking structure, and then down the elevator to the spot where we were to connect with the hotel shuttle. In total, this nice gentlemen spent one hour with us, and it was cold and late at night. We were his last customers of the day. We really had to force him to just leave our suitcases with us at the curb while we waited for our shuttle bus. We gave him $20, and felt like we still had received a bargain in terms of personal service.



I know other economies do not operate like the US economy, but people in the service industry in the US rarely make enough to actually support themselves. These are jobs frequently held by people with few English skills and little education but lots of ambition. They work hard, and most of them are friendly and inquisitive about your travel experiences. Almost none of them have ever been rude or unpleasant to me. I am happy to pay for such cheerful and competent service.



In Amsterdam it is supposedly inappropriate to tip. The service I received there was so absolutely dreadful I thought someone should have given me money. In my experience, you get what you pay for. Maybe if wheelchair staff in Amsterdam had to survive on tips they would not tell a physically impaired old man that he needed to walk to the connecting aircraft dozens and dozens of blocks from his arrival flight. I am not convinced that you get the same quality of service if the pay is guaranteed regardless of how badly you do your job.

I am now calm, two weeks after my experience at LAX. I am just going to explain our experience so that hopefully no one else has a similar event. We flew from Orlando to Anchorage with a plane change in LAX. When we landed we had to wait for someone to push our wheelchairs. The young lady assigned to push me was angry and did not want to push me. Eventually she found some pusher with an empty chair and made him come and push my husband.



We were switching from Delta to Alaska Air. I know that Alaska uses a different terminal than Delta, and that the two terminals are connected by a short tunnel. I was, however, frustrated because it had taken 45 minutes to get the wheelchairs. When the lady did not take the tunnel I asked her where she was going. She told me she was taking a short-cut.



She pushed us right outside of the terminal and onto the curb. Then she said we should watch for a bus to take us to the other terminal. I asked her why she did not take us to the other terminal, and she said the other terminal used a different company and she was not allowed to go there. Obviously this makes no sense. If wheelchair pushers could not move between terminals the whole system would fall apart.



She was large and loud and she dumped me out. The other pusher seemed lost and embarrassed and asked my husband to leave the wheelchair. Eventually a little shuttle bus came up. We told her we needed to go to the Alaska terminal. She asked us how we arrived at the curb. We told her, and she did not seem to understand.



About this time I realize that we are OUTSIDE the airport terminal and we will have to go through TSA again before we can board our plane. The shuttle driver takes us to a door. We get out, and she tells some man who is guarding this door that we need wheelchair service. He says he will take care of it. He makes a call on his walkie-talkie, and tells me "just a few minutes". At 15 minutes I tell him we are going to try and walk because we are going to miss our plane, but I hope 911 can come quickly because I might not make it to the plane. He tells me to wait. After 30 minutes had passed, and I had threatened to walk two more times, a wheelchair person arrived followed quickly by another.



This wheelchair pusher takes immediate control. By now I am positive we will miss our flight, but he assures me it will not happen. He then explains that the system works better if we request a wheelchair with our airline. I explain we had wheelchair pushers who pushed us outside and dumped us at the curb.



He is horrified and explains that should never have happened. He explains how every wheelchair request is scheduled every morning so no passenger has to wait. He said they could not come at the first request because they were dealing with their assigned wheelchair passengers from a flight to Mexico.



I could not believe it, but these two great guys got us thru security and to our gate just before the door closed. I always carry a bottle of water, and, of course, it was confiscated during the TSA procedure. My wheelchair pusher put me on the plane, put away carry-on, and left the plane. In two minutes he was back with a fresh bottle of cold water.



He requested that I contact the person in charge of wheelchairs at LAX and tell them what happened. I have not done that yet. It was a strange experience.....the worst and the best service we have ever had.



At any rate, if you are in LAX and a wheelchair pusher attempts to push you outside of the terminal, don't let her do it. Scream and yell and make her stop before you have to start all over again at the entrance to the terminal. Once you have been dumped at the curb there is nothing you can do. Her objection to pushing my wheelchair was that she had enormously long artificial nails that she had just purchased the night before and she did not want to ruin them. So watch out for the lady with the killer claws.

I’m a new member of the mobility impaired family (ruptured disks and muscle deterioration). Recently ended up in a power wheelchair. It is a monster of 250-300 pounds and needs a ramp or a lift to get into a vehicle. My car (Toyota Highlander) has a lift installed on it, so my USA travel is covered. However, I’m still kicking and screaming about going overseas. My taught was to ship my car ahead and follow by plane. Do not now if vehicles with ramps or lifts are usually available for rental overseas (primarily Europe, possibly South America). 



Any experience with this? Any idea who does vehicle shipping for what price range? Any comments, advice would be greatly appreciated.

I hate to say this, and I hope I'm wrong, but I think you face more problems than just getting your car shipped. 

For example, you can't take your chair onto the plane with you ... you'd have to transfer to one of those lightweight things and board in that, while your own chair goes into the hold. And given the weight, the airline might not be easily able to arrange to fly the chair at all, or only on a later plane.

Shipping the car will not be cheap. Cunard used to take cars on the QE2, so if you could afford it, you would have been able to cross to Europe that way, with your car. But I don't see anythung to suggest this is possible on the new ships. There are many companies who arrange to ship cars, but it's a longer process than you might be able to accept - cars are held, containerisd, wait for the ship, sail over at modest speed, then have to be unloaded and got through customs by the company for you, so could take a couple of weeks, minimum.

Now, if you can get your chair over, there ARE companies which rent cars with disabled access. This is the first one I found, renting cars with ramps http://angelvehiclehire.rtrk.co.uk/?scid=6136&kw=5774675 They have some fairly chunky vans, so ought to have something to handle your chair. Other companies, no doubt, exist. 

Where am I coming from with all this? I'm a big guy with diabetes (giving me peripheral neuropathy, ie weak and no feeling below knees) and heart failure, so for all but the shortest distance I need to use a wheelchair. My partner acts as pusher most of the time. So, based on my own experience:

 - make sure hotels have good access from car park to room. Some offer disabled rooms "just up a few steps", other offer lifts and doors which are too narrow, no turning room in the restaurant (again, just a few steps, it's a design feature!), lightweight fixtures inthe bathroom (look good, but can;t take the weight, or wobble/flex alarmingly) and so on. Also, coming to Europe, although there is a lot of talk about disabled access, one has to accept that you;re talking about buildings which could be 1,000 years old so the options are sometimes limited. Streets can be cobbled. Curbs may not be lowered, disabled parking may comprise two spots out of 200. And, living in what was behind the Iron Curtain only 25 years ago and though there is a willingness to make places accessible, there's limited money and many other priorities over and above getting people in wheelchairs into old castles! Two places I'd really like to visit, Auschwitz and the Wieliczka Salt Mine are essentially inaccessible (in truth, a very limited amount of access to both is possible, but so limited as not to be worthwhile). 

Finally, a thought. I believed for may years that there was no reason to holiday anywhere other than in the USA. I'd visited several times, and seen NY, DC, Orlando, New Orleans, Atlanta, Nashville, Memphis, Denver, Royal Gorge, Grand Canyon, Dallas, LA, SF, SD, Yosemite etc. And I loved it and wanted to see more. I believed that with so much choice in one country (and with knowing so much about the place, food, people, etc) there was no reason to travel elsewhere. So with the addition of Mexico and Canada next door and potentially driveable (I know, not so realistic) you have many, many choices - sea, river, lake, mountain, city, town, country, etc - that you may have to accept making the most of what you've got. 

Me? I discovered India and Japan, but that's another story!

thread_title: Travel insurance with a spinal condition
text:
I just purchased travel insurance. It has never been difficult for me to purchase a basic policy. Generally I just go to insuremytrip.com and select a policy that meets my most fundamental needs, and is also affordable. This year all 91 companies that this web site represents rejected our application. I am not sure if this was based on where we are going or our age. We never got to the stage of identifying previous illnesses.



I finally went to Squaremouth, where I found several companies with reasonable coverage for appropriate rates. We selected a policy with John Hancock. If we would have purchased the policy immediately after purchasing our plane tickets, they would have waived previous conditions. I did, however, just read the fine print of the policy, and previous condition is described as a condition for which you have received medical care in the last six months prior to traveling. I would think that a surgery twenty years ago would not exclude you from coverage.



In our case, my husband has been treated for his medical condition on a monthly basis, so he will not be insured for that condition. I do not think I have ever had a travel policy that included coverage for that condition. I generally just want a policy for an accident or some new illness. We are aware of the chronic condition, and plan accordingly. So I would try this site. https://www.squaremouth.com/travel-insurance-quotes



I do not know how they will respond if I have to make a claim. The reviews for claim management had some positive comments and a couple of negative responses. I can report that the purchase was flawless. I paid for the policy and received an instant receipt. A complete copy of the policy arrived in another hour along with a list of phone numbers to contact both for domestic and foreign travel.



You might try them.



Be sure to read the description of the type of medical coverage the company provides. Many of the companies on this site provide medical insurance only for accidents, not for an illness. I needed coverage for an infectious disease of an event like a stroke or heart attack.

Hi there,



My friends and I are planning to visit SanFransisco and LA in Jan-Feb, 2014.

We consist of 2 wheelchairs and 14 more people, total 16 people.

We will travel about 9-10 days.



We will have to rent a car.

We have searched for lift vans and buses but found out it is way too expensive.

found out that there is only one kind lift bus(for 50 people), and no smaller bus for us.

Please, is there anyone who knows where we can find the lift bus for 16 people or so?



Thank you

I cvanvirtually guarantee that you will not find one vehicle to suit you, but you may find two! Here are some sites to check out:

http://wheelersvanrentals.com/

http://www.wheelchairgetaways.com/california.htm

http://www.accessiblevans.com/index.php

I have spent lots of time in rented vans, and I can virtually guarantee that there is no van that will hold 16 people even without a lifting mechanism. John's suggestion for two vans is more realistic, but I think you will not be able to put all of you in two adaptive vans. To allow for the lift mechanism, the center seats of the van are removed, which leaves a front seat for the driver and a front seat passenger, and generally two to three seats in the rear of the van. At most an adaptive van could hold no more than 6 people, which would leave 4 of you having to rent a third vehicle.



Are the two members of your group who have disabilities completely confined to wheelchairs, or can they assist at all in their own transfer? It would seem to me that with fourteen healthy people it would not be an overwhelming task to help a disabled person into a standard seat and put the wheelchairs in the back, unless you are talking about large, electric wheelchairs, which would be more difficult to move. What do the members of your group who have disabilities use currently for transportation? Maybe the way they generally manage their movements can give you some insight into what you should try and provide for your entire group. How do the sixteen of you currently travel together?



Even if you are able to put your wheelchair users in standard van seats, it is still difficult to locate rental vans that will accommodate more than 7 passengers. There are a few 8 passenger vans, but difficult to locate. In my case I had trouble getting any rental car company to agree to provide an 8 passenger van with a reservation. It was generally reserve a van and hope, when you arrive, that it has 8 seats.



Finally, there is very little storage area in these vans. When we travel with 6 people in an 8 passenger van, there is room for our mobility scooters, when they are completely dis-assembled, and a couple of small suitcases.



Almost all car rental companies rent only 7-8 passengers mini-vans. Full size vans are still made in the US, but I do not know of one that holds more than 12 passengers, and that is without removing center seats to provide space for lift mechanisms. If you could locate two full-size vans with lift mechanisms you might be able to get your entire party in these two vehicles.



You should check the companies for which John gave you links and see if they rent full-size vans and what type of seating configuration they have.



The following links provide some more information on full-size vans with lifts. Maybe one of them can be helpful. http://www.betterlifemobility.com/Accessible-Vehicles/Full-Size-Mobility-Vans; http://www.mobilityworks.com/;

http://www.mobilityworks.com/Wheelchair-Vans-for-Rent.php;

Thank you for your suggestions.



Unfortunately, 2 people on wheelchairs use electronic wheelchairs and they can't seat on the car seats.



I don't think van is suitable for us.

We're looking for mini bus (for 25people or so) that has wheelchair lift so that we can all take in the same car.

But we are having a hard time finding the bus as well.



If you have any further suggestions, I'd really appreciate for your help.



Thank you,



Jisun

Those types of vehicles are not available in regular rental agencies inventories. They are generally only found in institutions that care for people with disabilities such as schools and nursing homes. Occasionally a community may provide a vehicle like this to help their citizens with disabilities. Hospitals in some larger cities provide this type of transportation for patients receiving out-patient care.



I cannot recall ever seeing one of these buses available to rent. I think you are going to discover that the only vehicles like this are owned by organizations that use them daily, and probably could not rent them to you anyway because of legal and insurance issues.



I suspect that you are going to have to discover some more creative way to make your trip. The most practical thing I can think of would be to arrange for three vehicles, two with wheelchair lifts and a third to take the rest of your group who cannot ride in the two wheelchair lift vans. This is going to be exceptionally expensive transportation.



I wonder how the people in your party are going to arrive at your departure point. Are you all flying into California from some other place? How do you all get around when you are together in your own home city? I know it is not possible to take an electric wheelchair on a plane, for example. People who cannot transfer into a regular plane seat have to use an aisle chair to reach their assigned seat.



Even a person who has profound disabilities cannot spend his entire existence in an electric wheelchair, so it would seem that there would be some way to make a transfer from a wheelchair into an automobile.

thread_title: Has anyone used the "TSA Cares" program while traveling?
text:
I believe that the function of this program is merely to provide information to people with disabilities who are traveling. I am surprised that you have had such inconsistent experiences from TSA. We have flown about 60,000 miles this year, and every TSA experience is essentially the same for us.



We put our carry-on bags on the conveyor belt along with our shoes, and our opened laptop computer. We walk through the metal detector, or when available the scanner. If the airport does not have a scanner then I have to wait for a pat-down because my artificial knees set off the metal detector. The only inconsistency I experience is the difference in the pat-down from one airport to the next. Last month in Anchorage I had the most invasive pat down I have ever received....hands in all kinds of places where other people's hands should never be.



Apart from that the whole TSA thing is quite standard from airport to airport. On Monday, flying out of Mardin, Turkey to return to Istanbul I did have a very unusual experience. My knees set off the metal detector, and so did the wand the lady used. I explained, in very bad Turkish, that I had artificial knees. She took me into a tiny booth built in the middle of the tiny airport and brought in another woman. I had to show them the scars from my surgery, which satisfied them. That was a first for me, but it was a tiny airport in eastern Turkey and I have no idea what training the have had. They may have been extra sensitive because it was near the Syrian border.

London "cabbies" are a very special group of people. They are the ones who drive the traditional black cab, not to be confused with mini-cabs, which can be almost any old beat-up saloon with a wheel at each corner. 



Licensed London cabbies undergo a very rigorous series of tests about driving skills, customer service, and knowledge of the thousands of street and roads in London. it is called " The Knowledge" and is very hard to pass.



Most are happy to chat and tell you a bit about London ( or themselves!) and I'm sure they will enhance your trip to London.



Few of them mind short trips, because of the standing charge that is on the meter at the start of the trip.



No need to tip for very short journeys, but if you get extra helpful service, or extra help with luggage, a £ wouldn't go amiss.

Any Black cab will be pleased to take someone from the USA purely because the know they are going to get a tip short distance or not!



Here is my tip for getting a black cab if you cannot find one on the street go to the nearest hotel and get doorman to whistle you one up ( he will expect a tip) if there is not one waiting outside.



As said before Black Cab drivers are very different from cab drivers any where else in the world.

They have to take an extensive test and have incredible knowledge of the streets of London. in fact said test is referred to as THE KNOWLEDGE.



I am also sure if you want to strike up a deal for your stay and speak to the right cabbie they would be happy to oblige for the right money.



In any case it wont hurt to ask, they can always say no!



Enjoy your trip.



Deb

I forgot to add NEVER flag down a mini cab as John said they should always be booked in advance through an office number.



This is for your safety, unfortunately there are a few unlicensed mini cabs who do not care for your safety their cars are not road worthy and they are not insured. And then you have a few who might well rob you and attack you especially if you are a woman or indeed a vulnerable person.



It's a sad fact but unfortunately true.

A couple of weeks ago in Istanbul the government closed down 150 "illegal hotels" leaving many visitors with confirmed reservations looking for other hotels. Most of these "illegal hotels" were, in fact, vacation rental apartments. It appears that people just placed their apartments on a web site and rented them out for the day, week or month. The owners did not meet any of the legal criteria for providing temporary housing for people on vacation.



While I understand that a property owner should be free to use his property as he wishes to use it, I also understand that as a renter, I expect some minimum standards to be achieved in terms of fire notification and prevention etc. So, I was rather of two minds about the events in Istanbul because I would want any short-term apartment to meet minimum safety standards.



I often rent from vrbo because I enjoy the feeling of living in a home rather than a hotel room, particularly when traveling in the US. I am less likely to use these types of accommodations when traveling outside the US because when I do not speak the language, I like the support I receive from a good hotel staff.



In Orlando there are a huge number of vacation rentals, but they are generally located in the same neighborhoods. We often rent a huge house when our entire family comes to Disney World. It seems to me as if every house in the neighborhood where we rent, is also a vacation rental. I do not know what the zoning laws are, but I suspect that not just any person in any neighborhood can rent his home for a vacation rental. Since I appreciate the desire of homeowners to protect their investments, I can rather understand why people might not like 52 sets of new neighbors moving in every Monday morning. It likely could diminish the value of other homes in the neighborhood.



I am not, however, supportive of measures that ban short-term rentals to protect the hotel industry. I do not think these properties prove a serious danger to the hotel industry, and I do not think there is anything wrong with a bit of competition.

Hi I have used airport assistance at Vancouver airport, be warned they drop you at baggage claim and leave you to it, so if you can't manage your own luggage you will need a porter. Its not far to walk out to arrivals lounge maybe 100 yards at most, but thats a long way with a walking stick and suitcase.



As for Vancouver it is a lovely clean city, I can't really help to much here as we only stayed for one night before we went on a cruise to Alaska ( stunningly beautiful) 



I hired a car and driver for the day to take us around the main sights so did not use public transport.



I think the best thing to do would be to also post on the Vancouver forum and I am sure people with local knowledge will help you and I think a simple google search " wheelchair hire vancouver " would answer your question on that.



Enjoy your trip and seeing your son.



Deb

You will not want to walk from the plane to Canadian Customs to the luggage carousel to the meet and greet foyer ar the exit doors to the street. I believe you need to make arrangements with your airline for assistance with that. Then I assume your son will meet you.



Vancouver is 100% accessible. Where there are stairs there will be also ramps. Where there are buildings there will be elevators. There are curb cuts on the sidewalks at all intersections. 



All transit is fully accessible, buses have slide out ramps to join the sidewalk to the bus and space behind the driver with priority to wheelchairs, walkers, seniors and strollers. All washrooms will have either a wider stall for wheelchairs. They are not "reserved" for wheelchair folk but the disabled will have priority when they enter the washroom. Some washroom setups will have a family room, between or near the men's and women's washrooms. These are for wheelchair users and they are spacious.



It was Rick Hansen, the Man in Motion and a local boy whose journey around the world to raise money for spinal cord research, who initiated the transformation of Vancouver, physically and in attitude, into a disability friendly city.

thread_title: Disabled assistance in listed stations for Trenitalia travel
text:
Just returned from Italy and Sala Blu was a life saver for us.

I used a UK (+44) cell phone and seemed to have problems getting 

someone to answer. I found that appearing in person at their office

the day before a trip was effective. 



At one office I found an agent who spoke good English and made 

arrangements for the following day. He also gave me a list of emails 

which he suggested I might use (see below).

This was VERY EFFECTIVE and I found that I could write a request,

use Google Translate to get the Italian version and then paste

both into an eamil. Response time for a reply was great (I am also

sure that this might vary greatly so don't wait to the last minute

to make your request). For most trains, it wise to note that one passenger 

is disabled when you are purchasing the tickets.



Information required

 train number

 PNR code

 departing and destination stations

 departure date, time

 car and seat number(s)

 number of persons traveling

 contact phone number

 type of assistance requested

 (chair lift onto/off of train, can you walk

 while on the train, luggage assistance).







If you have connections between your departure and destination,

assistance will be provided at every connection. BE AWARE however,

this does not apply to regional trains nor every station in Italy.

For example, coming from Chur, Switzerland to Torino, Italy there

was no assistance connecting to the train to Florence. 



Additionally Sala Blu will make arrangements with the destination 

station manager to provide assistance where Sala Blu does not operate 

(for example from Milan to Frankfurt via a connection in Munich, both German

locations provided assistance apart from Sala Blu. The German

dBahn trains were ICE or EC long haul, high speed trains).



Sala Blu requires that you arrive at their office in the station

you are using at least 30 minutes prior to departure.



They are a tad fussy regarding luggage; they will assist with one

bag for free and it's 5eu for every other bag.



Here is the list of emails given to me:



 Ancona SalaBlu.ANCONA@rfi.it

 Bari SalaBlu.BARI@rfi.it

 Bologna SalaBlu.BOLOGNA@rfi.it

 Frienze SalaBlu.FIRENZE@rfi.it

 (aka Florence)

 Genova SalaBlu.GENOVA@rfi.it

 Messina SalaBlu.MESSINA@rfi.it

 Milano SalaBlu.MILANO@rfi.it

 Napoli SalaBlu.NAPOLI@rfi.it

 Reggio SalaBlu.REGGIOCALABRIA@rfi.it

 Roma SalaBlu.ROMA@rfi.it

 Torino SalaBlu.TORINO@rfi.it

 Trieste SalaBlu.TRIESTE@rfi.it

 Venezia SalaBlu.VENEZIA@rfi.it

 (aka Venice)

 Verona SalaBlu.VERONA@rfi.it



In my experience, email addresses are case insensitive, but you can

always copy / paste from the above list.



This is the Italian link: http://www.rfi.it/rfi.html

Click the ENGLISH link on the top/right of the screen.

Then click on the Station Accessibility box on the left.

Often I get abused, harassed and swore at in public places when I use or ask to use disabled bathrooms, seating, etc...

I live in San Diego and most people are decent but many scream and swear and tell me they are fed up with accommodating the disabled. For instance...in the past week I went to the movie theater and was in disabled seating and was abused when I politely asked the healthy non-disabled seated patrons behind me to please remove their feet off of the disabled seating poles which were next to my head. I was repeatedly screamed at, told to get out of disabled seating because they didn't want to move their feet and had to get the manager to help me.

At a casino with my family I went to the women's bathroom 3 different times and politely asked if any women in line were disabled so I could take my turn after them and use the disabled bathroom. ALL 3 times I was swore at by healthy women in line and ORDERED to get back into line behind them! I was even told by a employee at the casino that disabled MUST wait in line with everyone else and CAN NOT go to the front of the line and use the disabled bathrooms! I thought disabled bathrooms were for the disabled before healthy people could use them...am I wrong???

Any suggestions? Do I have any rights?

thread_title: Help! What are my rights in public places in the USA?
text:
Jane, of course you have rights and your treatment is appalling. 

<<In 1990, the Americans with Disabilities Act became law, and it provided comprehensive civil rights protection for people with disabilities. Closely modeled after the Civil Rights Act and Section 504, the law was the most sweeping disability rights legislation in American history. It mandated that local, state, and federal governments and programs be accessible, that employers with more than 15 employees make “reasonable accommodations” for workers with disabilities and not discriminate against otherwise qualified workers with disabilities, and that public accommodations such as restaurants and stores not discriminate against people with disabilities and that they make “reasonable modifications” to ensure access for disabled members of the public. The act also mandated access in public transportation, communication, and in other areas of public life.>>

What can't be policed easily is the reaction of individuals to people with disabilities and I really feel for you. May I suggest you look for an organisation that works with and supports people with disabilities in your area. This will help you with ideas for where is welcoming as well as providing ideas for various responses you can make and letting you know exactly what your rights are.

Take heart and don't retreat.

text:
I agree, you do have rights, and this is appalling. I get so angry when I see young and obviously fully able-bodied people using the handicapped stalls, especially when there are plenty of others open.



If need be, don't hesitate to call the police if the management of the place you are in can't or won't help you. Seriously. It is illegal to discriminate against a disabled person, and behavior such as this is definite discrimination. And if they are actually threatening or hitting you deliberately, then you've also got normal assault and battery laws on your side in addition to the civil rights laws.



I've had to call the police when a restaurant refused to serve me with my service dog, and long story short, I was ushered in with great fanfare and profuse apologies and even comped my meal when the cops left. They can be a *huge* help for disabled people who are mistreated - and they will much more likely *remember* what they are told, which will help others who come after you as well.



Federal law is certainly on your side, and local law may also add teeth to it as well, as it does in California.



If you can't get satisfaction from the business itself, then also file a complaint with the DOJ and consider suing the business and any involved individuals whom you can identify.



It is, of course, going to be harder to deal with individuals who come and go, but if the business owner gets cited and/or sued for allowing such behavior, you can bet they will take steps to make sure it doesn't happen again. If you sue, you can also seek such specific relief as part of your suit, namely that they be *required* to take clear steps to stop this sort of thing in addition to any monetary compensation.



Abs140, I love the idea of those cards! 



I would definitely encourage people who are mistreated in any establishment for any reason to post about it in online reviews, at least if you have been unable to get satisfaction by other means.

With the exception of the disabled bathroom stall I have few complaints about the treatment I receive in the US. I agree that I think disabled people should have bathroom priority, but I have given up expecting that. The most popular place in the bathroom is the disabled stall. I live with that. 



I am almost always treated with exceptional kindness by total strangers. Today four different people in the grocery store wanted to help me reach items that were high on the shelf. Someone always helps put gas in my car. Restaurants go out of their way to provide space for my wheelchair. 



No one has ever used a swear word directed at me, or complained about my disability. Laws in the US provide legal access, but every day citizens provide all kinds of assistance. 



I do think it is important, regardless of your pain level, to treat others kindly. I try to smile, and I very rarely ask for any assistance. Your experience is vastly different from mine. We spend many weeks traveling and have been all over the US many times. People are unfailingly kind, compassionate and considerate.

thread_title: San Diego Zoo - Not Friendly For Those With Disabilities
text:
We were trying to develop a non-traditional Christmas, and decided to go to San Diego for the holidays. We always enjoyed visiting the San Diego Zoo when our children were small, and we thought our grandson would enjoy it.



Twenty years ago I was obviously unaware of how difficult the zoo would be for anyone using a wheelchair. There are large parts of the zoo that simply cannot be reached using a wheelchair because they involve stairs, and there is no alternative elevator.



We arrived at noon, planning to stay until 8pm to enjoy the Christmas lights after dark. After we picked up a map we spent 45 minutes trying to figure out what we could see easily (not much), what we could see with detours and out-of-the-way routes (mainly the panda bear display), and what things we simply could not reach (elephants, big cats and generally just about every exotic animal I wanted to see).



In five hours we saw a few monkeys, and we saw a large crowd in front of a window. We assume there was a large cat behind the window. Ultimately we left this display area. People continued to push in front of our chairs, and we could not see over their heads. No one was remotely interested in allowing us an opportunity to see the animal.



In addition to the absence of accessible facilities, the crowd at the zoo was rude. I have never been treated in such a manner as I was treated by other zoo patrons. I believe they could have easily tromped us to death.



The rest of our time was spent on a long journey up and down many hills before we finally reached the panda bear display. Here there was a moving sidewalk so we were able to see the mother panda bear and her baby for the brief period of time we were on the sidewalk. Too bad the zoo does not use similar crowd control measures at other popular displays.



We returned to the main entrance where there were a few Christmas lights. To see any additional lights we would have had to pay an extra fee for a trolly ride, which had no space for people with disabilities and did not even appear to have a boarding ramp. At least, no one working at the zoo had any information about how people with disabilities would be able to see the lights.



We left at 5:30pm, having seen almost nothing. It was a disappointing experience, and I would certainly caution anyone considering this adventure to think again. You really cannot justify the price of the ticket based upon what you can actually see.



Frankly, I remain amazed that so much of this very popular zoo is simply off-limits to people who cannot walk.

We just returned from three weeks in Southeast Asia. I would like to echo the advice of johnb121 and tortoise123_12. Bring:



1. Medication with original prescription (broken down or in original packaging)



2. Cooler container (could be just an insulated lunch bag with an ice pack inside)



3. Note from the doctor, explaining that the traveler is diabetic and needs to carry medication and supplies *including a sugar supply such as juice*. I advise translating the letter into the languages of every country being visited, as I found that security officials in Thailand and even Japan did not understand why a diabetic traveler would need a juice box.

thread_title: Getting around London with a disability
text:
Combo....



I am someone who lives in relatively central London, has to walk with sticks, and sometimes uses a chair..( as someone else says, it doesn't do much for me, but does help the people trying to help me). However, most of the time I drive myself.



You don't say how long you are coming for, what are the most important things you want to see, and whether you ever drive/ have a car



All of these are important..



If you have a car, or could rent one, this might help you some of the time. London is not a particularly disabled friendly city, and whereas there has been a huge emphasis on cycling, and walking, not too much has been done for those who can't do either.



If you are coming for a week, rather than two or three days, you might consider renting a small apartment..this is usually cheaper then hotels, as you can make some of your own meals and not have to pay restaurant prices all the time, and can also have a rest whenever any of you need to.



Try to decide what you really want to see...for example the area around Buckingham Palace is not the most interesting bit of London, and like anywhere official in the centre of big cities has huge wide open spaces which your father would find difficult. The best way to see the headline sites, the Palace, Westminster Abbey, St. Paul's etc. if only from the outside, might be to take one of the open top buses...they are all on web- sites..



There are parts of central London which are much easier to get around slowly and easily once you are there....look at the South Bank, around the Festival Hall, or Covent Garden, or even Soho.....and don't forget the river. The trips aren't cheep, but a ride all the way down to the Thames Barrier and back is something you parents would never forget.



I am not quite sure how this site works, but if it would help your planning to get in touch, please do so.



JY

I was talking with one of the India DEs about disabled access in India and Poland.

Here in Poland, it’s a pretty mixed bag. Not yet 25 years since the fall of the Iron Curtain, disabled access is still a long way down the agenda – though things are improving, thanks to the efforts of access advocates like Marek Sołtys of fundacja TPSW and new buses and trams are accessible, but still we lack drop curbs; shops, restaurants and hotels can be accessed only up (or down) 10 or 15 steps; and like many places with a long history, access to many historic buildings and places is limited to non-existent.

As someone who fell in love with India in his 40s and found himself in a wheelchair most of the time in his 50s, I’ve seen several parts of India – most notable the Kovai area in Tamil Nadu and Delhi/Agra/Rajasthan – the latter on a tour arranged by the said DE for my partner and I (yes, fat, wheelchair and gay. The gods do not always smile on me!). My friend, the DE, asked me how I’d respond when asked about disabled access in India and my immediate response was to say how good I’d found Amber Palace. Not perfect, but the Palace was built with ramps to allow .. well, let me put it this way. I commented on the ramps to our guide who responded that “even hundreds of years ago, people were injured in battle, born or became disabled or grew old”.

Hundreds of years later, architects building owners and the guardians of historic places still have not come to terms with the fact that failing to provide access denies their business, their property, their historic place to anyone with problems.

Three keys to access: ramps, rails and information

Ramps, because a wheelchair can’t climb stairs

Rails, because a handrail is so very, very helpful for anyone who struggle with stairs

And information, because without clear information about access people planning to visit India will be discouraged or else turn up and be sorely disappointed. How many people have cried tears of frustration and shame at the Taj Mahal when they found they could not climb the barrow, un-railed stairs to the platform? I was lucky, I could just manage to climb the stairs, then rested before entering the tomb, the afterwards before descending – but, again, who knew there are places where you can rest and recover?

So, given lack of information is the problem I hope TA members can help me address, what are my experiences?

Temples – it’s difficult for those with walking difficulties to take their shoes and socks on and off, and impossible for those in wheelchairs not to track” their wheels into temples. Where some areas are accessible without offence, i.e. where a disabled person could go in their chair without offending the temple guardians, this ought to be made easy and obvious. Things like the washing of feet in (often dirty) water are a problem too - neuropathy means I have no feelings in my feet. On one trip to India I went home with a blister on a toe. The toe was infected and I spent 13 weeks in hospital, in the early stages of which they discussed the point at which they might have to remove my lower leg. I’d taken off my shoes, washed my feet and walked barefoot around a temple …

Mysore Palace is worth an effort – some of the rooms are stunning, and you can keep your feet dry and wear socks. Some stairs.

Cochin Hill Palace – unless you can get your car to the door, not worth the climb. Interesting, but socks and stairs – lots of stairs.

Kodaikanal – too many unsurfaced paths as the only way to get to view points. Amazing mostly for the drive up and down – as a north European, coolness and rain are not such a big attraction, but the Carlton is very nice.

Humayun’s Tomb in Delhi is one of those places you perhaps put on your list of things to see “if I have time”. Move it up. It does not have 100% flat wheelchair access, and it’s a fair walk from the initial entrance, through several gateways, to the main building, but those gateways are the only problem getting that far – if you can, there’ll be a few steps up and down, then back to your chair.

Qut’b. Save for a ramp at the entrance, 99% flat. It’s very easy to see everything, and a nice place to take it easy while absorbing the age of India.

Delhi Cottage Industries Emporium is on several floors, but each one is connected by an escalator and there’s something to sit on at the top and bottom. For a one-stop for a carved elephant or a house-worth of beautiful furnishings (and a nice little café), its worth a visit if you can.

Rajpath. Although not flat, that’s because there is a hill. The road/pavement is smooth from India Gate to the President’s House.

Pushkar. Narrow, winding streets, poor pavements and steps at the ghats restricted me to the hotel, which overlooked it all

Jaipur. Unlike some places you’ll go, Jaipur actually has pavements, not for walking n, of course – they’re for the shops to expand onto. But they tried! The pink city is flat, but huge.

Amber Palace as above, not perfect but very good. I’ve no idea if you’d be able to go on an elephant, though. See not only the external ramps but the way they polished the “concrete” on internal ramp walls to reflect the light.

Observatory – not bad, but not good either. In truth, more of a place to get you photo with a weird looking thingy, but the “thingies” come in a surprising number of shapes and sizes, Some shallow steps.

Palace of the Winds. You know it’s a façade, right? The street side is what you normally see – behind it is basically solid scaffolding, from which the street can be viewed. Many steps on the back.

Jodhpur – Mehrangarh Fort was not designed by the same architect as Amber, sadly, so wheelchair access is going to be tricky. There’s a level courtyard initially, from which you can take an elevator to the upper levels of the fort. From there, if you can manage stairs down you’re OK – though in for a long walk. Basically, as you see the Fort you gradually descend – sometimes not so gradually – back to the courtyard you started off in, and where you’ll find a café. The slope down past where you’ll see the shrine to wives of the maharajahs of Jodhpur who have committed sati. is where it gets really steep … and of course there’s no handrail. And slippery in the (unlikely) event it gets wet. The view of the blue city from the heights of the fort is pretty amazing.

Ranakpur. I’m listing this because we found Ranakpur a wonderful place to chill. Mid-tour, a night or two at the Maharani Bagh could be just what you need (and it’s flat)

Udaipur. The Palace complex is quite big but past the individual gates we found access was not good, and there’s not much room to manoeuvre in narrow halls and stairways and small courtyards. The boat trip on the lake is a “must” if you can get onto the boat – you’ll need to get down 15/20 steps (at least these come with a handrail, and get from land to boat. The boat and shore are at much the same level, and the operators will hold the land … sorry, the boat steady for you. Everyone sits. If you like to shop, walk down from the Palace complex to the bottom of the hill and have your driver meet you there. The slope is not enough to panic, fairly smooth, and the crowds when we were there were thin to nil. So we were able to make our way down, stopping to look at and buy several things, and our driver waited for us, eagle-eyed as they all are!

Bundi. Maybe not a good idea. Once I’d scaled the alley to our hotel (no ropes needed, but a LOT of puffing, panting and cursing) AND the five floors to our room, I stayed in the hotel. The city is rundown, a bit (a lot) rough around the edges and the Palace and Fort have seen better days, though they were a LONG time ago. But for atmosphere and for watching the monkeys on the roof terrace, I’d still give it 8/10.

Ranthambore. Your views are probably different if you see a tiger. We did not, so the 5:30 alarm call, Jeep pick up and entry to the park all before dawn, then several hours hanging on for grim death as we bounced around the Park is not something we’d repeat. However, seeing so much natural nature was worthwhile. Climbing into the Jeep would be impossible unless you have the front seat. Otherwise, look at a cantor.

Agra – Taj Mahal. Until you reach the white marble are you’re OK. One or two ramps to negotiate, but that’s all (so long as you can get aboard the electric buggy from the ticket office to the gate).

Before climbing onto the white marble area you must put red overshoes over your shoes (they come with your ticket) and that’s the point at which problems start. How do you put overshoes (red or otherwise) on a wheelchair? How do you get a wheelchair or anyone with walking problems up to the level of the tomb? How do you stop what feels like 500 people trying to help? The answer, sadly and to India’s shame, is that you can’t.

What’s your experience of access in India? Share it with other TA members here, and let’s see what we can do to help other people with access issues to visit the India we love.

Hi,



 I've just booked a return trip to Egypt for myself and my mum. We've booked with Red Sea Holidays online, which we've done a number of times in the past.

 My mum suffers from osteo-arthritis in her ankles, knees, hips and spine and can't get in and out of the normal seats on the aircraft. In the past I've rang Red Sea and they've always pre booked us medical seats, so I had no reason to think there would be any issue this time.



 I've spent the last 3 days trying to get this arranged. Red Sea are telling me that as the flight is with Thomas Cook, they will not allow Red Sea customers to be pre book until 3-7 days before departure.

 My concern is if we have to wait until that close to travelling, if there are no medical seats left, my mum won't be able to travel.



 I've done some research on-line and found a Dept of Transport Access to Air Travel for Disabled Persons and Persons with Reduced Mobility - Code of Practice. Its a massive document but it looks to me as though the airline has a legal obligation to provide the necessary arrangements for disabled passengers.



 Has anyone else had any similar experience? And if so did you manage to get a resolution?

thread_title: Flying with a disability - Pre booking seats
text:
The airline we use generally does not assign the bulkhead seats until passengers arrive at the gate to the plane. Occasionally they will assign one to me in advance, but they make it clear that anyone with a service animal will have priority over me should they reserve a ticket after I am assigned a bulkhead seat.



I worry about that happening because then there would be nothing left in the front of the plane or in the Economy Comfort section of the airplane. Accordingly I always reserve a seat so I will have a decent place to sit. I often do not even request a bulkhead any longer. I do not like not being able to have my carry-on at my feet, and I really hate having to get it out of over-head storage after we have reached altitude.



I have very bad arthritis, so I appreciate that it is difficult to get in and out of a regular economy airline seat. It is not, however, nearly as difficult as many other things I am forced to do when traveling. If you can get an aisle seat with a movable arm rest you just have to turn into the aisle. My husband usually exits before I do, and then he provides stability for me as I rise from my seat. It is not the most graceful thing you see on a plane, but it works for me.



Now that we have the option of Economy Comfort seating, I have few difficulties getting in and out of my seat. I have not requested bulkhead seating for at least three years, and that was only because we were on a 12 hour non-stop flight and I was only three weeks out of hip replacement surgery.



So.....if it is not exceptionally expensive I would just purchase an Economy Comfort seat now, and not worry too much about the bulkhead seats.

Hi

I am wondering if anyone on the forum can recommend a good travel insurance company that covers people with learning disabilities without hiking the price up?

I have taken my mentally handicapped sister on holiday all over the world every year for about 20 years now with no problems. She always paid exactly the same premium as me as we are both fully fit and healthy, I always just made a point of telling whatever company that she has a learning disability, they were always fine with this, all they were ever interested in is if she had any physical problems which she has not.

Then 3 years ago it started,as soon as I mention the learning disability the price goes up 3 fold and we have to do a special totally pointless medical questionnaire, I say pointless because my sister is the fittest person I know!. Apparently learning disabilities are now classed as a medical condition.. My husband has a lot (and I mean a lot) of very serious medical conditions and she is being quoted more than him!. I think this is really, really unfair and borders on discrimination and is just an excuse to rip my sister off. 

I am wondering if anyone knows a company in the UK that is not classing learning disabilities as a serious medical illness?

Any help most appreciated
To clarify: do you mean something like developmental disabiliies (what used to be called mental retardation in the US) or something like dyslexia?

Yes mentally retardation or mentally handicapped as we used to say in the UK . My sister has a mental age of about 5 years old. She has no "label" to speak of ie no specific condition like downs or autism, no one knows why she is like she is, it has just been put down to the fact that she was born very premature. She is 100% physically fit though and totally addicted to sport, she does yoga, aerobics,football, running,swimming,horse riding (she has her own horse she mucks out every night after college) she also ,does sponsored walks and a half marathon last year and obviously she doesn't smoke or drink and is very slim.

My husband has diabetes,neuropathy,COPD,cholesterol.is over weight,out of breath most of the time,had to take the "fit to fly" test last time as his oxygen levels were too low, is always in and out the hospital as he also has joint problems.. His insurance is cheaper and he is also 20 years older.

It is all just crazy

I forgot to mention that both of them have been travelling for 20 years plus and neither of them has ever had a claim. My husband has always had to pay a fortune for cover due to his conditions but with my sister it is just purely a total rip off. Ok she has a mental age of 5 but how much do they charge 5 year olds, probably nothing.

Collectively between the 2 of them the cost is just becoming a joke

Finally found a company today that doesn't discriminate or rip off the mentally handicapped so we are all sorted finally!!



Goodtogo £29 (same price as me or any other healthy person)



Flexicover Direct £92 (shame on you). They even had the cheek to try and charge us an extra £5 for a medical endorsement form which literally had nothing on it as she has no medical conditions, (work that one out)



Virgin £86 (shame on you too)



Hope this helps others in the same boat

I am curious why you would have provided any information that you were not legally required to provide when applying for insurance. Insurance companies will find any way possible to earn more money by increasing premiums and reducing the amount and type of incidents they will insure.



I think this is a dreadful form of discrimination because your sister does not meet any of the criteria applicable to a pre-existing physical condition. There is absolutely no justification from the basis of an actuary to account for an increased premium. I have no idea what laws would cover this type of discrimination. Since you were able to obtain insurance I would probably not pursue the issue any further. In the future, unless you must respond to a specific question I would not mention the mental capability of your sister. If they do not ask, they do not need to know. The responsibility would be with their failure to ask rather than your failure to disclose information not solicited. My attorney often reminds me that nothing good can come from providing information not requested.

Requirements for insurance in the UK (where OP is from)

Are different than those for USA residents at a guess...

And laws and their interpretation thereof, also differs between the 2 countries.

So what you can/can't do, do/don't have to declare are possibly quite different....

Busy,



I am very pleased that the OP managed to obtain appropriate cover at a reasonable price, and I hope they all enjoy their trip. In the UK, insurance is a contract struck " in the utmost good faith" and the particular condition mentioned is a material fact, non-disclosure of which could have serious implications if a situation arose necessitating a claim. It is not a case of actuaries trying to gouge policyholders or evade their responsibilities.



Claims are only paid from the common pool of premiums, and sadly, experience shows that some conditions increase the risks and costs of a claim arising.

Yes, I thought things would likely be different "mon"

(Yep, I miss that jolly old jack tar, too, OTC is dull without him....)

Chrissy, your terminology is interesting and different from what we use in Australia. A learning disability (such as a reading disability) as defined by the DSM5 is not the same as an intellectual disability. An intellectual disability of the level you describe may make the person more likely to be unaware of danger and to perhaps take more risks than a person without such a disability. 

Nevertheless, it amounts to discrimination and there are laws such as the Disability Discrimination Act which are there to assist.

I link to a UK page for you and suggest you call the number listed for legal advice (free) on what your sister is entitled to (and maybe provide better services in the future for others)

http://www.nidirect.gov.uk/travel-insurance-for-people-with-disabilities

I am just glad I found this company that is not discriminating, just hope they don't decide to jump on the bandwagon like the rest next year!

Busy-retired I forgot to answer your point about why I disclosed the info. It was because you hear so many horror stories about how insurance companies have a nasty way of getting out of paying out by linking one ailment to another or saying such a condition was caused by such a condition so I always disclose everything for my husband too and even my pets. Only a few months ago my friends horse was not paid out on and she was left with a big bill as they managed to connect one ailment which it was no longer covered for in one leg with a new ailment in another leg saying that the uncovered ailment had caused the second which was total rubbish but they got away with it so yeah always disclose everything or they will start digging!

Chrissy,



I am truly saddened that you have been left with such a negative view of the UK travel insurance market, but I say again, I am glad that you found appropriate cover at a price that suited you.



I have spent over 26 years as a Medical Claims Consultant in travel insurance and emergency travel medicine, so I suppose I tend to view matters from the insurers' point of view, although my company is impartial, working as we do for lots of insurers and underwriters. 



In my business, as long as the policyholder has declared the things the insurers ask them to declare, in response to direct straightforward questions, and hasn't concealed a " material fact" which might have had a bearing upon whether the insurer would grant cover or not, then the policyholder gets the medical attention, service and support that they need.



As private individuals, my husband and I declare all our diagnosed medical conditions for our travel insurance, and, incidentally, we pay very significantly higher premiums to cover them all.



We are actually happy to do so for the peace of mind we have when travelling abroad.



Insurance premiums form a fund and the people who don't claim pay for those who do.



Insurers don't have a bottomless well of money. They are in business to cover their policyholders who need to make a claim, and only after those claim costs have been paid can they return a profit to their shareholders.



I hope you have a wonderful trip, that you don't need to make a claim and that all your travels will be safe and happy. If you do need to make a claim, then I'm sure you will regard the premium you paid as money well spent.



Regards

thread_title: Take your mobility scooter with you to the casino
text:
Although we do not gamble for recreation (or any other reason) we used to enjoy visiting casinos. We liked the opulent decorations, the lovely hotel rooms and the inexpensive food. Occasionally I would play a bit of Blackjack and my husband would spend an hour or so with the slot machines. 



When I lost my mobility I stopped even planning vacations in areas where there are casinos. They are just such exceptionally large structures I could not imagine trying to walk from one place to another, let alone getting to and from my room in a 3000 room property. 



This Christmas our youngest daughter was given charge of Christmas plans and she arranged for two days in Las Vegas. I took along my scooter. I could not contemplate getting around without my scooter, but I had no idea how I would be received or if it would be practical.



I never left my room without it, and the staff treated me very well. They always found an appropriate table for me, and on the gaming floor they provided similar arrangements. It made our experience so pleasant that we came home and went to Biloxi last week.



I am now wondering if a cruise ship would be a similar experience; although I know there would not be as much space.



I guess I am very late to this idea because I saw lots of people using electric wheelchairs and mobility scooters in all the casinos we visited.

Thanks. In all of our very extensive traveling we have never taken a cruise. My husband insists that it will feel similar to being in a prison, even if the accommodations are somewhat better than the average jail cell. I am hesitant because I do not even own any clothing that I could classify as "resort casual", and I am intimidated just by the idea that I might have to "dress" for dinner. Then I am afraid I will drink four Diet Cokes and require a loan from my bank to pay my beverage bill. Since I cannot imagine getting in a swimming pool on a cruise ship, and I am not interested in climbing an imitation rock wall or practicing my golf game on a putting range, or going into the casino where I could easily give into boredom and gamble away my next year's income I am not really sure what we would do on a cruise. It seems that you spend so much more time on the ship than you spend in the places where you make port.



A cruise has never been anywhere near the top of our "To Do" list, but I rather feel like I may be missing something in my perception because almost everyone I know take cruises on a regular basis. So, now that I hope I have solved my largest concern of just getting from my room to other parts of the ship I will have to begin research. Just one quick question. Does anyone know if it is necessary to make advanced arrangements if you bring mobility scooters. We do no need specially adapted sleeping rooms. We just cannot walk any distance.



Is Cruise Critic affiliated with TA? Several years ago I attempted to access a forum on cruise activities. It was associated with TA and I received a message that the sight was not available to those who did not use a PC. We have always been MAC based, so I just never looked at that site again.



Recently what enthusiasm we might have had for a cruise has been dampened by stories of ships that return to port when 2/3's of the guests and crew are ill, or the ship breaks and leaves people stranded without food, water of bathroom facilities, or a cruise ship actually runs into something and the captain jumps overboard while the passengers, who received no information on how to leave the ship are left to manage on their own. I know these are very rare when compared to the number of people who enjoy successful experiences on cruise ships, but I see these events covered extensively on my local news, as we are near several cruise ports. It seems to happen more frequently than I would wish.
