When I moved to Florida I continued to use my Disabled Badge that I had used in Idaho for the first few weeks we were in the state. While parked in a private lot at Walmart I received a ticket for using Disabled Parking without a valid permit. The cost of the ticket was $250. I found the officer in the lot that was issuing tickets. I pointed out my Idaho permit, and he responded that it was not legal in Florida because it did not have an expiration date on it, and in Florida, a permit must have an expiration date.



I did a bit of research, and then I called the officer's supervisor because, in fact, Florida reciprocates with every state, and there is no rule requiring an expiration date. The ticket was revoked and the officer was forced to call and apologize (which he did at the unseemly hour of 6:00am).



I tell this story only to illustrate that it is very easy to get a ticket when you park in a Disabled parking place, regardless of whether or not it is on the city street or in a private parking lot. I also want to warn visitors that occasionally police officers assume more authority than the law allows. As for compassion? I certainly received none from the officer who ticketed my car, and the sight of me in a wheelchair did not make him any less determined to give me the ticket.

It sounds as if you had a cascading catastrophe of events, and I am so sorry for what happened to you. I appreciate that you identified the guilty parties in this disaster being Mobility Source and the Westin Hotel Emerald. People should know to avoid both of these places.

For many years when visiting Disneyland, Sea World and the San Diego Zoo I just used to rent the ECVs that these parks provide for disabled guests. I have, however, rented mobility scooters in cities, including New Orleans, San Francisco, Seattle, New York City, Washington DC, Houston, Phoenix, and several other cities. I have never had a bad experience. I almost always use Scootaround, and have been pleased with their service.



Eventually I reached the point where I could not walk well enough to manage on what I could do with a rented scooter, and I purchased my own. It was the best thing I have ever purchased. It helps me manage in airports. I can use it in the parking lot of Sea World, inside the mall, the flea market, the farmer's market, the state fair and all those other places I would just watch from a bench were it not for my scooter. It is exceptionally portable, which was never the situation with scooters I rented. It fits nicely in the trunk of my Chrysler Crossfire, and no piece of the scooter weighs more than 30 lbs. I can put it together myself in less than 5 minutes. It solved many of my mobility issues. Now if I could just use it internationally as easily as I can in the US I would truly be a happy traveler.

thread_title: mobility source scooters/wheelchairs my horrible experience
text:
I generally charge my scooter every night when I am using it all day. If I use it modestly I only charge it once a week. I am sure that the batteries are expensive. I had an old huge model before I bought my little more portable model. I replaced the battery on it and I think it was about $100. I supposedly can get 14 miles from one charge. I have never exhausted my batteries.



I cannot imagine it takes much electricity. Both my husband and I have scooters and I have not noticed any increase in our electricity bill when we are charging them nightly. Oddly, that is not something I ever even thought about.



The models that are available for rent are generally large scooters that are very difficult to transport in a regular passenger car. I prefer my scooter because it is small and can be taken apart so it fits in a very small space. It is much more convenient to use when traveling because it goes into the trunk and comes out again very quickly. When I was renting a scooter we had to rent a large van or SUV to have room for the rented scooter, which was much more expensive than a regular passenger car.



As for a husband wanting to purchase a mobility scooter, these are my thoughts. I resisted using a scooter for several years. Then my children came to me with a plea that I use a scooter. We do many activities with our children. According to my children I moved so slowly that I kept people from fully enjoying their experiences. My husband also joined this argument claiming that my mobility issues diminished his pleasure of doing things with me.



While I do not believe any of them would ever leave me home, I certainly did not want to feel obligated to miss our family adventures. So I purchased my first scooter for the convenience and mental health of my husband and children.



I do not think a scooter reduces mobility. Pain reduces mobility. I continue to walk when I shop, visit around in my neighborhood and I use no assistance in my home. When I know I am going to be moving more than a couple of blocks I take my scooter. Walking in pain does not increase or even maintain existing levels of mobility.



I spend part of every year in Turkey, generally in Istanbul. Istanbul is an ancient city and there are barriers to using a scooter or wheelchair. The curbs are very high. the cobblestones are exceptionally rough. Almost every place we go involves narrow stairs. It is not easy to use a scooter on public transportation. Currently it is still more trouble than it is worth in Istanbul. We make generous use of taxis, and depend upon the kindness of friends with automobiles. I also walk very slowly and take lots of rest breaks. There are many times when I wait on a bench while my husband goes up the stairs for a better photo or around the block to collect the laundry.



We both took our scooters with us when we went to Italy last February. We managed them quite well there. There is a special train car for scooters and wheelchairs. Most of the curbs have cut outs. There are generally cars parked in the walkways, but we were able to navigate around them. Our only major problem in Italy was that many of the elevators were so small that we could not get even one scooter into the elevator without taking it apart.



We both have Pride Scooters, and they are the "Go Go: model. Without my scooter I would be exploring the world from the back seat of a vehicle or waiting on a bench while my family went ahead. It keeps me off of the rocking chair on the front porch just watching the world go on without me.

Both my husband and I are older. I have had a disability problem for many years, and in the last three years my husband has also developed a problem. Accordingly, when we do not travel with our mobility scooters we request wheelchair assistance at the airport.



Several weeks ago in Amsterdam I allowed myself to be lured from the airplane with the promise that wheelchairs were waiting at the end of the jetway. I know better than to do this, but I did it. Of course, there were no wheelchairs waiting.



Eventually a small golf cart type of transportation arrived, and there was one seat available. The man driving the cart said my husband was not entitled to ride it because we had not made an advanced reservation. He told him he would have to walk but the gate for our next flight was very near.



I rode to the gate while he started to walk. The gate was a huge distance. It was in another complete wing of the airport, and I would estimate that it was at least 15 blocks. We did not have much time to make the plane change. When I saw how long it took us to reach the gate I requested that the man with the cart return to get my husband, but he refused. I then spoke with the KLM agent at the gate. He did say that my husband was registered as needing a wheelchair, and he agreed that he should not have been expected to walk such a huge distance, but he then shrugged his shoulders and said that the wheelchair people were contracted and there was nothing he could do.



My husband eventually arrived at the gate, just before they closed the doors to the plane. He was, however, in so much pain that he could barely move for the next few days.



I did complain to Delta Airlines, which is the airline that obtained our KLM ticket. We received some frequent flyer miles as an acknowledgement of the problem, but that did not change the quality of service we received in Amsterdam, nor did it give us back the vacation days we missed while my husband was recovering from his journey in the Amsterdam airport.



I try to never write things on a TA forum such as "Never go to the Amsterdam Airport" because I understand that our experience may not be typical. I had been informed that this airport was one of the most helpful airports in the world, but that was not our experience. Between the lack of assistance, the arrogance of the people who did not manage our problem and the magnitude of the problem we had to manage on our own, we will not be traveling through Amsterdam again.



If you need to go through this airport I advise that you check several times to make sure that your wheelchair request has been processed, and then, do not leave the airplane until there is a wheelchair there for your use. As long as you are on the plane the flight crew cannot leave, and it is in their interest to make sure you can leave quickly.

Virgin Atlantic did the exact same thing to me at Heathrow. We waited at the top saw the crew go by, and it was maybe 25-30 mknutes before a passing staff member said "can I help you?" and went off in search of our missing assistance. 

So I agree 100% - don't get off until the chair is at the plane door.

I am sorry your husband had this experience. I have travelled through Amsterdam and had wheelchair assistance provided perfectly OK.



Last Saturday I arrived in London Gatwick and had pre-booked assistance. However, I had checked in a mobility scooter I did not need the assistance as they brought the scooter to the door of the plane for me. In the meantime, the buggy driver was complaining he had more customers on his buggy than he was expecting. Obviously passengers who had not booked assistance had got on the buggy, but nobody had checked this.



At the originating airport there was my self and two other people who had assistance. One of the pax was still on the plane awaiting to be lifted off, I was on my scooter, so who did he have on his buggy. The buggies in LGW can take 7 passengers, so he'd obviously messed it up.



I think it unfair and selfish for other passengers to do this and half the time there is absolutely nothing wrong with them, apart from lazyitis.



I sympathise with your husband having had such a long walk and hope he enjoyed the remainder of his holiday.

The US has laws that provide for equal access for disabled people so there is rarely any problem using a wheelchair in any urban area in he US. I would rent a wheelchair or a mobility scooter and have it delivered to your hotel so it is available when you arrive.



As others have mentioned, even getting around in these huge hotels in difficult if you do not walk well. Certainly getting from one hotel to another is very difficult for those of us with mobility problems. If you have a wheelchair or a scooter it is very easy to get around in a hotel, and equally easy to move from one location to another. There is always a place to enter and exit using a ramp rather than stairs, and elevators easily accommodate wheelchairs.



I am able to walk for short distances so I have never asked for a disabled room in a hotel, but if you need a roll-in shower, or a room with wheelchair accessible light switches you can request a disabled room as well.



You will have a much more pleasant experience in this city if you use a wheelchair or a scooter. There are several companies that rent wheelchairs in Las Vegas. This is a link to the one I used to use frequently. http://www.scootaround.com/locfinder.asp

We visited Vegas in June 2010 and Sept 2011. My husband uses a motorised wheelchair and we saw advertising in the hotel for motorised wheelchair hire. 

Though I don't need to push my husband, I need to go with him and we found that this increased the distances I walked considerably. The major roads are crossed by pedestrian bridges accessed by escalators which of course we couldn't use. Lifts are provided but they are not always close to the escalators. This meant we spent a bit of time and extra walking finding these and getting across roads. Twice we found that they weren't working at all. Once we'd got to know where they were, we got up and down the strip more easily. 



Our son thought that he'd be helpful and buy us both monorail tickets. In reality, we spent more time walking through the hotels and trying to find the disabled access lifts etc that it would have taken to just walk outside to where we wanted to go. I wouldn't recommend using the monorail as it is a very long walk through the hotels to access it. 



We found Vegas a bit more stressful than other US cities from the getting around point of view but we still enjoyed it enough to go again and intend to do so again in the future.

I almost always find that any new city is challenging. It seems to me as if they place the elevators in the most obscure locations they can possibly find. It is also true that if you are walking with a person in a wheelchair you will probably increase the number of steps because the person in the wheelchair has fewer alternatives to reach a specific destination. Public transportation can also be difficult. In some places not every tram or bus is equipped for disabled passengers and I find myself either waiting for the "right" bus or having to move to a different bus stop.



It actually takes me a couple of trips before I am completely confident that I have memorized all the routes I need to follow along my way. Hopefully, having now experienced Las Vegas you will have more practical information and your next trip will be less difficult for you.



I admire people who continue to make the effort to travel with the inconvenience of a wheelchair. Congratulations to you brave husband, and special congratulations to you for faithfully following along.

Thank you Busy-retired. My eyes were opened when my husband became a wheelchair user. Fortunately he can walk very short distances which helped in Paris when I had to carry his manual wheelchair down the steps to the boat on the River Seine. No one helped. Paris was the worst city that we have travelled to. This isn't because of the cobbled streets etc, which were difficult, but you expect that in an old city. It was the rudeness of the people. I was sworn at and reduced to tears on more than one occasion as I was not moving quickly enough. I didn't get help at all with carrying the empty wheelchair down numerous flights of stairs/steps and getting hubby up kerbs where drivers had blocked the few dropped ones there were, was a nightmare. 



Paris is a beautiful city but we won't go there as a couple again. 



As for Vegas, we were told that the Deuce bus prioritises disabled people who automatically go to the front of the queue. We didn't get to try this out but apparently everything stops until that person is safely boarded. Maybe the OP could try this and report back? We have travelled fairly extensively in the States and find it pretty user friendly from a wheelchair users point of view. It is just some of the older things such as the San Francisco Cable cars that can't cater well for people in wheelchairs. 

Thank you for your kind comments, though people with disabilities don't have a choice in struggling with these things if they want to do anything or go anywhere. It does get very wearing as I am sure you well know.

As my doctor often says, the alternative is a rocking chair on the front porch while you watch the world go by. I expect I will continue to make the effort until that rocking chair looks more attractive that it does today.

thread_title: travelling to orandia with a passenger in a wheelchair
text:
Orlando is my home airport, and we fly in and out of this airport many times a year. The only thing that you have to do is request wheelchair service. It is best to do this when you make your original reservations.



You generally have to stay on the plane until all the other passengers have departed. Then a person with a wheelchair meets you at the door of your plane and takes you wherever you need to go. If Orlando is your destination, the wheelchair person will push you onto the tram, take you down to baggage claim on the elevator and provide assistance with your baggage and on to whatever ground transportation you are using. Your traveling companion may just walk right along with your wheelchair.



The wheelchair service in Orlando is outstanding. The workers are concerned for your safety and comfort. They are happy to stop for you at a restroom. They have also stopped for me to purchase a cup of coffee, a sandwich and even a magazine. 



I always tip my wheelchair person, and if he helps me with some difficult task such as moving through TSA security as I am departing, or managing several suitcases when I arrive, I tip a bit more generously as these services are worth a great deal to me. They will, however, take you where you need to go without receiving a tip.



Orlando is a very wheelchair friendly destination. I am sure you will have an enjoyable time. If you have any other questions regarding this destination and physical disabilities feel free to ask.

We are becoming elderly but are not disabled. Nevertheless, we were recently given a room with an "accessible" bathroom. Accessible room if you used two separate elevators and went along very long corridors, but the bathroom had a shower over a bath and a very wide lip on the bath where I presume you could sit before entering. It was the scariest, most slippery thing to negotiate that I have ever met. Is this normal?

I have had rooms with great roll in showers but this just seemed weird. It was in a modified convent in Spain, now a posh hotel.

I see lots of different "modifications" for those of us who are disabled. In Turkey there are almost no accommodations for disabled people, and often what is available is not useable. Today I noticed a tiny ramp built next to twelve steps. The ramp was at such a steep angle that it would have been folly to attempt it with a wheelchair or a scooter.



I have long sense given up hope that I will live to see one of my favorite places become more accessible so I "cope" by making whatever accommodations I can make on my own. If the floor is slippery I ask for extra towels, and occasionally I travel with a small rubber bath mat. It takes up almost no room at the bottom of my suitcase.



When I cannot use my scooter and am forced to walk I plan my trips carefully so I do not waste any steps going in the wrong direction. I make generous use of taxis, and I stop and rest often. I find that shop keepers in Turkey are happy to bring out a stool if I stop in front of a store. Usually they offer a glass of tea as well.



I understand the frustration with post three, but I also know that there are still many places in the world that have not yet become disabled friendly. In the case of Turkey I cannot imagine that all of these ancient streets and buildings could be made accessible in less than fifty years and with a huge expense. So, without any intent at being offensive, and with the recognition that we are certainly entitled to equal access, I am appreciative of those countries that do accommodate my disability. If I have to live with a disability I am thankful that I live in this time period where so many things are easily accessible, and I really appreciate the legislation in the US that makes living with a disability so very easy.

Here in Poland we have a mixture of very sensible, plain stupid and no adjustment for the disabled at all. Many many shops are upstairs - either with stels up to the door or with the enrtraces of several shops off a gallery accessed only by stairs. Shopping malls have no lifts - one in Nowy Sacz has shops on a semi-down floor and a semi-up floor, so neither is accessible.One hotel we stayed in gave us their only accessible room - which had an lordinary bathroom plus a disabed wetroom, so from that point of view was excellent, and was a double-sized room too, but it was the room furthest from reception and the restaurant, along very long corridors (fyi Lynn!). Trains are steps up from the platform, many buses are minibuses and not at all accessible.And so it goes on. 

Poland is an "old" country - until the 1790s a powerhouse and with the most advanced constitution around, but it's only 20-some years since it came out of from behind the iron curtain, and it still has a lot of catching up to do.

john, I imagine that you experience some of the same barriers that I face in Turkey. In the US an "old" building is rarely more than 200 years old. In Europe 200 year old buildings are often of the "newer" variety. The task of retro-fitting ancient buildings is always controversial because often changes in the design and/or structure are necessary. In truth, I do not even know how some of the places in Turkey could ever be made accessible to those of us in wheelchairs.



I ultimately just have to conclude that there are some places, like Mt. Everest, that are never going to be experienced by a person in a wheelchair. Since I will never hike into the valleys in Cappadocia I have to be satisfied with the things I can see from the accessible paved walks and from the road.



When we are talking about an entire country, however, it is a different issue. I am sure that it is very difficult to live in a country that cannot yet provide equal access, and yes, I am appreciate of the fact that legislation in the US has made my own country much easier to manage.



In the US the ADA legislation was a long time in coming, and there were many howls of horror as it was implemented. There are still lots of places that are not fully compliant with the law. For some small business owners creating equal access entries, and/or equal access bathroom facilities has been almost prohibitively expensive. The kind of changes that must be made to the basic infrastructure are slow in coming, and they are expensive.



I hope Poland is soon able to accommodate your needs better both for your sake, as well as for those of us who would like to visit.

thread_title: laos for those with physical impairment
text:
My husband has mobility problems although NOT a wheelchair user. 

We have just returned for 18 days in Laos and I hope you will find some of this information useful. Please feel free to ask any other questions.

Temples-you need to take off shoes to enter but there is not always someone to sit down to do this. 

Toilets- when on the road in the countryside all the restaurants have toilets readily available. However, they are the squat type; there is a porcelain step about 8 inches high on which you stand. There will be no handrails to keep your balance and often there is a hosepipe running making the floors very slippery. 

Hotels- beware of the mats laid out everwhere , a real trip hazard 

LUANG PRABANG 

Si Kuang Waterfalls- If you are in a private car, ask at the ticket office if the driver can take you up to the picnic site, from there it is approx.50 metres relatively flat walk to the viewing platform, where there are seats .. Otherwise it is approx. 300 yards uneven walk from car park.

Bear rescue Centre- approached by approx 60 metres slightly inclining track. A few steps up to the viewing platform but very low handrails. 

Boat trips- the banks of the Mekong are very step with either steps or slippery banks. The access to the boats is either by a rickety plank of narrow wood or by clambering over other boats. 

Royal Palace Museum and Wat Pra Bang- access is by steep steps with no handrails. No shoes are allowed in the Museum and there is nowhere to sit to take them off. 

Wat Xieng- access via the Mekong side is by steeps steps, no handrail. Ask your driver to take you around to the other entrance.

Wat Visoun- ask driver to take the vehicle right up to the temple. 

Hotels- Villa Chitdara- ground floor rooms are flat from street. However several steps down to the garden and up to the restaurant. However, they would serve breakfast on your balcony, Laotians are very helpful.

Ban Lakham – several steps up from the street but a gate post to hang on to. Again, breakfast can be served on your balcony overlooking the river. 

PHONSAVAN

Plain of Jars – site 1- a slight incline of about 100 metres (no places to sit) to the jars from where you can view the whole site. No official seating but plenty of Jars to sit on.

Site 2- difficult ,uneven incline to see Jars

Hotel Anouleklao- ground floor rooms and lift but 3 steps to hotel entrance, no handrail. Only breakfast is served , nearest eating place is about 50 metres away. 

PAKSE

Villa Sisouk, a few steps to enter hotel but it does have a lift and you can arrange to eat ,by advance booking , at the hotel in the evening. 

Hotel Pakse- this has a great rooftop restaurant , unfortunately the lift stops short of one floor so the access is only by a winding staircase with limited handrails. However, they were very happy to serve us on the street terrace which is 2 or 3 steps up from the pavement. 

Tad Fane waterfall- 150 metres walk from carpark to viewing point , the ground was damp and slippery. 

Wat Phu- an electric trolley train will take you to the foot of the site but not back to the ticket office unless you ask. At the site there is a limited amount to see and nowhere to sit, although the local seller offered his chair to my husband whilst I visited the site. The site is only accessible to the fittest, the steps are high, uneven and very ,very steep. If you have already seen the Angkor complex in Cambodia , I would say not to bother with Wat Phu. 

Khone Phanee waterfalls- for a few dollars per person return ,the golf trolley will take you to the viewing platform although there are a few steps on uneven ground to get up to the platform. Seating is available at the platform.

 4000 ISLANDS- only Don Kong island is accessible by vehicle. To visit the rest of the islands and to find the Irrawaddy Dolphins involves steep river banks, unstable wooden boats etc. I would say the whole area is probably not worth visiting if you are impaired as you would be limited to what you can see.

Border Crossing to Ubon airport, Thailand- it is not necessary to get out of the vehicle. The border officers allowed me to fill in the relevant forms on behalf of my husband. Otherwise, it is approx. 200 metres to walk across the border and involves stairs down to an underpass

 I have cervical spondylosis I require a very hard mattress to sleep otherwise I will be in agony. My husband & I would like to go on hoilday at some point somewhere in the sun. I am unsure how I could find a hotel which could cater for my needs.

 The other problem I am unable to lift or pull anything heavy which means my husband is left to carry the cases he is now nearly 65 years old. Is there a travel company which could pick us up from home & sort all the luggage out so we both could just relax? 

Any suggestions would be very welcome.

I would imagine the only way to find out if the hotel has firm mattresses would be to decide where you want to go and then actully call or email the hotel.



i have just returned from Ibiza where the mattress in the hotel was firm.



There are companies where you can send your luggage from home to your destination, which means you do not have to lift it at all. I think Saga Holidays, Virgin, Kuoni and some of the more upmarket tour operators can supply transport from your home at an extra charge. You need to do a bit of research.



However, I find that the majority of airports these days are very efficient in helping disabled passengers, you just need to advise them in advance of your needs.

Hi

Thank you for such a fast response. All the information is very helpful & has certainly given me a starting point.

Regards

Heather

Maybe not something you'd thought of, but India is a wonderful destination and you're basically guaranteed a firm bed as the majority of "mattresses" are simply a many-layered cotton pad. 

As H has said, airlines and airports are very disabled-friendly and you can arrange a wheelchair via the airport or airline (could you walk from mini-cab to check-in?) If you would find a wheelchair helpful, they'll usually collect you from check-in and take you through the security etc to the departure lounge, then collect you again to take you to the gate and down to the plane. If your husband can push the luggage on a trolley from mini-cab to check-in, that's the last you'll see it till the other end. Or you could pick up a porter, curbside. (Maybe it would be worth visiting the airport in advance and talking with the porters and info desk about what can be arranged?)

At the other end, you'd again get a wheelchair to the arrivals hall and you could pick up a porter in baggage claim so all your husband has to do is identify your cases and they'll go with you through to arrivals. What happens in and after arrivals is down to what you've booked. Your husband may have to push the luggage trolley, and you walk, to your car/taxi/transfer bus. But the key point is to check who can arrange what, book it early and check it again just before departure.

Incidentally, I believe the right order of things in the UK is for you to arrange assistance via the airline, but for the actual assistance to be provided by the airport. Same process overseas, so you'd not have to arrange anything with the foreign airport - the airline will do it for you.

I think we all try to do too much, and not to see or consider or ask what help may be available (some of it free-of-charge, like wheelchairs and a pusher to get you through the airport, some at a cost, like porters). As we get older and/or less abled (I'm 53, but have to use a wheelchair, or crutches for short distances) we either draw back our horizons and accept a limited existence or we accept out limitations and plan to get the most out of things, whether it's arranging a wheelchair place at the cinema or theatre, accepting stares and being dealt with in the third person (and would he like a drink? Is there anything he needs? Well, asking me direct might be more polite, for a start!) or broadening your horizons, choosing a wonderful holiday destination, researching just how you're going to get there and how you'll get around, checking that you and your husband will be able to tackle what you must while others do all they can to help, and going for it. Don't forget, there is a worldwide industry which can come together to make your journey and holiday as easy as it/they can

Go for it Heather, the world really is still your oyster.

I am not sure if I should post this under the Maui thread, but I have just returned from a two week experience on Oahu, and have a few observations regarding traveling to this island with a disability.



My husband and I both use mobility scooters for any walking greater than a block. We can manage a flight of stairs and we can walk for short distances, but anything beyond that is difficult and painful.



Starting with the airport, we had exceptional difficulty obtaining our scooters from the plane. I have a theory that the ground crew does not see many scooters because they did not seem to know how to get them from the plane to the door of the plane. We waited so long that our luggage had already been collected and placed in the Delta Luggage/Storage area.



We also seemed to create a bit of a problem when we left Oahu. The airline staff seemed somewhat perplexed by our scooters and did not know what to do with them. After talking with several people we were able to help the final gate agent understand what was to be done with the scooters, and they did arrive in Orlando so they did figure out what to do.



We were very surprised that there was not a separate line for disabled people moving through TSA screening, but we had to use the same line as all other passengers. It slowed the line down significantly, and I felt badly for the people behind us, but we had no alternative. The TSA agents were also perplexed by the scooters, and we drove them through, then took them back again twice before they decided how to handle them. I just do not think they have had lots of experience with them. There seemed to be a huge misunderstanding about who should drive the scooters through security. The right answer is the owner, not the TSA agent, but you had to let them determine that on their own.



We rented a vehicle from Alamo. It was a Chevrolet SSR, and it was almost perfect for us. We could put both of our scooters in the back without having to break them down. This was a huge advantage for us because it took no more than five minutes to load and unload them. Alamo was great for us. They selected a vehicle that met our needs and it was ready and waiting when we arrived. We were exceptionally pleased with the rate, which was below $20/day.



Our condo on Nahua was on the 15th floor. It had been advertised as having a large balcony. The balcony was long, but it was no more than 18" deep. It was certainly not large enough for our scooters. Moreover, the roof top terrace was not fully available by elevator. The elevator went to the penthouse floor, and the terrace was one flight above, requiring the use of stairs.



We can walk short distances, and we can manage a few stairs, so we did not actually look for a disabled modified condo. We have no room to complain about the absence of these modifications because we did not ask for them. Overall, however, the location was excellent for us. We could easily reach the beach with our scooters as well as travel all over Waikiki. Our parking place was right next to the elevator, and our condo unit was also next to the elevator, making arriving and leaving very easy for us.



Many of the smaller gift shops were not accessible. Generally rows of merchandise were too close together to permit us to use our scooters. It was a loss for them because we did not spend any money in stores we could not enter.



Generally we had no difficulty finding alternatives to stairs, but the elevators were often rather hidden. We had to hunt for them in the Ala Moana shopping center as well as a couple of other shopping centers. One evening we ate at California Pizza. We had no difficulty getting to the second floor using the elevator, but when we finished our meal the elevator was no longer working. Fortunately, the adjoining restaurant had a service elevator we used to reach the ground floor. It did put us out in a dark alley, but at least we got back to the ground.



Most major attractions were exceptionally easy to reach. Everything at Pearl Harbor was excellent. We had no difficulty managing the museum or the trip to the USS Arizona. It is almost a textbook perfect execution of good modification.



Reaching the beaches was not difficult. We had no problem finding beaches with paved sidewalks in front of them. We did not use our scooters in the sand, but we were able to park them near us. Often we elected to relax on the grass before the beach sand, and this was exceptionally nice. We just drove our scooters on the grass.



We liked Hanauma Bay. Several walks were easily navigated. The paved path to the beach looked quite steep so we did not attempt it since we did not wish to go in the water. I am sure our scooters would have been able to do it if the batteries had been freshly charged.



We spent an afternoon and evening at the Polynesian Cultural Center and it was completely accessible. We even took the boat ride, while PCC employees drove our scooters to the arrival location. The employees were exceptionally aware of our difficulty in seeing over the tops of the peoples heads, and they made sure we had good views of everything. I would recommend that people with disabilities purchase the Ambassador Package because it will permit you to select seats nearer the front. We could not use our scooters to reach our seats for the evening performance of Ha, but we left them at the top of the staircase and slowly made our way to our selected seats.



We also had no difficulty at the Dole Pineapple Plantation. Everything there is easily accessible, and the store was fun because there were no aisles that were too narrow for us. They made special access at the train so we could ride right up to the train. The bathrooms were clean and very accessible.



We did not use any public transportation, but I noticed that the public buses were capable of kneeling for handicapped passengers as were several of the tour buses we saw. The Alamo shuttle had a huge van with a ramp, and it was easy to just roll right on. That single advantage would encourage me to select this company again.



Restaurants were generally not difficult. The only places that did not have alternatives to stairs were Roy's Hawaiian in Ko Olina and the Panda Cuisine in Honolulu. In both of these cases we had to navigate a few stairs, but they were not steep or difficult.



Most parking lots we encountered had disabled parking spaces, but we found very few that were not occupied. I did not, however, ever see one of these spaces that had a car parked in it that was not eligible, which is not always the case in other locations.



It is my general observation that most places need a few more handicapped parking places. I did some research prior to leaving to determine laws about handicapped parking. I could not find out what Hawaiian laws were. A public safety officer at the zoo told us we could park anywhere for two and one-half hours. We took him at his word, and we did not pay any parking meter. We never received a ticket, but I do not know if that was because we were legal or just not noticed.



When we visited the Plantation Village the homes all had steps leading to the front doors. Our guide took us up paths that led to the back door, and made the facility completely accessible. The Iolani Palace did not permit us to use our scooters, but they did provide their own wheelchairs. Because there were only ten rooms we decided to just walk. This was a serious mistake that dramatically reduced the pleasure we received from this museum, but it was completely our fault. There were, thankfully, benches on both the first and second floors, and the staff gave us elevator access to the basement eliminating the need to walk down a flight of stairs. If we visit it again, we will use the wheelchairs provided by the attraction.



Of course, there were places we could not visit. We could not climb to the top of Diamond Head or hike in the botanical gardens, but it seemed as if everywhere it was practical to do so, arrangements had been made to provide equal access for disabled visitors and residents.



The gravel paths in the Valley of the Temples were OK for our scooters, but it would be difficult to manage a push wheelchair over this terrain.



Overall we felt that the general population was exceptionally hospitable and kind. Many people did not seem familiar with our scooters, and we did only see three other scooters while we were in Hawaii. Several times people stopped and asked questions about them. Everyone was very gracious to us.



Next to Disney World, where we spend a great amount of time, Oahu ranks as a premier location in providing access for those of us with disabilities, at least with our type of disabilities.



It is certainly a destination that we plan to visit again.

thread_title: UK Airport Security - Travelling with metal hips!
text:
Hi Stacey



The check only takes a minute or two and mostly people are quite cheery and careful. If your hips are not metal then you probably won't even set the alarm off. 



If your hips are metal then a few things I feel help are: wear shoes you can get on and off easily and wear clothes that are not too bulky. If you are in any pain tell the person checking you so she can be careful.

In the US, since November of 2010 I have not seen a wand. Everything is done either with a scanner and/or a physically pat down. I have not been in a single airport where the scanner was actually working. I would prefer the scanner because even though my nude body appears somewhere on a screen no one is touching me.



I do not know about touching skin. The TSA worker always wears gloves so maybe it is OK for a hand clad in plastic to touch skin, but I have lots of skin touched. I have tried to be reasonable about this because if you fly you have absolutely no choice about the procedure.



In truth, however, it is something I dread more and more. There is lots of poking and prodding that is exceptionally invasive. I have finally requested that they just do "their thing" without the verbal explanation, which just seems to make everything last longer and be even more degrading.



The worst part of all this procedure is that there are still plenty of ways for someone to get on the plane with an explosive device, and the only way to prevent that is to do a body cavity search of every person. Since I do not think that is going to happen, I just think the dog and pony show I have to endure is TSA Theatre designed to make the flying public "feel" safer. 



Or perhaps it is part of the economic stimulus plan, because I do not think the average TSA worker formally worked as an executive or even had a skilled career. I think they were all previously unemployed. I really hate the attitude that most of them have. They are so authoritative, and one can do absolutely nothing except comply with whatever they ask one to do regardless of how ridiculous or demeaning that request might be.

The folks over at the Air Travel forum suggested that I post my question about passenger assistance here as well.



I will be accompanying my 88-year old father to Ireland later this month. We are flying Vancouver - Heathrow (plane/terminal change) - Dublin and then in reverse at the end of the trip. He uses a cane, but cannot walk long distances. 



Our travel agent has requested airport "passenger assistance" and it has been marked on the travel documentation we received back. However, I am not sure how this works in practice. 



I am assuming that the assistance will take the form of a wheelchair. Our travel agent says that we will be assisted gate to gate through Heathrow. However, I am wondering about what happens when we arrive in Dublin. Are we assisted right through immigration and customs procedures to baggage pickup and into the public areas or ??? Similarly what happens on our return to Vancouver International?



I would be grateful for any information regarding experiences with passenger assistance. I suspect that I am beginning to fret a bit too much and all will go well. However, this is a trip that my father has always wanted to do and I want to make it as smooth as possible for him.



Many thanks.

All airports are basically the same.

Assistance usually starts at the airport check-in desk and will take you through security into the departure lounge, you will normally be met again at boarding time and taken to the gate and assisted to the plane door (aisle chairs are available if needed). Depending on distance they may use wheelchair or golf buggy.

On landing wait on the plane until assistance arrives and you will be taken through immigration and baggage claim and to the terminal doors - some will take you out to the car parks / car hire.

Tipping is optional - $1-2 range.

I have no experience of how they handle terminal transfers at Heathrow.
Thanks very much for this, mymsman. With the advice received on both forums, I understand the process much better and feel more comfortable about it.

You might want to consider whether it is worth buying/borrowing a wheelchair to take with you so you have one available while you are in Dublin. 

Your father may not wish to be considered wheelchair bound but it could make sightseeing a lot easier if you don't have to keep taking breaks. Even if he doesn't sit in it all the time he could push it and use it as a walking aid. 

Airlines don't charge to carry wheelchairs and it doesn't count towards your baggage allowance.

Thanks again, mymsman. You are correct. Having a wheelchair full time would, of course, make sightseeing a lot easier. However, that is a step that he is not ready to take at this point and I must respect that. We are spending a few days in Dublin on our own and then going on a bus tour. I've already told him that we will do just what he feels comfortable with. If, at any time, he doesn't feel up to getting off the bus or going very far, we'll find a cafe to have coffee/tea and watch Ireland go by. I think it's as much the idea of being in Ireland that is important to him rather than seeing anything in particular.

I don't mean to annoy your father in any way, but pride can mean we fall foul of trying to do too much and risking harming oursellves.

If your father is not yet ready to give in to the wheelchair, have you looked into things which are not, on the surface, chairs? I hated using a wheelchair, but have accepted that (a) I DO need one, because (b) it means that I can see and do far more than I would otherwise be able to and (c) the rest of the world may stare, but that woman has awful hair, that child is ugly, and what did HE think he was doing when he bought those trousers? We can always find someone to stare at,

But back to the point, one possibility would be something like this http://www.abilitymatters.ie/walkingaids.html which could help your father to walk but, as soon as he needed to rest, could be turned around and becomes a seat. 

Or a folding, lightweight, wheelchair like this http://www.aamobility.co.uk/wheelchairs.php which you could carry, bagged, until he needs it.

The idea is not to force your father into a chair for long stretches of time, but to have something which you (folding chair) or he (walker) could have as disguised back up to help him if he's walked too far, or something is further away than he thinks he can manage, or is simply there if, for example, you're in a long queue for something.

Oh, and definitely ask your airline for ground assistance (the rule is that you arrange the assistance with your airline and THEY book it with departure and arrival airports. As mymsman has said, they'll get you from check-in to plane and from plane to arrivals hall.

I am the OP on this thread. I have reported back on our experience on the Air Travel Forum. Here is a link, in case it is helpful to any readers - 



http://www.tripadvisor.com/ShowTopic-g1-i10702-k5378454-o10-Passenger_Assistance-Air_Travel.html#41106347



Note to johnb - Many thanks for your post and the very helpful comments. Unfortunately, we were already away when you posted. In the end, we did manage, although both you and mymsman were so right. We were limited to a considerable extent. However, I think that my father was so thrilled with just being in Ireland, that it didn't matter that we didn't see everything.

Think of it as a Judi Dench role and learn some lines for the occasion. :-)

You are within you right to ask them not to push you. I travel with my daughter, who is a full-time wheelchair user. She pushes herself in her chair to the plane. 



 However, they are required to operate the aisle chair, if one is needed, to actually board the plane. 



At times, the jet bridge has been too steep on departure. At that point, we ask for assistance, and someone will push her up. However, she does direct them as to the speed she wants them to go.

I am a wheelchair user and my partner and I are cruising to the fjords at the end of June on the Arcadia. We are stopping at Bergen, Flam, Olden and Stavanger. I would appreciate any tips, comments etc. re wheelchair access in these places.

Not sure where you will dock in Bergen, but from the Festningskaien you have a flat, though not necessarily smooth, progree right along the side of the harbour, Bryggen, past the fish market and into the main drag through the city centre, which is a very nice, wide, pedestrian street. Turn left before the fish market and you'll see the funicular. Steep to the entrance, not sure in wheelchair access. The alternative place the ship might dock is farther from the walkabkle area, and they'll most likely have buses laid on,

Bergen is a beaufitul city, and the "voyage" amongst the islands into and out of Bergen is stunning.

My partner and I did a Norwegian Fjords trip last year. I have mobility issues due to severe arthritis so we decided to borrow a wheelchair from the Red Cross.



As already stated bergen is very accessible along the seafront. There is also a HOHO bus which we decided to do as it was raining extremely hard the day we were there. I don't use a wheelchair at home, so can manage some walking and steps.



In Flam we did the Flam Railway and the guard put out a ramp and pushed me onto the train. The station is about 200m flat ground away from where the ships dock. very easy to buy the ticket and do it on your own. However, I would look up on the internet to see how many ships in port that day. We were the only ones there the day we went. I looked to see what time the ship's excursion was leaving and ensured we went after that. I think we got the train about 11am and it was reasonably empty.



In Olden there was a 'Dotto Train' at the dockside, so we did the trip on this. It took us around the village and local countryside to a lake. It was very pretty. Alternatively, the walk to the village is not far and is on the flat.



In Stavanger it is flat all along the seafront. Again here we did the HOHO bus and the driver dropped us off back at the ship.



We also went in June, so the days are very long. The scenery is absolutely stunning. In fact we want to go on another cruise to the Lofoten Islands and Arctic Circle. We didn't do any of the ship's excursions as they are always so overpriced. However, we found that we didn't need to in Norway. We found everyone friendly and helpful and of course, all speak good English.



Remember that Norway is VERY expensive. We didn't buy anything at all as we found the prices fairly exorbitant, but we had a wonderful holiday.



Please don't hesitate to ask if you need any further info. You may also want to have a look at the forums on CruiseCritic.
Many thanks for youir detailed response, it is very helpful and much appreciated

if you like us are keen to to do DIY tours because of a wheelchair. Buy yourself the lonely planet book on Norway. It will give lots of info plus email addresses so you can write to the tour people direct to find out about wheelchair acessability. We find this invaluable and makes trundling round with the buggy a lot easier

thread_title: Mobility Scooter - check through or check at gate?
text:
Have rented mobility scooter for hubby in the past and we now purchased one. Previously, we had a wheelchair meet us at the airline gate to provide him transportation between gates, baggage, etc. We will be traveling to Vegas in March 2012 and are trying to decide if we want to check his scooter through to Vegas or check it at the gate.



Taking into consideration that attendant with wheelchair knows the fastest route between gates, we can see the benefit of simply checking the scooter through to Vegas. But at the same time, we are concerned about the scooter being damaged in transit and think that checking it at the gate would be best for it so it will not be banged around on the luggage carts etc. We are also considering a mixture of both. Have wheelchair for hubby so we can benefit from the attendant's knowledge, and me use the scooter to keep up with the long-legged attendants who seem to walk a mile a minute. There are advantages and disadvantages to all of the scenerios.



If you have any info to share with us about traveling with your scooter via air, we would GREATLY appreciate you sharing with us. This is a new experience for us.



THANKS for ANY input you can give us.

thread_title: Mobility Scooter - check through or check at gate?
text:
I have never checked my scooter with my luggage. I always take it right to the door of the plane, and I pick it up there after we land. I find it so much more convenient to have my own transportation rather than wait for someone to push my wheelchair.



Your second alternative would provide you with the assistance that comes from having someone with good knowledge of the airport accompany you to your next gate or the luggage claim area. In your situation it might be a wise choice.



It is not something I would do because I pretty much know the way around the airports I use on a regular basis. I probably would feel guilty using someone to push a wheelchair for the primary purpose of guiding me, if I could accomplish them same thing by myself. There never seem to be enough wheelchair pushers to go around. I suppose I still take pride in doing as much for myself as I can. 



I also like to plan my lay-overs with a couple of extra hours so we can get something to eat, browse in a bookshop or even visit the stores. I can do none of these things if I depend upon someone to push my wheelchair.



If you are extremely unsure of your ability to navigate the airport, then it might be best if you used a wheelchair pusher. I would not, however, tell anyone that you are using this person for navigation reasons rather than physical needs.

Under your circumstances I believe it would be very prudent to put your husband in the hands of someone who will push his wheelchair while you take charge of your scooter. Hopefully the scooter will be delivered to the door of the plane prior to the arrival of the person who pushes the wheel chair.



My husband has your role in our marriage, and I know if I were to become any more forgetful he would need assistance getting both of us to our next gate. You have a very legitimate need for additional help in transferring and/or reaching the luggage carousels.



I do not know what to tell you about the backpack on your scooter. I am thinking that the crew who loads the scooter would not even pay any attention to it. I travel with a C-Pap and I always put it on the back of my scooter. About half of the time I forget to take it off, so it goes with the scooter into the plane. No one has ever said anything about it. I do have an address tag on my C-Pap. I would make sure to include that with your backpack. I have luggage tags on all of my luggage including my carry-ons.

thread_title: Mobility Scooter - check through or check at gate?
text:
I have a Prism Pavement scooter because my walking distance is limited and I am very slow. This model is small and light enough to lift and it will break down into three pieces if required. So far I have travelled with it from Glasgow or Edinburgh to France, Teneriffe, Gran Canaria, Kuala Lumpur via Dubai, Kuala Lumpur to Langkawi and Bali without problems or damage in transit. I have always been allowed to drive it to the gate but once there it depends upon the facilities as to how it is loaded into the hold.

a) if the plane is on the tarmac, the scooter can be taken at the gate or a special hoist vehicle may be used to transport wheelchair/scooter passengers direct to the door of the plane, after which the wheelchairs/scooters are loaded in the hold.

b) If the plane is linked to a moveable passage, then usually I am asked to drive the scooter right to the door of the plane from where the porters take it and load it in the hold. If there is a lift from the waiting area at the gate, sometimes the porters will take the scooter down to the hold that way and I will walk to the plane.

The porters are not supposed to lift the scooters for health and safety reasons, but they often carry mine down the steps at the plane door to the tarmac! I will always show them how to disengage gear for easy pushing,

At the end of the flight the scooters usually come off with the baggage and are taken to the baggage hall belts for retrieval. In that case a wheelchair is provided for transport from plane to belt. Just don't get mad when you find it sitting up on the belt as has happened to me twice!! On occasion I have found my scooter has been brought up to the door of the plane, which is wonderful.

A tip: Clearly label each section of your scooter ie. detachable seat, basket,

Print and laminate a clear instruction label to stick on front and back of your scooter ie' Lift by Handle' or ' Lift knob to disengage gear ' It could prevent unecessary damage being cause.

This is all borne of my own experience and I hope it is useful.

thread_title: Mobility Scooter - check through or check at gate?

In the US scooters are generally taken from the gate to the baggage hold of the airport using an elevator, but they are not collected with the regular luggage. My cart is also light weight and often they just take it down the stairs to the plane. 



I try to sit on the left hand side of the plane so I can watch my scooter. Once no one took my scooter from the gate and the plane had started to back away before I could notify the flight attendant. 



I also recommend using a laminated card with operating instructions because all scooters do not work in the same way. 



We now have a more complicated situation as my husband's last spinal procedure failed and he is now also using his own mobility scooter. Both of our carry-ons are now on wheels so we each pull one beside us. TSA screening is more complicated than ever, but as long as we can move we will continue to travel.

thread_title: Mobility Scooter - check through or check at gate?
text:
Now I need to amend my post. We had a non-stop flight yesterday between Salt Lake City and Orlando. I took my scooter to the gate. It was kind of a last minute decision so all the seats on the left side of the plane were taken, and we were on the other side. I asked the flight attendant to make sure the scooter was loaded on the plane before the door closed.



I had talked with the gate agent three times before we got on the plane. She had placed a gate check tag on the scooter. It is still amazing to me that she then walked down the jetway and closed the door to the plane with my bright red scooter sitting right there next to the door. Nonetheless, my scooter did not greet me at the door when we arrived in Orlando.



We waited while they completely emptied the hold of the plane. Then it was "officially" not there. They sent a wheelchair for me, and we went to baggage claims, picked up our checked suitcases and filed a claim. The Delta employee in the claim office called Salt Lake, and they located the scooter immediately. It was on the next plane and arrived before mid-night.



Since we live 40 miles away from the airport, and we had to return to the airport today we just asked them to hold it, and we picked it up. Delta was exceptionally good about fixing this problem. They offered to rent a scooter for me until mine arrived. I did not need that since I was going straight home and straight to bed, with no walking plans before our return to the airport.



When we picked up the scooter today they gave us an envelope with 2 $50 Delta vouchers enclosed. I felt that not having my chair was a huge inconvenience and worrisome until I knew for sure where it was. In spite of these concerns, I was very satisfied with every Delta employee who helped with the problem.



I do, however, need a work-around to prevent this from happening again. Any suggestions would be appreciated.

text:
My scooter is very small, and I am very large, but I have never had a problem with inclines in any airport I used.



I did, however, have an bad experience last month with my husband's scooter. We try to sit on the side of the plane where we can watch our scooters. Leaving Atlanta for Orlando we saw the luggage crew drop my husband's scooter from the gate of the plane to the tarmac. We immediately contacted the flight attendants.



When we arrived in Orlando we were met by the airport wheelchair staff and two representatives from Delta. This was impressive because it was well after mid-night when we arrived. They put my husband in a wheelchair and helped us collect our luggage. They sent the scooter to a repair facility, and offered to rent a substitute for my husband until his scooter was repaired. It took them 36 hours to fix it, and it was then delivered directly to our doorstep, and we live 40 miles from the airport.



I do not know if every airline takes such good care of disabled passengers as Delta, but Delta gets an A+ in my book.

I don't call this discrimination against having a service dog. If you return a car covered with dander and dog hair, aren't you "discriminating" against the next renter, who may suffer from severe dog allergies?

I have very limited walking ability, and I use a wheelchair or mobility scooter. I have been flying with this situation for at least the last decade. You should have no difficulty at all flying with this type of disability.



Generally when I fly I either use my mobility scooter or I request wheelchair asistance when I check-in. Actually I request wheel-chair assistance when I make my reservation and then remind them when I check in.



An attendant will seat your husband in a wheelchair, manage his carry-on luggage, help him through security and deliver him to his departure gate. From here the gate agent will wheel him up the jet way to the door of the airplane.



If one is completely incapable of walking there is an aisle chair they can use to get him the rest of the way to his seat. If he manages at all with crutches, I would probably use these to reach my seat. It is a bit less difficult than the aisle chair. The flight attendant can then help put the crutches away and get them again should he need them in-flight for any reason.



When you arrive at your destination you will be greeted by an attendant with a wheelchair for your husband, and he will take you to baggage claim, generally help collect your luggage and help you reach whatever transportation you will use when you leave the airport.



I do tip these attendants generously for help through security and help with luggage because it is this assistance that makes it possible for me to fly.



On other occasions I take my mobility scooter. When I have it I just drive it to the door of the plane. It is gate checked from the door of the plane and returned to the door of the plane when I arrive. I like this better because I do not have to depend upon someone to push my wheelchair, but the extra help with security and luggage is also nice.



I do not travel with my push wheelchair. I have one at the home of each of my children and that is where I most often visit. When I go other places I generally prefer my mobility scooter. If I need a wheelchair it is so much less expensive to rent a wheelchair than a mobility scooter.



Also, when I have my own push wheelchair it is more difficult to get an attendant to push you. Generally my husband was expected to push the wheelchair, and that was a bit much for him with his own carry-on luggage. I would arrive early and kind of insist that I received a wheelchair attendant. It just took a bit more time.



I guess it kind of sounds like lots of trouble, but it is really quite easy. In fact, on some other forums you will read passengers complaining about all the people who use the wheelchair service because they are too lazy to walk to the plane themselves. If it looks attractive to the ambulatory it cannot be too difficult.

We are looking to go on a family vacation (wife, 6year old daughter, and myself). My wife can only do minimal walking because of her bad feet. We thought about going to a beach. Does anyone have any other vacation ideas that involve minimal walking?

Is your wife willing to use a wheelchair, and would you be willing and able to push her? We had a marvellous holiday touring Rajasthan last year, with me in a wheelchair or walking short distances on crutches. Crutch travel was hugely eased by the many spots to rest throughout the sites we visited - Taj Mahal (you only have to walk on the white marble bit, until then you can go by chair).Amber Palace and Jaipur, Jodhpur, Udaipur (even managed to get into the boat for a two-hour cruise on the lake) and so on. Wonderful, and with our agent's help, hotels were prepared with ground floor bedrooms, special meal arrangements to ease matters further. 

Honestly, if a chair/crutches combination would work for you, the world is still your oyster. (Airports easy with a pusher provided by the airport both in the UK and India).

An alternative could be a coach tour? See the world through a bus window, and use chair/crutches at stops so your wife is now stranded on the coacvh while everyone else gets off. 

I've not suggested a cruise, as (a) puching and walking distances on modern cruise ships can be huge, some ships would be difficult to negotiate with a chair, and getting on/off could be a problem, again stranding your wife on board (gangways at best, tenders propbably very difficult)

I can walk, but not too far and not alot, so I too am limited when I travel. I like the hop on/hop off bus tours in the cities (I had a great one in Singapore in March). I try to find places where I can sit and rest after a while, even if I have to go to a coffee or tea shop. I personally find independent travel the way to go because you can go at your own pace and you're not herded around like cows. I was on a tour of St. Peter's and the Coliseum offered by the ship from the port in Civitavecchia and found that that type of tour wasn't suitable for me. The pace was far too fast and I couldn't keep up (and I wasn't the only one either).



I had a cruise from Galveston, Texas to Rome (Civitavecchia) and it was wonderful. Yes, the ship was large and there was a good bit of walking around the ship, but it was doable. Embarking and disembarking were no problem either. None of the port calls on this cruise involved a tender and the brows (gangplanks) were low and easy to do. The food was good and there were alot of activities onboard for those who wanted them or you could just sit on deck and read, your choice. I would recomend a cruise for those with limited mobility.

I too have limited mobility and have done 4 cruises. We always arrange our own excursions in each port, but I put in a lot of research beforehand. We have never had a tender port, but I would manage as I can get up and down steps.



Alternatively, you could try a river cruise as you stop in city centres. Most Euopean cities are accessible, but again you need to check it all out carefully.





It all depends on what you want to do and your likes. You could base yourself somewhere and go out on day trips by car.

Cincinnati, Do you want an international destination or were you thinking more of doing something in the US? Maybe if you could tell us some of the places you wanted to visit we could provide opinions and suggestions about those locations.

Thanks the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) building codes have changed in regard to accessibility to public facilities for physically challenged people - how is the room equipped to accommodate ADA guidelines, such as passages, counter heights, door hardware, bathroom fixtures, and roll-in showers,

• Does the hotel provide any special disability services? 

• Are the rooms ADA compliant? 

• Can the beds and other furniture be moved in order to make the room more comfortable and accessible? 

• Does the hotel provide a wheelchair accessible shuttle to nearby tourist attractions and public transportation? 

The bathroom:

Doorways must be a minimum of 32 inches wide to accommodate wheelchairs and walkers. Doors should swing out rather than in, with clearance on both sides.

A roll in shower with shower seat 

A wall-mounted grab bars in the shower

Install a seat at the head of the tub or inside the shower enclosure

A wall-mounted handheld showerhead, preferably mounted on a slide bar so someone of any height can use it.

The threshold of the doorway should be even with the adjacent floor.

The sink has knee clearance. Make sure a wheelchair can roll up to the sink with knee room underneath.

A toilet raised with full grab bars or with full grab bars attached to the toilet. Wall-mounted grap bars in both sides of the toilet. Are the grap bars "L" shaped, horizontal and/or vertical?



Are there sufficient emergency exits for wheelchairs?

best regards

Betty

All hotels are required to meet minimum guidelines to meet the needs of the disabled. Many of the things you mention on your list are not part of the requirements of the ADA. For example, the ADA does not mandate that a hotel provide a wheelchair accessible shuttle to tourist attractions.



The ADA mandates larger doorways and modifications in the bathroom for disabled people. Some rooms have adaptive equipment for deaf guests. I have been in ADA hotel rooms that did not have space with knee clearance under the sink, and I have certainly been in hotels that have no emergency exit in case of fire except the staircase. Elevators are not to be used in emergencies. I have been in ADA rooms that did not have full grab bars attached to the toilet.



I have not stayed in a hotel in NYC that has all of the features you seek. I think your best alternative is to select a few hotels that appeal to you in terms of location, amenities, etc and write and ask them what particular accommodations they make for physically disabled guests. You could include your list so it would be quick for the hotel to determine if they meet each of your expectations.



Unless, of course, some visitor to this thread has a suggestion for a NYC hotel with the features you desire.

The scooters that most rental places have available to rent are large, heavy-duty scooters that can be a problem to transport. I used to rent these before I purchased my own mobility scooter. It took my two strong sons-in-law to get my rented scooter inside the giant SUV we drove to Orlando.

Apart from the problem of moving your scooter from one place to the next, there is no place easier to manage with a wheelchair than Orlando. That is one of the major reasons we elected to live here. Virtually everything is available to you in a scooter or wheelchair.

text: Hi Marybeatles, have you already gone on your trip? If not, I have info that may help you. We just got back from Disneyland, and I needed a scooter to get around on due to a foot injury. I could transfer but not walk far. The hotel we stayed at was helpful, have wheelchair accessible rooms even though they were quite small, but could get my scooter inside. The tub/shower combo might be an issue is you can't step over. It was very close to the main entrance- it was maybe 3-4 businesses south of the main crosswalk. It was the Ramada Maingate Hotel. Best surprise ever- there is an independant scooter and wheelchair rental spot right on the property called Scooter Village Inc. ph. 888-956-2246. They rented scooters cheaper than Disney, even let me keep mine overnight. Best of all I did not have to walk all the way to where Disney rents and risk them being all gone, plus I could take it out of the park to go to restaurants or downtown Disney. They also said they take scooters all over the area, so maybe you could work out something with them. Knott's Berry Farm might be a fun place to go, not far from Disneyland. I don't know about the city buses from experience, but they must be handicapped accessible. Maybe there is a website that would tell you for sure. There might be a shuttle service too, not sure because we had our own car. We also went to Huntington Beach for the afternoon. Down the street from the pier they had electric bicycles for rent- maybe this would be an option if the scooter could not be transported that far. Huntington Beach is about 45 minutes from Disneyland I think, maybe a city bus could get you there as you make only a few turns on main streets to get there (down Katella a few miles, then on Beach Blvd which runs right into the beach) The pier is several lights to the north from there. If you have not gone yet and want more info on what I experienced in Disneyland as a scooter user, send me a message and I will try to help you.
