I planned to go from Anaheim to Los Angeles to San Diego, Ca with my daughter. I am disabled and needed a scooter. I was referred by the Westin Hotel Emerald in San Diego to Mobility Source. 



I phoned the co, and the man was a bit strange, but seemed very reasonable price wise, and was willing to bring my scooter to Anaheim. He said he would pick it up at San Diego. I thought that was great. 



Unfortunately, my scooter had a problem that I believe was electrical. The scooter wouldnt start then it would, and the power was getting lesser and lesser but the battery was fully charged. I unplugged it and started it again a couple of times, then called the owner/one of two I was told. I have forgotten his name now, as it is around 2 months after my trip. 



I was so upset for so long that I didnt want to write about this, but then decided I had better warn others. I have had time to calm down about the treatment I received. When I spoke to the man from mobility about the scooter not working properly, he was a nervous wreck shouting at me. He ordered me to do this and that, and practically hysterical. He did not even let me finish one sentence without yelling at me.



He told me that he was sure that it was because I HAD A CELL PHONE THAT WAS CAUSING THIS. My cell phone wasnt even with me when this happened, but he decided that it was from mine and others. The scooter had worked for a day fine, and then just started to act up. I was already in Disney and for sure all the phones there would have caused it to break there if he was right! 



Anyway he told me to unplug it and then plug it again and call him back. I was crying I was so upset after his behavior. I had been calm, and he interrupted me constantly was snapping at me like an animal. I called him back as he instructed and said it was doing the same thing again. He said he would come there and bring another scooter. 



However, after the way he behaved, I was so upset, and didnt want him to ruin my entire trip if he gave me a defective scooter, I didnt want to deal with him. I just said never mind plz come and pick this up Ill get another scooter somewhere else. HE said that he would refund ALL MY MONEY. I said, fine. Well, he did Not refund my money, and I had to get my bank to go after him for it. I got my money from the bank. 



After that I was lucky and there was a company right on the same block as my hotel in Anaheim right across the street from Disneyland. They brought me a scooter and I had no probs whatsoever.



 Next I went to Los Angeles, and ordered another one /no probs from Sherman Oaks Medical. The guy was terrific. Then, I asked the concierge from the Westin to find another co for me as I explained what happened. The concierge Molly said she loved that guy from Mobility. She kept having me repeat over and over what happened, and just infuriated me after a while; as she would not just say she would look for another company. She kept making me re live it over and finally I snapped and told her to just find me a company and call me back with the phone number.



 I called Scootaround; as they gave me that phone number to call., and was told that they could get a scooter to me by 3 that day. I said fine, but I would be on a tour and would get back by 5. When I returned from the tour, the scooter that was left did not give me room for my legs and feet, so I called back the co and left a msg requesting a change if possible. 



My daughter had received a call and the hotel room had msgs on it from some frantic nut saying he was there with my scooter (previously at 3pm before I got back from my tour), but that i had not been there! All this hysterics for what? I couldnt believe it. The scooter was left there; why did I need to be there? I told them Id be on a tour till 5. 



Anyway I left a msg requesting if they could get me a different one, and then the guy called back and said I better meet him downstairs because he was coming to get his scooter and would not give me another one. He said he had been there earlier and I wasnt there! He was angry! I told him I had told the person I ordered from that I wouldnt be there till 5. He then said, OH i heard about you having problems with another company! obviously these two nasty people were friends or related. 



I got 3 calls from this nut, and I was sick in the bathroom from all this aggravation and he demanded that I meet him downstairs in 5 min from wherever he was on the way there. I just went down even though I was sick, and he told me I would get my money back. By the way HE HAD THE NERVE TO INTIMIDATE ME BY GRABBING THE SCOOTER WHEN I GOT OUT OF THE ELEVATOR, HE DIDNT EVEN LET ME WALK TO THE FRONT DESK! 



 WELL I DIDNT get my money back from him either! ! I called another co Eric's medical supply. The guy came right away and was so NICE! ITOLD HIM ABOUT WHAT HAPPENED, and he said that the scooteround guy worked for him but HE FIRED HIS A-- because he was crazy! He said to ME you better call that bank today and tell them because he will not give you your money back!



 I told the hotel about the nice guy and asked them to refer to him, but I just called there today, and they are still referring to that animal I spoke to orig from mobility source. Ill never forget the RAGE in his crazy voice! And, to top it off, after I came down to ask a question to a concierge at the hotel, she said to me, OH YOU MUST BE MS..... I could tell by your voice, and you have a scooter/poor whatever that guys name was at mobility, he went thru so much with you. I said, What? What are you talking about? She told me that she decided to call him and get his side of the story! That poor man tried so hard to please you. I said, IM the victim here!



 Anyway, I could see she was difficult and i walked away to find someone else to ask about where I needed to go in town. The man looked like a manager, and so I asked him if he was, he said no...he asked if I wanted one. I said no, i just wasnt comfortable with how I was treated by the concierge molly and wanted to find out how to get to the ferry.



 Well, all of a sudden, that molly went looking for a manager, and comes out looking for a fight, and says YOU want a manager? Heres a manager.....he comes out and is looking at me and I just walked away. I wasnt going to start in with that when I already had enough! I was on my way to rush to the ferry, and would talk to a manager when I wanted too!



 later on I came back to the hotel and was ordering food at the hotel, and started to cry. The waitress was so nice and told me that she would ge a manager for me to talk too. She felt I needed too. The guy came over and we talked about the prob plus others at the hotel, like no air circulation in the rooms, hot/ how the room was dirty, and cups etc was dirty and dust everywhere and how I came to that hotel for the hottub and it was taped off. How I had gone again to the hot tub, and it was supposed to work as I called first and then it didnt. 



I paid more for this hotel than the Ramada in La and that hotel surpassed all my expectations. This one was just a mess, for the exception of a nice front desk girl named Melissa. I totally wasted my time talking to the manager as he did nothing, said nothing to the other managers, even though I requested that. It was just more of my time ruined on that trip. 



By the way its like a monopoly on the scooters at the san diego zoo and other places that guy/mobility source has his scooters there. Seaworld you could rent a scooter from them thats theirs i believe. The whole thing was a horror and made me sick and I spent a fortune on this trip to take my daughter away before she started college. I cant believe that people have said good things about this guy at mobility source. I guess they were lucky enough to not have one break on them and they didnt have to suffer the wrath of that guy! 



ERics medical supply was reasonable and very accomidating. I have rented scooters so many times, and even had one that broke down on me, but never ever was treated like these 2 guys treated me.



San Diego good company for scooters= Eric's Medical Supply

Los Angeles good company for scooters: Sherman Oaks Medical.

Anaheim I forgot the name, but was right across the street from Disneyland.



Hope you all have great safe trips with no misery like mine was.

thread_title: traveling with a child with autism
text:
My son is 19 now. He still has meltdowns from time to time. My advice for younger kids is to provide enough distraction (whatever works, food, books, games, etc.) It also helps to tell the people around you what the situation is. I have found that most people are very understanding when they realize you are not a bad parent with a misbehaving child. And you will have to remind your child not to kick the seat in front of him!

I worked my son up to transatlantic travel by starting with Mc Donalds. We started with fast food, then with chain restaurants with menus you can color on, working our way up until we got to the Four Seasons.

As for the plane ride to Europe, I hope this doesn't make me sound like a bad mother, but Tylenol PM (tylenol and benadryl) worked great for allowing both boys to sleep on the plane. I will caution you that some children have a paradoxical reaction to benadryl and become agitated, at least that's what the literature says.

I would also recommend getting out early, seeing the sights, having lunch out, and getting back to your hotel or villa for a swim or other decompression time. Then dinner and early to bed.

The best advice I can give is give your boys enough varied experiences at home that an airplane will not seem so strange. We were lucky because my inlaws live 3000 miles away and we have been flying since both boys were infants. Also, depending on how impaired the child is, or his age, you might consider creating a picture book (using photos) explaining the process of baggage check, gate check-in, security, boarding, etc. so it is all familiar.

The TSA can be a problem. My son has been pulled out of line for for a full check. Some agents are kind-- others have looked at my son and required him to re-sign his passport, as his signature is childish, and he looks like a grown man. And my sons are biracial, so look like they could be anything, so get flagged all the time. Telling the TSA that your child is autistic does not always help. On the other hand, once European security realizes that you are a mother with children, you will be fine.

I realized early on that I would resent my son if I never got to go anywhere again. We are on vacation in North Carolina right now, and my son had a meltdown in front of the neighbors. So I will go over there later and explain, and he will apologize for being rude. It doesn't end, but trust me, it gets so much better.

thread_title: Fiji and New Caledonia Islands - wheelchair access
text:
Yes we did the cruise and went on to tour New Zealand, Australia and Singapore! Mainly had a great time, but I didn't get ashore at any of the tender ports - the special lift that should have made this possible was broken throughout our cruise. Overall we were not impressed with Holland America and will never cruise with that company again.



In Fiji, we booked a private tour through Pooja Natasha at Tour Managers and had a guide and driver for the day. They were both excellent and we learnt so much about the island and its people. Both were also very good at getting me to otherwise inaccessible locations - we went to some villages/crafts, visited overlooks and viewpoints as well as the orchid gardens of the sleeping giant. Terrain not good for w'chair but area around reception is ok and we had a mini tour with an orchid expert. Had a beechfront/lagoon lunch at a very nice hotel.



In Pago Pago (American Samoa) we had an excellent day with Rory West from North Shore Tours. We booked a private tour and went all over the island, including the museum, national park and some lovely secluded beaches. We sampled local fruits and leant a lot about the history of the island. Rory is so knowledgible about the island and is a wealth of information and a genuinely nice guy. We all had a meal together at the end of the tour.



In Hawaii we just hired cars for each of the islands and managed to get to all the places the official tours went to but we went at our own pace and it was vastly cheaper too - made the cost of the private tours affordable as we saved so much by hiring cars.



In Noumea we just went to the town, but there were plenty of vans with drivers touting for business. I didn't get ashore at Ile de Pins and Lifou, but my partner did and he enjoyed snorkling and swimming. He also said access was nowhere near as bad as the picture given by the ports of call presentation on the ship. There were lots of locals who would have willingly helped had I been able to get off the ship!



If you are on a cruise, join the roll-call on www.cruisecritic.com - that way you might be able to join up with other people on your cruise. The site is also good for getting info about ports of call. I usually email the tourist board for each place and ask if they have an access guide or similar info for wheelchair users and that is usually a fruitful line of enquiry. If you can transfer to a vehicle then there are many options to explore for private shore excursions. On other cruises we have joined up with other couples and thats been a successful way of having an enjoyable day and spreading the costs.



Good luck on your planning and I hope you have a wonderful time.

thread_title: travelling to orlando with an autistic 3 year old
text: Hi I'm travelling to orlando next May for 18 days I wonder if anyone could give me any tips about getting around the theme parks with an autistic 3 year old I don't want to push in on queing but I also want my 10 year old to have a good time too,does anyone know if they might do baby change for parents of disabled children so that both parents can get on a ride with our daughter if our son won;t go on that ride.Thanks any advice greatly appreciated.

thread_title: travelling to orlando with an autistic 3 year old
text:
make sure you take documentation with you specifying the disability - letter for doctor etc , this will get you a special pass reducing queue times 





18 days is a long time , if planning multiple park visits make sure you have adequate rest/break days . 



Plan breaks outside the park during the day visits -don't spend all day in the park 







You know your own child best but any autistic spectrum toddlers i've known would have been totally freaked out by being left with strangers in a place with unfamiliar noise [repetitive music, machinery noises, other kids people shrieking , constant distractions from lights things moving , crowds , , smells and sight of food, strange smells of people's perfume and fabric softener or general BO , people dressed in big headed costumes



I would allow plenty of chill out time , work out calming strategies , consider ear plugs or noise canceling headphones [get the child used to these before you go]

make sure you have any security objects , and try an implement calming strategies well in advance 



Plan ahead- know exactly what to expect -ask on relevant forums for specific info on rides - esp related to darkness, sudden noises, jolting , drops , spinning etc 



Things that neurotypical people find mildly amusing or mildly scary/disorienting can be horrific to someone on the autistic spectrum- and it does not have to rides- queueing with someone smelling strongly of perfume or stale smoke , or sudden noises can be just as horrifying 



Be prepared for your child not to want to go on any rides at all unless you already know how he reacts to crowds, noise, rides etc - have a back up plan for this eventuality.

thread_title: travelling to orlando with an autistic 3 year old
text:
I suggest that you investigate rides before putting your child on them. This is something I would tell every parent, not just the parents of an autistic child. I destroyed the magic of Disney World for both of my grandsons because I took them on my favorite ride "Pirates of the Caribbean" on their first visit to the park when they were both toddlers.



Now the eight year old will not even get on the boat for "It's A Small World" and the six year old begs to go only to Epcot, and will not go to the Magic Kingdom.



Parents know what types of things disturb their children, and I wished I would have paid better attention to my own grand-children. Our own children loved it so much it just did not seem possible I could scar the grandsons for life, but I did.



Apart from that. Take a physician's note to Guest Services. They will give you a special card which you can give to the cast members operating the attractions. With that card you can ask for special consideration for your child, and usually cast members are great in providing whatever assistance you need.



Having learned the hard way, I now limit the exposure to loud noises (ear plugs or better yet, noise-canceling ear phones for fireworks). We do not go into attractions that have strobes or any type of flashing lights.



It is very warm here in May. I would plan to arrive early, leave by noon, and return after 6pm. Actually, what we prefer to do is not to arrive at the park at all until 6pm if we have enough time to see Disney World during their vacation period by taking it in 6 hour periods. I prefer to go in when it is starting to cool. I pass all the other parents taking their cranky miserable children and we walk into the entrance with ours, who are fresh and ready for adventure.



We also plan many activities that are not related to any amusement parks. Of course, our grandchildren like the water parks. We also take them to the beaches. We prefer the Gulf Coast beaches, but the beaches at Melbourne are also nice.



Do not worry about asking for what you need for your child. Your primary obligation is to meet the needs of this child, and I would ask for anything I needed to make that possible. I also would not push, force or encourage your child to do anything he is unwilling to do. When the child is done for the day, leave. It will make morning much easier.

thread_title: Report On Experience With Mobility Scooters in Italy
text:
We received an invitation to spend two weeks in Italy with very little advance notice. We knew that the itinerary would involve much walking, and based on our research we assumed we would not be able to see many things because our walking is so limited.



After much discussion we decided to at least take our mobility scooters and see if they might make it possible for us to see some of the sights. We decided if they were not useful we would just leave them in our hotel room.



Our flight with Delta Airlines involved one code-share flight on Air France from Florence to CDG. This became a serious problem because Air France did not want to permit us to check our scooters. I spent over three hours on the telephone obtaining permission to check our scooters, and was notified that we had to be at the airline terminal four hours prior to our departure.



When we arrived at 6am there was no one working for Air France so we waited at the check-in counter for a bit more than one hour. Eventually a gentleman approached us and ask if we were the passengers who wanted to check scooters. We said we were, and he explained that they had to be boxed. We then watched as several employees wrestled our dis-mantled scooters into large cardboard boxes.



I do not know what happened to the boxes but when the scooters came out in Atlanta they were not in boxes and their various parts were taped to the main body of the scooters. My scooter sustained some minor damage which Delta addressed promptly upon our arrival at our home airport.



I was generally pleased with the process of transporting the scooters to and from Italy, but in the future I would attempt to avoid using any airline other than a US carrier familiar with mobility scooters.



The other transportation issue we had was when we went from Rome to Florence via train. We had to apply to bring our scooters 24 hours in advance. This involved physically going to Termini in Rome and finding the tiny office for disabled passengers. Lots of paperwork was filled out, and we were instructed to arrive 60 minutes before our train on the following day.



When we arrived at Termini we were directed to a waiting room. We waited there for about forty minutes and then two men came with a lifting device that they used to take our scooters to the train and lift them into a special car with wheelchair accommodations. The rail trip was pleasant and uneventful.



Transportation from the train and airport was a bit challenging. In Rome I made an advanced reservation with Rome Cabs. They provided a small van. The driver met us at the airport even though our flight was nearly two hours late. The driver put the scooters into the van and easily transported us to our apartment.



In Florence we took a taxi from the train to our hotel. We took our scooters apart, and both of them fit into the trunk of the taxi along with most of our luggage. Transportation on the ground was not a problem.



As for our success, Italy proved much easier for our scooters than we expected. There were occasional curbs that were too high for our scooters and we had to lift them by hand over the curb. We were with other family members who helped us do this. On a couple of occasions where we were alone we were able to manage on our own, but someone always offered to help.



We were able to fully explore the Coliseum and to a more limited degree the Forum. We easily reached the Pantheon. We were not permitted to take our scooters into the Vatican, but the Vatican did have wheelchairs which our family members were able to push. My only comment about our Vatican experience is that the wheelchairs were in dreadful repair, and very difficult to push. Our daughter really earned the calories she consumed in her evening meal after pushing us through the Vatican all day.



Florence was generally even easier than Rome. We had virtually no problem with curbs. It was easy to get into most of the churches and museums. The Galileo Museum was an exception. They would not let us use the mobility scooters, but did have one wheelchair. It was difficult to use this wheelchair because the lifts were not operating, and there were multiple levels.



Restaurants were generally accommodating. On a few occasions we just left our scooters near the entrance to a restaurant or small shop, took our keys and returned to find our scooters safe.



The only other surprise was the elevators. I had carefully researched to locate places to stay that did not involve stairs. Both of the places where we stayed had elevators. I did not realize how exceptionally small the elevators would be. They were smaller than a phone booth, and we had to take our scooters apart to put them on the elevators. This process takes no more than ten minutes and was not a huge inconvenience, but it would be nice if elevators were a bit larger.



We avoided the problem of the typically small size of European hotel rooms by renting a self-catering apartment in Rome, and reserving a suite in Florence. In both places we had room for our scooters. 



Our conclusion is that it takes some extra work to arrange for our scooters, but it makes seeing a city possible. Our experience in Italy was great, and we would certainly take our scooters again if we return.

thread_title: Report On Experience With Mobility Scooters in Italy
text: I'm so glad your trip worked so well for you, Busy-retired. Your report will be invaluable to others coming to this forum looking for info about Italy and scooters.

thread_title: Report On Experience With Mobility Scooters in Italy
text:
My husband was very hesitant to take them. He was afraid we would break them on the streets or the airlines would damage them. My philosophy is that I purchased it to use it. My goal is to see and do everything I can. I would rather die with my scooter scratched and dented and a head filled with memories than pass away leaving my scooter looking like new and my bucket list unaltered. Every scratch and dent represents some great adventure.

Although not a tour operator, many bed and breakfasts cater to guests with dietary concerns. The Iron Mountain Inn B&B in the mountains of Northeast Tennessee is one. You can do a search on the PAII (Professional Assn of Innkeepers International) for other B&Bs which cater to gluten free diets.

thread_title: Disabled access in Bangkok and Beijing
text:
I just returned from both cities and was very frustrated at the lack of access. I am ambulatory, but cannot walk long distances, can only go up a few steps with assistance or a handrail to hold on to and cannot climb ramps or stairs. I was unable to enter the Temple of the Recling Buddha in Bangkok because it had 4 high steps and no handrailing and I was alone without anyone to help me. I didn't even try the Temple of the Emerald Buddha or the Grand Palace because of that.



In Beijing I walked up a steep ramp to the landing, but was so out of breath when I got up to the top, I had to sit and rest for a half hour to get my breath. I had a young man for a guide that I hired outside the Forbidden City and he helped me up the ramp and then took me down the closest ramp to exit. Since it was clear that I was not going to be able to actually go into any of the areas, I then left. And, again, based on that experience, I didn't try the other sights such as the Temple of Heaven, Summer Palace, etc.



Based on my experience, I would suggest that anyone who has problems in this area please check out the issue of accessibility before planning a trip to avoid such frustrations. It is very aggravating to go so far and then not get to see the major sights due to health issues.

text:
Hi Christal! I think I can answer your question for Banff, Alberta. I did a little googling and found this:

http://www.servicealberta.gov.ab.ca/pdf/mv/Placard_Info_FAQ.PDF

(see questions #15 & 16)

To summarize - if you have a placard for your car at home, bring it and use it in Alberta, making sure it's clearly visible in your rental car. If you don't have a placard, then you can get a temporary one for use during your visit from any Alberta registries office. You don't need to present your own placard or have a medical certificate to get a temporary visitors' placard valid for your visit. There might be a charge for this, but it would be no more than $10. It's also pretty likely that the temporary Alberta placard would also be recognized in BC (Vancouver), but I'd have to look into that a bit more to be sure.

To find an Alberta registry, use the search box at the bottom of this page:

http://www.servicealberta.gov.ab.ca/1641.cfm

After Nov. 1, 2010 regulations changed. Once I went through the scanner, which was fairly quick, but on every other flight the scanners have been broken and I have had to have a complete physical pat-down, which is so obnoxious that if I experienced it with any other person I would report it as a sexual attack. In addition, after having probed into every area of my body, some TSA employees will still not let me leave until they run the gloves that they wear through the machine that detects explosives.



I carried both a card and a letter from my doctor, and the TSA person laughed at me and told me to not bother because certainly a terrorist could obtain a card and letter. It was completely useless, both in the US and in foreign countries.



Generally this is the same experience I have in most foreign countries; although the physical pat-down is not nearly as aggressive any where as it is in the US.

Any good web sites out there for best places to visit in Canada in a wheelchair? would love to go whale watching and to Banff on the Rocky Mountaineer but slightly concerned about city transport etc

In the city of Vancouver everything is very accessible, buses, skytrain and taxis. In the hinterland not so much for accessible transportation. The Rocky Mountaineer is supposedly fantastic but not sure how accessible excursions are. But the all terrain bus that goes on the glaciers is accessible

Hi blackscorpion ~



Yes, I can vouch for Vancouver and Victoria being totally wheelchair friendly. There is always an elevator option. And the Rocky Mountaineer is accessible as well. I'm not sure about wheelchairs going on the whale watching boats but my guess is they have a system, because they cannot deny people access because of a disability. BC has clear laws about it. 



Rick Hansen (Man in Motion) has been instrumental in improving accessibility for people. Google him for more info.



The problem comes with individual restaurant owners and individual hotels. Some restaurants have handicap washrooms in total compliance with the law, but the odd one stashes highchairs or extra supplies in the way and hotels differ from property to property. Some think a handicap room means grab bars in the bathroom. Others have full roll-in showers and lowered light switches. The onus is on the traveller and there is a great checklist here on this forum (just down the list) called Checklist for Accessible Hotels (or similar) 



Unfortunately there is no "place" in Canada that is more favourable for wheelchairs except the 3 provinces in the middle of the country, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta which are completely flat but where there is very little in tourist attractions. Quebec City is marvelous but has cobblestones and many ups and downs. Ottawa would be a great place to visit. The downtown area is very flat and there is a lot of Canadiana there. The excellent Museum of Civilization is across the river, about 20 minutes by bus, in Gatineau, Quebec. Here are things to do for Ottawa. The National Gallery is wonderful. The War Museum is wonderful, Sparks Street is underwhelming, The House of Commons is commonly called The Hill and is indeed on a hill. The Rideau locks and the boat tours on the Rideau canal. But Ottawa in the late spring or early fall is a great place. I would think a week would do it. I'm not up on their accessibility laws.

http://www.tripadvisor.com/Attractions-g155004-Activities-Ottawa_Ontario.html



Back to BC and Alberta. You could consider flying into Vancouver, visiting the city and Victoria (even the ferry across the Strait is accessible), then back to Vancouver to take the Rocky Mountaineer to probably Banff, rather than Jasper. Have a look at Brewster Tours for what they offer up the Icefields Parkway out of Banff or Calgary. Then get to Calgary for the flight home. This is a very common itinerary for UK folks who come here. If you do decide on this destination, I would suggest you plan mid-June to mid-September. There is ice on the lakes and snow on the trails up to about mid-June. July and August would be your best bet. And 2 - 3 weeks would give you enough time to see Vancouver 5 nights, Victoria 3 nights, RM 1 overnight in a hotel on the way. Then 3-4 nights in Banff, 3 nights in Jasper and finally 1 night in Calgary before your departure day.



I notice you have posted on the Banff Forum and been directed back here. What I would suggest you do, if you are really interested in exploring Vancouver and the Rockies, is post on the British Columbia forum. There are a whole bunch of us over there who can help you with your research. The reviews for the RM and whale watching are there. There is one poster who is a tour guide and goes to the Rockies many times in a tourist season. He can assess and compare Tour Company programs for you. As well there are some Alberta posters who "cross border shop" by reading both the BC Forums and the Alberta Forums. You will be in good hands.



Because Banff and Jasper and Lake Louise are all in Alberta, I cannot speak to their laws about accessibility, but someone on the forum could tell you.



When it comes to hotels, you really have to build your own checklist and do the contacting and checking. The same with tour companies BTW. But email is pretty easy these days. Someone was posting on the Victoria Forum and I remember this resource website:



http://www.access-canada.ca/site/about/index.htm



I'm just going to link the whole thread for you. It contains quite a few links.



http://www.tripadvisor.com/ShowTopic-g154945-i207-k4581330-Hotel_Accessibility-Victoria_Vancouver_Island_British_Columbia.html



When you have thought about it a bit more and if you want to explore BC, Alberta and the Canadian Rockies, I would suggest you open some of the threads that interest you on each of the forums for the 3 just mentioned destinations. Reading what other people ask and the answers given will prepare you quite well for general awareness of our part of the world. 



I hope this helps. I have no more thunder left! for when you post on the BC forum.

http://media.metronews.topscms.com/images/44/c4/1a51a9df434cae8feaad4d69ac87.jpeg

"Rocky Mountaineer will make every effort to meet any special needs, including the requirements of our disabled guests. Some of the Rocky Mountaineer coaches are wheelchair accessible. GoldLeaf Dome Coaches have elevators for guests who have problems using the spiral staircase. Please inform us at the time of booking if any assistance is required."

My suggestion is that you take enough meds for a few extra days than your basic itinerary. You never know when a flight will be delayed or when a volcano will erupt or some such! :-(



Take your meds in the original containers with labels in your name.



Also, I would suggest you consider taking your prescriptions with the generic name of the meds, as that will be known by chemists world wide. For example, not all chemists will know the Trade name Advill but all will know the generic name ibuprofen. (Both will also have a chemical identity.) Then if anything goes sideways, you will be able to get what you need.



I hate to say it, but the paperwork from your GP is almost worthless. Anyone can produce a counterfeit letter from a GP from a printer that they don't mean much any more at Security or Customs. But do have them with you.

I've had good luck with asking my pharmacist to give me bottles with labels that will hold the amount of the drug I need to take with me. This makes it easy to pack small amounts or larger amounts in the right sized bottle and the label with the drug name is attached "officially." They will add the generic name as well if you ask.



Hope this helps.

We spent a day in Barcelona having gone there by train from Salou, and my wife is in a wheelchair. The Placa Catalunya station has no lifts and is underground, so we had problems there, but once in the streets we found the place quite wheelchair friendly, the Ramblas is a fascinating street market and easy to get along, but there are some more outlying places which would probably need you taking taxis. We never stayed there but I have a link which may help.



http://www.enableholidays.com/holiday_search/holiday_search_results.asp?destination=Spain&resort=54&rating=0&submit=Search



I would advise seeing the Spanish Village ( Poble Espanol ) and also the Sagrada Familiar, but you would need taxis to get to these. 



PLEASE be aware that pick pockets are rife in Barcelona and you would not believe how skilful these people are, keep mobile phones, cameras etc out of sight and have money in a secure body belt or neck wallet under your clothes, believe me I have been on the receiving and and these characters can get into a velcroed or buttoned pocket in a second without you feeling a thing, it just seems as if someone has bumped into you, apologised and hurried on. Don't let me scare you off though, Barcelona is one of the most beautiful and fascinating cities in the world and I would tell anyone to visit it.

text:
Historically Disney World is very crowded during this week; however during all of 2010 & this year we have been exceptionally surprised by WDW. We have gone on Christmas Eve, the week after Christmas, Spring Break, July 4th week-end & Labor Day. Magic Kingdom is more crowded, but still not bad. 



I do not know if Universal is impacting WDW, but since their attendance increased by 30% last year compared to 1% at WDW I think it is responsible. 



Even if the parks are crowded groups with a person in a wheelchair move to the front of the line at many attractions. My family love to go with me because they do not wait in many lines. 



Sea World also does not seem crowded. We went between Christmas & New Year's and it was lovely. They also have preferred seating for wheelchair guests & families. 



I would rent a villa. You can stay in a large home for much less than a moderately priced hotel. The villa we like to use has been adapted for wheelchair guests. Rent a car, stay in a villa & eat a few meals at home & Orlando is a bargain especially when you factor in the exchange rate. 



If you get tired of amusement parks there are scenic drives to beaches on the Atlantic & the Gulf of Mexico as well as NASA tours & hundreds of factory outlet stores which people from the UK really seem to enjoy. 



I think if you avoid Universal the rest of the attractions are not excessive. The weather is generally lovely. Prices are cheap for UK residents & your children are a good age for you to create great Disney memories. 



As a person in a wheelchair Orlando is more user friendly for me than anywhere I go. If you would like some hints about how to maximize wheelchair benefits send me a PM & I will try to respond when I get back to my laptop. The iPhone I am using is difficult for longer responses.

text:
We purchased plane tickets for our annual trip to Turkey last summer. After buying the tickets, my right hip generally ceased to function. It took me a long time to get an appointment with a reliable surgeon. When I saw him he said I needed a new hip, but that was on Oct. 4 and we leave for Turkey on Oct. 30.



He did the surgery on Oct. 5, and I started physical therapy the same day. I have really worked to try and bring myself into the highest functioning level possible.



So......we leave day after tomorrow. I am walking slowly with a cane, but I do improve every day. I am sure it is foolish to take such a huge trip so soon after major surgery, but those tickets were not refundable.



Has anyone else traveled so soon after major surgery? Are there potential problems of which I am not aware?

Otherwise, take it slow........use your cane.......Dont do stairs unless you have no other option. Maybe learn "Where is the elevator (or escalator" in Turkish.

thread_title: Traveling three weeks post hip replacement
text:
Unfortunately, Turkey is most unfriendly to mobility scooters or wheel chairs. The walks are often cobblestone, or have huge holes, or involve steep stairs. Many times they are not passable because a merchant has set up shop on the sidewalk or a restaurant has placed tables there. In addition the curbs are six to eight inches high, and there are no cut outs making it impossible to cross from block to block. I would have taken my mobility scooter for the last four years if it would have been practical.



I really cannot even use the standard walker that many hip replacement patients use. I have been training with a cane since a week after my surgery because it is the only walking device that is practical. Elevators are also rare in the hotels and restaurants we frequent. Fortunately taxis are plentiful and inexpensive and I plan to make generous use of them. My husband also speaks the language well enough to communicate my needs.



I am going to plan every outing carefully so I do not take one step that is not necessary, and we are going to start very slowly. I really believe I can do this. If I end up spending my vacation in the hotel lobby it is still a more interesting place to recover than my own living room.



My surgeon has authorized this trip. I think he might be a bit ego involved because he has a building reputation in a small area as a leading surgeon for hip and knee replacements. I suspect I will end up discussed in an article in a medical journal if I make the trip successfully.

thread_title: Traveling three weeks post hip replacement
text:
I am happy to report that our trip as been successful thus far. I did not follow my doctor's instructions last week and did somethings that were not allowed. I paid a price, and I was not able to walk as well this week as last.



Fortunately Delta airlines was fantastic. When I explained that I had recently had surgery they gave us bulkhead seating (and first class seating for all of our domestic flights).



Delta also met every plane with a wheelchair. When we arrived in Istanbul the man with the wheelchair actually got on the plane and came to my seat to escort me out of the plane. He went to the head of the line to obtain our visa and took us through the diplomat gate for passport control. He also managed all of our luggage, and when I realized I had left my jacket on the plane he went back to get it.



I am going very slowly, and I balance one day of high activity with one day of low activity. I am very happy that we decided to come. Even if I could do nothing but watch the street from the window of my hotel room, recovering in Istanbul is much more fun than recovering at home.



Fortunately, I am generally able to walk for short distances so our plans have not been badly impacted. This was a very good decision.

thread_title: Traveling three weeks post hip replacement
text:
Hi Sarah, We are still in Turkey and having a wonderful experience. The first week was a little tough, probably because I went right out and did much more walking than I should have done. I spent two days in the hotel room recovering.



From that point forward I get a tiny bit better every day. Now, on most days, I walk about a mile. We have good friends with cars. My husband is fantastic, and we do not mind using taxis. Most importantly, the Turkish people are kind and hospitable. They are quick to run to your side when they see you with a cane. I have never crossed a street or climbed a stair without the help of some stranger.



I am so sorry to hear of your difficulties. Infection has always scared me. I looked for a surgeon with a very low rate. My surgeon, and all of the operating team, wore contamination suits with re-breathers so they never exhaled into the sterile operating room. It makes a huge difference in terms of infection. I did not let anyone come near me in the hospital unless they sanitized their hands, and my family were tested (with nasal swabs) for staph infections prior to my surgery. Some people can carry staph without symptoms.



I think it is very important to be as pro-active as possible in preventing infection, but regardless of how careful we are, it is just one of those things that can happen to anybody. In terms of a hip replacement, it is a really terrible complication.



I hope you are feeling better and that the hip you received is not one that is being recalled. I cannot imagine going through all of the trauma of replacement all over again.

Best Wishes - BR

thread_title: Boarding the plane with an amputee

Hi Ozzy, First you have to tell whoever you book with that you have someone who is unable to climb the aircraft steps. Now I will tell you what happens .When you book in at the airport you will have to have a label attached to the wheelchair by the checking in staff at the check in desk and you will be given a form to take to another desk pointed out by the check in staff to inform the aircraft about a disabled person that needs to be boarded. The person on this desk will tell you which gate you will be boarded from as sometimes disabled are boarded at a different gate. When its time to be boarded someone will come for you all and ask if the disabled person can walk at all and then you will all be taken to the ambilift which is a Van with a cabin on it that rises and falls and will take you all to the plane.Your Father in Law will in his wheelchair that will be then put in the hold after he is taken to his seat in a special wheelchair that can be wheeled down the isle of the plane.If your plane is at a tunnel he will be wheeled down to the door of the plane and then taken to his seat the same way .

Just make sure you are at the gate about an hour before official boarding time as disabled people board first.

The same thing will happen on the return journey.

The difficulty with meeting accessible needs is that there are no worldwide standards for hotels, restaurants or attractions. This kind of traveller really needs to do a fair bit of homework to reduce surprises upon arrival - at hotels mainly. You might be interested in looking at the Accessibility Checklist which is in first position of the topics listings on this forum, with a sticky against it. The Disability Standards are pretty fierce in Australia, having been in place for about 20 years. Public places are now pretty well obliged to have access or face the wrath of the law through the Human Rights Commission

http://www.hreoc.gov.au/disability_rights though I would certainly check with any hotel first as the law is being introduced in stages as it applies to hotels.

Any theatre except perhaps heritage ones will have access and places for wheelchairs and there are accessible toilets all over the place, even in my local shopping centre, though sometimes you need to get a key from someone in more remote places. (There is a MLAK key system where eligible people can purchase a key that will open these toilets. http://www.masterlocksmiths.com.au )

This site may be helpful

http://www.travelintelligence.com/luxury-hotels/australasia/australia/new-south-wales/sydney/wheelchair-accessible-hotels

but I haven't personally checked.

Just had a lovely night at Bells at Killcare and had the wheelchair accessible room. Very nice though I would have thought a bit cramped for easy movement without them moving some of the furniture. (I am not a wheelchair user) The shower was fantastic.

I don't think I have ever seen so many scooters around as there are in Australia and the cities really are pretty well set up for them.

Hi Lynn ~



I would think that the standards for public spaces are well implemented and getting around the cities is easy. That is so here. I wouldn't expect any problems getting around the cities.



I was meaning to point out to the OP that wheel chair access means different things to different hotels which are not public places. Some think that grab bars in the shower make it accessible, when in fact a wall mounted shower seat or even a roll in shower and a hand held shower head would be more fitting. So the hotel says, "Yes, yes, this hotel room is wheel chair accessible" but in fact does not meet the needs of the traveller. There are also doorways to consider: 80 cm exterior and 75 cm interior will handle a wheelchair. Maneuvering space on either side of the bed. Raised toilet. Lowered hanging rod in the closet.



These are the things that require the homework. It can be very frustrating to arrive at a hotel to find that the hotel answered the "is this an accessible room" in the affirmative when in fact it falls short of the mark. I also think that it's a good idea to get the actual room number confirmation in writing because we all know that travellers can arrive to find the "accessible" room has been changed to another one.



And then there are restaurants. What to do if the lovely renovated handicapped washroom has two steps up to it. My best suggestion is - do the homework.

I too would recommend checking but the guidelines for places like hotels are quite stringent, right down to width of doorways and lifts and the architects had better know this stuff. It helps that our Human Rights Commissioner is blind. Mind you, the person on the desk may well not know what is required.



The difficulty is mainly in implementation within a timeframe, so only a percentage have to be compliant by a set date. And there is always the "unjustifiable hardship" clause. Easyjet just won when a woman sued because they wouldn't carry her on the flight she wanted, but it turned out they had already accepted 2 other wheelchair customers for that flight and that was the max space they could allocate per flight. They did offer a reasonable alternative flight but she sued instead. All very interesting and passions run high.



I have just checked our Sydney Morning Herald Good Food Guide and wheelchair access is listed, but of course, as you say, the three steps to the washroom may not be mentioned.

http://www.goodguides.com.au/sydney/ 

I hope Kropos finds we have done a good job.

Hi there,



We live in Australia and have a disabled teenager who is in a wheelchair. 



Generally speaking most public spaces are accessible. Transport is also quite accessible, with most train stations now having elevators/lifts, ramps etc. Some buses also are accessible. However some of our older buildings are not fantastic for access. For example the Art Gallery of NSW, the access is at the back of the building with very poor signage in the front. So it takes a little while to figure out how to get into a building. This was a few months ago, and things may have changed...



We recently went on holidays to Victoria and stayed in the Mt Buller area. We checked that the hotel had disabled access, but got a room that we couldn't find a way to, with a wheelchair! It was a bit of a shock, as we had assumed that all rooms were accessible. So we had to change our room....

Also some of our restaurants are not accessible. We went to a famous restaurant in Daylesford Victoria (a Spa town) and we had requested a table which we could access with a wheelchair. The main dining area was down a few steps, so they very kindly set up a separate table in the foyer area for us.

thread_title: Vacations for folks on kidney dialysis
text: My husband is on kidney dialysis, and we live in western NY. Vacations are good for him, but of course we need to arrange for hemodialysis, so this is a significant complication in vacation planning. Does anyone know of any destinations that are especially suitable for dialysis patients (i.e. have dialysis centers that are receptive to visitors?) We especially like lakes, rivers, horses, zoos, farms, and history. Thank you very much for any leads.

thread_title: Vacations for folks on kidney dialysis
text:
Hi Julia,



Welcome to TripAdvisor. I'm relatively new to hemodialysis (about 6 months or so) I've only dialyzed outside of my home clinic once so far, during a long weekend out of town - and we are going to the Washington Coast for Christmas and New Years. 



I live on the other side of the country from you, so I don't know of any places closer to you than the West Coast of the US. :) But I've been doing my research! I'm surprised how many smaller towns have dialysis facilities. Pretty much if they can support a hospital - they can support a dialysis clinic. Of course they are smaller - the one i went to last month only had 6 chairs (my home clinic has 24)! 



That being said - DaVita put our a press release of their "top 10" places to visit in the US for vacations on D. Of course, they are all big tourist destinations and they all have DaVita clinics, but some of those destinations might appeal to your like of history and rivers: http://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20111129005925/en/DaVita-Announces-Top-Holiday-Travel-Destinations-Dialysis



I don't live in a tourist area, but I'm surprised at the number of visitors our clinic gets. I haven't noticed any irritation by the staff to this - in fact I think they are happy to see some new faces and hear some new stories. :) At the clinic I visited in November, they seemed happy to oblige and everything went smoothly. 



You might just do what i did - and pick where I wanted to go, checked with my home clinic if there was some place nearby and let them worry about it! I checked all the coastal towns I normally visit, and they all have or a near a clinic. Perhaps it is because so many people, out here, go to the coast to retire.



Have you and your husband traveled while he was on hemo, before? How did that work for you? I've heard that your access can be a problem when you travel because no one at the clinic will know your access...so I'm learning to set my own needles so that I can learn it and feel more confident when I travel. I used to travel a lot -KD slowed me down, but now that I'm on hemo, I'm gearing up to travel much more than the past few years!



I dont think TripAdvisor gets much dialysis traffic, at least people don't mention it often. Have you check out: http://ihatedialysis.com/ they are a very active message board and they have a travel section that might be able to help in finding specific locations where you want to travel.



Anyway - nice to meet you. I hope you find what you are looking for here.



Noah

text: Thank you so much for your kindness and information - I plan to use the links that you provided. My husband has traveled three times in the three years that he's been on hemodialysis (also twice when he was on peritoneal dialysis, which was easier) but it sounds like your area is much more dialysis-friendly than ours. thread_title: Delhi and Rajasthanh with walking difficulties
text:
This is something I put together elsewhere on TA:



Simply - some places are better than others. Do you need a wheelchair? If you do, you can still see a lot if you can manage a few steps or walk a short distance. Good examples:

- Delhi a/p - flat, get your airline to book a pporter to push as it's a long way to the exit

- Qut'b - one upward ramp on the way in, one section needs some walking, but you can see a lot from a chair, including the actual column

- Humayun's Tomb - some gateways with a few steps, but do'able

- Pushkar - narrow streets and steps

- Amber Palace - very accessible as there are (original) ramps in places

- Jaipur Observatory - OK

- Jodhpur - Palace is not so accessible, due to stairs

- Jodhpur lake cruise - you need to manage about 12 stairs and get onto/off the boat

- Bundi - steep!

- Ranthambore - you need to be fairly agile to get into a jeep. Maybe consider going by Canter

- Fatepur Sikri - I could not climb onto the bus to FS from the visitor centre, so passed!

Taj Mahal - some ramps. You need to be able to get onto a low'-floor buggy type thing to get to the entrance from the ticket office. When you get to the base of the white marble, you need to be able to walk and climb about 15 stairs - or at least our guide did not know of any provision for w/c users. I w/c'd as far as I could then managed the rest (slowly!) with two crutches and the help of my partner. There are places to rest as you see the outside of the tomb

Other - Hotels, make sure you get a ground floor room and still expect some steps. Getting around, a lot of the time the pavement does not exist and the road is busy and ill-repaired - but hey, you're in India!! Bathrooms, you'll find european style toilets in tourist hotels and restaurants, but may occasionally have to cope with a "squat". Use toilets when they're availabe! Staring, you WILL get started at and your picture will be on a thousand mobile phones. You will also be asked a lot oif questions, especially by school kids, so you'll feature in many a "report on our trip to the Taj" essays. People are generally very polite but at the same time inquisitive. 

When all's said and done, you will manage to see and do a lot. And you'll be in INDIA. This is what I said to a lady who asked about India:

“India is the most foreign place I have ever been, hot, wet, dirty, incredible poverty, filth, stinking open sewers, horrendous public toilets, noisy, chaotic, beautiful, fascinating, historic, amazing, wonderful , friendly, delicious, incredible, great helpful inquisitive people, stunning scenery, I would live there if I could and be the happiest man in the world.”

And I stick by that !

Then this a couple of days later after a couple of other TA members had added comments:

Literist - Sanjiv makes a very good point. I was dissuaded from following up on this (hiring porters to travel with us) when we visited by our tour company who made the (vaild) point that hiring a "pusher" would not make bumpy streets and "off road" areas comfortable or even possible. In my case, I limited my walking to short distances and stairs. A w/c can get you around on the flat and smooth and within reason where the surface is less than smooth. Arranging porters could be the answer for you, as you can't walk, but I fear you may still find yourself limited - the "inaccessability factor" will also depend on your nerve and the ability of the porters to carry you and your chair up narrow and steep staircases, often with a lot of other people trying to crowd around (and often trying to help).

I don't mean to scare you off. For me India is worth every discomfort, every drop of sweat, every twinge of pain and every stare, but you and your tour company will need to check out just what is going to be possible, in hotels, in transport and in sight-seeing. There is a lot of information on TA, on the web and via email for info on hotels. Use it to judge how much you will be able to achieve. But please give India a try.
Edited: 14 years ago

thread_title: Skiing with two children with Asperger syndrome
text:
private ski lessons work really well for kids with aspergers - google 'skiing with Oliver' - our 9 year old daughter has aspergers as well and is becoming a nice intermediate skier with even a little racing behind her (didn't like falling or losing but we are working on that). lots of patience and lots of time required to get her to the hill some days....same thing with skating etc.

Some great locations that make it easy to do a trip with kids in tow plus on hill accomodation nice and not too much money- Ellicotville! excellent with great web deals so not too $$$$ and a short drive from Toronto - don't forget your passport!. 

Some great vaction packages with our major airlines to Kelowna - big white and silver star are exceptional with kids - secure sign in and out procedures, just call ahead to find and book a recommended instructor who could be on site for your vacation days to provide continuity with experience teaching kids with autism and/or adhd plus lots of other activities. talk to the airlines about how to make your flight more comfortable - try to fly direct to keep it short and sweet the first time with lots of back-up entertainment/books/food due to weather or mechanical- the reality of flying! Don't overmedicate for the flight but take according to the doctors orders(if you do at all - we don't use any medication), stay hydrated and well fed and ask for a tour of the flight deck before the start of the flight if time permits to reduce anxiety - most pilots love to say hello to the kids before the door has to close if they aren't too rushed.

Take lessons at a small hill ahead of time and again - don't hesitate to set up a lesson or two with an instructor that can work well with your kids and be flexible with weather to make it as smooth a transition as possible! Key - easy as possible for you and fun for the kids - allow lots of time to get the clothes and equipment set - up if they are touchy about that stuff! 5 hours of prep for 1 hour of skiing - but it is all about the journey right?

To the naysayers - yes lots of adults can do lots of things with aspergers but they have already developed their coping mechanisms - this gives us all hope!- but keep in mind these folks are just starting to get the ball rolling and hopefully can look forward to some great vacation memories with their kids with a little travel advice! It is tough when you are in the trenches man!

Since I last made any major contribution on this forum my life has changed a bit. My husband now requires a mobility scooter, in addition to my own need for my scooter. He has developed some mild dementia which means he easily becomes disoriented in new places and requires observation. We have decided to meet our grand-daughter in Rome next week. She is studying in Europe this semester.



After attempting an Art Fair last week-end it is completely clear to me that we will not be able to enjoy anything if we do not have our scooters. I have spent a week, but I believe I have located an apartment with no stairs. I also have located a gentleman who can transport our scooters from the hotel to which ever area we wish to visit each day.



My major question is how much or Rome can we access with our scooters. I asked this question on the Rome forum, and got kind of a mixed response. Some people said that the general tourist and historic areas had been adapted. Others suggested that we leave them at home.



I understand the problems of infrastructure and mobility scooters. I never take them with me to Istanbul; however, since I did not take them when we went in November we spent too much time in our hotel room because we simply could not walk anywhere.



If anyone has used a mobility scooter in Rome I would love to read your evaluation. If you have visited Rome and have any observations about the adaptation of infrastructure for scooters or wheelchairs I would appreciate hearing anything about what we can expect.



Thanks for your help.

Hi we were in Rome a few years ago with my sister who uses a wheelchair. We found the access surprisingly good and people were very willing to help. There are 2 lines on the tube- one with no wheelchair access and 1 with wheelchair access so make sure you get the right line - the one with access. This means you can get on and off the trains as they are low to the platform and at the stations they have lifts up to the attractions. The stations with lift access are marked on the underground map so maybe try to get one of these before you go. We stayed in a hotel slightly out of the city centre for better access and we also got buses and found many of the buses had been adapted to go down low to get the wheelchair on. Most of the main tourist sites have good wheelchair access- the Vatican my sister got in free as she was in a wheelchair and I got in ata reduced rate as her companion. We also got through a special queue. There were a few areas she couldn't access in the Vatican but overall it was fine. Round the Colusseum the ground is all cobbled so a bit bumpy for the wheelchair but again we got in on a separate queue so no waiting and we got a reduced price. We couldn't get right down into the main area but got to see plenty and get a feel for the grandeur of it all. We found alot of the old streets int he tourist areas cobbled so were at times bumpy and a bit harder to get down but we coped well. If there are any stations at things you want to see that don't have lift access just get off at the station before and go down- the main tourist spots are all reasonably close so you can wander about not on the underground and get to see everything. The zoo was lovely- we went through the park which had some beautiful statues etc and the zoo was very wheelchair friendly- again reduced entrance for wheelchair users and their companion. thread_title: What can be done when a hotel doesn't deliver?
text:
We've all had it happen ...



Careful planning ... Assurances of the appropriate accessible accommodations ... Confirmation and re-confirmation ...



And then you get there ... and life happens.



So what can be done? I propose we start by sharing our experiences here, because no big hotel chain wants to identified in the thread.



Let's do it, be specific, be honest, but please done sling mud because we won't be taken seriously if that happens

thread_title: What can be done when a hotel doesn't deliver?
text:
So I'll go first. My wife and I are pretty seasoned travelers. She's a strong para and been in her wheelchair since she was a kid. She has worked in international health since the late 70's. As a globetrotter, working in mostly in developing countries, you can imagine what she's been through in terms of tough travel and hotel accommodations.



So, now we're both retired, working off a huge cache of hotel and frequent flyer points. Traveling in retirement is waaaaay better.



One of our hotel programs, Starwood Preferred Guests contacts us and says: "As a valued SPG member, we'd like to make you an offer".



It was pretty straightforward. Come down to Mexico to the Cancun Westin Laguna Mar for 6 days / 5 nights for cost. No obligation, look around, see if it's for you and we'll talk. The offer was actually for me, but she took the call from the SPG rep. So she explained she was in a chair, and that any reservation would have to be for accessible accommodations. No problem!



So there's a follow-up e-mail, she once again reiterates her situation. The reply once again is no problem.



The concierge calls us the night before we come down. Again, we reconfirmed the need for an accessible room. No problem.



We arrive and guess what? No accessible rooms available. So, we march up the management chain and no joy. They'll try and get one for us tomorrow. OK. So we go and see the concierge to make some dinner plans and tell him the story. He says: "Don't worry." Takes it up his management chain, which is different than the front desk chain. No joy.



In the meantime we're contacted by the Starwood Vacation Ownership folks who ask if we'd listen to a presentation for a perk of some bonus points. It's raining so we say sure. After the dog and pony we say: "We like the model, can we see an accessible unit?" We get to the director of marketing and she asks us how we like the property. We tell her it's nice but what about accessibility? She tells it's the only accessible pool in Cancun. We say great, where's the lift, because no one else seems to know? She doesn't know either. We tell her about the problems with our room. She's horrified and tells us she'll get right on it. Oh, by the way they can't show us an accessible model.



So I'll cut to the chase. It's four days later, still no joy and after picking my wife up and putting her down for the toilet, the bath and on and off the bed, I've got a pretty sore back. What's really has got me steamed is that I know it's a simple training issue, but it's Starwood? I don't expect this kind of thing from them, normally they're more on their game. They paid for us to come down, to impress us, and earn our future business. Big company three organizations in the company: operations, marketing and bell services, and nobody stepped up.



I wonder if they'll read this ... probably not ... but there's a person turning 50 every 10 minutes. Their target marketing demographic, and many will have a mobility impairment at some time in their life.

thread_title: What can be done when a hotel doesn't deliver?
text:
I'm beginning to believe that there has been a steady erosion of rights for the disabled over the last decade or so. At least that's what I've seen in my travels.



After the ADA was passed, there was a focus on awareness of the needs of the disabled, not to provide special treatment, but more about improving access for all persons.



The realities of competition in the travel marketplace have forced the industry to look where they can cut costs, and probably this is where a lot of the erosion develops. At least where accessibility problems are concerned. I, for one, believe that universal design is the right answer, not special accommodations for the disabled.



We have to remember that someone turns 65 every few minutes in the US. And many of them will become mobility impaired, even if only temporarily, at some time in their lives.

thread_title: Travelling in Asia with a lot of life saving drugs
text:
My husband is on several life saving drugs and we want to travel to Vietnam for a month. He is pretty self sufficient and can measure his INR for the Warfarin - that is not a problem. I just wonder if anyone has any advice for storing such a number of drugs while travelling in Asia. We would need to take a month's supply, and would have to return to Aus if something happened to them. 

Regards DG

thread_title: Travelling in Asia with a lot of life saving drugs
text:
Hi,



Generally speaking as a non-resident tourist you can bring in most medications which are:



a) specifically prescribed to you,

b) in quantities that are only for your period of stay

c) are not for re-sale, gifting, etc.

d) are not specifically prohibited in that country.



Vietnam, like most of SE Asia is very aware of and takes the issue of narcotics smuggling very seriously.. so while legal drugs pass Customs control with little issue, things that are prohibited or regulated may get closer scrutiny. So, you'd be wise to just double check with the VN Embassy or CG in your area for a definitive ruling.



As far as storing it, in most hotel rooms your room will either be controlled by a it's own A/C unit, or via central A/C-- so maintaining a reasonable 'room temperature' should be easy.. 



In the cases where your room is not climate controlled, you might be able to store it in your in-room fridge-- but-- be sure you let the hotel know and your specific room maid/housekeeper as well.. just so it's not accidentally thrown away during the daily room servicing process..



As a last alternative, many hotels can arrange for it to be stored in their kitchen refrigerator or can provide a supply of ice to cool it.



Travel Safe,

thread_title: Travelling in Asia with a lot of life saving drugs
text:
Thanks GOPBI, some good hints in your response. We will only be staying in two hotels this time, so your tips should be easy to put in place.

No narcotics involved. However the drug routine is pretty new to us and even though we have travelled to Asia many times, we did it without this addition to our luggage - although it will get smaller as the days go by!

thread_title: Travelling in Asia with a lot of life saving drugs
text:
Hi,



Obviously when you're actively traveling, the drugs should remain on you or in your immediate carry-on and within your control at all times.. never, ever let it go in checked bags.. while the statistical probability of a lost or late bag is very, very small, since the consequence can be severe, you need to take that risk to as close to zero as possible.. so when traveling, keep them on your person.



In the hotels, if the medications need to be climate controlled-- like being kept in your room refrigerator, I would do a few things..



a) Place a note on the fridge door *and* inside on the medication itself (in local language) that they are not to be thrown away.. 



b) speak to your rooms actual maid/housekeeper *and* the front desk or housekeeping manager as well..



Medications aren't widely known to be high theft items as their re-saleability is limited... Not like cash, cameras and the like which can be re-sold quickly.. Things that get stolen are generally things that can be quickly turned to cash or used themselves.. so, unless the thief also has the same medical condition, the notion that it's likely to be stolen is, in my mind, very low.. 



If your meds don't need to be kept cool, then store them in your checked bags and keep those bags securely locked when unattended in your room. If you really want to go one step further-- and I know people who do this-- you can also ask to store them in the hotels front desk safe..



In any case, it's always wise to know your prescription and have access to it and know the name and address of the best western medical clinic in the towns you'll be visiting.



Travel Safe,

thread_title: Travelling in Asia with a lot of life saving drugs
text:
Hi,



Unfortunately within the Asia region there is a small risk of adulterated drugs as unlike many 'western' nations, the national control over dispensing drugs-- that's pharmacy issues and not illegal narcotic trafficking-- is not as tight or comprehensive as it is in the west..



That said, it's not "common" per se, but you DO need to be aware of what and where you source your meds.. The best way to protect yourself is to buy only from reputable local sources.. 



One of the better ways to know who is or is not a reputable source is to check with your local Embassy in that country.. Most Embassies maintain a publicly available list of accredited medical providers and clinics in that country and that speak your native language.. 



Many Embassies, by policy, can't or won't formally recommend one provider or clinic over another, but the list is who they know to be credible and reliable.. In lots of cases, these doctors or clinics are where the Embassy personnel go for care themselves..



In your case, as it appears you are an Australian national, the AU Embassy in Hanoi has this exact list here:

That way, if your luggage goes missing, as ours did for 3 days on arrival at HCM, he has enough drugs for the holiday. With the big buisness of counterfeiting in Vietnam, I would be very wary of trying to obtain the drugs there. He also carries a letter from his doctor, as one of the drugs is regarded as a 'controlled' drug in the UK, plus a copy of his prescriptions , just to prevent any hassle at customs. We had a lovely trip in the Central Highlands but was glad we did not go the whole way Dalat to Hoi An. 3 days was enough as we like our comforts, and as the roads were bad in places I think my husband would have seen it as more of an endurance test than a holiday. Thanks for your posts.

thread_title: How do people with disabilities manage in Europe and Canada?
text:
Hi, Belinda. A bit about your disabilities, and Canada: 



Travel within cities, or between them, should be quite similar to what you find in Australia. There is government mandated accessibility (if you assist your walking with cane/walker/wheelchair). Since mobility assist devices travel free on airplanes, I'd check through a rolling walker with seat for yourself. 



I have a friend who is both celiac and diabetic, so I'm sensitive to your food issues. This is a bit harder to predict. A restaurant which is great with server A can turn into a nightmare with server B. Gluten free menus are not all that common. Upscale restaurants, and even "family" restaurants in cities should be able to help you pick. 



However, many chain restaurants with the worst food have the best written documentation! Canada's ubiquitous fast food, Tim Hortons, features coffee, deli food, and doughnuts. Almost the only items you'll be able to order are the coffee and steeped tea (at least it's ready brewed, no waiting for a tea bag to tint tepid water). 



Enormous distances involved within Canada. Example - Sydney to Cairns is about 2500 km, isn't it? Well, if you started near Canada's eastern most point, in St. John's Newfoundland , 2500 km would take you as far as Montreal, in the province of Quebec. You'd need another 2500 km to get from there to Winnipeg, Manitoba. And another 2500 km to get from Winnipeg to Vancouver British Columbia on Canada's west coast. Very rough distances, but you get the idea. 



You would normally fly west to see Europe? You might continue west from there to Canada. Then west again home. Eastward time zone hops are much tougher than west ones for those with fatigue issues.

Two years ago I had two very unpleasant experiences in the Atlanta airport within the same week involving the person who pushed my wheelchair. The first time I just ignored the event, but the second time I was really unhappy and I called Delta. They immediately corrected the situation, and ask me to give them another chance.



Recently we completed a trip. Normally I book travel to allow for at least two hours for connecting flights in ATL. For this trip I was more interested in price, and paid no attention to the connecting times.



It ended up that we had only 40 minutes in ATL both on our way to our destination as well as returning. I was worried that we would miss our connection on the outbound flight, and since it was an afternoon flight on Christmas Eve, we really wanted to make that connection. As our travel date approached we were able to see that we would land at "A" terminal and depart at "T" terminal, so we would have to move terminals.



I called ATL and explained my situation telling them that I did not have time to wait for the wheelchair pusher to come down the jetway after all the passengers have left the plane. This process normally takes 15 to 20 minutes.



I was assured that they would make sure I made my connection. When we arrived in ATL there was a wheelchair waiting at the door of the plane, and I was permitted to exit the plane before the other passengers. We made our connection with time to spare.



I made no special request for the return flight because it was not critically important to me to catch the connecting flight. There was another flight only one hour later. Nonetheless, I was contacted by email and told that I should expect the same service on the return trip.



We returned last Wednesday. The wheelchair person met me at the door of my plane and pushed me to the connecting flight and right on to the connecting plane. Delta's promise was that I would be "whisked" to my connecting flights, and that was an apt term for what happened.



I would never make it a policy to provide for such a small window of time to connect with a different flight, but I remain exceptionally impressed by the way Delta managed our situation.

What good news and congrats to the airline. If an able bodied passenger can make a connection in that time then a person with a disability should also be able to do it. You got to experience the adaptations necessary to help you function like a person without disabilities which is what it should be. May that happen more and more. I hope you let them know and maybe also wrote a letter to the local paper. Spread the news that this is possible and desirable.

I immediately wrote to the director of the service and her supervisor. I doubt my local paper would print a letter of that nature, but it is a good suggestion which I will attempt. I think it is so important to acknowledge these things when they happen. In my case it was choreographed so well that it was almost poetic.



It is always nice to experience something like this.
