Hi Folks, We bare intending to take a Mobility Scooter abroad.

can anyone tell me if the whole scooter travels in the hold, or does the dry cell battery have to be removed?

My mum travels with hers by air and has had no problems. If the battery is dry cell it can stay on the scooter, although some ground staff have insisted on disconnecting it (but it still stays with the scooter).



Her scooter is fairly small, the seat lays flat on the footplate, the tiller folds down over it and we have a large zip up bag that it goes in after folding it down. We leave it on freewheel and remove the key before allowing the ground staff to load it.



Normally mum drives to the door of the aircraft on it and we pack it up there. She just walks on the plane then. At the other end, depending on the airport, she either gets it delivered back to the door of the aircraft or it is delivered to oversize baggage and she has an airport wheelchair and pusher to take her through immigration to baggage reclaim.



You will need to inform the airline that you are travelling with a scooter and they will want to know weight/dimensions and battery type. We also take a copy of the manufacturers documentation to prove it is a dry cell battery.



The ONLY issue we have ever had is with First Choice who would not allow us to take the seat arms on board with us as they were deemed as a weapon. After a lot of discussion I suggested that they take them off us at the door of the aircraft and then hide them so we couldn't get at them during the flight, which they were then happy to do!



We have only ever done one charter flight with it (the First Choice one mentioned above) but we have taken it on multiple transatlantic scheduled flights on American, Virgin, BMI, United and others.



Hope this helps.

Unfortunately, compliance with disability legislation doesn’t necessarily mean suitability. Slap a handhold on the wall and presto, you’re compliant. Add a ramp, even if it’s on the other side of the building, and you’re compliant. Add one table in an out of the way area to accommodate one wheel chair and you’re compliant. Accessibility is an “add on” rather than an initial design concern. I realize that economies and standardization dictate designing for the “average” but it seems to me that we can do better. (If there are enough people to make “Big and Tall” a going concern, where is that “Short and Chubby” that I need?)

Every city you visit has great "walking" tours, but I would never manage the one or two hours they all seem to take. Does anyone know if these companies also hire out wheelchairs?

Thanks.

Hi Perilous, have you thought about hiring a mobility scooter and then your companion won't have to push you.Here in the UK every shopping centre in town has a mobility hire place and they will hire you one for an hour or day/s. I travel to Spain a lot and I take my wheelchair in the hold of the plane free of charge and then hire a mobility scooter there .The plane would probably let you do the same with your walker , but you must inform them when you book.I too have (rhuematoid) arthritis and have had to do a lot of research and ask a lot of questions since I got it three years ago and still wanted to travel.

Seavale, you are right, that is often the way for already existing buildings and I can sort of understand that. Once in one of our schools the only way to construct wheelchair accessible paths to the playing fields and hall was to build an enormous zig zag ramp, underpinning a few buildings on the way, at a cost of almost a million dollars. And it would have taken her so long to negotiate the path the lesson would have been half over by the time she arrived. This for a school of fewer than 1000 students. We found a motorised scooter did the job instead, at a cost of about $4000

However, each new school being built now complies with disability access requirements.

We were really pleasantly surprised in Barcelona to see that every train station was equipped with a lift for people with disabilities and that public toilets all had foldable rails, lower basins, angled mirrors and lever taps. Most of the buses were wheelchair accessible. Wow!

Goes to show if you design for disability everyone is advantaged, even us short and chubby ones for whom station steps are becoming a difficulty. I always remember an advocate for this principle using curb cuts as an example, helpful for mums with prams, bikes, shopping trolleys AND wheelchairs.

In the UK walkers have no rights in law they can go in wheelchair spaces on buses or trains but if a wheelchair boards they have the right to the space not the walker.

I searched online for information but wasn't able to find much of any use so in the end I bit the bullet and just went. First to Thailand about two years ago and this January to Vietnam. Here's what I found...

My trip to Thailand which, as a nut allergy sufferer, was interesting! 



Firstly, peanuts are ubiquitous in Thai cuisine; if they're not in something, they're on it. Add to that the dangers of cross contamination (nut allergies are extremely rare in South-East Asia so they don't take the same precautions as we in the West do) and you have a recipe for disaster, if you'll pardon the pun! 



Fortunately there are a number of Western fast food chains in Thailand such as McDonald's, Burger King, KFC etc which provided most of my nutrition the whole time I was there. 



Where I went and what I found that was safe to eat: 



Bangkok - Pretty much everything from Starbucks to McDonald's and loads of Sushi places too. You'll have no trouble finding safe food here. 



Ayutthuya - The ancient capital of Thailand is now just a small provincial town. No luck here apart from the 7-11 stores, crisps and drinks. 



Kanchanaburi - Home of the bridge over the River Kwai. One KFC near the bus station about 2 1/2 miles from the actual bridge. That's it. I asked in the official tourist office. 



Koh Samui - Thailand's version of Ibiza was great, Chaweng, the largest town on the island has McDonald's, Burger King and an English owned bar called the Green Bottle (Chaweng Beach Road) which serves English and other European food which is entirely nut free. The owners understand the risk of nut allergy and were able to assure me the food was safe for me to eat. The food is all home cooked as well, it was lovely! 



The next town down the coast is called Lemai and is a bit more upmarket, it too has McDonald's but I'm not sure about anything else as I was only there briefly. 



 It's not a comprehensive list but if you wanted to go to Thailand but were unsure about the food then this may help calm any fears you have. It's an amazing place and well worth a visit!

Vietnam, having had a long Chinese influence, does have a few nuts in it's cuisine, much more so in the North so it's always best to ask what's in a dish. Although everywhere I went the standard of English was good enough to get the message across and most restaurant staff I spoke to understood the concept of nut allergy. As a precaution I took a Lonely Planet phrase book which has a section on allergies and if I had trouble explaining myself I could at least point to the relavent sentence!



Where I went:



Ho Chi Minh City (Saigon) - Huge number of restaurants (including some Western fast food chains like KFC and Lotteria) best one was HHL on Pham Ngu Lao, very friendly staff, perfect English and knowledge of allergies. Food was excellent. Try the Pho (pr. fer) and the Hot Pot!



Nha Trang - The Rusty Nail, a recently opened ex-pat bar on Tran Phu opposite the beach (head South from the centre past the turn off for the old airport) a variety of Vietnamese and Western dishes and obviously English was spoken perfectly. Other places I ate at included Veranda (also on Tran Phu), Lanterns on Nguyen Thien Thuat and the Why Not? bar on Trang Quang Khai. No problems in any of them.



Hoi An - Slightly more expensive town (probably something to do with it's World Heritage status) but again no problems. Most staff understood allergies and were very helpful.



Hué - Getting further North the Chinese influence is much stronger and you'll have to be more carefull here. Although reasonable English is spoken there are a lot more Chinese style dishes and the risk of cross contamination is probably higher. Personally had no problems but it was more difficult to get the message across.



Hanoi - Being the capital city there are restaurants everywhere but be cautious: many don't speak good English, the dreaded peanut is everywhere and there are only a few Western style outlets in the centre to fall back on. Personally, unless you're a particularly intrepid traveller, I'd avoid it!



Hope this helps some of you and If anyone has any info on food in Cambodia, Laos, China and Malaysia I'd love to hear from you!
How did you find travelling on airlines? Some parents on the forum are rather in despair about taking their kids.

Generally I've had no serious problems on airlines, apart from being offered a packet of peanuts which obviously I declined! 



The only real problem with travelling by air I've noticed is that if you try and select special meals in advance you are offered all manner of exotic choices like Kosher, halal, vegan, vegetarian etc. etc. but there never seems to be a nut free option! As a result of this I resort to asking the cabin crew when meals are offered and the general response is 'it's not got nuts in it but we can't guarantee it's 100% nut free' so I make a judgement call: if it's a full English breakfast for example it should be ok, if it's a curry or Chinese meal then I play safe and abstain.



 There are often things included like yoghurts, fruit etc. which should be safe but if you or someone you're travelling with has a life threatening allergy (mine is serious but not quite that bad) then contacting the airline directly in advance and/or taking your own food is probably your best bet.



Hope this is of some help!

Can we pressurise airlines to have an allergy section in their pre-booked flight meals? I am allergic to peppers (capsicum) and have really struggled to get a peppers-free meal on a number of different airlines. (This includes going on the website in advance, getting an e-mail telling me to phone a certain number the day before the flight and STILL getting a salad with peppers in it. Thankfully I could see this and therefore didn't open it - the smell of peppers makes me very sick!!)

Also, it would be really helpful if the cabin crew had a list of all the ingredients in the meals even if that can't be supplied to individual passengers.

I have posted questions about this on various web sites, as soon as I get any useful information I will post it on here and if anyone else has any information on this please feel free to post it!

Thanks a lot - that would be very helpful. It is quite hard to be on a long journey and only to be able to eat bread and cheese! Even stewards and stewardesses just say "you should have asked in advance", which I did!!

I can't see why they don't have a list of all ingredients in meals, just as there is on the side of the yoghurt pot!!

Hi,



As an airline employee- one who works on the airplane-- let me share with you a few issues make this "nut-free" issue a challenge..



First, most airlines now use third-party catering companies for the entire on-board catering process-- that is everything from ice, to drinks, to food and all the set-up.. One of the issues that airlines have to account for is menu consistency and availability across their system.. That is insuring that the same meals (or regional variances of them) can be prepared and provisioned at each and every one of the various cities that the airline may service-- and for global carriers that's a lot of cities where similar meals must be available.. 



That is why you may see somewhat the same meal selection across many different cities of the same airline.



The next issue-- and arguably the most difficult one-- is that it's very hard to make a truly guaranteed nut-free meal when the production facility, food storage areas, food preparation areas, food packaging/assembly areas and all equipment for such are all shared-use and do come into contact with nut products at various point in their use. 



Quite simply, no matter how much cleaning and sterilizing you do, you just cannot truly guarantee a nut-free product.. therefore, catering companies and the airlines are reluctant to take the risk- and liability- of producing and labeling a meal as "nut-free" when in reality it may be been inadvertently cross-contaminated at some point in the process.

 

Some catering companies do provide airlines a list of the ingredients to be used in their selections meals once the meal plan is established.. it looks very similarly to how you would see them on pre-packaged products sold at retail stores- but airlines don't regularly publish this information- in part because there's been little to no demand by the passengers for it- and there is no regulation or requirement by any governing body that such be provided... but it is known to the airline when they set their meal order with the caterer.



As to the concept of a "xxx-free" seating zone.. That's something that gets suggested to the airlines literally all the time.. However, you may or may not be surprised to hear about just how many different things get suggested as being necessary exclusion zones for health related issues.. It ranges from perfume-free, dust-free, dander-free, nut-free to fragrance-free and a few more.. The problem is that it's just not realistic that the airline can sub-divide a cabin for each of the different allergy needs in such a manner *and* guarantee that there won't be any of the offending material in that zone carried by another passenger.



Most airlines now don't directly serve nuts on board (in the Economy cabin).. however beyond that, there is just no practical or reliable way for the airline to *guarantee* that the flight is truly nut-free-- be that from the airlines catering or other passengers who may bring nut-materials on board themselves.



This isn't meant to diminish the importance of the issue-- rather to highlight the realities involved in the process and the operational challenges that would have to be addressed.



Travel Safe,

Thanks, GOPBI. That is very helpful.

Hi,



Pressing the cabin staff isn't going to help you if that information wasn't boarded at the origin point.. quite simply, they can't give you something that wasn't provided on the ground.



In most cases, the crew only gets a listing of all offerings and the "plating" instructions-- that is what components go with what meals and how it's supposed to be put on the plates or trays-- and not what's specifically in them by ingredient or even nutritional values. This is why when you ask "what's in the salad?" they have to sneak a peek.. the information we get as crew only lists it as "dinner salad"..



My best suggestion is to ask the airline before departure if they can provide you with this information.. Catering choices are made months in advance so it's a reasonable expectation that a menu listing or basic ingredient listing is available..

I am also allergic to capsicum and avoid peppers. I have never even thought to ask if my meal contained peppers. In all the years of flying I have done I have never had a meal with peppers. I have, on one or two occasions, had the option of selecting a Mexican-style meal. I avoid that and take the other alternative.

Peppers are never pureed. They are always diced and it is always possible to see them in your food. While it takes a bit of time to remove them, it is not like you have any other important task to complete while flying on a plane.

text:
I travel with my scooter all of the time when flying domestically in the US. I have not gone through initial TSA screening at LAX, but I did fly into this airport last summer with my scooter.



I do not know if your mother will have to go through security again. I terminated my flight at LAX so I just left the airport.



Typically however, the airline crew will deliver your mother's scooter to the door of the plane. The airport is constructed so that a disabled passenger has equal access to everything an able-bodied person. I have never been in an airport in the US that did not place disabled people at the front of the security line. Usually they will have one line where they want you to go and you will be directed. If no one tells you which line to use or invites you to move to the front of the line, just ask the person directing TSA traffic where she should go.



I cannot imagine that you will not automatically be directed to the front of one designated line; however, since you had a poor experience in LAX several years ago I would be prepared to explain to the TSA agent that the scooter cannot be manouvered through the regular line and you need to move to the front of the line.

thread_title: LAX AA Terminal 4 Transit With Scooter Advice Please
text: I have traveled at LAX with my scooter several times, both Int. and Dom. I have always landed in Tom Bradley Terminal if it was Int. If they are traveling AA through to LAS they should not have to deal with their baggage, that should be transfered by AA on through even if they have to change planes. I would imagine that they will only be responsible for any carry-on's they may have and go from Bradley to the dom. terminal. AA should give you more information than they have. Call them again and explain to them again that there will be a scooter traveling and that your parents are elderly and require assistance from one terminal to another. This has been my experience with one exception and that was landing in Paris De Gualle Airport. I was supposed to have an assistant to take me from one terminal to another as it was a time issue but no one showed up. That airport is HUGE and we had to take shuttles from one side of the airport to the complete opposite side. Well, we ended up missing our flight and had to stay overnight in a terrible hotel...nightmare. LAX is much different. The terminals are all within scooter distance and walking should not be a problem for someone assisting her. Make sure that just before you land to remind the Flight Attendant that you have a scdooter and it must be brought to the entrance of the plane AND you will need an assistant to guide you to your next bording platform (even if it is just one bording area over) and insist on having some help. They have plenty of people employed just for this service, but unless you insist they are sometimes lazy and will not do their job. This is especially true since you are flying AA from start to finish. Good luck, and keep a cane with you, if for no other reason than to prod people if you don't get the service you paid for.

text:
I can't see that you have nominated a particular place, which makes helping you more dificult. However, I can give some guidelines.



# Google something like <<accessible accommodation in XXXX>> That magic word accessible actually works for many places and may be all you need.

# Luckily you do not need wide rooms or wheel in bathrooms, but you do need elevators. Make sure any hotel has elevators.

# You could look into scooter hire in the town you choose. Again <<disabled scooter hire>> or similar will find what you need.

# If you are looking at museums etc, look on their site for <<disabled access>> <<wheelchair access>> and of course <<disabled parking>> or <<accessible parking>>

Note: Some hotels think that access to the foyer means they are accessible. Check all the way up to and into the room. Even then they may have 3 stairs at the entrance. The mind boggles.

Of course you will find sites that do not match what you are looking for, but you will find many that do. It is learning the language that relates to disability that opens the doors.

Good luck

Lynn

thread_title: Fully accessible motel room in Whakatane
text:
Quite by chance we were given an accessible room in the Tuscany Villas motel at Whakatane in New Zealand. It was lovely to see that this motel had two such rooms available. As it is part of a chain of hotels it is possible that others also have such rooms.

The room was set up with a ramp in from ground level (slight sliding door lip) a king sized bed with space enough for transfers and a door connecting it to the next room, also an accessible one. The bathroom door opened right back to allow entry and was extra wide. There was a wheel in shower and a shower seat and rails attached to the wall. Light switches were accessible. The basin extended over the top of the counter but was not really something you could roll under. There was one rail on the toilet wall to assist transfers.

The place was also equipped with a mini kitchen but a great deal of that was not accessible, such as high shelves for mugs and glasses. There was a table and two chairs and an easy chair.

All in all, a good effort and pleasing to see.

The town itself also has ramps for access along the waterfront wharf to restaurants and boats. Not sure about access to the boats themselves though.

I'm hoping to get some advice or suggestions. 



I am traveling with my son on Air Canada to LHR and I'm a little worried about pre-boarding. 



I'm hoping to pre-board with him as to get him settled before a long flight. Short version, he's has been diagnosed with a TBI (cleared to fly years ago). Between the hour of the flight (11pm) and the fact that he's going to be excited, I'm hoping to get on before the rest of the plane as to settle him in his seat without people bumping into him. 



I'd also like to be able to switch seats to a bulk-head seat as to give him a bit more room to move to the washroom and such. Our TA was not able to book those seats for us and told us that we had to try at check in. 



Please let me know if anyone has had any problems with AC. Positive stories are much appriciated as well.



Oh I should mention we do have a letter from his doctor. 



Thanks!

Hi,



Here's my suggestions as someone whose been a Gate Agent early early on in my career..



Many airlines have eliminated the formal "pre-boarding" policy allowing families and such early access.. and many now use a formal two-tier system-- as Air Canada does-- that lets their First Class/Business Class and top tier mileage members board first or at any time in the process.. followed by economy class- usually by rows or zones.. 



Here's where I suspect that Air Canada would be willing to bump you to the front of the line.. I can't see any real reason why you couldn't be allowed to board at the beginning of the Economy cabin.



My suggestion is to arrive at the gate *early*.. when the first agent(s) arrive-- don't ask once boarding starts, it's too hectic at that point.. Once you get to the gate introduce yourself to the lead agent (if there is a differentiation in rank) and explain your situation *briefly* and state your request.. No need for the letter at that point unless they ask for it.



I'd recommend that you politely *ask* if you can board at the beginning of the Economy cabin or whenever is best.. I say to ask in this manner for a reason... This way you're not seen as "pushy" or "demanding" (some people do that stuff) and the request you've asked for is one that should be reasonable to accommodate and fits the situation... They may surprise you and allow even earlier, but see what they say.



If they say yes, then stand on the side of the podium-- but nearby so that they see and remember you, but that you're not blocking the podium.. This way once it's time for you to pre-board it's not a big "show" that someone is being allowed early access.. you'd be surprised how funny people get when they perceive that others are getting "special" treatment.



As far as bulkhead seating.. That's going to be harder since these seats are seen as premium seats and will most likely already assigned to AC's high status fliers, so I wouldn't be expecting them... But.. I'd ask about them at the check-in counter when you first arrive at the airport.. If they're already assigned at that time, then you're pretty much out of luck.. If there are some left over (remember that you're going to need two seats side by side) at check-in then *ask* the check-in agent if you can be assigned them or if not, can they list you for these seats and see if they can be assigned at the gate.



As a side note, if you do ask about or try to get bulkhead seats, be sure that you disclose or ask about your sons condition as some of the bulkhead seats that face exits are restricted seats and have minimum age (usually 15 or more years old) and physical requirements that must be made met.



Best of Luck.

Taking a Mobility scooter on a plane? Range for Orlando?
text:
Hi,



Virgin will handle this, as most all airlines do pretty much like this:



They would allow you to use your own scooter--for your own mobility use-- all the way to the plane-side departure gate.. The scooter will be screened at the security check-point as all your hand-carry will be.. Once at the departure gate, you would be "transferred" to a manual push-style wheelchair (with a pusher) and your scooter would then be tagged by the gate staff and be taken downstairs to the ramp or aircraft level and loaded into the cargo hold.. 



You may be asked by the gate staff how to disconnect the batteries (if applicable) and how to operate it, but most scooters are rather simple operation devices. 



One piece of advice, please do NOT leave anything on or attached to the scooter that can easily "fall off" or isn't properly or permanently attached to the scooter itself.. The scooter will remain right-side up while in the cargo hold (it's not laid on it's side), but I have seen things like special custom seat cushions become separated and lost in transit..



You would be escorted- or pushed- in the wheelchair from the waiting gate right up to the aircraft door itself. If you need assistance from the aircraft threshold (door) either a ground agent will assist you further to your specific seat, or the airline will transfer you to a specially-design "aisle chair" which is nothing more than a regular push wheelchair, but very narrow to fit between aircraft aisles. They have to use that special chair since normal wheelchairs can't/don't fit down aircraft aisles..



Upon arrival in MCO, your own scooter would be brought up from the cargo hold for you to either a) the door-side at the aircraft, or b) just at the end of the passenger loading bridge.. If, for some operational or security reason it cannot be returned to you at either of these two common points, you'd be taken by a manual push wheelchair to the point where you own scooter is returned to you.



Obviously, on the return from MCO back to the UK, the process will be substantially the same.



In the US, there is a series of Federal Laws, known as the Air Carrier Access Act (ACAA), which defines what types of assistance, methodology and the like an airline *must* provide to legitimately mobility impaired passengers to assist them in their travels. These regulations also apply to non-US carriers (like Virgin) when arriving into *or* departing from a US airport.. Do know that ACAA explicitly prohibits any airline imposed charges for the transport of any legitimate mobility use device when such device is being actively used by the passenger for his/her own mobility use.



I will tell you that it is very, very common for airline staff to handle these scooters and you will find that the whole process is rather well defined and comprehensive.



Travel Safe,

I have just completed my 8th plane trip in the past 30 days. I try to use the restroom in the terminal when we have a lay-over. In each of those 8 experiences I did not find a handicapped stall in any airport restroom that was vacant. None of them were occupied for a short period of time. It seems as if the traveling public has converted the handicapped stalls to their own private dressing rooms. I see suitcases open. In one case a mother called her daughter (who was behind me in the line) to come to the stall so she could change her clothing after Mom already changed her clothing.



I appreciate that the larger stall is more convenient if you are changing your clothing, but when the only occupied stalls are those for disabled guests, it seems a bit abusive to convert them to dressing rooms.



Several times when I had enough time I waited until the disabled stall was vacant. Five of my trips had very brief layovers and there was no time to wait. I do not object to waiting in a general restroom line until a restroom is available, but I do not think I should be forced to wait in a line to use the facility that was constructed to meet my needs.



Thoughts?

Hi,



Unfortunately, unlike parking stalls that have explicit regulations for their use, lavs generally don't have the same protections or limitations/restrictions.. I've only once seen a special "restricted for handicapped use only" sign, and that was in the Narita airport.



I do notice that I see more "family" bathrooms so that kids who need to be changed and the like have somewhere to go, that doesn't infringe on the handicapped stall use..



I also happen to make an announcement on the aircraft that there is handicapped accessible lavatory (and I say where it is), and I also mention to "please kindly give preference to those needing this specific lavatory."



Do I use them? Yes, I do.. However, I am also conscious that those who have a disability or other have other legitimate needs for one has preferential priority over waiting people-- like myself-- who may use them, but after legitimate needs people.. If I do use one, I try to be as brief as possible, because I am aware that as Murphy's Law is-- the minute I get inside, a person with a disability shows up.



If there was a sign specifically stating they were for disabled use *only* then, I'd comply accordingly. I have a tendency to think that so long as people use some level of courtesy that we can manage this without the need for explicit legislation to the contrary... But I also acknowledge that I am not handicapped myself, so I can't really say that I can 'experience' it from that perspective, but try to be as accommodating as possible.

I can tell you that from an employee's perspective there can be a whole host of reasons.. 



Example: My airline allows me to use a jump-seat-- those are the small folding seats that your FA's sit on during taxi, take-off and landings-- when there isn't a regular passenger/cabin seat on the aircraft.. In selected cases, I *must* be in uniform to use these seats.. 



In other cases, some other airlines mandate that employees *don't* wear their uniforms when pass-riding.. Each airline has their own rules and can be different as the travel case may be.. 



So, there can be a very valid reason that I (or another employee) will need to change clothes before travel... Again, this isn't the *norm* per se, for most people, but just highlights that there are reasons out there for needing to do so.



Also, most airlines don't allow their own employees to use their lounges to do so-- after all, it's for their paid passenger members and not as an employee changing room.. and I agree with that.... Some carriers are really extreme in this rule and don't even allow their employees to become members, even if they were to buy a regular paid membership.



Again, this isn't to make an excuse for able bodied persons from using and occupying handicapped stalls for changing or even using it for-- shall we say more 'traditional' bathroom functions-- but to recognize that there may be very valid reasons for needing a place to change..



I will tell you that within my own airline and the unions that represents our FA's and Pilot groups, they do remind the general membership to be aware of and in compliance with any special restrictions for bathroom use when in passenger terminals and even on our aircraft itself.. and if appropriate to do, to yield the facility to others behind you of demonstrated need.



In the end, I don't think that they should be an able-bodied persons *first* choice, and if other stalls are open, they (handicapped) stalls should be left open, nor do I believe that they should be for things like, as you note- hiding from BF'/GF's/DP's, or for using a cell phone (I don't make *or* receive calls from people in or on the toilet).



In the end, I agree 100% with your statement of "... If you have the ability to use a regular stall I think it is preferable to do so rather than require a disabled person to wait for you." and I think that if an able-bodied person were to spend one full day in a wheel chair-- and experience it from that perspective-- you'd have a very different appreciation for these stalls and what they mean to you. 



Travel Safe,

thread_title: If you wish to rent a portable oxygen concentrator...
text:
I rented, paid for, and was assured, a particular oxygen machine and batteries from Oxygen to Go two months before a planned trip. When I called to re-confirm the order a week before I left, they'd already rented the unit they promised me to someone else, saying my card would not go through. After telling me they no longer had the machine I’d paid for, they stated that they’d tried to contact me by phone and email. I received neither, and since I’m disabled, I am home all the time, so I would have gotten at least one of the messages they claimed to have left. They would have realized that the only problem with my card was a reversed number in the expiration date, if they'd only contacted me.

The unit they sent me was a larger, heavier machine, which they would have obviously not even sent if I had not called them to re-confirm, put out less oxygen, and was harder for me to handle, and whose batteries did not last as long. In addition, they also sent me a defective battery. I had to get up in the middle of the night to change out batteries in the charger just so I'd have all fresh ones the next morning. I felt like I was charging and recharging batteries all the time, so I would not run out of oxygen. My vacation was ruined, as I was unable to go to places I'd planned, as I was afraid my batteries would run out before I returned. And, as anyone who has cruised is aware, there are only two plug in’s in the cabin, and since I was constantly having to use the charger, I was only left with me one plug to use with my continuous flow oxygen concentrator at night, and for everything else I needed to plug in. Needless to say, the plug in’s stayed hot.

I called the only contact number on their equipment tag which put me in touch with a man in a far away state who had no idea what was going on and who said there was no way he could get another battery to me, and could not help me. I was stuck, and just prayed I wouldn’t lose any more batteries to malfunction.

Oxygen to go has not offered to refund any of the money I paid them to rent the original machine I’d reserved from them, even though they clearly were in the wrong. They have not bothered to contact me regarding this at all. Even though they are supposed to assist people with disabilities, I would never depend on them again for any reason. Better beware before doing business with these people.

thread_title: Dad with dementia wants to travel
text:
Dementia can be a very slow as it progresses. We traveled with my husband's mother for as long as she could remember who we were, and as long as she wanted to travel. My greatest worry would be if an Alzheimers patient wandered away in a strange location. My mother-in-law was in a wheel chair so we did not have to worry about her taking walks alone and becoming lost.



Certainly traveling with a person who is easily disoriented can be a challenge, but I would do as much as you possibly can while your father can still travel. You may not be making many memories for him, but you will make them for yourself.



We treasure all of our memories with my mother-in-law, especially those e made after we knew that her memory and knowledge was diminishing.



Just try to allow plenty of time and do things in a relaxed and casual manner. Dementia is exacerbated when people are rushed and forced to do things they do not understand. Provide plenty of breaks, and eat three proper meals each day. Do not cram lots of things into one day. Just to be safe, I would put a tag around his neck with his name and the name and telephone number of your hotel. If he does wander away someone can help him return to you.

text:
Hi,



Itchy, Setati raises an excellent point, you do have some very defined rights-- which you may invoke at your sole discretion when traveling by *air*, called the Air Carrier Access Act or ACAA for short.



I've written a short high level summation of it here:

http://www.tripadvisor.com/ShowTopic-g1-i12336-k3828194-As_Information_Your_rights_under_ACAA-Traveling_With_Disabilities.html



I happen to be one of my carriers designated CRO's for ACAA issues so I'm pretty well versed on what it says, and what it doesn't say... 



I will say that one commonly held miss-belief is that ACAA supersedes airline or regulatory safety or security policy-- it does not... It speaks to accommodations that carriers and airports must make available to passengers *but* while still remaining within existing security and safety framework.



Sometimes, it's a juggling act, but in the end, in the vast majority of cases it can be done.. The other thing is that all newer aircraft are much more 'friendly' to those with special needs.. be that movable arm rests, larger bathrooms, etc..



I'll agree that for the most part you need to ask for these accommodations, this is in part for several reasons.. First, a carrier may not assume that a persons needs or wants such accommodations and they cannot (for the most part) mandate you to use them.. Also, not everyone is as well versed in the ACAA rules and lastly, it can be a sensitive or uncomfortable issue when speaking to someone about their needs... I know that when I do so, I exercise a large degree of discretion to insure that my conversations are private- to the extent possible- and that they are as sensitive as possible.



I find that it's more on the airport side where difficulties exist.. but I understand that some of this is infrastructure based roadblocks as most of the US airports are well over 30+ years old and built in a time when ACAA or the notion of disabled travelers wasn't nearly as prominent as today.



Travel Safe,

I'd like to share my experience traveling with parent w/dementia. It shows we can still have a sense of humour when dealing with a difficult situation.

This is an excerpt from a travel blog I posted last year. My father passed away in April, and travels now, free of mental and physical encumbrances.



"Took my dad (87/alzheimer's) and sister's FIL (Grandpa John,90, tiny, alert and very grumpy!!) to the airport (gate pass for me, rev tkts for them) [I am an airline spouse--added note]



TSA!!! 

Last minute detail--Grandpa John has pacemaker!! Surprise! New to me!

 

My dad kept saying he'd "never done this before"--shoes, xray etc--of course, he forgot)

John has something in every pocket, 4 shirts a jacket and cap. 

TSA guy: do you have anything else in your pockets? Yep. Yep. Ditto, ditto, wink wink (I think he recognized me) 

Final tally in 2 bins plus carry-on duffle: 3 metal writing instruments, one checkbook, one address book, one wallet and one billfold, one wool shirt, two shoes and a cap, one rollaboard and tote bag. And a handful of loose change! I think he left 20# on the conveyor belt. 

Over to hand screening...

Meantime, Dad is still muttering about all the "new" system, why do I take off my shoes, getting cantankerous, but I already had him put his cap and jacket in his carry-on (John wasn't listening, of course)

John's telling the TSA guy to watch his billfold and Dad's getting belligerent and...we made it through without being arrested for something...manslaughter came to mind--NO--Just kidding!!!



Sat one down to get "recombobulated" while the other watched. Then had John sit down and get dressed--had to put the wallet in the inside pocket of shirt 3 and make sure it was buttoned--looked like a hamster getting out of his chest!! Then each pen went in each pocket, then the checkbook, address book and billfold and change. I think it took 20+ minutes and there was no one in front of them when we started!!

I apologized to everyone behind us and wished them a Merry Christmas! Everyone was smiling--talk about Holiday Spirit!"



So, that's my story in a nutshell--it's much longer when I verbalize it with people who know them. And a bit more fun to tell again. 

Patience and preparation and more patience...Good luck, bon voyage!

I have depended on a wheelchair for airport transfers for a decade. I use a large mobility scooter at home, but it is too large to use when traveling. Recently I purchased a more portable scooter.



It is a small scooter that comes apart into three sections so it fits in the trunk of our Chrysler Crossfire along with a week's worth of luggage.



I have been using it as we have been flying this summer. I check my checked luggage and then go to the TSA disabled line. Since I never travel without my husband he can keep track of carry-on luggage and I do not miss the services of a person pushing my wheelchair.



I take the scooter to the plane and it is gate checked after we board. At almost every step of our air travel this summer the gate check process has not been without problems.



In Atlanta the scooter was left at the jetway. When the jetway rolled away from the plane my husband saw the scooter still sitting there. We contacted the flight attendant and she stopped the plane and they loaded the scooter.



Flying into Oakland earlier this week, we waited for nearly an hour for the scooter to be delivered. Ultimately the co-pilot had to go and check. He found the baggage handlers carrying my little scooter along with a huge scooter. I leave my key in the scooter and it is easy to drive. The other scooter, however, did not have a key, and it was not in free-wheel mode. The baggage handlers were attempting to manhandle it up the stairs. This did not work. The co-pilot explained how to put the chair in free-wheel mode, but it still took them another 30 minutes to deliver the scooters. 



I knew when we got the baggage claim our two suitcases would be rolling around all alone. I was wrong. The baggage handlers had spent all that time dealing with our scooters, and had not unloaded any luggage. The entire plane load of people were waiting.



The other lady with the large scooter complained that her scooter had been damaged on her trip. The headlight had been broken and the steering mechanism also damaged.



So far, I am still feeling that I have more positive experiences using my own scooter than I have negative experiences, but I would appreciate hearing from others who use a scooter for airport transfers.



I wonder if there are things we could do to increase the reliability of the people who manage the scooter once it is gate checked.

First of all I am fascinated by the fact that your scooter comes apart in three pieces and stores in the trunk of your Crossfire! Along with luggage! My fold-up wheelchair took the backseat or trunk - but I am particularly curious about the weights of the pieces individually and whether or not you are able to lift or if it requires your husband to do so. 

I do agree with your observations regarding the air-travel and confusion - although I have been in and out of wheelchairs for years, just recently required one again and it took a beating through handling. 

I can only imagine the gasp of seeing your chair setting on the tarmac as your plane rolled away! 

My experience with a chair was that the handlers could not manage to stow it without causing paint damage, minimal, but it was a brand new chair (each leg of our trip resulted in chips/scratches and we watched it be tossed into the hold of the plane like a bit of flotsam - and the folding and removal of foot rests had to be explained and done by us. The foot rests had to be stowed in the overhead with our carry on luggage. My husband certainly had his hands full, but I did gratefully accept the assistance of the persons on each end of flights to get us up the ramp and into the terminal. 

We have found each airport to handle things like security and loading a bit differently, some of them far more efficient and respectful than others. I do greatly prefer having my own chair rather than relying on the ones that the carriers have available - but I confess the idea of a power scooter is highly appealing to my independent nature. 

I completely agree that some form of education might be a good idea for those who are required to handle these items. Unfortunately the handling of belongings has long been a sore spot with the public in general, improvements have been made - but far from fault free. I also think that the new regulations are causing some changes for the better, but as with most things it will take time for the adjustments to 'sink in'. 

Thank you for this report - it is most helpful.

I am a Brit, and notice the two people who posed here are American, but I may be able to say something helpful.



My wife has arthritis and we have both a wheelchair and a scooter. We only take the wheelchair abroad but we have seen several Brits take smaller scooters without any problem. We usually pick a resort where we can hire one rather than take our own.

Mobility scooters in Britain fall into two categories, pavement (sidewalk) models, and road models. The road ones are bigger and heavier and usually don't come to pieces easily. The pavement ones, like ours, usually come to bits in moments without tools and stow easily in a car. The heaviest part of ours, the motor section, weighs about 45 pounds and a fit man can lift it off the ground easily. A strong woman could too.I'm sure America must have similar scooters, and I would think it should be easy to find one that comes apart quickly and easily.



I have seen wheelchairs come off planes with damage to them, but not often.We have never had to remove the footrests from ours and take them as overhead luggage, this seems odd. Like Busy though I have seen handlers carrying a scooter because they had no idea how to put the thing on freewheel, I had to tell them to look for the lever. Maybe they should get some training in this as more and more disabled people are travelling on planes, certainly in Europe anyway.



Different airports seem to differ greatly in how they handle disabled people too. Some have special queues and are very helpful, others seem to have no idea or simply not to care. They still have a long way to go.

As to scooters that come apart, my husband has a Lexis-Light. It comes apart into three pieces. They heaviest piece is 26 pounds. The total weight of the scooter is only 54 pounds. 



It is the lightest travel scooter on the market. It is manufactured in Israel. The only US Distributor is Planet Mobility in Michigan. You can find them on the internet.



The only drawback of this scooter is that it is not super powerful. You can only use it on pavement and it does not have a lot of power to get up steep hills. But that is the tradeoff for the light weight and travel convenience.



We can easily take it apart and fit it into pretty much any car's trunk.

We have just completed a five week trip around the US, involving six flights. My scooter looks almost as good as it did when I first checked it.



Along the way I learned to (1) Take a photo of the scooter so I can establish what it looked like before being handled by luggage staff (2) Make sure that I have my ID and address on every part of the scooter (3) Include brief instructions on how to operate scooter and place in free-wheel mode (4) Make sure I get gate-checked tag from gate agent before it is time to board. (5) Confirm that the scooter is not still sitting in the jet way when it is pulled away from the plane. (6) Do not leave the plane until scooter is delivered. The FA and pilots cannot leave the plane so long as passengers remain on it. If I stay on the place someone is motivated to eventually find my scooter, and pilots seem more effective with the ground crew than one passenger.



I loved traveling with the scooter. It made my airport experience something all together different. I could shop, buy food and beverages, browse books and magazines and I did not have to depend upon any other person to do any of those things. I also think that in addition to saving money renting scooters at my destinations, I will also save the money I tipped to the person who pushed my wheelchair. I just wished I had made this decision two or three years ago.

Hi,



I'll add from my years as a baggage handler early in my airline career the issues that ground staff encounter with scooters..



In many cases it boils down to a facility issue.. Many scooters are not of the size, shape or weight to be safely taken down the jet-bridge stairs-- regardless of the number of people who are helping.. A simple baby stroller is one thing, but scooters are generally a whole different matter.. 



In most cases, this means that at least one person off the "crew" will have to take the scooter to the nearest elevator that has both passenger/concourse and ramp level accesses.. Again, a time issue as there are not that many elevators with both levels of access-- for obvious security issues...



Also, how the scooter was loaded by the previous station plays a part in how quick we can get it out.. Some stations put scooters in first (a big no-no) and then they get buried with bags.. so the crew can't get to it until the very end.. In other cases, due the size of the cargo door (notoriously on B737's) some scooters simply can't fit into the cargo compartment right-side-up-- this means you have to either tilt or lay the scooter on its' side to clear the door.. Again, a time element..



In the case of a scooter with old style wet-cell batteries there are hazardous materials forms that may require a "check-off" by a qualified agent to insure that the scooter and batteries are being transported safely.



Lastly, some scooter are easy to maneuver around-- others require a masters degree in mechanical engineering to figure out-- there is no uniform standard of scooter operation.



Again, while all this is going on there is the pressure to maintain an on-time departure for the aircraft's next flight..



To correct one small matter-- within the US, there is NO requirement in place for *pilots* to remain on the aircraft while passengers are on-board-- there IS however a provision that a certain number of Flight Attendants or other properly qualified personnel remain on-board while passengers are present.

 

Travel Safe,

I appreciate the time you took to add your perspective to our scooter issues. We also visited with a baggage handler about this issue after a one hour delay with the scooter.



His complaint, and a valid one, was that they had received no training in handling scooters. While I agree that a few scooters are complicated, I tried out the six leading brands before purchasing, and all of those "portables" operated in the same way.



Nonetheless, I have a small operating instruction card on my scooter. I also leave the key in the ignition so baggage handlers can drive it if they need to get to an elevator. Finally, we print instructions on how to put the scooter into free-wheel position. This seemed to be the issue which caused the most difficulty for the baggage handlers on our last trip. 



I also have instructions explaining how to collapse the steering mechanism down onto the floor of the scooter. That is all I have to do to put it in the trunk of any standard automobile, and I hope it is sufficient to place it into the luggage compartment of a plane. I do not have instructions to completely take the scooter apart. I worry that if it is taken apart I will never see all of its parts again.



I appreciate the efforts that airline personnel make to assist my disability. While there may be no rule requiring a pilot to remain on the plane until passengers have left, I have never been left on the plane by a pilot. On several occasions I have had a pilot go get a wheelchair and push me to my next gate or to the luggage carousel, but none of them have left me.

I flew from Manchester UK TO Palma Majorca this July

thread_title: As Information: Your rights under ACAA
text:
Hi,



Just thought I'd let people know, who may not be familiar with what exactly your rights and responsibilities under the Air Carrier Access Act (ACAA) which applies to all US carriers operating anywhere in the world, as well as (with some exceptions) to foreign carriers when operating to/from the US.



DOT ACAA:

http://www.dotcr.ost.dot.gov/asp/airacc.asp



There is also an excellent "Q&A" from the DOT as well:

http://airconsumer.ost.dot.gov/rules/FAQ_5_13_09.pdf



Take a moment to read thru the guide and the Q&A's as they are very well written and easy to understand...



*****************

A few points that I'd stress to those who may need/want to avail of one or more of these rights:



a) you need not disclose the nature of your disability, nor do you need to have documentation of such,



b) an airline may not force you, nor automatically make you an ACAA-subjected passenger against your wishes. You may voluntarily elect not to use one or more of these regulations.



c) you need NOT pay any additional sums to the airline or airport operator, to avail of any of these specifically outlined rights.



d) an airline must have and make available to you (by phone or in person) within a reasonable period of time after your initial request, a specially trained and certified complaints resolution officer (CRO) available to you. 



Also... a few things the airline is generally >>not<< required to do:



a) airlines may not be required to force, displace or mandate other passengers yield their assigned seats to accommodate any ACAA needs passenger.. There can be seats which have special features that are designed for the ACAA-needs passenger and they would have first priority to these seats.



b) airlines are not required to physically move or assist with the dispensing of any medication or application of medical devices.. Common examples are the administering of IV medications or the use of any lavatory functions.



c) airlines are generally not required to provide any form of medical assistance while on the aircraft.



d) airlines may deny travel to any service animal *so long as* such denial is based on a demonstrative violation of an applicable US or foreign safety regualtion and/or any applicable State/Federal or foreign animal health (quarantine) regulations.



Airlines overall have become much more user-friendly in terms of the travel needs of those with special needs, but it always helps to know what the specific regulations are... or are not... to make your trip less stressful and easier on you.



Travel Safe,

text:
Hi,



I've been asked, via PM, for some further explanation on items "a", the disclosure of your condition, and item "d", the CRO.. So, I'll post that here..



Item "A"... The ACAA doesn't require you to disclose to the airline nor any other party the specific nature to/of your disability.. In some cases, the airline may *ask* your condition so that they can be prepared and to be able to provide the necessary and proper services and/or resources on-board. You are not under any obligation to answer.. If you do disclose, any information provided must be treated by the airline as confidential passenger information to the same extent- but no more or less than all other general passenger manifest information.. Do know that the airline can-- within limits-- deny you travel if they can demonstrate that your travel would pose a demonstrative risk to the safe, efficient and/or inimicable operation of the flight.. Carriers don't go down this road lightly--as it's seen as a 'last resort' decision.. but can or will do so, if there is a demonstrative risk..



Item "D"... The CRO, or Complaints Resolution Officer/Official.. This is a formally trained and certified person.. The training and certification must be on file with the DOT.. S/he is usually a direct employee of the airline, but doesn't have to be by statute.. The airline must make one available to you, but that doesn't have to be face-to-face.. it can be via phone if that is the most practicable and time efficient means to do so.



In some smaller stations, the airlines' CRO may not be in that airport itself, but may be at their head office or another hub city.. However, regardless of location, one must be made available to you within a reasonable time period.. The airline need not delay a flight to make one available to you, nor may they willfully withhold one before flight time. 



The CRO is specially trained to know the specifics of the ACAA.. what the rules are, what they are not and what the role and responsibility is of each party.. They are also charged with the duty to properly record any complaints lodged and provide the complainant with the required documentation of his/her compliant against the carrier.. If the complaint involves items not carrier controlled, they are to direct the traveler to the CRO for the airport or other provider.. 



ACAA does have some very specific rules about how complaints must be handled.. ACAA does also grant the CRO some additional authority in some regards to resolve issues between the passenger and the airline.. However, the CRO does not, and cannot override, supersede or contravene any security, safety or regulatory rules that may exist.. The best way of viewing this person is that they are an ACAA-eligible passengers' *advocate* in the matter.



Travel Safe,

thread_title: As Information: Your rights under ACAA
text:
Hi,



I've been asked for some information about this topic-- ACAA-- in relation to being overseas.. Let me post this for the larger community..



Q: Does the ACAA rules apply overseas?



A: Yes and no.. The ACAA rules DO apply to ALL US based airlines no matter where the flight originates OR departs.. So, if you are flying a US carrier FROM an overseas location, you still have all the same ACAA rights as you would if you were traveling domestically within the US.



The ACAA rules do NOT apply to non-US carriers when the flight originates from OUTSIDE of the US.. They DO apply to foreign carriers when the flight originates INSIDE the US. The ACAA rules also do NOT apply to non-US airports. 



Simply the US Department of Transportation (DOT) does not have jurisdictional authority over non-US carriers when flying from overseas points nor do they have any overt authority over non-US airports.



Q: If I think my rights were not met overseas who I do complain to or file a complaint?



A: If the issue is with a foreign AIRPORT, you will need to file the report with the actual airport operator- or the national transportation agency that manages the airports.. In some cases overseas, the airport is run as a private business.

 

If the issue is with a foreign AIRLINE *and* the issue stems from an action or incident that occurred overseas, you need to file the complaint with either the airline directly and/or the national transportation agency in the country of departure.



If the issue is with a US airline and it occurred outside of the US, then you would file the complaint with either the airline and/or the DOT. In this case, because it is a US carrier, you would have full ACAA protections regardless of the fact you started overseas.



Q: Can I get compensation for any failures to meet ACAA rules?



A: The ACAA does not formally establish a passengers automatic right to any pre-set level of financial compensation for failures to meet any of the prescribed provisions. Unlike the rules in place for denied boarding and the like, there is no provision for automatic cash/credit compensatory payment to a passenger for any failure of the ACAA- be that unintentional or otherwise.



However, the DOT as the governing agency has the authority to impose administrative fines or sanctions for non-compliance, and if warranted, the US Department of Justice may also intervene if the matter moves into a criminal matter.



This does not preclude any individual passenger from bringing the matter to a court of competent jurisdiction and seek legal redress as they deem necessary or appropriate.



Travel Safe,

Hi,



"... However, if you are injured on the plane while it is in flight, isn't the airline responsible for your medical expenses?"



Maybe yes, maybe no.. It depends... 



Courts have ruled inconsistently on the issue.. There is some divergent thinking on the matter.. Many courts have held that if the immediate action that led to your injury were not airline controlled-- turbulence is the most common example-- *and* the airline took all reasonable measures to protect passengers, then they are not liable for these injuries as they are essentially weather related and not carrier controlled. This is why you see and hear more announcements about seat-belt usage and FA seat-belt checks..



But again, some courts have ruled differently.. Also, when you travel internationally, you are now bound by one of the two travel conventions-- the older Warsaw Convention or the newer Montreal convention.. These conventions put into place limits on how much an airline may be liable for in case of injury or death while on a common air carrier *if* they are found liable at all.



To assume, hope or expect that the airline will cover any or all of your expense if injured on their aircraft- a a blanket statement-- I would think is a dangerous thing as it will be very situational and many factors would come into play.



You can do internet searches and find people who have been successful in seeking compensation and claim, and others who have not.. There unfortunately, is no clear pattern of actions taken by the courts.



Travel Safe,

Subject: Paris

Location: Ile-de-France, France, Europe

Title: Paris not for everyone

ID#: 64651286



I returned from Paris two days ago and although it is a beautiful city it is not a place to go to if you have any problems walking, climbing stairs, or standing for long periods of time. Stairs are everywhere and many places don't have any railings to hold on to. Most restaurants and other places tourists frequent have the restrooms in the basements. The Metro and RER Stations(train) have many, many stairs going from one to the other and if you are lucky to find an escalator going up, you usually will not find one coming down. Versailles has cobblestones you have to walk on, about the distance of a football field before you get to the entrance and even with an advanced ticket there is a lot of standing in line, which is the case of almost all of the tourist attractions. If you can not use the stairs in Versailles you can ask one of the gentleman working there and they will take you to a special elevator that only they know about. I am not saying people with handicaps should not go to Paris, just be aware.

I was in Paris several years ago and agree with much of what you said. The stairs and cobble stones were very difficult for me at the time - I had a bone tumour removed just prior to our trip so walking was painful, and going downstairs very difficult. The one bonus I found with Paris though was that there were benches everywhere to rest on. I just took my time and enjoyed the slow version of Paris. I also went prepared with medication to help me deal with the increase in pain due to the extra walking. I had a great time and hope to go back one day and enjoy a pain free visit!



I also experienced one of the worst asthma attacks I've had in years my last day in Paris. I found every time I used the Metro I'd be left coughing, so I eventually avoided it. I'm not sure what it was, but my lungs definitely suffered in Paris. I will ensure I take my preventative inhaler regularly before and during any future trips to Paris.

Best of all, the location can't be beat, there are plenty of outdoor (ground floor) cafes nearby as well as a grocery store, and it's not expensive.

The metro was a nightmare. As the OP says, if there were escalators one way, then there wasn't in the other. Hubby had to struggle up the stairs while I dealt with his wheelchair. It was very rare for someone to offer to help. Any drop down kerbs on the pavement were nearly always blocked by parked cars.

It is an old city so our expectations were lower but we couldn't contemplate going back as a couple.

I am agree with you . I went to paris last year and i have also suffer this type of problems . I have the problem of climbing stairs . So i have too problems in paris . And there are also yellow cab service is not available for hire the taxi .

We go to Paris for several months every year and have found that although few Metro stations are handicap accessible, many buses kneel for easy wheelchair access. For those not in wheelchairs but who have other disabilities and for the elderly and expectant mothers

there is priority seating fairly near the front of the bus. Priority seating is also available on the Metro. 



The long lines for museums and other attractions often can be bypassed if one has ID indicating that one is disabled, and frequently the tickets are reduced in price. You just need to ask. 

At some museums they even have loaner wheelchairs available for free for those who have difficulty being on their feet long enough to tour the exhibits.

thread_title: Where is a great, dry, temperate destination?
text:
First place that came to mind was San Diego, California. In August average high is 25°C and low about 19°C and the climate is semi-arid. Although it can get to 32°C that would not be typical and prevailing winds are off ocean. Along the water there are plently of flat areas. And of course California wines. Although a fairly long flight.



Similarly Seattle, Washington has its dry season in August (later is better) and only occasionally hits 30°C or above. Only problem is that parts of that area are very hilly. The town of Sequim, WA across Puget Sound is quite flat along the water and has a great climate. Also Washington wines are very good. Across the Strait in Canada the city of Victoria has the same climate and relatively flat walking at Butchart Gardens.



Another option might be Bermuda which is very temperate and mostly very flat except right along the water in some places. Although when we visited in 2008 their public bus service was very wheelchair unfriendly but I have heard that has changed since and they are more attuned to disability issues. . Lots of nice hotels although value could be a question. Closer to UK and there may well be direct flights.

travelling with a post operative arthroscopy knee,any suggestions?

This is not a difficult recovery, particularly if you are more than 4 weeks post-op. If you are experiencing pain and swelling prior to your flight I would take an ice pack, and whatever medication for pain prescribed by your doctor.



If you are flying First Class you should have no problem. Nearly all First Class seats have enough space so you can get good extension with your leg. If you are flying coach, try to get the airline to release bulkhead seat assignments for you prior to your flight. These seats are normally not assigned until just before the boarding process, and they are assigned by the gate agent. If you have a medical need, however, you can usually get assigned to bulkhead before your flight.



When you make your plane reservations request wheelchair assistance. Someone will meet you with a wheelchair, help you through security and deliver you to your gate. Once you are at the gate ask the gate agent where you should be for pre-boarding, and have the person who is pushing your wheelchair leave you in that location. Someone will push you up the jetway to the door of the plane before they start regular boarding, giving you time to get situated before boarding starts so you do not delay other passengers.



When you land, you will need to remain on the plane until all the passengers have left before they will send the wheelchair to pick you up. This means that you will arrive at the luggage carousel just about the time the luggage starts to show up, so it is not a big deal to wait for the wheelchair.



If you are taking a long plane trip it is wise to get up and walk the length of the plane and back every 90 minutes or so.



I took a transatlantic flight 3 weeks post op from a complete hip replacement. I walked every hour to prevent blood clots, wore support stockings and took Warfarin to further reduce the possibility of blood clots. Bulkhead seating gave me enough space to extend my leg, and I had no difficulties on the flight.

Hi Julie, Obviously your best option transAtlantic is a first class upgrade. I have never flown on Virgin so I am not familiar with their seating arrangement. On our last transAtlantic flight we were on Air France, and we elected to sit in the back of the plane. It was convenient for me to be located near a restroom, and in a location where I did not block huge areas of the aisle when I stood up.



However, if your husband requires an aisle wheelchair to reach his seat, that is a long way to go down the aisle.



Often the gate agent holds bulkhead seats until boarding and then gives these seat assignments to disabled people because they are near the front of the plane and have a bit more leg room. I personally do not like bulkhead seating because I like to have my carry-on by my feet, and that is not possible if there is no seat in front of you.



Most people object to the back of the plane because it takes longer to get off. When you are waiting for wheelchair services, or for your own gate checked wheelchair to be brought up from the luggage compartment you are going to have to wait until everyone else is off the plane anyway. Air France also served meals from the rear of the plane so it was just a very nice location for us with that airline.



You should look at seatguru.com. Every seat in every airline is evaluated, and it makes it easier to make a decision. You can make sure you get a seat that reclines, and one that offers maximum leg room. Seat pitch and leg room space differ from seat to seat, even within the same airplane.



What are your plans when you reach Orlando? I can provide some information about this destination. We spend lots and lots of time in the Orlando area. We have season tickets to most of the parks, and often get up on a Sunday morning and decide to drive down for a day. We also take our grandchildren down for a week at the time and rent a villa. The last time we rented a villa, we rented one that was re-modeled to provide for a person with a disability. Of course, all hotels in the US are required by law to provide rooms for people with disabilities. The Orlando area is very friendly for disabled people.



Good luck! I admire you for being willing to continue to travel under less than perfect conditions.

Hi lilyana, I have thought about your question for a couple of days, and I believe, that on a whole, I find airlines and airports to be exceptionally helpful to me with my level of disability.



There are some advantages disabled people enjoy in the process of flying. Be sure to request wheelchair transportation when you make your reservation. When you check your luggage remind the agent that you need a wheelchair transportation.



If things work right, and 95% of the time they do, you will not have to do anything major once you are in the wheelchair. The wheelchair takes you to the front of the line for TSA screenings. It always takes us a little bit longer in this area because I have to go through the pat down area, but I never have to wait in line.



I always arrive at least 90 minutes early when flying, and I plan on at least 2 hours for plane changes because I know it is going to take me longer, and if my in-coming flight is late there is no way I can run to catch my next flight.



Usually once you reach your departure gate, the gate agent will board you ahead of the rest of the passengers. This gives you the option of having plenty of overhead space for your carry-on, and you can get settled in your seat without inconveniencing other passengers.



Of course, none of these little benefits compensates for being unable to move yourself from the entrance to the airport to your departure gate, but it makes life a bit more pleasant for both a disabled person and her traveling companion.



It is important to remain on the plane until you have a wheelchair at the door. Do not let a flight attendant talk you into walking up the jetway to wait for your wheelchair. So long as you remain on the plane the flight attendant has to stay there with you, and she is motivated to make sure your wheelchair arrives. Once you are off the plane you are not the responsibility of any specific airline employee and you can wait a long time at the end of the jetway.



Almost all of our flights have been uneventful and generally pleasant. Even our international flights are managed well.....with special processing through customs and immigration.



We had a couple of bad experiences with Delta in Atlanta at the end of October. The first one we decided to ignore until we had a similar experience five days later. I called Delta from the airport, and within five minutes I was surrounded by people who wanted to help. Delta also sent us a couple of $100 vouchers by way of apology.



When things do not go well, it is good to have a back-up plan. I have telephone numbers of people to call at Delta, and we fly 98% of our flights with Delta because they have our loyalty program and they serve the airports we frequent.



There are some tricks that enhance the experience of a disabled person traveling by air, but on a whole, I generally have a very positive experience whenever we travel.

You'll need to notify the airline in advance that you need a wheelchair.

Airlines do vary, and also if you can walk a short distance will affect things.

With Singapore Airlines we could check in at any row, then walked a short distance to the Special Needs area, where I was given a wheelchair.

Thai airways insisted we used one specific check in, which was the furthest from the entrance. I think a wheelchair then collected us from check in. It took 2 hours from getting out of the car to getting to the departure lounge.

Yes, once you've got to check in, just relax. You'll be taken express route through security, to the lounge. Then collected from the lounge, either by chair or buggy and taken to the gate.

Depending on your walking ability, they might wheel you to the aircraft and let you walk on, or they can use a special chair to get you right to your seat.

I live in Australia, Mum's visiting from UK. Can I arrange it all or is she best booking through a travel agent that can sort it out? Would appreciate any advice that can be given please. Thanks

Hi Renshen

We always book direct with the airline. If she can find a travel agrent who specialise in caring for the disabled that might be an option, but I'd always book with the airline, that way nobody else is between me and the airline.

We always book online, then phone the airline to tell them I need a wheelchair. Sometimes we'll phone again a week or 2 before the flight, to make sure everything is organised.

There will be an attendant to push the chair, and also help get hand baggage through the security checks.

She'll be directed to the wheelchair place at check in, then taken to either the disabled lounge, or a pay lounge. She'll be collected from there when the time is right, and taken to the aircraft.

You might want to consider paying for a lounge at Manchester and Singapore. We were not impressed with the 'lounges' provided for the disabled. At Changi, it was a significant walk to the toilet, and just a vending machine for snacks. Compared to the overall cost, the lounge isn't that much.

Minimum transit time at Changi is 50 minutes. For somebody disabled I'd advise at least 2 hours, ideally 3 to make a stress free connection.

Do buy a through ticket from Manchester to Brisbane, otherwise there are various complications, which are a lot worse for the disabled.

I live in North Wales but prefer to fly from Heathrow. Much better choice of flights, so might make the transfer easier.

Don't worry, she will be looked after.

There is not much more I can add to Heatseekers response. Back in Oct I had my first real experience of special assistance when flying from Gatwick to Changi via Dubai and except the very last part of the return journey at Gatwick it was very plain sailing. I was looked after from the minute I arrive at the airport, even with my husband there they were still very attentive, when left in a lounge they find a seat for you as they take the wheelchair away and return with it later but they placed me where all that I needed was easily at hand. I agree with heatseeker regarding to buying a through ticket to make things less complicated. We were very impressed and will definitely do it again.
