“ My understanding is that as long as it's declared ahead of time, Spinal Cord Injury is covered as a pre-existing condition.”



Some insurance providers may cover it, others may exclude any claims relating to the injury, and others may refuse all cover. You need to check with your provider and get it in writing. Just make sure you provide full details and don’t make any assumptions.

I ended up using https://www.squaremouth.com/ to compare plans and ultimately buy one. They were referred to me by a coupe people in another forum and also had a good writeup on Forbes.com. They let you input your travel dates as well as the date of your first purchase or deposit for the trip. Then based on that, they show you policies that will work from various carriers. There's a whole list of things you can click that you need coverage for, one of them being pre-existing condition. When you click that, any policy that will not cover it is removed from the list.



They also have a phone number you can call to ask questions before you buy. I found the whole process to pretty user-friendly and straight forward.



The *one* thing I'm not doing backflips over with my particular policy is that they will not give it to you in writing ahead of time that that they will cover your *specific* pre-existing condition. I was expecting to show my proof (Dr. note or SSDI letter) of spinal cord injury and have them send something back saying 'we've reviewed the proof you submitted and will hereby cover you for your spinal cord injury", but I was told the only time that process happens is in the event of a claim. So even though my condition sounds like it meets the criteria they set forth in the policy details, I won't know for sure unless I actually have to use the insurance... fingers crossed I never have to find out. 



That was possibly just for my particular policy, TravelSafe Classic. I didn't have many options since I bought my first flight back in February. This policy has a 21 day window within which you must purchase, but from what I've been told, a lot have a 3 day window. My guess is that buying within the 3 day window gives you way more options.



I'm still not 100% sure what to do about the chair for flights *not* originating or ending in the USA. I've added it to my renter's insurance. Once again, let's hope I don't have to use it. 



Anyway, I hope this might be of some help to anyone as lost as I was. Feel free to ask for clarification on anything I mentioned.

Dave, that's not an impressive way of handling pre-existing conditions. That would worry me enormously.



In the UK you go on an insurers site, they give you a basic premium, then ask you about your pre existing medical conditions, and then provide you with an updated price to cover your conditions. You pay the price, and get back immediately by return an insurance document listing your pre-existing conditions, and confirming you have declared them and that they are therefore covered. 



If it's not too late, in your case I would be researching other insurers as right now you have no guarantee your policy will cover you.

text:
I've never flown in the USA so my comments are generalised.

Normally you leave the rollator near check-in (staff will tell you where to go) and then are transferred by wheelchair to the gate.

If you need a rollator you almost certainly walk slowly, so need help to get through security and to the gate in reasonable time. Do let the airline know soon after you book your tickets that you'll need a wheelchair at the airports.

The rollator will be handled like check in luggage, and when you reach the destination, tell the wheelchair attendant you need to collect your rollator, and he'll find it for you, normally near the baggage carousel.

I've only done a few flights, and suffered no damage. My only complaint was Thai Airways stuck a label on it, which was impossible to remove. Remove the stick holder, or turn inward so it doesn't protrude and hopefully all should be fine.

It's depressing how every journey becomes a real challenge when you're disabled, but it's still great to get around. I'm sure you'll have a lovely time.

thread_title: Tips on to Travel (Domestic) with a Rollator
text:
Sorry if this seems negative--it's just the facts plus a bit of my personal feelings



There is a real lack of training lately (maybe covid; maybe not.) You need to be extremely explicit to the point of being bossy, you need to solve their problems for them; you need to remind them politely of their legal obligations--- all while being sweet as pie. Good luck with that. I have had some experiences that involved sexual assault in front of appalled passengers (and I am not talking about TSA pat downs.



All of this is based on my personal experience during the past 3 years. One of the key requests you need to make in writing and repeatedly is for a transport chair to travel with you in the interior of the plane. ALL planes are supposed to carry them; only 1, Alaska, has had one-- and that only one direction. A transport chair is a narrower wheelchair that can get down the aisle to get you to your seat and to the bathroom. (Oh yes: not transport chair = no way to get to the bathroom!) You ask to take your walker/rollator to the jetport where they help you transfer to the transport chair (aka the aisle chair). Let them strap you in and then keep your eyes closed as they get you across the gap from the jet port into the plane itself! Not having an aisle chair on British Airways (well, an aisle chair that was narrower than the aisle) meant that I had to crawl over and around about 15 rows of seats, much to the amusement of fellow passengers who were allowed to board before I reached my seat. They also got to watch as the "manager of accessibility" for most of the international airlines at LAX followed me, not offering any help but slowly and carefully smoothing my blouse down my chest and over my torso at every step. 

 

LABEL everything. It may even help....it hasn't helped me: I lost the battery and cord for a scooter which was never found or replaced during a month-long stay at one location in Scandinavia (and nothing sold there fit my rented scooter.) On my last trip, AA managed to break my wheelchair into several pieces. The airline replaced it....several weeks after I got home! I am considering putting my wheelchair in a nylon bag at the gate, which will unfortunately hold up other passengers even more.

he

 Yes, the rules are on the books. They are mostly ignored. At best, you may get a cheery "sorry" out of someone. There may be some young people who know how it's supposed to work but are mostly powerless. I have written letters and filed complaints, but haven't heard a word back. To be honest, I was more likely to get what I had been promised (and was entitled to, like an extra bag to carry medicines) when I increased the volume of my voice just a teeny bit, all while smiling,asking for a supervisor, and simply stating what had been agreed upon.



If I didn't like to travel so much... staying home would be much easier!

Hi Larissa

You haven't told us where you live! Without that info, we can't give you a definite answer. Normally disability badges are only accepted in your home country.

You'll get more local information and a more accurate answer by asking in the destination forums for each of the places you intend to visit.

To find the correct forum Google Tripadvisor forum [destination name].
Most if not all US states recognize "Blue Badges" hanging from the rearview mirror or placed on the dash.
In some cities the "handicap parking" on metered streets requires " all must pay. " In others, not. Read signs carefully.
I have the blue tag and use it wherever I go. I have never been contradicted .

You also need to verify EXACTLY what your pass will allow.My friend is a NYC resident but her pass is a NYS pass. The privileges that she does NOT have are a. No need to pay meters, b NYC pass holders can block hydrants and park in no parking zones - she can not!

https://drhandicap.com/insights/handicap-parking-permits-valid-states/



My experience is that placards are now accepted among US states pretty much universally. BUT the conditions under which they can be used vary. CA is among the most liberal: time limits don't apply. No need to feed meters, but you still pay in private lots. If a space is identified handicapped, anyone with a placard can park there (so no "this handicapped space is reserved for the person who lives nearest.") Most importantly, if parking is ever forbidden, it is forbidden to all (No parking 8-10 am for street sweeping is NO PARKING, for anyone.) 



It is murky as to whether a public institution can limit the use of handicapped spaces to people who live work or go to school at that institution. Our local university claims it can; I disagree. The Portland Rose Garden just doesn't recognize out-of-state placards. Nice.



You can usually look on a city's website to get info. For a definitive answer, call the city's police department and ask to speak with parking control They are used to answering this question.



I am hearing that EU countries recognize US placards, but I haven't confirmed that the states recognize the placards of EU countries.

thread_title: Airline travel with both rollator and wheelchair

The problems of air travel when you're disabled are horrendous.

I normally send my rollator as hold luggage, and it's never been damaged, but I do remove the stick holder which looks vulnerable. The worst was Thai Airlines who stuck labrls on it, which couldn't be removed.

I think your mother would have to hold on to the rollator while she's in the wheelchair, but there might be problems if she's taken by a buggy, where space can be limited.

Unless she books a premium lounge, she will be taken to a lounge for those with special needs. Normally wheelchairs are available, but I've never needed to use one. In my experience these special needs lounge don't have a toilet, and it's often a significant distance to one (i.e. difficult to walk if you use a rollator normally and have to rely on a stick).

She'll then go in a wheelchair directly to the plane entrance.

How far can she walk with a stick?

Sorry this is a bit vague but I rely on my wife to help me and would really struggle to cope on my own. Perhaps somebody else will have more information. I admire her determination.

They just pointed.



The day before, NS Assistance called us and told us that our trip to Schiphol was changed to a trip to Amsterdam Central and then a taxi would pick us up and take us back to Schiphol. So we did ride to Amsterdam Central, but no taxi was waiting for us. There was an NS Assistance person at the train, but she didn't speak English very well and she also didn't help my wife off the train. I had to do it.



So is this normal for European rail travel for disabled travelers? The websites of the rail carriers make it sound like it's very smooth. But it seems to be very difficult.

I’ve replied on your other thread, as follows



There are over 50 countries in Europe. Every country is different as is the assistance available. In the U.K. it seems to work very well but, as with most countries, including the US, must be booked in advance. 

On the issue of language, it’s not really fair to expect everyone, even those offering assistance, to speak English. Some will, some won’t but may speak German, French, Spanish or another language. thread_title: Rail travel for disabled people in Europe
text:
I have walked with an all terrain Veloped which is larger that your average rollator and sturdier,for the last 15 years. Here in the U.K. if possible I book the ticket in advance and my Veloped and I are booked into the wheelchair space in advance. On local journeys I just appear at my nearest station’s booking office which is then closed and a ramp put up for me on the next train.



On Eurostar and the TGV to Switzerland it is booked as a wheelchair and I sit either on it or the accompanying seat. On those journeys I am allowed a ramp. On journeys within Switzerland I’m not to allowed a ramp (it is a lift actually and strictly for wheelchairs). As more and more Swiss trains become easy access it becomes much easier. Once on the train my Veloped usually sits folded in the wheelchair space or if the train is busy I just sit on it.



You need to read the rules for each country that you are visiting. I think you will find that many actually use lifts and don’t allow rollators on them. Many of the countries only refer to wheelchairs and mobility scooters. Some of them do refer to rollators but do not appear to understand why someone would use one. 



As there are 2 of you, you might consider having a very lightweight foldable wheelchair for use during your travels which would allow you the use of the lift or ramp and carry the rollator with you.



Unlike here in the U.K. I think assistance generally has to be booked in advance. There are some documents about disabled people travelling in the EU on line. The last time I looked at them was some years ago and they may have altered since then.

thread_title: Service dog with non American accreditation
text:
Hi Isabella

We have now received a very helpful and lengthy reply from the charity which supplies service dogs for Autism in the UK. I hope it helps you identify areas where you need more research. It's a complex subject, but I hope this helps you have a really good time in the USA.

This is their response:

The assistance dog laws in the US, and from state to state differ from those of the UK and the West Indies. 

Under the American disability act, service animals in the state of Texas are protected, and that a person is not entitled to make demands or inquiries about qualifications or certifications of a service animal for purposes of admittance to a public facility except to determine the basic type of assistance provided by the service animal to a person with a disability. If a person’s disability is not readily apparent, for purposes of admittance to a public facility with a service animal, a staff member or manager of the facility may enquire about whether the service animal is required and what type of work or task the service animal is trained to perform. 

However, it is important to note that in Texas, a service dog has different protections to what we know as a ‘assistance dog’ in the UK.

I would advise the you to purchase a specific jacket stating Autism Service Dog in order to be covered by the service dog laws. Hopefully this should also prevent your disability not being ‘readily apparent’ and allow you to be protected under the service dog laws. 

This is quite a good link to look through: https://gov.texas.gov/organization/disabilities/assistance_animals

Hopefully this is enough info to start your research, but it would be my recommendation that you gather as much evidence as possible and become familiar with the local assistance dog laws.

For example, has the dog been owner trainer, or trained by a charity or organisation? Any certificates from approved Assistance dog companies, such as ADI (Assistance Dog International) accredited organisations. What can you provide to prove that the dog is qualified and trained? Proof of the dogs public liability insurance to be used as a working dog, and that they are covered in the US

In regards to a card that you can use to show, on Etsy, there are lots of creators who make these exact cards that can be shown to facilities and customised.

An example of cards that we use for our partners and their assistance dogs can be seen below: 

[the writer inserted a picture, this is the text]

You have just met Makka!

Makka is an autism assistance dog, he has been highly trained to p[erform a variety of tasks that directly mitigate my disability. Some of the tasks that Makka performs for me are:

Pressure therapy

Anxiety alert and support

Finding an exit or a certain person

Maintaining eye contact with me so I feel safe when talking to strangers

Being a visual aid to show I may need help

Being my best friend and companion

text:
A lot will depend on the medication you are taking and how well it controls your epilepsy.

Travel insurance: Like all disabled people you need to declare the issue, and answer further questions as required. I'm not aware of any companies which specialise in epilepsy, but a charity which helps epiletics might be able to give help.

For advice on cruises you could also ask in the linked Internet site at https://boards.cruisecritic.com/forum/69-ask-a-cruise-question/

If you are involved with a charity which helps epileptics, that may be your best source for advice.

Regarding the transport problem, many choose not to hire a car on holiday, I'm often surprised that so many manage without a car. I haven't hired a car for years, which is why I've often visited Singapore, where there's a great public transport system, and car hire is not a good option for tourists. I do avoid destinations where I consider a car essential, and where I'd find the driving challenging. So first think where you'd like to go, then ask in the destination forum. To find the destination forum Google tripadvisor forum destination.name

All of us disabled find planning a holiday difficult. I'm sure you'll get something sorted, and will enjoy a lovely holiday.

Where to begin. I have a big ask. I (64 years old) will be sailing on a transatlantic cruise from Ft. Lauderdale to Europe (either to Barcelona or to SouthHampton...TBD) with husband 64 who is a paraplegic and uses a manual wheelchair. I would need to have a van delivered to the port, and then 5 weeks later picked up at a different port (definitely Southampton for return trip). I have found a couple of sites on line that suggest they do wheelchair rentals in Europe, but I can't get specific details of the extent of their services. I have tried e-mail and website inquiries with no response. Am I in a dream world or is this doable?. Is there anybody on this forum that has done something similar? I am at the point now where I am seeking a disability travel specialist but even that has yielded zero responses. (I am beginning to think my internet only does outgoing and no incoming HAH) I am stuck. Any advice?

Hi Teri, and welcome to TripAdvisor

Picking up a vehicle in Europe and dropping off in Southampton is unlikely to work, the UK is a separate country, not part of the EU, so vehicle insurance won't cover you in the UK, and most hire companies would not allow you to leave the EU area. Normally there is no problem about driving within different countries in the EU, but it would be wise to check. We drive on the left in the UK, which is another problem if you were to bring a European car into the UK.

I admire your determination, but think you may have to simplify, and either spend the time in the UK or in continental Europe. Or treat it as 2 separate zones, and cross into the UK and rent a vehicle after the crossing. 

Hiring a suitable vehicle is difficult, made more complicated if you would like hand controls.

if you don't get help here, there are a number of forums dedicated to helping the disabled (this is just a small part of general travel advice), which might be more useful. My wife suggested Scope https://forum.scope.org.uk/

There is also this Facebook group https://www.facebook.com/groups/DHorizonsTribe/

You could also ask in the destination forum for suitable places you'll start your trip. To find the destination forum Google tripadvisor forum destination.name

I hope you get something sorted. It is difficult, but I'm sure you'll have a great trip.

I agree with post #1 regarding hiring a vehicle in Europe and dropping off in Southampton. You could consider ending your journey in Paris, Amsterdam or Paris and taking Eurostar to London. Their Special Assistance is second to none and they give wheelchair passengers plus a companion discount plus upgrade.



Facebook has lots of forums for disabled travellers. You could begin by looking at The Accessible Travel Club.



I think Avis is one of the few companies who hire adapted vehicles.

Thank you both for your advice. I will look into the Eurostar as an option to and through the UK. I signed up for the Scope Forum, the DHorizons Tribe and Quora to see what information I can glean. I feel like I have a lot of time to plan all of this, but the Transatlantic cruises to and fro have a shorter window of opportunity and I hope to have most of my big questions answered before I book. 

Thanks again for your help.

thread_title: Trip report traveller with mobility issues Japan by train
text:
I am writing this report to try and help others with mobility issues.



We had trips to Japan back in 2011 and 2016 and promised ourselves we would return to this fascinating country. Unfortunately Covid restrictions got in the way and they had to be cancelled.



Fast forward to 2024 and we had the chance to take the trip. Things had changed in that my wife now has to walk with the aid of poles and finds it difficult to walk much more than 1 km at a time. So our days of wandering for hours were over. 



We decided to miss out Tokyo and Kyoto in favour of less well known places. And to use our JR pass taking lengthy train trips most days. So we could it down and watch the world go by.



We had booked assistance for both flights which worked well at both Heathrow and Haneda. We arrived at Haneda on a dull grey morning and after clearing the airport formalities picking up a pocket wifi and getting our JR pass we were good to go.



We had tried to cut down on luggage so we had one wheeled suitcase, a bag which fitted on the handle and a camera backpack. It was my job to handle the luggage so Dianes hands were free for her poles. 



I had the Navitime app on my phone as well as googlemaps and googletranslate all of which proved helpful. I usually made seat reservations at ticket offices but did use the green machines sometimes. The ticket gates were easy to use and although I was nervous at first putting my valuable and irreplaceable JR pass into a machine fearing it would be swallowed up the machines worked perfectly and our tickets always popped out the other end. Where we made a point of collecting them and tucking them safely into a coat pocket.



We made a point of booking good quality hotels at or near the stations we were using.



We took the monorail changing at Hamamatsucho to a local train before arriving at Tokyo station around 1300. Like most stations we used there were elevators as an alternative to escalators or stairs which was helpful but we did find that the elevators were often quite full with able bodied travellers even those without luggage using them and not giving priority to travellers with mobility issues as usually happens back home.



We had 90 minutes until our first Shinkansen so looked for somewhere to have lunch where we could sit down and also have room for the luggage. This was not easy to find but eventually we managed to squeeze in to a small noodle bar.



Our first journey was from Tokyo to Akita by Shinkansen, a 4 hour which did not involve any changes the weather was dull and although we were surprised to see snow on the ground we did doze from time to time following our long flight.



It was dark by the time we arrived. There was snow underfoot but fortunately our short walk to ANA Crowne Plaza Akita was mostly under cover. Our hotel package gave us evening food and breakfast so after a good nights sleep we were ready for the start of our adventure.



Our destination was a Kyokin by the sea in Miyako this involved returning by Shinkansen 1.5 hours to Morioka the weather had picked up and we enjoyed watching the snow covered countryside and the distant mountains. We had lunch at a small café in the station before catching a local rapid train for the delightful 2 hour journey over the hills to Miyako.



We had arranged a transfer to Jodogahama Park hotel which I will review separately and proved to be one of the highlights of the trip. Our package included dinner and breakfast as well as transfer back to Miyako station.



JR trains back to Morioka are few and far between. We could have taken a bus but instead chose to take a train north along the coast to Kuji this train is on a private railway not covered by JR pass so we needed to buy tickets costing 1890Yen for the journey.



Initially we were disappointed as the train passed through a series of tunnels but eventually we came to the coast and saw the sea defences which had been erected as a result of the 2011 Tsunami a sober reminder of the devastation and loss of life which it caused. The train paused on a couple of occasions to allow passengers to admire and photograph some stunning sea views.



At Kuji we changed back to a JR train for our onward journey to Hachinohe where we could catch the Shinkansen back to Morika. Kuji station was one of the few we came across without elevators so we had to use steps over a footbridge.



At Morioka we were booked into the Richmond hotel which is just opposite the station. Getting to the hotel involves crossing a main road but fortunately there is an underpass, which can be accessed by elevators. We did not have meals booked but took advantage of the 24 hour convenience store attached to the hotel.



Next day we headed south to Kumamoto a journey of around 1000 miles involving 3 Shinkansens. Not everyone’s cup of tea I know but a demonstration of the comfort and efficiency of the JR railways.



We had been told that breakfast at the hotel would have been slow and crowded. I couldn’t find any cafes open at 0900 at the station so we stocked up on breakfast food from the convenience store for our 2 hour journey to Tokyo. We were surprised that trolley service was on the train so I had a coffee but I understand this is soon to be withdrawn.



I had built in a window of 1.5 hours at Tokyo Station so was able to get a coffee and buy drinks and Bento boxes for our onward journey. 



The next step was 4 hours to Okayama. South of Tokyo we were hoping to catch sight of Mount Fuji. It didn’t look promising as many of the lower mountains we cloud covered but as we approached Fuji station a snow covered Mount Fuji rose majestically above the clouds. Magical!



Changing trains at Okoyama was easy then it was a further 2.5 hours by Sakura Shinkansen To Kumamoto. I found these with their wide seats to be even more comfortable than the previous Shinkansen. 



After a long day of travelling we were ready to check in for our three nights stay at Blossom Hotel Kumamoto. This was only a few meters from the station and was attached to a large shopping centre so getting supplies of food and drink was easy.



Our plan for the next day was to visit Kyushu Ceramics Museum at Arita. We took the Shinkansen 1 hour to Hakata and then a limited express train 1.5 hours to Arita. We were unaware that there were reserved seats on this train and sat in a reserved carriage. The ticket inspector politely informed us of our mistake and we were able to find seats in the next unreserved carriage. 



The walk to the museum was just under 1 km but did involve climbing some steps. We could have taken a taxi from the station instead. I would highly recommend this museum for those interested in art and ceramics, exhibits were informatively labelled in English as well as Japanese. The museum was light and airy without an admission charge and there was a small café with great views on the first floor.



We then repeated our steps on the return to Kumamoto although reserved seats were fully booked on the train to Hakata we were able to find seats on the crowded unreserved carriage.



The next day was our only slight disappointment. My plans involved the Yufuin no Mori tourist train which only has reserved seats. I tried to book the night before but there were no seats available so my plans went out of the window. Moral book tickets for busy trains well in advance!



As an alternative we decided to go to Miyazaki. Sakura Shinkansen 1 hour to Kagoshima Chuo then limited express 2 hours to Miyazaki. The highlight was the run along the coast looking out over the bay to Sakarujima Volcano. We had a good lunch at Izakaya restaurant in the station and then retraced our train back to Kumamoto noticing the increased activity from the volcano.



I’m pretty proud of the planning for the rest of the trip. We took the Shinkansen for the 2 hour journey to Hiroshima arriving around 1030 where we were due to stay two nights at the Granvia hotel which is within the station.



We were able to leave our luggage at the hotel before catching a local train for the short journey to Kurashaki aka The Venice of Japan a flat walk of around 1km took us to the old shops and canal side of this historic town. We enjoyed a lunch in a small café run by a quite old man who insisted on immaculate service. A stroll along the canal side a cup of coffee then back to the station and our hotel.



Our package included both evening food and breakfast in the 21st floor lounge with amazing views over the city.



The next day was a trip to one of our favourite spots Miyajima. Regular trains from Hiroshima take 30 minutes or so to the ferry terminal for the JR ferry which is covered by the JR pass. You do however need to put a 100Yen coin into a machine to pay a tourist tax. A lovely sunny day and the island was not too busy so we were able to walk to the floating Tora before having a delicious Oyster lunch at Torii restaurant.



It is worth noting that on the ferry at the same level as the car deck there is a small cabin with seating so passengers with mobility issues can avoid having to climb stairs. Our return journey to the hotel went smoothly.



All too soon our trip was coming to an end and we had to return to Haneda for our flight home. I was concerned at arriving in Tokyo with our luggage at busy times so I booked later trains to arrive around 2000. 



This gave us the bonus of an extra morning in Hiroshima. Leaving our luggage at the hotel we took a tram to the A dome and visited the Peace Park which for us is something of a pilgrimage. 



As well as the children’s memorial and the eternal flame which we always find moving we visited the Rest House with its interesting exhibits a café and the remarkable story of Eizo Numara who by chance was in the basement of the building and was the only survivor of the 37 people who were at work in the building when the A bomb exploded.



We also had time to visit the Hiroshima Museum of Art housed in two remarkable buildings nearby. We particularly enjoyed the collection of impressionist paintings. Some have questioned the 600Yen admission charge for a small gallery but I would argue quality over quantity. The black cat café within the museum provided very welcome coffee and ice cream.



A return by tram to the station and lunch at one of the busy restauants in the station shopping centre and it was time to collect the luggage and catch our train.

1.5 hours to Shin Osaka and then a diffuct chage which involved waiting for three trips for a space in a crowded escalator to an underpass finding the correct platform for our Hikari which started from Shin Osaka which we made with 3 minutes to spare. For the 3 hour journey to Shinagawa.



As I had hoped the local train and the Monarail were not crowded so our journey to Haneda was straightforward, We were staying at the Royal Park Hoten which is inside terminal 3 next to checkin N.



The next day our return flight was delayed from 0945 to 1230 so we had the benefit of our hotel room to wait in rather than the terminal. After checkin assistance worked well and we were able to wait at a lounge by the gate until it was time to board the aircraft.



So Diane was able to enjoy our trip despite mobility issues. In fact on a couple of occasions we saw wheelchair passengers whose journey must have been booked in advance being met by station staff with ramps so they could alight from their train. I would suggest that with careful planning others with mobility issues could tour this fascinating and beautiful country.

Hi Katie and welcome to Tripadvisor.

Cobbles are a nightmare for the disabled. Walking sticks can easily slip. Small wheels on wheelchairs or walkers get stuck, or shake the user. By contrast I use a rollator with 14ins (355mm) wheels and hardly notice them! So large wheels are best.

For the Rhine cruise try asking for advice on the Cruise forum https://www.tripadvisor.co.uk/ShowForum-g1-i10703-Cruises.html

For help on travel in Switzerland, you'll get advice from local experts on the Switzerland forum https://www.tripadvisor.co.uk/ShowForum-g188045-i336-Switzerland.html

I do feel that at the moment your trip sounds difficult. Coping with a walker and a wheelchair and luggage while travelling won't be fun, and you've made things more complicated by combining train travel and a cruise, so lots of transfers.

I prefer to stay in one hotel throughout a trip, then I get to know the area, and don't have too many transfers, which are very difficult when you're disabled.

First step is to follow these links and get advice from those who know the areas you want to visit, then see how you feel.

thread_title: Traveling with special needs- Avoiding Scam Companies
text:
I do not recommend Special Needs Group (AKA Special Needs at Sea) for medical equipment rentals.

https://www.specialneedsatsea.com/



My experience with this company was extremely disappointing. I visited their website and initiated a rental request for an electronic scooter, understanding that my card would not be charged until availability was confirmed.

However, just ten minutes later, I received an e-signature document, a rental agreement that I was expected to print, sign, and bring with me to pick up the scooter. The email stated I should click the button to review and sign the agreement. Crucially, I did NOT sign this agreement.

Despite this, my credit card was charged $265. When I immediately called to cancel the request (to free up the scooter for someone else), as my husband decided we should just take our scooter, a representative named Shella informed me that they would only refund $215, keeping $50 as a cancellation fee.

This cancellation fee was never disclosed to me, and I had not signed any document agreeing to it. I never received confirmation that the equipment was available. To add to the poor experience, the representative was unsympathetic and unprofessional.

Based on this experience, I strongly advise against using Special Needs Group for your medical equipment rental needs. I urge others to thoroughly research customer reviews before engaging with this company, as I wish I had done.

thread_title: Mobility assistance from Delta at Atlanta airport
text:
It is difficult to have a Meet ad Assist for your airport arrival. They have no idea when you will arrive, how you arrive and where you will be let out of the arrival car.

The Atlanta Airport usually has several people working around the arrival area. You could get out of the arrival transport, have your luggage on the sidewalk with you and ask an airport porter for assistance. Once you are checked in, ask the airline to help getting to the gate. thread_title: Mobility assistance from Delta at Atlanta airport
text:
It seems like Atlanta may have some sort of working system. I think I woul call the office of the director of the airport, if only to get the proper direct phone numbers. Most airports have people to help transport you between the check in and TSA. (whixh is probably the easiest part!) Other than that, it's mostly theoretical and I have not been able to arrange much help. You have some challenges ahead.I 

starting as much as five months ahead of my flights, and after many hours of phone calls to EACH of seven airlines, I was told, unequivoally, that all US airports and major European airports have a "kiosk" marked with a wheelchair symbol which has a phone.. All you have to do is pick up the phone and the mobility coordinator will come out to meet you. During trips to Austin, DC, Philadelphia, London and Copenhagen in the past year, I was unable to find any handicap sign, much less a kiosk or a mobility coordinator (or anyone who had ever heard of such a thing, including skycaps and airport police. At LAX, and after we persisted for an hour and a half, someone finally presented himself as "the disability coordinator for all the international airlines." It is a serious understatement to say this person gave no evidence of having had any training. Despite all the effort I spent before multiple trips to communicate (over the phone or via email) my needs to the airlines never made it to my reservation, except wit h SAS. You need to advnce plan every segment through each airport don't forget that you may need an aisle chair to get to you set or to the restroom (There is supposed to be one stored on every plane. There isn't.) We had drivers drop us off near the skycap. They could call someone to come push my wheelchair through the airport but it took up to half an hour for someone to show up. Overall, we find that we need 1 1/2 hours more than the suggested time inernational travelers are told to allow. I can normally propel my own chair, but not with carryon luggage.Supposedly you can have a companion escort you to the gate but I have heard people say the compsnion is only allowed as far as TSA. We haven't tried this. The whole system (or non-system) operates to make travel exhausting, inconvenient, and at times nearly impossible. The best airline we've experienced? SAS. The worst, by far, was BA. Alaska was surprisingly good. American was somewhere in the middle but they broke my wheelchair! I think this is all pretty outrageous and clearly in violation of federal law. The question I am repeatedly asked is, if it's so hard, why don't you just stay home? It would certainly be easier all around if we did, But I like to travel and I have friends and relatives all over. I just wish there was some enforcement of existing law.

thread_title: Service Dog - Four Seasons - inconsistent accommodation
text:
I have had a medical alert service dog for 10 years. She alerts me by sensing changes in my breath that signal a medical condition. 



For the past 5+ years, she has accompanied me to a Four Seasons, where she sat on a pool lounger with me or next to me OR a beach lounger, with me or next to me. 



On my last stay, a manager questioned if she was a service dog and pried about my medical condition. I told her I was happy to provide paperwork and contacts, as they were required to fly her. She asked more than she should have, but I complied to keep things peaceful. 



On this stay, I went to the pool and asked for chair setup. The staff greeted my dog by name and said they would have chairs set up for us. A few hours later, the same nosey manager from last time informed me that she would not be able to sit on the beach chair with me bc it was food and beverage outlet and it was a surface they serve food on. I asked her why the change and she said they were choosing to enforce state law more strictly and she was just enforcing the law. (Last I checked, a pool manager is not a law enforcement officer.)



Over the next few hours, I was told this had always been the resort policy, they were just not enforcing it prior, that I should put my dog in a pack and play on the beach, that she could sit on the sand, but not in the lounger, this was required by state law since they were a food and beverage outlet, and that owners of property at the resort who claim they have service animals would also want their dogs to sit with them and this couldn't be allowed. 



I asked for documentation of the statutes and was not provided any. I pointed out that the ADA was federal, which trumps state law, and I showed them that on each of my last 4 stays - which were all multiple weeks - they allowed my dog to sit on a towel on the beach lounger. 



For the dog to check my breath every few minutes, would require constant jumping up from the sand, or me bending down to the sand. This is ridiculous. 



There is code in the ADA that allows for elevation as an accommodation. My understanding from my attorney is that resort should allow their prior accommodation, a towel on the beach chair. 



I am trying not to be an unreasonable guest or difficult. If I had known this change had taken place, I wouldn't have come here. I do not push my animal on people or places. I go where we are accommodated with minimal effort. However, we are here now, on an unrefundable trip, for the next 2 weeks. It has been 20 hours and the resort has not offered another accommodation. 



The other reality is that the beach chairs sit outside overnight. They are not wiped down or sanitisezed. They are on the beach exposed to the elements. Everyone places a fresh set of towels on the chairs to sit on them, whether eating or not. And also, people's butts and feet are on them. How is a dog on a towel any different? 



Suggestions?

thread_title: Advise please-booking a wheelchair accessible holiday abroad
text:
Hi Rochelle and welcome to the forum.

Most of us prefer to book directly with the airline and hotel, so this may not be the best place to ask about agencies.

Go through past posts, and you'll find lots of help on problems and solutions.

It is difficult to arrange a wheelchair friendly holiday. You'd need to seek advice where you live on agencies that organise trips for the disabled, perhaps if a charity helps your daughter, they might have suggestions.

Europe is mostly good for the disabled, but watch out for cobbles in towns.

We visit Singapore a lot, and that is very disabled friendly, although wheelchair taxis are rare, can she get into a normal car, and leave the wheelchair in the boot/ trunk?

I suggest you think of places you'd like to visit then ask for advice from local experts on the destination forum. To find the correct forum Google Tripadvisor forum destination name.

It's going to be difficult, but you'll have a great time when it's all sorted.

thread_title: Manual wheelchair or electric scooter for Europe
text: We go to Poland from the US often, so I can be specific regarding Krakow and Zakopane, Poland. We love Krakow and Zakopane, but a lot of the sidewalks and streets are paved with cobblestones -hard to use a wheelchair, but possible. in the right situation. In addition, Zakopane is hilly. I push my wife, who is not very heavy, using a collapsable "transfer wheelchair." I am 81 years and this can be difficult and tiring, but we manage if we take it easy. I take a "golf seat" so I can take a break. The wife can walk for short distances to overcome curbs and very bad spots and that is important. If she was heavy or couldn't walk at all, it would be very much different. In addition, Poland is a great place to visit and reasonably priced, but it is only beginning to make accommodations for disabled people. In Krakow, baby carriages are everywhere, but wheelchairs are few. Not at all like the USA. When booking a room, look for first-floor or elevator-accessible rooms. Taxis are very available and very reasonably priced compared to the USA and are a good alternative for getting around and almost all will take your wheelchair.

We have done this four times in the last six years. We have recently purchased an "all terrain'" manual wheelchair with balloon bicyle-like tires and attendant brakes on the handles. We will try that out on our next trip to Poland and will report back after that. I am not saying this is better than an electric mobility scooter. It is just something that works for us. We have an electric mobility scooter that my wife uses in Florida, but we have not tried it in Europe. Be warned, however, that what I wrote above applies where there is a person to push the wheelchair. It does not apply to a situation where one has to operate a manual wheelchair on their own or an electric wheelchair. 

 One bit of caution is that if you check a wheelchair into baggage and there is only a short time to your connecting flight, they might not have time to transfer the wheelchair. It may take a day or two before you see it again, not to mention the hassle of retrieving it. This is worse if two airlines are involved. There is something called a "gate check" that could prevent that, but it doesn't work smoothly all the time.

 HAPPY TRAVELS

They don't have tons of staff going out in the world to check on this stuff....

There's some would say that, useful as this is, it is not really in the true spirit of diversity or inclusion because it is 'positive discrimination'.....

thread_title: Miami Accessible Taxis - Don't get scammed
text:
Warning for wheelchair users visiting Miami: accessible transportation options for motorized wheelchairs can be very limited, and unfortunately that can leave passengers vulnerable to questionable taxi practices. During my trip, the meter showed one amount, but after arriving I was told the credit card machine was unavailable and was asked to pay a much higher cash amount instead. Because accessible transportation is not easy to find, I felt pressured to pay it.



Just a friendly warning to other wheelchair users: before starting the ride, confirm that they accept cards, ask about all charges in advance, and if possible take a photo of the cab number and meter. I’m sharing this so others can avoid being caught off guard like I was.

It’s wheelchair accessible and the harbour front is pretty level all the way around from the village to the yacht club (which has ramps and nearby accessible toilets). We often have coffee or a light lunch at the yacht club or nearby cafe. 

In the village itself (the other side of the bay) there are loads of waterfront cafes and restaurants all with level access to the outdoor tables. Note: I’d consider few of the waterfront cafes to have accessible toilets but I haven’t checked. 

It’s a very different atmosphere to SP so might make a nice change.

ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST FOR HOTEL ACCOMMODATION



Accessibility is not standardized in the hotel industry and can be easily interpreted in different ways by hotel employees. Rather than look for “wheelchair friendly” hotels in the forums, have your criteria and needs ready and deal with the hotel directly. Often hotel websites will show that they have accessible rooms, but their definitions may differ widely and they may not be designed to meet your needs. At this point, you call directly.



Some things to ask a hotel:



Common areas:



1. designated handicap parking with a priority location in the parking lot.



2. step free access (level or ramped) and/or lift access to main entrance.



3. automated door opening.

 

4. ground level/lobby level accessible washroom.



5. elevator to above ground accessible accommodation.



6. level or ramped access to public areas.



Rooms:



1. wider entry and bathroom doorways – external 80 cm, internal 75 cm. Easy to open? 



2. mid-height light switches and power outlets



3. lever type door handles



4. maneuvering space on each side of the bed – 90 cm



5. roll in shower



6. wheeled shower chair and/or wall mounted shower seat



7. grab bars in bathroom



8. raised toilet



9. lower hanging space in closet



 

Neighbourhood:



1. proximity to markets, pubs, restaurants ... up to 500 m distant.



2. proximity to health services.



Tips:



1. Call hotel directly.



2. Keep notes: names, dates, times, topics, what’s agreed and confirmation numbers. Take these notes and print outs with you on your vacation.



3. Ask to talk to someone who is familiar with handicap rooms because they have been in them.



4. Ask questions that will elicit information rather than a yes or a no.

 - Describe ...

 - Tell me about ...



5. Check that you have a credit card GUARANTEE for an accessible room and a confirmation number. Not just a REQUEST for an accessible room if available at the time of check in.



6. Reconfirm your reservation for a guaranteed accessible room a couple of days ahead.



7. When you arrive, check out the room before you check in.



8. Again, take your notes and print outs with you on your vacation.



More tips:



Be prepared, in the unlikely event that:



1. the hotel does not have the accessible room available for you when you arrive. The hotel will need to find you an accessible room, even in another hotel. (See #6 just above) “Where will you put us up for the night?”



2. the complimentary hotel shuttle may not be accessible. The hotel will need to accommodate the service in some other way. “How will you provide alternate shuttle service for us?” 



Be cool, be persistent, use a sense of humour and your vacation will be much more a pleasure than a nightmare.

Thanks for your comments Noah. Yes, "accessibility" generally means mobility issues that require some physical modifications of a hotel room. When you say "other forms of disabilities" what do you have in mind? Needs will definitely vary and this list is meant to be a reference guide for people to take from as they need. And you are right, hotels in a given country are often not required by law to meet standards in terms of accessible properties. Even in Canada, with standards that are quite high regarding mobility issues, a hotel can design an accessible room the way they want to. 



My hope is to provide a checklist of some things to keep in mind when booking a room. A hotel that says their room is accessible just because they have installed grab bars in the bathroom really doesn't have an accessible room. And a guest can be in for a rude surprise if their only question has been "Is the room accessible?"

I think most people these days know enough not to rely on advertised “accessibility” and are more proactive than in the past. Visit http://www.disabledtravelers.com/ to see a good resource. In relation to TripAdvisor, I see your list as more of a guide for the abled to access the appropriateness of a facility for disabled guests – should TA add such a tool. 



One thing not on your list is the bathroom sink arrangement. In most of the establishments I visited you can’t wheel under the counter and the sink taps are too far to reach from the side. If you can’t stand, the shower (or maybe the tub) is the only option to simply wash your hands. Pack hand wipes!

MMandM, 



By other forms of disabilities that might benefit from accommodation, I mean:



- folks with Visual impairment

- folks with hearing impairment

- folks with cognitive impairment

- folks of short stature



Folks with visual impairment might benefit from having a phone that beeps to indicate a message waiting, instead of with a flashing light, braille labels for switches and a verbal or audio description of the room by staff upon checking in. Or a braille or recorded "guest services" guide and room service menu.



Folks with a hearing impairment might benefit from a visual door knock indicator, awareness of the staff of a hearing impaired person is in the room so a phone call may not be the best way to contact them. Alternate ways of contacting staff for services or ordering room service can be worked out.



Folks with cognitive impairment benefit from the staff being aware of the situation and a plan on what to do if that person appears to need assistance. 



Little people may benefit from a well placed step stool, or simply having amenities placed within reach instead of on tall shelves.



Simple awareness of the staff of specific situations can go a long way in preventing misunderstandings, lost business and not to mention law suits. We aren't all traveling in North America where accessibility is often much easier to come by than some other parts of the world.

Hi folks,

This is a very useful forum. 

Most of us who have a disability or live with people who have a disability pretty soon get to know what does and does not work in terms of accommodation, access and suitability related to our particular needs. Before our daughter came along we made a lot of assumptions (presumptions) about "special needs". Unless one is directly affected, one simply won't know. Hence a lot of hoteliers thinking they are providing a useful service that may in fact be limited.

Thus there is a primary responsibility on we, the users, to ensure providers of accommodation have facilities that are suitable.

However, I do believe that any building or room that is accessible (in its widest sense) to disabled users will be accessible to ALL users. Wheel-in, wet-area shower/bathroom arrangements could be put in all new hotels, if not all new hotel rooms. Older buildings can allow for upgrades to match. I do think we the disabled community needs to be even more pro-active in informing architects and designers to look not just at the regulations but the variety of user needs as mentioned by some of your correspondents.

For example, ALL light switches and power points could be set lower, say at thigh height (OK, yes, whose thigh?) rather than adult elbow height or at the ankle setting. Things are improving generally and we are grateful that people keep up the fight. But caveat emptor is always a good motto to live by when booking accommodation.

Thanks for the opportunity to join the form.

John C

Caveat emptor, exactly. Asking specific questions can make such a difference to your hotel room stay.

1a) - how many disabled parking spots are there....and the distance to the main entrance (or disability entrance)

1b) what options are there (if any) if all the spots are full? This one comes from trying to stop at a major attraction with 2 whole spots near the building and more located more than 500ft away. Great in a wheelchair, not so good on canes or walker.

While waiting for my wife at the doctor’s today, I read a great article about accessibility issues, and how business owners “think” they’ve done things right.



One example was where a restaurant had redone the bathroom to make it wheelchair accessible, but the bathroom was located in the basement, which required you to take the stairs.



Another example was where the restaurant had a wheelchair accessible bathroom on the same floor, but stacked all their extra chairs in the hallway making it too narrow for a wheelchair to get through.

This is great. So often my daughter has been at bars/restaurants/clubs where spare chairs are stacked not just in the corridor but in the "disabled" toilet. Complaints always bring apologies but next week, it's back the way it was. I was in an internet cafe today and there was a large disabled toilet but no access between the desks bolted to the floor, and a step up to the shop anyway. You what ... ?

As to car parks ... I have started to take digital pix of cars illegally parked and on the occassions the drivers have seen me doing this I tell them I am e-mailing the pic, with their registration plate visible, to the City Council parking office. Boy does that get a response.

And we left. He was still there whe we got back. Not happy. I hope he learnt his lesson.

A wiki-style list of good and useless hotels would be great. Can TA help or do we do this ourselves?

Hi, folks,



I'm delighted to find this thread and forum, and although I'm fairly new to the ranks of those needing to take accessibility into account to one extent or another, I'm not new to the concept or necessary parameters as a long-time former paramedic and interior designer who specializes in aging-in-place and accessibility, mostly in the residential market. 



I do agree that it's high time that Trip Advisor start building in mechanisms to review locations for accessibility, but since they do not, I've started adding accessibility comments to my own reviews, and would suggest that all here do the same. At minimum, knowing who some other disabled travelers are should give us a place to start to look for reviews that at least consider accessibility to one extent or another.



I'd also just like to point out in the discussion of what to look for that in no location will you ever find consideration for *all* types of disabilities as part of the built environment. The standards, where they exist, are designed to account for the "average" person (who of course doesn't really exist), including "average" reaches, heights, etc., and for the most common disabilities, which translates to basically the wheelchair-bound, blind, and deaf. Nice as it would be, it's really not reasonable to expect businesses to try to anticipate every possible need. And even if they could do so in a room or three, there's nothing saying that those particular rooms would always even be available when *you* needed one. 



Rooms are also designed with current design trends in mind, which pillow-top mattresses already mentioned in this thread illustrate, and even if a hotel equipped some rooms with lower beds, there's always going to be someone who ends up with one of those rooms who needs a higher bed, or vice versa. This is part of why they go for the "average", because then everything is standardized. Furniture is also bought in bulk at reduced costs for larger hotels, often manufactured to order in the far East, and anything that falls outside of the standard becomes *astronomically* more expensive for the business.



Ignorance and lack of required modifications contribute to locations not being accessible (because the fact of the matter is that if the law doesn't require it, most businesses simply aren't going to do it, not to mention how greasing palms, etc. can often get people around the requirements), but two of the biggest obstacles are simple cost to the building owner, and physical possibility. In most cases, at least in the US, businesses are not required to make modifications if, basically, the cost would be prohibitive to the business, or if the basic structure or nature of the building precludes it. One would probably not be required, for example, to install an elevator in an historic house that is open to the public, or in a small building in which it would take up an inordinate amount of space required for the operation of the business like a large chunk of the dining room in a small restaurant. 



Building and business owners have rights, too, and rightfully so. Accessibility laws attempt to balance those with the needs of the disabled public. 



Unfortunately, this means that more older and historic properties will not be accessible, period, and that those for whom this matters need to look more to newer ones.



We think it would be so easy to put grab bars, ramps, and elevators everywhere, for example, but when a business is faced with the expenses involved in equipping hundreds of rooms with even *one* single new item like a grab bar, the costs multiply well beyond what is apparent to the average traveler. 



Likewise, to install an elevator is an expense of probably *at least* $100,000, and not all businesses can afford that - nor is it even possible in all locations like many older and smaller buildings. Ditto with ramps. 

Sometimes there just isn't the space given how the building and neighborhood are configured - Georgetown in Washington, DC just provided me with a very graphic reminder of these issues myself. It's unfortunate, but some places like many of these older, small, converted houses are simply never going to be accessible because to make them so would create a greater hazard and obstruction problem for everyone.



So, by all means, make your checklists and ask about your needs and desires, and good luck with finding what you are seeking. I would just ask that you keep in mind that we are not the only population with needs to be met with regard to the built environment, and to keep some of these issues in mind when making judgments about what a given business has or hasn't done to accommodate the disabled, because oftentimes what is there is the result of a careful balancing act in an admittedly impossible quest to be most things to the most people possible.
